name: Ufuk Yanıkoğlu
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46284/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who was born in 1971, lives in Ankara. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 31 January 2002 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the remaining complaints to the Government. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility on 7 November 2002. The application was filed by Mr Ufuk Yanıkoğlu (“the applicant”), on 16 January 1999. The applicant was sentenced to three years' imprisonment. Both the applicant and the public prosecutor appealed. On 27 November 1997 the Ankara State Security Court applied the decision of the Court of Cassation and sentenced the applicant to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment under Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code. The court held thirty-three more hearings after this date, in search of one of the accused persons, who was on the run. The applicant was released from prison in September 1998 after serving his sentence. The application for appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Justice on 17 September 1998. The case has been adjourned pending the outcome of the appeal.

name: Hasan Aydoğan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41967/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Six Turkish nationals, Mr Hasan Aydoğan, Ms Türkan Özen, Mr Hüseyin İşeri, Mr Süleyman Evren, Mr Ünsal Varol and Mr Hürriyet Öztürk (‘the applicants’) were accused of aiding and abetting an illegal armed terrorist organisation. The applicants were represented by Mr M. Filorinali and Ms Y. Başara, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (’the Government’s Agent) represented them. The case was adjourned 11 times between 10 September 1999 and 19 October 2001. The court ordered the continued detention of Mr Aydoğan and Ms Özen at the end of each hearing. In October 2001 the Istanbul State Security Court, after having examined the evidence in the case file, convicted them as charged and sentenced them to death. As to the other applicants, the court decided to defer the imposition of a final sentence, pursuant to Law no. 46. The evidence included verbatim records of reconstructions of events, search and seizure protocols, forensic reports, statements by others tried before another State Security court and testimony from a number of witnesses. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The decision indicates that their lawyer, despite having requested the court to hold a hearing, had failed to attend it. The court refused them leave to appeal since the decision in their respect was not open to appeal. No information was submitted by the parties as to further developments. On 24 September 2002 Mr Aydoğan’s and Ms Özen's sentences were commuted to life imprisonment. The couple were released on bail and are now serving their sentences in a Turkish prison. They are also appealing their release from prison to the European Court of Human Rights.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7436/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 1 June 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. name: Mehmet Erdagöz
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the Government of the Republic of Turkey on 18 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 21890/93) against Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under Article 25 by a Turkish national, Mr Mehmet Erdagöz, on 1 May 1993. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Gölcüklü, the elected judge of Turkish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention), and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 June 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Martínez, Mr Kaplan, Mr Yılmaz and Mrs Akçay. Mr Walsh was unable to take part in the deliberations on 22 September 1997, Sir John Freeland, substitute judge, replaced him as a member of the Chamber. The outcome of these proceedings is not known. The circumstances of the case are as follows: A brawl broke out between the applicant and members of his family on one side and a Mr H.A. and his friends on the other. The police arrived on the scene half an hour later – before the applicant, who was not on the premises, had even been informed – noted that the windows had been broken and made out a damage assessment report. H.A. was convicted of threatening use of a firearm, criminal damage and an offence under the Firearms Act. He was acquitted for lack of sufficient evidence. The Court of Cassation upheld this judgment on 28 February 1994. The application was dismissed on the grounds of the applicant’s lack of liberty and the applicant was suspected of fabricating evidence. In a judgment of 28 June 1993, the Criminal Court acquitted H.A., who had allegedly organised the attack out of animosity towards the applicant. The court also ruled that the applicant had been illegally deprived of his liberty. The applicant was also ordered to be transferred to security police headquarters for detailed questioning. The first complaint was lodged against the chief inspector and Deputy Inspector S.K. on 17 September 1992. He alleged that during the inquiries into the altercation of 3 June 1992 the former had abused his authority by drawing up a biased report of the incident. Mr Erdagöz was released the same day, at a time which has not been specified. The Adana public prosecutor, after conducting an investigation, discontinued the proceedings. He concluded that the allegation of abusing authority was unfounded and decided not to pursue the investigation concerning the chief Inspector. The applicant’s complaints against the police were dismissed on 29 December 1992, and he was released. The complainant went to the police station to lodge a complaint against the person responsible for smashing the windows of his shop and bringing two bullets as evidence. He was asked to produce evidence or name a witness; he left the station and came back two hours later with the two bullets. The police officers accordingly went to his shop with the bullets, but there were no bullet marks in the shop. The officer in charge of the investigation, Enver Tunç, ordered the complainant’s first statement to be altered and sent a squad to the premises. On the same day this squad made out a report noting that there wereNo bullet marks whatsoever in his shop, the inference was drawn that the complainant had falsely produced the bullets in question for the sole purpose of ensuring that [H.A.], the person he had accused, would be arrested. Chief Inspector Tunç accordingly referred him to the criminal investigation branch for questioning. The complainant was referred to the public prosecutor’s office by an order of 17 September 1992. The applicant appealed against the above discontinuation order to the President of the Assize Court. He alleged in particular that his detention in police custody had lasted for two days and had been due to the resentment the police felt towards him on account of his previous complaints to the European Commission of Human Rights and the domestic courts. On 7 March 1994 the President  dismissed the appeal and on 24 June 1994 the Minister of Justice refused a petition in which Mr Erdagöz had asked him to lodge an appeal in the interests of the law.

name: Krzysztof Wersel

The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant, Mr Krzysztof Wersel, is a Polish national who was born in 1970 and is currently serving a prison sentence in Brzeg. The applicant was convicted of three counts of armed robbery and sentenced to a prison term of three and a half years. He was committed to Zabrze Remand Centre in July 2005. The Government submitted that as of 26 November 2009 the applicant had been detained in Brzeg Prison, in a cell in which the statutory minimum space of 3 square metres per person had been respected. The applicant did not complain to the penitentiary authorities in connection with the living conditions as regards the more recent period of his detention. He did not bring a civil action in tort to seek compensation for the infringement of his personal rights. The appellate court held that the applicant be exempted from all costs of the appellate proceedings, including legal assistance. The applicant drafted his own cassation appeal and filed it with the Katowice Regional Court. The applicant, once more, asked the court to grant him legal aid for the purpose of his appeal proceedings. No formal decision was served on the applicant to that effect. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their plots of land had been illegally seized by the administration for dam construction without any payment being made. The court ordered the administration to pay the applicants an amount of increased compensation, plus interest at the statutory rate, running from 1986, when the plots of lands were submerged in the waters of the dam. In 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning insufficient interest payable in respect of additional compensation, the delay of the authorities in payment of the additional compensation. The cases could be characterised as compensation claims arising from expropriation. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgments of the first-instance court only in respect of the date from which the statutory rate of interest began to run from 19 August 1993. The National Water Board appealed. On 11 November 1998 the administration paid the applicants the amounts due together with interest. The cases were settled out of court in a settlement of $1,540,000 (EUR 1,100,000) and $424,914,000 ($2,155,000), respectively. The case was heard at the Baskil Civil Court of First Instance.

name: Rajko Medenica
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20491/92) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Assize Court of the Canton of Geneva had tried and convicted him in absentia. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 16 December 1999 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided to dispense with a hearing of the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) and decided to allow the application to proceed. The applicant was accused of causing Yugoslavia’s welfare institutions to sustain substantial losses with the complicity of an official at the consulate of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Geneva. He was arrested on 27 October 1982 and charged with fraud, intimidation and forging documents. On 1 February 1984 the applicant paid the stipulated sum and was released. He then travelled to the United States of America, where he acquired American nationality and practised as a doctor specialising in the treatment of certain serious forms of cancer. The case might be set down for trial between January and May 1989, but it was adjourned until 17 April 1989 after a further hearing on 13 March 1989. One of the applicant’s American patients applied to the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina, Charleston Division, for orders requiring the applicant to continue to treat him until he could be replaced by another doctor. He maintained that his life would be in danger if there were any interruption in the treatment he was receiving from the applicant. The American court issued a restraining order prohibiting the applicant from leaving the territory of the U.S. and requiring him to surrender his passport. That decision was served on the Swiss authorities, including the Principal Public Prosecutor of the Canton of Geneva, who was given sixty days in which to respond. The Canton of Geneva Assize Court convicted the applicant in absentia and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment, of which two years, eight months and twenty-five days remained to be served. The applicant was also found guilty of forgery of documents for procuring the signing by his secretary of seventeen false receipts for expenses in a name she no longer used. The jury assessed the amount of alleged damage at approximately 1,000,000 Swiss francs. On the other hand, the applicant was acquitted by the jury on 672 counts of fraud. He was also made an order excluding him from Swiss territory for ten years. An application for the applicant’s immediate arrest made by the Principal Public Prosecutor after the delivery of the verdict was dismissed by the Assize Court. The offences to which the convictions related had been committed between 1973 and 1981. The applicant lodged an application with the Court of Justice of the Canton of Geneva for the conviction in absentia to be set aside, under Article 331 of the Geneva Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 42 below) He maintained that good cause had been shown for his absence at the hearing on 17 April 1989, as he had been compelled to comply with the enforceable decision of the American court – which clearly constituted a reason beyond his control. The appeal was lodged on 26 April 1989, that is to say a week after his trial had actually begun, and his application for an adjournment had been dismissed. By that juncture, for reasons of time, he could no longer reverse the course of events he had helped set in motion. The Court of Justice described his attitude as irresponsible. The applicant was also held to be at fault for having delayed in appealing against the decision of the American court. The appeal was dismissed by the Canton of Geneva Court of Cassation on 14 February 1991. It held that the argument concerning the refusal to remit the case had been conclusively disposed of in its judgment of 27 June 1990. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court, seeking to have set aside the Canton of Geneva Court of Cassation’s judgments of 27 June 1990 and 14 February 1991. He alleged, inter alia, a violation of his right to be heard and to attend his trial. The Federal Court dismissed his appeal. It held that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention did not preclude a trial being held in the defendant's absence if the defendant refused to attend or was unable to attend through his or her own fault. It considered that the applicant had misled the American court by making inaccurate statements, notably regarding Swiss procedure, in order to secure a judgment. The applicant was arrested at Munich Airport (Germany) on his way to a conference. He was extradited to Switzerland and transferred to Champ-Dollon Prison. An application he made for a pardon was refused in February 1996. He served the remainder of his sentence, spending part of it in a secure wing of Geneva Cantonal Hospital. On 20 December 1996 he returned to the United States. The Federal Court's opinion is that it was the applicant’s own fault that he had been unable to attend his trial. It was possible to infer that the aim of the defence had been to obtain an adjournment of the trial in Switzerland.

The American court issued a restraining order prohibiting the applicant from leaving the territory of the US and requiring him to surrender his passport. The Swiss authorities were given sixty days in which to respond. The applicant lodged an application with the U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina to have the restraining order of 28 March 1989 set aside. In a judgment of 26 May 1989 the Canton of Geneva Assize Court convicted the applicant in absentia and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment, of which two years, eight months and twenty-five days remained to be served. The applicant was also found guilty of forgery of documents for procuring the signing by his secretary of seventeen false receipts for expenses in a name she no longer used. The jury assessed the amount of alleged damage at approximately 1,000,000 Swiss francs. On the other hand, the applicant was acquitted on 672 counts of fraud. Conviction in absentia had been set aside under Article 331 of the Geneva Code of Criminal Procedure. He maintained that good cause had been shown for his absence at the hearing on 17 April 1989. An application for the applicant’s immediate arrest made by the Principal Public Prosecutor after the delivery of the verdict was dismissed by the Assize Court. The offences to which the convictions related had been committed between 1973 and 1981. The Court of Justice held, in particular, that the applicant had been seriously at fault in not transmitting his medical knowledge to other practitioners despite knowing from 1 February 1984 onwards he would one day stand trial. His trial had eventually begun five years after his release on bail, so he had had ample time to pass on his experience. The Court of Justice of 20 November 1989 dismissed the applicant's application for relief from his trial. On 8 March 1990 the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina set aside the order of 28 March 1989 and ordered the return of the applicant’s passport. On 16 May 1990 the applicant attended the hearing before the Canton of Geneva Court of Cassation. In a judgment of 27 June 1990 the Court of. Cassation dismissed the appeal as unfounded, holding that he had brought. about the situation that had prevented him from leaving his patients and. appearing before the Assize Court by his own conduct. In addition, statements he had made to the. United States. District Court cast doubt on whether he had genuinely intended to travel to Switzerland to stand trial. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court, seeking to have set aside the Canton of Geneva Court of Cassation’s judgments of 27 June 1990 and 14 February 1991. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The judge elected in respect of Turkey withdrew from sitting in the case. The Government appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties, the Court found in favour of the applicant. The case was brought against the applicant by the Ankara Security Directorate on suspicion of membership of the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court convicted the applicant of membership. The Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi). The applicant appealed the conviction, but the appeal was rejected. The case is still pending in the Assize court.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his pre-trial detention had exceeded a “reasonable time’ within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. The President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Polish Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, Warsaw, had been given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Constitutional Convention and Rule 44 § 2) The applicant was born in 1956 and lives in Polanica Zdrój. The applicant was detained in August 2002. The Warsaw District Court extended his detention until 31 October 2002. On appeal by the applicant, the Warsaw Regional Court upheld the decision of 21 August 2002 and extended it until 31 December 2002. In March 2003 the Warsaw Court of Appeal extended the applicant’s detention until 21 June 2003. In November 2002, the applicant appealed against a decision of 28 October 2002 extending his pre-trial detention. No ruling was given on the appeal on 27 February 2003. The applicant appealed again on 4 November 2002 and his appeal was dismissed. On 7 December 2002 the application was dismissed and his detention was again extended. The case is pending before the first-instance court. The applicant was detained in 2002. He asked for his detention to be lifted and replaced by bail. The Prosecutor of Appeal dismissed the application on 2 January 2003. On 19 April 2004 the applicant was subjected to a medical examination at his own request. The results of the medical examination did not reveal grounds for release. On 17 August 2004 the Warsaw District Court lifted the applicant’s detention and released him on bail. On 18 January 2006 the applicant lodged, under the Law of 17 June 2004, a complaint concerning the length of the examination of his appeal against the decision of 28 October 2002 prolonging his pre-trial detention. The court found that the applicant had not obstructed the proceedings. The complaint was made in 2003. The Warsaw District Court refused to entertain the appeal on 27 February 2003. On 28 February 2006 the Warsaw Court of Appeal declined to consider the complaint. It referred to the fact that the complaint concerned proceedings prior to the entry into force of the 2004 Act. The 2004 Act produced legal effects as from the date it entered into force. The complaint was settled out of court for about 10,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approx. EUR 2,500) in a settlement of around £1.5 million (EUR 1,000,000) in 2005. The case was settled in court in 2006 for £1,500,000 (Eur 1,600,000).

name: Stuart Gray
train_texts: The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) by two British nationals, Mr Stuart Gray and Mr Rory Gray, on 10 September 2009. They complained that shortcomings in the British health system in connection with the recruitment of locum doctors and supervision of out-of-hours locum services had led to their father’s death as a consequence of medical malpractice by German locum doctor U. U. The application was declared partly inadmissible on 18 December 2012 as being manifestly ill-founded as regards the complaints against the United Kingdom and the complaints under Article 14. The applicants are the sons of the late David Gray (hereinafter referred to as “Mr Gray” or “the deceased”) who died in the evening of 16 February 2008 at the age of 71 at his home in Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom. Mr Gray suffered from kidney stones and from 2004 on he had regularly been attended at home by his doctor, a General Practitioner. The GP had routinely administered injections of opiates, in particular pethidine at a dosage of 100mg, for pain relief. On several occasions between 2006 and 2008 Mr Gray had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by “Take Care Now’ (“TCN”), a private agency that recruits locum doctors within the United Kingdom or from abroad. Dr U., a German national, had recently been recruited by TCN through an agency on a self-employed basis to provide out-of-hours care. U., at the time aged 65, had qualified as a doctor in Germany in 1972 where he was practising as an aesthetic surgeon. U. administered 100mg of diamorphine from the respective ampoule included in the palliative care box by intra‑muscular injection. Two hours after U. had left, Mr Gray’s partner realised that he was no longer breathing and called an ambulance. The attending emergency services confirmed that Mr Gray had died. On Sunday 17 February 2008 TCN suspended U. from duty, terminated his engagement with immediate effect and advised him to return to Germany. U. was suspended from the British medical register on an interim basis. He apologised for the medical malpractice in connection with the deceased’s treatment and again explained that he had confused the opiates. A post mortem report issued on 25 June 2008 by a forensic pathologist in the United Kingdom established as the cause of the death diamorphine poisoning in association with alcohol intoxication and hypertensive heart disease. The Cambridgeshire police commenced criminal investigations against U. for manslaughter. U. has since been cleared of any wrongdoing by the Medical Board of England and Wales (MBE) and the British Medical Practitioners Association (MPA) Cambridgeshire Constabulary made an application for assistance to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation (Bundeskriminalamt) in March 2008. The CPS asked the German authorities to carry out the respective investigations and to arrange for hearings of the relevant witnesses in Germany. Bochum Chief Public Prosecutor ex officio initiated preliminary criminal proceedings (Ermittlungsverfahren) against U. in Germany under file no. 49 Js 174/08 on suspicion of having negligently caused the death of Mr Gray. In Article 152 § 2 of the German Code of Criminal Procedure in conjunction with Articles 222 and 7 § 2 no. 1 of theGerman Criminal Code (see Relevant domestic and international law and practice below) Cambridgeshire police officers visited Germany on several occasions in the period from July until September 2008. German police officers heard representatives of U’s professional indemnity insurance company, of the public health authorities at the Arnsberg District Government and the Westphalia-Lippe Medical Association (Ärztekammer) as witnesses. A forensic expert opinion was obtained from a professor of Essen university hospital on the question whether the treatment of the deceased by U. had complied with medical standards. In his final report issued on 18 September 2008 the expert confirmed that the cause of Mr Gray's death had been an overdose of diamorphine. U. availed himself of his right not to testify. U. not sufficiently investigated the cause of Mr Gray’s acute pain and had not verified whether the medication administered and its dosage had been an appropriate therapy under the circumstances. The expert concluded that U.’S treatment of the deceased had thus been inadequate and had violated basic principles of medical care. Cambridgeshire Constabulary requested the German public prosecution authorities to assure that no criminal proceedings would be instituted against U. in Germany prior to finalisation of the investigations in the United Kingdom. According to a file note by the Bochum public prosecution. authorities of 5 November 2008, the German prosecution authorities had informed Cambridgedgeshire. Constabulary in reply to a similar request made over the phone that day that they had been obliged by operation of law to institute. preliminary criminal proceedings against U in Germany. U. acting as joint plaintiffs to the prosecution (Nebenkläger) the right to inspect the files in such preliminary proceedings. The Chief Prosecutor found that while the fact that U. did not have a criminal record, had made a full confession and had apologised to the victim’s relatives had to be considered in his favour. A draft of the penal order was attached to the application. U., represented by counsel, had declared that he would accept the envisaged sentence of 9 months in prison and a payment of 5,000 euros (EUR) to the treasury. U. was arrested on 12 March 2009 for allegedly having caused the death of Mr Gray. The EAW was forwarded by the British authorities to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation on 13 March 2009. On the same day Cambridgeshire police was informed by the Hamm General Prosecution authorities that execution of the EAW had been halted in view of the criminal proceedings pending against U. in Germany. On 20 March 2009 the Witten District Court issued the penal order (file no. 49 Js 174/08) against U as applied for by the prosecution authorities. On 14 April 2009 newly appointed counsel for the second applicant practising in Germany asked the Bochum prosecution authorities for information. It follows from a subsequent letter by counsel dated 19 May 2009 that his request for inspection of the files was granted. U. had nevertheless committed a grave error in the deceased’s treatment. U. had been convicted by final decision of a German court for the offence underlying the extradition request and the sentence imposed upon him was currently in the process of being executed. His extradition would therefore be contrary to the ban on double jeopardy as reflected in section 9 (1) no. 1 of the Act on Cooperation in Criminal Matters. The Hamm Higher Regional Court, endorsing the reasoning of the Hamm General Prosecution Authorities, declared U’s extradition inadmissible on 14 May 2009. On 1 July 2009 a meeting between the representatives of the Bochum prosecution authorities, the CPS and Cambridgeshire police took place at Eurojust in The Hague. The content of these discussions is confidential. The Westphalia-Lippe Medical Association applied for the opening of disciplinary proceedings against U. for breach of his professional duties in connection with the incidents in the United Kingdom on 16 February 2008. U. under file no. 49 Js 174/08. As a consequence of the German authorities’ decision not to extradite U., the criminal investigations in the U.K. were discontinued. There was nothing to establish that U. would commit a similar error of treatment in Germany or that he lacked the necessary qualifications for practising medicine. Consequently, the health authorities held that there was no need to suspend or revoke U’s licence to practice medicine in Germany and discontinued the proceedings. An Inquest into the circumstances of the incident was held by the Cambridgeshire Coroner from 14 January to 4 February 2010. U.D. in particular for having committed a grave error in the treatment of Mr Gray, and fined him 7,000 EUR. The GMC Fitness to Practice Panel considered that U. had breached several of the basic principles of good medical practice and decided to formally strike U.’s name from the medical register in the United Kingdom. In addition, in 2009 the applicants brought civil claims for damages for unlawful killing arising out of negligence with the High Court against U., TCN as well as Cam Bridgeshire PCT.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25706/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’s Convention”) The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr T. Kochanowski, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. On 19 June 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The Polish Government, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings (Article 36 § 1 and Rule 44), did not indicate that they wished to exercise that right. The applicant was not informed about the foster parents’ place of residence for almost two years and was thus prevented from exercising access rights. The child suffered from a serious emotional disorder which had been caused by family tensions. The decision on custody and access rights should be suspended until the child had stabilised. On 9 July 1998 the applicant consented to the child’s remaining with the foster family for the duration of the necessary psychotherapy, which she estimated at one year. The Child and Youth Psychiatric Service convinced the expert that S. was not in need of psychotherapy. It was proposed to instigate contacts between the child and her parents under psychotherapeutic or pedagogical guidance. The child's father and mother have been unable to reach an agreement on how to return the child to them. The court ordered that the child be returned to the parents as soon as possible. The child's parents have not been able to find a way to return her to them yet. They are waiting for the court to issue a ruling on the child's return. The boy's mother is waiting to see if she will be allowed to see her son again. The father is waiting for a decision on whether to send the child back to his parents. The mother is also waiting to hear if the father will be able to see the child again. S. was removed from her foster family in 2001. The child had been in the care of her parents for five years. The parents did not want the child to stay with them. The court agreed to let the child stay with the parents. The case was adjourned for two years. S. was returned to her foster parents in April 2004. She has since made a full recovery and is now living with her parents. She is expected to return to the foster family next year. For confidential support call the Samaritans on 08457 90 90 90 or visit a local Samaritans branch, see www.samaritans.org for details. On 5 March 2002 the applicant requested that a court decision be given immediately. On 9 February 2002 the child’s curator informed the court that she would need another six weeks to prepare her submissions. On 28 June 2002 the court requested the Youth Office to report on the child's present life circumstances and on the discontinuation of therapy. On 24 April 2003 the Pankow-Weissensee District Court, following a hearing attended by the applicant, ruled that the child should stay with the foster family until the child reaches majority. However, the District Court proposed that the parents should abstain from making use of access rights for one year and that contact should be carefully re-established afterwards. The District Court considered that the applicant was unable to accept the child’s wishes and her present life circumstances within the foster family. She was, in particular, unwilling to accept that a parent-child relationship had developed between the child and her foster parents. The Court of Appeal ruled that parental authority had to be withdrawn from both parents and transferred to the Youth Office. Furthermore, visiting contacts between theChild and her parents were suspended for one year. The decision was made by the District Court on 9 July 2003, and the applicant lodged an appeal with the Berlin Court of appeal (Kammergericht) on 8 August 2003. On 13 November 2003 the child's curator submitted her comments. She considered the measures taken by the Court to be disproportionate. The Court of Appeal quashed the District Court’s decision, transferred sole parental authority to the child's father and granted the applicant visiting rights once per month for five and a half hours each. The child had consistently expressed the wish to live with the foster family as a full family member. The Court of appeal conceded that the alienation between the applicant and her daughter had to a substantial degree been caused by the period of time which had elapsed since her placement. The proceedings could and should have been conducted in a considerably more stringent way. However, the decision had to be taken in accordance with the child’S welfare, which was not defined by earlier shortcomings of the proceedings. The applicant lodged a complaint against the Court of Appeal’s decision, in which she gave a full account of the proceedings before the civil courts. She alleged that the impugned decision was disproportionate and violated her right to the enjoyment of her family life under Article 6 of the Basic Law. The Federal Constitutional Court, sitting as a panel of three judges, refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint for adjudication. If the applicant wishes to appeal, she can do so by writing to the Berlin-Brandenburg Administrative Court of appeal (Oberverwaltungsgericht) on 19 September 2005. The applicant can also write to the German Federal Court of Justice (Bundeskriminalamt) on behalf of the applicant if she wishes to.

In the course of the discussion the Child and Youth Psychiatric Service convinced the expert that S. was not in need of psychotherapy. The child is now being cared for by a foster family. S. is expected to make a full recovery from her ordeal in about a year's time. The family is still waiting for a decision on the future of the child’s home. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court of Luxembourg. In the meantime, S. continues to receive care at the home of her foster parents. For more information, go to www.fosterhome.org.uk. name: Jørgen Kristiansen
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1176/10) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings leading to his conviction he had not been afforded a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 July 2013. The High Court ruled in favour of the applicant, who was convicted of attempted rape on 9 March 2008 in a car parked near a petrol station in Sarpsborg, Norway. The City Court did not find credible the applicant’s explanation that he and Ms A had kissed and to a little extent touched one another voluntarily and that he had NOT forcibly attempted to rape her. In 2009, the Borgarting High Court (lagmannsrett), hearing the applicant’s appeal with a jury, convicted him on the attempted rape charge. It ordered him to pay 60,000 Norwegian kroner (NOK) (approximately 7,500 euros at that time) in compensation to Ms A for non-pecuniary damage. The High Court described in detail how the applicant, after he had called Mr B (who could not come straight away), had attempted to obtain sexual contact with Ms A by force. It stated that in the beginning, when the applicant had tried to kiss and touch her, Ms A had told him that she was not interested because she was the girlfriend of Mr D. Counsel for the defence requested that J be disqualified from taking part in the further proceedings on grounds of lack of impartiality. The High Court observed that “the jury member had formed a picture [bilde] of the victim from many years ago where she at the time had experienced her as a quiet and calm person” It decided that a member might be disqualified if the person in question had particular reasons for identifying himself or herself with the victim or if there were any other circumstances to the effect that he or she had a prejudging attitude. However, that was not the situation in the present case and the High Court decided that J ought not to withdraw. Juror J took part in the entire trial before the High Court, including the jury’s deliberations and vote on the charge of attempted rape. The High Court had special regard to the fact that the parties to the case had requested that J recuse herself, but it found the absence of partiality so clear in this case that this could not be decisive. Neither had counsel for the defence alleged before the Supreme Court that this was a sufficient ground for disqualification. The majority did not consider that her attendance at birthday parties and class outings with the victim in itself indicated an identification of the victim or weakened in any other way the confidence in her impartiality. Victim could easily perceive a verdict acquitting the defendant to mean that the jury believed that she had made an unfounded and serious accusation against the defendant. The minority shared the majority’s view (see paragraph 16 above) that previous contacts between the victim and J could not, of their own, disqualify the latter. It could possibly be maintained that one could draw the conclusion that a calm girl would hardly make a fuss without any justifications for doing so. However, there was no basis for such a conclusion and there was in any event no reason for attaching weight to such a possibility. The timing of J's statement was of considerable importance. For the persons present in court it could seem conspicuous that the juror had not confined herself to informing about her previous contacts with A. J's affirmation could easily have given the impression that J expressed a positive assessment of the victim. That J had expressed a view on how she had perceived her “at the time’ was of secondary importance. Both counsel for the defence and the assistant advocate had demanded that J recuse herself. Under Article 6 of the Convention, “the standpoint of the accused [was] important but not decisive’. In this case the “fear” of lack of impartiality by the applicant had been “objectively justified” (see Ferrantelli and Santangelo v. Italy, 7 August 1996, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996‑III).

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40555/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr F. Babaoğlu, a lawyer practising in Ankara. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The case against the applicant continued before the Istanbul State Security Court. On 5 April 2004 the applicant was released pending trial. The case was still pending before the domestic courts when the applicant died on 14 June 2005. The Constitution was amended on 18 June 1999 and the military judge sitting on the bench was replaced by a civilian judge. In the course of the proceedings the applicant's requests for release were rejected, taking into account the nature of the alleged offence and the state of the evidence.

name: Gerda Rieg
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 63207/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a German national, Ms Gerda Rieg. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her right to remain silent and not to incriminate herself had been breached in criminal proceedings against her. By a decision of 18 March 2004 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The applicant was fined 1,500 Austrian schillings (ATS) with two days' imprisonment in default. She claimed that the obligation under section 103 § 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act to disclose the driver of her car violated the presumption of innocence and her right not to incriminate herself. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant's complaint for lack of sufficient prospects of success. The incident was not prosecuted for exceeding the speed limit, but for failing to give the correct address to the District Administrative Authority on 12 March 1997.

The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 18 March 2004 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant was fined 1,500 Austrian schillings (ATS) with two days' imprisonment in default. She claimed that the obligation under section 103 § 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act to disclose the driver of her car violated the presumption of innocence and her right not to incriminate herself. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant's complaint for lack of sufficient prospects of success. The applicant was not prosecuted for exceeding the speed limit. The case was settled out of court in 2000, and the penalty was not more than ATS 10,000 (ATS 1,000,000) with no important legal problem at stake.

The applicant alleged that he had not had a fair trial as there were insufficient guarantees to exclude legitimate doubt regarding the independence and impartiality of the tribunal which tried him on criminal charges. The Crown case was that D.G. had been summoned to the scene by the applicant and another co-accused, M.H., using a mobile telephone belonging to D.M. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1) The applicant was charged with attempted murder and making threats to kill. Crown case involved video recordings from closed circuit television (CCTV) cameras near the scene. Crown contended that the applicant could be seen making certain calls. There was also eye witness evidence of him making at least one of the critical calls. In total, the Crown case was that six relevant calls were made from M.H.'s mobile telephone to D.G. or one of his associates. The applicant's case at trial was that he had made no calls on M. H.'s phone. He said that he was a drug dealer using his own telephone and that the calls were for his own criminal purposes and were nothing to do with the summoning of D. G. The judge told the jury that should they wish to view the recordings again, they only had to ask. The jury subsequently retired. On the second day of their deliberations, they indicated their wish to start reviewing the video evidence in the afternoon. Counsel were advised of the jury's request and the court convened with junior counsel for the applicant among those attending. The only issue that arises as a result of the CCTV request is who exactly is present in court when they view the material. The general view is that if they are able to watch it on their own, it would be much more constructive – if counsel and your Lordship were not present. Officer M cannot do anything other than operate the video machine, and there is to be no other communication with him – or any communication from him – than simply asking him to play you what you want to see. Judge instructed the jury to return and directed them as follows: “Ladies and gentlemen, having discussed this matter with counsel, what we are going to do is this: we are. going to leave [OfficerM] in this court with you, and he will play any part of the video that you have seen, andHe will play it as you think fit. Remember that there is more than one camera that operates – that sometimes you are viewing camera no. 1. Jury left alone in the court room with Officer M at 2.05 p.m. to begin reviewing the video evidence. The jury spent almost two hours viewing the video recordings in the presence of Officer M. When the court reconvened, leading counsel for the applicant directed the judge's attention to various authorities, including Archbold's Criminal Pleading, Evidence and Practice. Judge: 'The unusual circumstance is this ...: we cannot put the equipment in the jury room'. The judge agreed to reconvene the court at 4 p.M. as he did not wish to interrupt the jury's viewing of the videoevidence. Counsel for the applicant suggested that the police officer could continue to operate the equipment but that the presence of a jury bailiff in the jury room would ensure that there was no communication between the parties. Judge: 'And the problem is this: that those who sit behind the dock are essentially put on trust in relation to thePolice officer's lack of communication' Judge: “If the Jury bailiff's oath is that they are to stop any approach by any outsider to the jury, then any communication as to which section of tape the jury wish to see should, in fact, go through that conduit'” Judge: “And essentially, that communication can only be complained of if it came from the officer' Judge observed that there was a need to protect the privacy of the jury while preserving the integrity of the situation. However, he pointed out that “the die had been cast” and that: “... either the procedure in the circumstances of this particular case is acceptable, or it is not.” It was then suggested that either the jury themselves be instructed how to use the equipment or that the video be played in open court in the presence of the judge. The following morning, a solution was agreed which would allow the jury to operate the equipment themselves, with information provided to assist them in locating the part of the recordings that they wished to view.  applicant found guilty of attempted murder and making threats to kill. He was sentenced to 25 years in prison. His co-accused, M.H., was found not guilty. He appealed, arguing that the approach taken to the viewing of the video recordings amounted to a fundamental infringement of the integrity of the jury's deliberations. On 20 June 2006, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. The court summarised the matter before it as follows: “[Counsel for the applicant] contends now, as foreshadowed in his submissions to the judge on his return to court, that the course taken amounted, however unwittingly, to an infringement of ... the jury’s deliberations.” Court of Appeal refused to receive witness statement from Officer M. The court agreed that a fair trial required that a jury should not be improperly influenced during its deliberations. The Court observed that this was not a case where any bias, or apparent bias, was in question. The question was whether the conviction was safe, and in particular whether the unusual course taken meant that there was an unacceptable risk that the jury may have come under improper extraneous influence after the close of evidence in the case. This was not that kind of a case. There was no challenge whatever to the manner of investigation. The issue was what the evidence, which the police were accepted properly to have gathered, did or did not prove. The court noted that the approach adopted in the present case occurred with the authority of the judge and with the consent of all parties. It emphasised that no question arose as to the applicant's right to a fair trial being waived. The safeguard of the integrity of the jury system lies in the respect that jurors have for the serious oath that they have taken, reinforced by the directions and warnings that they are given by trial judges, rather than in requiring formal rules attempting to insulate them from contact with the outside world. “He directed them, as we we.” said the court. Jurors should be entitled to review the same material as has been put in evidence in court, says judge. The judge in this case, we are satisfied, was absolutely right not to permit them to be given a substitute poorer quality VHS recording. If the necessary equipment can be provided in any particular court by agreement as to compatibility of machinery between parties and the court, then so much the better. The ultimate responsibility, however, for the presentation of evidence lies not with the court but with the parties seeking to adduce it. We take leave to doubt that that will ever be so with a little forethought -- then we think that the normal course should be followed. The judge ruled that the trial was not entitled to be heard in public. The verdict was returned in favour of the defendant, and the case was dismissed.

The case originated in an application (no. 8400/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had not had a fair trial as there were insufficient guarantees to exclude legitimate doubt regarding the independence and impartiality of the tribunal which tried him on criminal charges. The Crown case was that D.G. had been summoned to the scene by the applicant and another co-accused, M.H., using a mobile telephone. D.M. survived but suffered permanent brain damage after being shot in the back of the head in 2004. Crown case involved video recordings from closed circuit television (CCTV) cameras near the scene. Crown contended that the applicant could be seen making certain calls. Eye witness evidence of him making at least one of the critical calls. In total, the Crown case was that six relevant calls were made from M.H.'s mobile telephone to D.G. or one of his associates. The applicant denied the Crown contention that it showed him making a call at a relevant time. He accepted that eye witness evidence and CCTV recordings demonstrated that he had used a telephone at certain points. However, he said that he was a drug dealer using his own telephone and that the calls were make for his own criminal purposes. Jurors were asked to view the video evidence again on the second day of their deliberations. They indicated their wish to start reviewing video evidence in the afternoon. Counsel advised of the jury's request and the court convened with junior counsel for the applicant among those attending. The only issue that arises as a result of the CCTV request is who exactly is present in court when they view the material. The jury retired and the case was adjourned until the next day. The judge concluded by saying that there was no reason why the recordings could not be taken into the jury room and played there by the jury if required. He added that any time the jury wanted to see the video, they only had to pass a note. The judge instructed the jury to return and directed them as follows: “We are going to leave [Officer M] in this court with you, and he will play any part of the video that you have seen. He will play it as you think fit. Remember that there is more than one camera that operates – that sometimes you are viewing camera no. 1, and I think at other times camera No. 2' No assent was recorded from junior counsel for the applicant but no objections were raised to the course of action proposed. Judge: 'Does anyone have any objections to the court being cleared, along with the defendants and the public gallery, and simply leaving [ Officer M] there?' Jury left alone in the court room with Officer M at 2.05 p.m. to begin reviewing the video evidence. The jury spent almost two hours viewing the video recordings in the presence of Officer M. When the court reconvened, leading counsel for the applicant directed the judge's attention to various authorities, including Archbold's Criminal Pleading, Evidence and Practice, and the following discussion took place: “The court has, for all purposes, during this afternoon, whilst the jury have been reviewing the material, really been an extension of the jury room –' ... Counsel for applicant: 'And what has happened, in reality, is that an individual – he happens to be a police officer – an individual has, in fact, been within that jury room' Jury could not work the equipment. Judge: 'And that is the first problem ... The second problem is that the jury could not worked the equipment' Counsel for the applicant: '...we understand that [Officer M] was able, in fact, to instruct another officer how to use this machine in pretty short order' Judge: ‘Perhaps, but that is how it was presented to me –' Judge suggested that the police officer could continue to operate the equipment but that the presence of a jury bailiff in the jury room would ensure that there was no communication between the parties in light of the oath to prevent any communication with the jury. Judge: 'I am not sure I would want to change it now. I mean, counsel can consider all of this overnight –’ The judge later advised the jury that he would give counsel a chance to consider the matter overnight. The following morning, a solution was agreed which would allow the jury to operate the equipment themselves, with information provided to assist them in locating the part of the recordings that they wished to view. The jury will be shown in open court, with everybody present, how that equipment works, and you will then be left to it. They will decide exactly who is to operate it, and what you wish to see. The jury viewed the video recordings alone for about an hour. They continued their deliberations for the rest of the day and into the following morning. He was sentenced to 25 years in prison for attempted murder and three years, to be served concurrently, for making threats to kill. His co-accused, M.H., was found not guilty. The applicant appealed, arguing that the approach taken to the viewing of the video recording amounted to a fundamental infringement of the integrity of the jury's deliberations. On 20 June 2006, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. The court noted that the officer in question was a member of the investigating team of police officers which had conducted the enquiry. Court of Appeal refused to receive a witness statement which had not been seen by the applicant or his lawyers. Court examined trial transcript and found that all counsel concerned gave assent to the presence of Officer M while the jury viewed the CCTV footage. Court agreed that a fair trial required that a jury should not be improperly influenced during its deliberations. Court observed that this was not a case where any bias, or apparent bias, was in question. The question was whether the conviction was safe, and in particular whether the unusual course taken meant that there was an unacceptable risk that the jury may have come under improper extraneous influence after the close of evidence in the case. The court noted that the approach adopted in the present case occurred with the authority of the judge and with the consent of all parties. Jurors approach what is a difficult and often anxious task with a remarkable sense of duty. The safeguard of the integrity of the jury system lies in the respect that jurors have for the serious oath that they have taken, reinforced by the directions and warnings that they are given by trial judges, rather than in requiring formal rules attempting to insulate them from contact with the outside world. The court further referred to the “careful direction” given to the jury that there was to be no communication between them and the officer operating the equipment except for the purposes of finding the correct place on the video. The court noted that the suggestion mooted before the trial judge of having a jury bailiff present demonstrated that there could be no absolute prohibition on contact with the jury. It further observed that there was no indication that the jury had been in any way inhibited by the presence of the police officer: they spent considerable time viewing the recordings. The court concluded (at paragraph 55): “We are satisfied that on the facts of this case, whether or not what occurred should have happened – and we will come to that in a moment – the hypothetical informed and fair minded observer would be aware of all the factors to which we have called attention” Jurors commonly ask questions on all manner of topics. Some of them call for the jury to be reminded of a particular area of evidence. The judge in this case, we are satisfied, was absolutely right not to permit them to be given a substitute poorer quality VHS recording. If the necessary equipment can be provided in any particular court by agreement as to compatibility of machinery between parties and the court, then so much the better. It is not desirable that equipment should be provided which can only be used in open court, because although it may turn out to be possible to proceed as was done here on the second day of viewing, that will often not be possible. On 22 August 2008, the applicant was denied leave to appeal to the House of Lords. ‘‘This case. ought to take place in open court.’’ said the applicant’s lawyer. The application was denied and the judge ruled that the case would have to be heard in court. The appeal was dismissed on 24 August 2008. The judge said the case should have been heard in an open court and not in secret. The case was heard in the Lords on 21 August 2008 and the ruling was upheld on the same day. The trial was adjourned until the next day at 11.45am on 22 August.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39482/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a fair trial by virtue of the prosecution’s failure to disclose all material evidence in their possession. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The applicant was convicted of the murder of Christopher Nugent and sentenced to life imprisonment. The pair were convicted of conspiring to break into a bank to steal money. The money was meant to be used to pay a man who had broken into the bank and stolen it. The two men were sentenced to prison but were released on bail. The case has been described as one of the worst in the history of the UK. It is alleged that the money was used to bribe a man in exchange for his silence. The trial was adjourned until October 1992, when the defendants were released from prison. The prosecution claimed that the release of evidence from the bank would be prejudicial to the prosecution's case against the two men. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26589/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the respondent State had failed to take steps to protect the right to life of their relative Mr Şevket Epözdemir (“the deceased”) The applicants also alleged that during a meeting with political party representatives, General K.T., who was the commander of the Tatvan 6th Armoured Brigade, had threatened their relative and one of his colleagues. The General had told the two men that “they would meet their deaths very soon”. Şevket Epözdemir left his house to go to his office, which was nearby. When he failed to arrive the family became concerned and contacted the authorities. At midday the following day the first applicant went to the police station in Tatvan. She told the police officers that when her husband had failed to come home the previous evening she had telephoned the local prosecutor and asked him whether her husband was arrested. But half an hour before she went to police station her husband's body had been found by soldiers in a ditch in the vicinity of the nearby town of Güroymak. He was blindfolded and there was a gunshot wound on his face. Doctors established the cause of death as cerebrovascular haemorrhagic shock caused by the gunshot wound. and the body which, according to the doctors, had been caused by physical trauma. The applicants sent letters to the offices of the Van and Tatvan prosecutors and asked to be provided with information regarding the steps taken in the investigation over the course of the previous ten years. The Van prosecutor’s office decided that it had no jurisdiction ratione loci to investigate the incident and forwarded the applicants’ letter (mentioned in the preceding paragraph) to the office of the prosecutor in Tatvan. The Güroymak prosecutor took a decision of non-jurisdiction ratione materiae and sent the letter to the prosecutor's office at the Van State Security Court. Şevket Epözdemir's body was found in Tatvan in 1993. The applicants brought compensation proceedings against the Ministry of the Interior. In their petition the applicants argued that the perpetrators of the killing had not been found, despite the fact that more than one year had elapsed since the incident. On 16 December 1997 the Van Administrative Court decided to award compensation to the applicants, in accordance with Article 125 of the Constitution (see paragraphs 32-34 below). It held that when carrying out their duties the public authorities had an obligation to take the necessary measures to protect the deceased’s life. The compensation proceedings have now been settled. The Ministry of the Interior appealed, arguing that it had not failed in that obligation because the reason for the killing and the identity of its perpetrators had not yet been established. The applicants lodged an appeal with the Supreme Administrative Court against the decision and argued that a citizen need not officially seek protection from the authorities in order to trigger the State's obligation to protect such a citizen’s life. The Van Administrative Court re-examined the case in the light of the decision. and decided to reject the applicants’ claim for compensation. In reaching its conclusion, the administrative court noted that the investigation into the killing was still ongoing and, in any event, the deceased had never sought protection. from the State. The appeal lodged by the applicants was rejected by the Supreme Administrative Court on 17 April 2003. The applicants maintained that the authorities had failed to take the necessary steps to prevent the attack on their relative and to find the perpetrators. The Ministry was therefore responsible for the pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage arising from the failures on its part. The final decision was served on the applicants on 3 January 2006. name: Waldemar Szulc
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 63679/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Waldemar Szulc (“the applicant”) was unrepresented before the Court. The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Leicester. His wife died on 16 February 1996, leaving two children of ten and twelve years of age respectively. His claim for widows’ benefits was made on 9 February 1997 and was rejected on 18 February 1997 on the ground that he was not entitled to Widowed Mother’s Allowance. After various rejections, on 20 September 2000 the Inland Revenue confirmed he was ineligible for WBA as he is not a woman.

name: Nuri Akalın
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23480/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Nuri Akalın (‘the applicant’) was arrested on suspicion of being a member of an illegal organisation in 1997. The medical report drawn up by the doctor indicated that there was hyperaemia on the applicant's thighs. The applicant stated before the İstanbul State Security Court that his statement in police custody had been taken under torture, but he did not give any details. The case against the applicant was subsequently resumed before theİstanbul Assize Court. The case is pending before the Court of Cassation. The applicant objected to his continued detention and requested his release. The 11th Chamber of the İstanbul Assize Court dismissed the applicant's objections on 14 January and 15 April 2009 respectively, having regard to the nature of the offence in question and to the state of the evidence. No hearing was held. According to information in the case file, the case is awaiting review by the Court of Cassation, and the applicant may be tried in front of the Supreme Court of Justice, which could take up to two years. The case is currently before the court of cassation.

Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Nuri Akalın (‘the applicant’) was arrested on suspicion of being a member of an illegal organisation on 3 March 1997. The medical report drawn up by the doctor indicated that there was hyperaemia on the applicant's thighs. The applicant stated that his statement in police custody had been taken under torture, but he did not give any details. On 26 April 2002 the İstanbul State Security Court convicted the applicant under Article 146 of the former Criminal Code. On 12 May 2003 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment. The case is pending before the Court of Cassation. No hearing was held. The applicant objected to his continued detention and requested his release. The 11th Chamber of the İstanbul Assize Court dismissed the applicant's objections on 14 January and 15 April 2009 respectively, having regard to the nature of the offence in question and to the state of the evidence. On 2 April 2009 the İstanbul Assize Court convicted the applicant. According to information in the case file, the case is pending before the Court of Cassation. The appeal is expected to be heard within the next few weeks.

On 19 May 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applicant's application at the same time (former Article 29 § 3). The application was brought by a Turkish national, Mr Nuri Akalın (‘the applicant’). The applicant was represented by Ms İ. Kadirhan and Ms G. Tuncer. On 2 April 2009 the İstanbul Assize Court convicted the applicant. According to information in the case file, the case is pending before the Court of Cassation. No hearing was held. On 25 December 2008 and 9 April 2009, the applicant objected to his continued detention and requested his release. The 11th Chamber of the  İ Istanbul Assize Court dismissed the applicant's objections on 14 January and 15 April 2009 respectively, having regard to the nature of the offence in question and to the state of the evidence. The applicant's request for his release was denied by the 11th  Chamber. The case is still pending.

name: Imad Al-Khawaja
train_texts: Cases originated in two application (nos. 26766/05 and 2228/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. First applicant alleged that his trial for indecent assault had been unfair because one of the two women who made complaints against him died before the trial and her statement to the police was read to the jury. Second applicant alleged his trial. for wounding with intent to do grievous bodily harm had been. unfair because the statement of one witness who feared attending trial was. read to jury. Both cases took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 January 2008. Mr Al-Khawaja was charged on two counts of indecent assault on two female patients while they were allegedly under hypnosis. One of the complainants, S.T., committed suicide (taken to be unrelated to the assault) before the trial but, several months after the alleged assault, had made a statement to the police. The judge allowed the evidence to be admitted at trial. The jury heard evidence from a number of different witnesses and the defence were given the opportunity to cross-examine other witnesses. In his summing up, the trial judge directed the members of the jury, on two separate occasions, as to how they should regard the read statement of the deceased complainant. The applicant was convicted by a unanimous verdict on both counts of indecent assault. The Court of Appeal concluded on 3 November 2005 that the applicant's right to a fair trial had not been infringed. Relying on Doorson v. the Netherlands, judgment of 26 March 1996, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996‑II p 66, the court held that admissibility of evidence is primarily a matter of domestic law. It then found: “Where a witness who is the sole witness of a crime has made a statement to be used in its prosecution and has since died, there may be a strong public interest in the admission of the statement in evidence” The Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords but certified that a point of law of general public importance was involved in the decision. The applicant was charged with wounding with intent and also with attempting to pervert the course of justice. He was found not guilty of the charges against him. The court also considered that the applicant had been able to attack the accuracy of the deceased complainant's statement by exploring the inconsistencies between it and the evidence given by witnesses and experts. On 30 November 2005 the applicant petitioned the House. of Lords on the point oflaw certified by the Court of. Appeal. On 7 February 2005 the Houseof Lords refused the petition. Prosecution argued that T. was too fearful to attend trial before the jury and that he should qualify for special measures. The trial judge heard evidence from a police officer who testified that the Iranian community was close-knit and that T.'s fear was genuine. T. himself gave evidence to the judge from behind a screen. The judge ruled that leave should be given for the statement to be read to the jury, saying: “I am satisfied in those circumstances upon the criminal standard of proof that this witness is genuinely in fear.” He added that the defendant's evidence, if he chooses to give it, would be sufficient to rebut and to challenge the evidence that is contained in that statement. The applicant's appeal was referred directly before the full Court of Appeal. The applicant argued that the inability to cross-examine T. infringed his right to a fair trial. The appeal judges were satisfied that if they were to refuse leave, under the CJA 2003, to have T.'s statement read at trial there would be unfairness to the prosecution. On 29 April 2005, the applicant was convicted by a majority verdict, principally of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm. He was later sentenced to nine years' imprisonment to be served concurrently with a term of fifteen months' imprisonment for doing an act intended to pervert the course of justice.  leave to appeal on conviction was refused on 24 January 2006. Court of Appeal held that the jury was informed of all matters necessary to its decision-making process. The applicant's sentence was reduced to seven years' imprisonment. Trial judge warned the jury in detail as to how they should treat this evidence and properly directed them as toHow they should consider it in reaching their verdict. Although the applicant maintained that even a proper direction by the judge could not cure the unfairness, the Court of Appeals ruled that the judge had given the jury all the information they needed to make a fair decision. The trial judge had explicitly warned the trial judge in. first instance, stating that there was available not only cross-examination of other prosecution witnesses but also evidence from the applicant himself and the potential for evidence from other bystanders in order to prevent unfairness.
