train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24746/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his son Pearse Jordan had been unjustifiably shot and killed by a police officer and that there had been no effective investigation into, or redress for, his death. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building on 4 April 2000. The case was heard by the President of the Court, who held that proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of McKerr v the. United Kingdom, no. 28883/95, Kelly and Others v. the United UK,No. 30054/96 and Shanaghan v the United. UK no. 37715/97. The applicant’s son, Pearse Jordan, aged 22, was shot and killed in Belfast by an officer of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (the RUC), later identified as Sergeant A. Treacy. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Treacy and declared the application admissible on 4 April 2000. The facts of the case, in particular concerning what happened when Pearse Jordanian was shot on 25 November 1992, are in dispute between the parties. The application is denied and the case is adjourned until further Notice. Four civilians stopped and had an unobstructed view across the road. They heard a crash behind them and turned to see on the opposite side of the road the red police car pulling alongside a car (Pearse Jordan's) and ramming it up onto the footpath. The civilians heard no warning shout or challenge given by any of the officers and saw nothing in Pearse Jordan’s hands or anything threatening in his actions. The police carried out a search of the car. The four witnesses followed the ambulance which took Pearse. Jordan to hospital where they stated that they were subjected to hostile and threatening remarks by. members of the security forces. The Independent Commission for Police Complaints will supervise the RUC investigation. Sergeant A thought that this was possibly the re-supply of terrorist equipment taking place. He was carrying a Smith and Wesson 59 pistol and a MP5 Heckler and Koch. The car possibly reached the speed of 60, maybe 70 miles per hour at the fastest. Sergeant A’s car drew level with the Orion and he signalled for it to pull over. The Orion slowed falling behind and then shot past on the passenger side, accelerating down the Falls Road in the direction of the city. Sgt A told his driver to pursue him and force him off the road. The officer was then shot dead by the Provisional IRA. Sergeant A said that he called out “Police. Halt.” or “Halt. Police” The driver of the Orion turned around towards him. He could not see the man’s hands which were below his waist. He feared the man was armed as he had spun round so quickly. He fired a short burst from his MP5 at the trunk of the man. The driver fell flat, toppling over. It was realised at that stage that he was seriously injured. Sergeant A quickly searched the car, while other security force personnel administered first aid to the driver. The military took over the first aid. Sergeant A said he had a clear view of the deceased from the waist up. When the deceased turned to face him, he did not make any movements towards him. In that short space of time, he formed the opinion that the deceased was a threat to his life. The man’s actions had not been of someone about to surrender. He was certain that there were no viable alternatives to discharging his own weapon. Inspector M gave evidence in relation to the shooting of the police officer. Interviews were conducted with the other police officers and army personnel involved in the incident.Forensic examinations of the cars involved in. the incident were carried out. During the investigation, appeals were made by the police in newspapers and broadcast media for potential eyewitnesses. A number of civilians made statements to the police and subsequently gave evidence at the inquest. In May 1993, the RUC concluded its inquiry. Its report on the investigation was submitted to the Director of Public Prosecutions (the DPP) on 25 May 1993. The DPP’s department issued a direction of ‘no prosecution’ in respect of the fatal shooting of Pearse Jordan. It had been concluded that the evidence was insufficient to warrant the prosecution of any person. Following that decision, the Coroner decided to hold an inquest. The Coroner held a preliminary hearing on 20 December 1994. Defence issued a certificate in which he identified information whose disclosure at the inquest he believed would be contrary to the public interest on grounds of national security. He made an application that the identities of certain military witnesses be withheld and that they should give their evidence from behind a screen. The Coroner sat for three and a half days, hearing evidence from 19 witnesses, including the applicant, 8 civilians, Soldiers V, W and X, 7 police officers and a pathologist. The proceedings were adjourned on 16 January 1995, at the request of Pearse Jordan’s family, to enable the DPP, in the light of new evidence, to reconsider the decision whether or not to bring a prosecution. The applicant’s legal representatives made an application for the Coroner to discharge himself from the Inquest on the grounds that he was not conducting the inquest fairly. The Coroner refused the application. The applicant sought orders of certiorari to quash inter alia. the refusal to give the next of kin access to the statements of the witnesses before they gave evidence at the inquest. Legal aid was granted to the applicant for this purpose. The judicial review application was heard on 9 and 10 November 1995. By judgment of 11 December 1995, Lord Justice Carswell refused the applicant's claims. In doing so he had regard to the inquisitorial nature of inquest proceedings. The applicant appealed against the decision of Lord Justice Carswell. Appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland on 28 June 1996. House of Lords also refused leave to appeal to the House of Commons. Inquest was due to recommence on 1 December 1997. It was adjourned on 19 November 1997 by the Coroner, after consultation with the parties, pending the outcome of a judicial review application in the High Court. Final judgment was given in the case of Sharon Lavery v. the Secretary of State and the Legal Aid Department, in which a challenge concerning the unavailability of legal aid for inquests was dismissed. Coroner said he intended to resume inquest on 1 November 1999. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. On 7 December 1992, the applicant instituted civil proceedings, alleging death by wrongful act. The applicant served a statement of claim in the civil proceedings on 5 October 1995. On 24 October 1995 the Ministry of Defence served their defence. On 8 October 1999, the Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial. The case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. On a date unspecified between 4 April and 2 October 2000 the applicant was provided with the witness statements of persons whom the Coroner has decided should be called to give evidence at the inquest.

They saw nothing in Pearse Jordan’s hands or anything threatening in his actions. An officer about 12 feet away fired a number of shots. Some of the shots struck PearseJordan. He staggered a little further then turned to face the police who, when they caught up with him, verbally abused him and pushed his face into the ground where he was kicked and searched. The police carried out a search of the car. The four witnesses followed the ambulance which took Pearse Jordanian to hospital where they stated that they were subjected to hostile and threatening remarks by members of the security forces. Sergeant A had been at a briefing at 11 a.m. the day before concerning reports of a planned distribution of kit and munitions, including weapons, explosives and mortars. A surveillance operation was to be mounted and he was in charge of the teams on the ground which were going to intervene if possible to intercept the munitions. At about 3.20-3.30 p.m., following reports ofa car acting suspiciously at White Rock leisure centre, he and his teams left Woodbourne police station to wait at Andersontown police station. The red car from the leisure centre arrived in Arizona street. Sergeant A thought that this was possibly the re-supply of terrorist equipment taking place. He was told by radio to gather his people together – car crews with call signs 8, 9, 3 and 12. Sergeant A said that he called out ‘Police. Halt’ or ‘Halt. Police’ The driver of the Orion turned around towards him. He could not see the man’s hands which were below his waist. He feared the man was armed as he had spun round so quickly. He fired a short burst from his MP5 at the trunk of the man. The driver fell flat, toppling over. It was realised at that stage that he was seriously injured. Sergeant A quickly searched the car, while other security force personnel administered first aid to the driver. He did not know that car 12 had come into contact with the Orion or the deceased. Sergeant A said he had a clear view of the deceased from the waist up. He said the man’s actions had not been of someone about to surrender. He was certain that there were no viable alternatives to discharging his own weapon. Forensic examinations of the cars involved in the incident were carried out. Interviews were conducted with the other police officers and army personnel involved. Only officer D heard shouting coming from the call sign 8 direction before the shooting. In his statement of 6 December 1992, Sergeant H, from the car call sign 11, stated that on arrival at the scene he had instructed car 12 to be moved to facilitate the movement of a bus which stopped very close to the injured man. The RUC concluded its inquiry into the shooting in May 1993. Its report on the investigation was submitted to the Director of Public Prosecutions (the DPP) On 16 November 1993, the DPP’s department issued to the Chief Constable of the RUC a direction of ‘no prosecution’ in respect of the fatal shooting of Pearse Jordan. Following that decision, the Coroner decided to hold an inquest. The inquest began on 4 January 1995 and was held at the Royal Courts of Justice in London. The jury was returned a verdict of unlawful killing. The verdicts were returned by a jury of seven men and two women. The Coroner decided to protect certain categories of information from disclosure on the grounds of national security. Defence issued a certificate in which he identified information whose disclosure at the inquest he believed would be contrary to the public interest. The Coroner rejected the request by the applicant’s counsel to withdraw the protection of the identities of the RUC witnesses. The proceedings were adjourned on 16 January 1995 to enable the DPP, in the light of new evidence from the taxi driver, to reconsider the decision whether or not to bring a prosecution. The DPP decided that the evidence remained insufficient to warrant the prosecution of any person in relation to Pearse Jordan's death. On 10 March 1995, the applicant’s legal representatives made an application for the Coroner to discharge himself from the Inquest on the grounds that he was not conducting the inquest fairly. The Coroner refused the application. The applicant sought orders of certiorari to quash inter alia (a) the. Coroner's refusal to give the next of kin access to the statements of the witnesses before. they gave evidence at the inquest and (b) the decision. of the Cor coroner to grant anonymity to RUC witnesses. The judicial review application was heard on 9 and 10 November 1995. By judgment of 11 December 1995, Lord Justice Carswell refused the applicant's claims. He had regard to the inquisitorial nature of inquest proceedings. Inquest was due to recommence on 1 December 1997. It was adjourned on 19 November 1997 by the Coroner. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland on 28 June 1996. Final judgment was given in the case of Sharon Lavery v. the Secretary of State and the Legal Aid Department, in which a challenge concerning the unavailability of legal aid for inquests was dismissed. The Coroner informed the interested parties that he intended to resume the inquest on 1 November 1999. On 2 February 2000, the applicant was informed that the Chief Constable would provide copies of the statements of the witnesses who were to appear at the inquest. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. On 5 October 1995, the applicant served a statement of claim in the civil proceedings. The applicant did not reply to this request until a date unspecified subsequent to 27 August 1998. On 8 October 1999, the Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial. The case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. The Coroner has decided that 12 police officers and Soldier Y involved in the anti-terrorist operation in which Pearse Jordan died should give evidence at the inquest.

The application was heard on 9 and 10 November 1995. By judgment of 11 December 1995, Lord Justice Carswell refused the applicant's claims. He had regard to the inquisitorial nature of inquest proceedings. He referred to the remarks of Griffiths J in Ex parte Peach: “A coroner's inquest is a very limited objective indeed.” The applicant appealed against the decision of Lord Justice Carswell. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland. The applicant’s application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused. The inquest was due to recommence on 1 December 1997. It was adjourned on 19 November 1997 by the Coroner, after consultation with the parties, pending the outcome of a judicial review application in the High Court concerning the availability of legal aid for legal representation for the family of the deceased at inquests. The Coroner informed the interested parties that he intended to resume the inquest on 1 November 1999. On 2 February 2000, the Chief Constable would provide copies of the statements of the witnesses who were to appear at the inquest. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. On 5 October 1995, the applicant served a statement of claim in the civil proceedings. The applicant did not reply to this request until a date unspecified subsequent to 27 August 1998. On 8 October 1999, the Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial. The case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. The Coroner has decided that the witness statements of persons whom the coroner has decided should be called to give evidence at the inquest.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 12305/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1974 and lives in İzmir. On 19 March 2007 he resigned from his job to perform his military service. On 12 April 2007 the applicant was paid 16,985 Turkish liras (TRY ‑ approximately 9,200 euros (EUR) in respect of severance pay and he signed a release discharging the City Council from all liability. The Labour Court held that the applicant’s discharge from the military shortly after he had been enlisted fell under the provision of the collective agreement, which called for the suspension of the employment contract. The first-instance court had ruled in favour of the applicant. The City Council appealed against the decision and reserved its right to submit additional observations once the reasoned judgment had been served on it. The Court of Cassation quashed the first‑instance court’s judgment. No appeal was possible against this decision. The applicant could not technically ask to be reinstated. The decision was served on the applicant on 22 September 2008. The appeal was not communicated to the applicant at the time. The case was decided on points of law in July 2008, and the case was not heard at a hearing. The judge found that the applicant had resigned from his job and that he had been paid severance pay.

In his statements before the public prosecutor and the judge, taken in the absence of a lawyer, the applicant denied that he had been involved in the activities of anillegal organisation. The judge in the case ruled on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to 12 years and 6 months' imprisonment. The court awaited enactment of a new provision to replace the annulled Section 1 § 4 of Law no. 4616. The new Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) entered into force on 1 June 2005. The Istanbul Assize Court reviewed the applicant's conviction in the light of the provisions of the new Criminal code and decided to reduce his sentence of imprisonment to six years and three months. The case against the applicant and his co-accused was transferred to the Istanbul Assizes Court. The applicant was released on 21 October 2004 and the judgment became final on 14 August 2005.

name: Georgiev Cvetan Rangelov
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Bulgarian national, Mr Georgiev Cvetan Rangelov (“the applicant”), alleged that the execution of the preventive detention order against him violated Articles 5 § 1 and 14. The Government of Bulgaria, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, did not indicate that they wished to exercise that right. The applicant entered Germany in 1979. He has been convicted some fifteen times since 1980. He is currently detained in Grad Vraca (Bulgaria). The applicant’s previous convictions, the order for his preventive detention and for his expulsion from Germany. Munich I Regional Court convicted the applicant of eight counts of burglary and attempted burglary, committed only a few months after his release from prison. It found that by breaking into different shops, the applicant had stolen goods worth some 140,000 Deutschmarks (approximately 71,581 euros) The city of Munich ordered the applicant’s expulsion to Bulgaria and prohibited him to re-enter Germany for an indefinite duration in view of his criminal convictions. The applicant served his full prison sentence until 19 June 2003. Since then, he was remanded in preventive detention. The application was dismissed on 25 November 1997 and the applicant was released in January 2002. On 1 December 2003 the Nuremberg Court of Appeal, allowing the applicant’s appeal, quashed the decision of 21 August 2003 and remitted the case to the Regional Court. The Regional Court found that it was very likely that the applicant would reoffend if released. He had been convicted of burglary on numerous occasions and had reoffended shortly after having served long prison sentences. The refusal of the Straubing Prison authorities to allow the applicant's defence counsel to inspect his personal files had violated the right to a fair trial. The applicant was subsequently granted access to his own personal files. On 26 February 2004 the Regensburg Regional Court, having heard the applicant on 15 January 2004 and the applicant and the two experts W. and T. on 19 February 2004, again decided that the execution of the applicants preventive detention was necessary. The court considered that it was illegal to retain a convicted person in preventive detention for an indefinite period of time only as a consequence of his foreign nationality. The Public Prosecutor’s Office would have to consider this issue when deciding on a fresh motion lodged by the applicant to suspend his preventive detention pursuant to Article 456a of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 45 below) The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint and to grant him legal aid (no. 2 BvR 1079/04). It found that his complaint had no prospects of success. There was nothing to indicate that the criminal courts, in reaching their decision under Article 67c § 1 of the Criminal Code, had failed duly to consider human dignity and the right to freedom. The Federal Constitutional Court confirmed that measures relaxing the conditions of detention were a decisive factor for the prognosis of a convicted person’s dangerousness. The applicant neither claimed to have applied for such measures in the course of his preventive detention nor to have been unlawfully refused such measures. The decisions of the criminal courts were also not based on the fact that until then, no such measures had been granted. The criminal courts had rightly pointed out that there were no suitable measures to prepare him adequately for his release. Subsequent developments in the case have led to a review of the applicant's preventive detention order. The Regensburg Regional Court refused to suspend the execution of the applicants preventive detention Order on probation. The Regional Court considered that the applicant’s continued preventive detention was still proportionate. It conceded that it was problematic that no measures at all were planned by the prison authorities to further the applicant's reintegration into society. The court would have to decide at the next periodic review whether the applicant was to be released for reasons of proportionality, despite the fact that he had not previously been granted relaxations in the conditions of his detention and had not been considered as no longer posing a threat to the public. There was still a risk that the. applicant would commit further serious offences against the property of others (but no violent offences) if released. Munich Court of Appeal ruled that the prosecution’s balancing between the public interest in the continuation of the applicant's preventive detention and his interest in his personal liberty had – at least at that time – not been unconstitutional. On 30 November 2009 the Korneuburg Regional Court (Austria) convicted the applicant of two counts of murder, one count of attempted murder and robbery with firearms, committed on 1 June 2009 in Austria and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The judgment was upheld on appeal. The applicant was subsequently transferred to Bulgaria in order to serve his sentence. He was expelled to Bulgaria on 13 December 2007 in accordance with the deportation order issued by the city of Munich.

The case originated in an application (no. 5123/07) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the execution of the preventive detention order against him had violated Articles 5 § 1 and 14. The Government of Bulgaria, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, did not indicate that they wished to exercise that right. The application was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant is currently detained in Grad Vraca (Bulgaria) The applicant was convicted of eight counts of burglary and attempted burglary. He was sentenced to eight years and six months’ imprisonment. The applicant served his full prison sentence until 19 June 2003. Since then, he has been remanded in preventive detention. The court found that the applicant had a propensity to commit offences by which serious economic damage was caused and was therefore dangerous to the public. The city of Munich ordered the applicant’s expulsion to Bulgaria and prohibited him to re-enter Germany for an indefinite duration. The expulsion order became final on 30 December 1997, the regional government of Upper Bavaria having dismissed the applicant's appeal on 25 November 1997. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of 21 August 2003 and remitted the case to the Regional Court. The Regional Court found that it was very likely that the applicant would reoffend if released. He had been convicted of burglary on numerous occasions and had reoffended shortly after having served long prison sentences. The refusal of the Straubing Prison authorities to allow the applicant’s defence counsel to inspect his personal files had violated the right to a fair trial. The applicant was subsequently granted access to the applicant's personal files at Straubed Prison. He was sentenced to three years in prison but was released after one year. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Regional Court’s decision of 26 February 2004. The court considered that it was illegal to retain a convicted person in preventive detention for an indefinite period of time only as a consequence of his foreign nationality. The applicant, represented by counsel, lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. He notably argued that his right to freedom as guaranteed by Article 2 § 2 of the Basic Law was violated because his preventive detention was disproportionate. He claimed that the refusal to admit him to a social therapy due to his imminent expulsion discriminated him because of his Bulgarian nationality. It found that his complaint had no prospects of success. There was nothing to indicate that the criminal courts, notably in finding that the applicant was still dangerous, had failed duly to consider human dignity. The Federal Constitutional Court confirmed that measures relaxing the conditions of detention were a decisive factor for the prognosis of a convicted person’s dangerousness. The applicant neither claimed to have applied for such measures in the course of his preventive detention nor to have been unlawfully refused such measures. The decisions of the criminal courts were also not based on the fact that until then, no such measures had been granted. The criminal courts had rightly pointed out that due to the applicant's persistent refusal to accept responsibility for his offences there were no suitable measures to prepare him adequately for his release. Subsequent developments in the case of the applicant have led to a judicial review of his detention. The Regional Court considered that the applicant’s continued preventive detention was still proportionate. It conceded that it was problematic that no measures at all were planned by the prison authorities to further the applicant's reintegration into society. The applicant could not expect any relaxations in the conditions of his detention. He could not critically reflect on his criminal behaviour. There was still a risk that he would commit further serious offences against the property of others (but no violent offences) if released. The court would have to decide at the next periodic review of his preventive detention whether the applicant was to be released for reasons of proportionality, despite the fact that he had not previously been granted relaxations. Munich Court of Appeal ruled that the prosecution’s balancing between the public interest in the continuation of the applicant's preventive detention and his interest in his personal liberty had – at least at that time – not been unconstitutional. The applicant was convicted of two counts of murder, one count of attempted murder and robbery with firearms, committed on 1 June 2009 in Austria, and sentenced to life imprisonment. On 13 December 2007 the applicant was expelled to Bulgaria in accordance with the deportation order issued by the city of Munich on 16 April 1997. He was subsequently transferred to Bulgaria to serve his sentence. The judgment was upheld on appeal and the applicant is serving his sentence in Bulgaria.

The decision was appealed by the applicant. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of 21 August 2003 and remitted the case to the Regional Court. On 26 February 2004 the Regensburg Regional Court again decided that the execution of the applicant’s preventive detention was necessary in view of its objective. It found that it was very likely that the applicant would reoffend if released. He had been convicted of burglary on numerous occasions and had reoffended shortly after having served long prison sentences. As the applicant was not a German national it was unlikely that the prison authorities, having regard to the usual measures, would have relaxed the conditions of his detention (Vollzugslockerungen) Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Regional Court’s decision of 26 February 2004. The court considered that it was illegal to retain a convicted person in preventive detention for an indefinite period of time only as a consequence of his foreign nationality. The Public Prosecutor's Office would have to consider this issue when deciding on a fresh motion lodged by the applicant to suspend his preventive detention pursuant to Article 456a of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 45 below) The applicant, represented by counsel, lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court on 27 May 2004. He notably argued that his right to freedom as guaranteed by Article 2 § 2 of the Basic Law was violated. The Federal Constitutional Court confirmed that measures relaxing the conditions of detention were a decisive factor for the prognosis of a convicted person’s dangerousness. The applicant neither claimed to have applied for such measures in the course of his preventive detention nor to have been unlawfully refused such measures. The decisions of the criminal courts were also not based on the fact that until then, no such measures had been granted. The criminal courts had rightly pointed out that due to the applicant's persistent refusal to accept responsibility for his offences there were no suitable measures to prepare him adequately for his release. The judge found that psychiatric expert A.C. had consulted a psychiatric expert it had consulted. There was still a risk that the applicant would commit further serious offences against the property of others (but no violent offences) if released. The court would have to decide at the next periodic review of the applicant’s preventive detention whether the applicant was to be released for reasons of proportionality. The applicant had not previously been granted relaxations in the conditions of his detention and had not been considered as no longer posing a threat to the public. In these circumstances, a therapeutic treatment was without prospects of success. There was no starting point for beginning with measures preparing the applicant's conditional release. As he contested having committed the property offences he had been found guilt of, he could not critically reflect on his criminal behaviour. Munich Court of Appeal found that the prosecution’s balancing between the public interest in the continuation of the applicant's preventive detention and his interest in his personal liberty had – at least at that time – not been unconstitutional. The applicant was convicted of two counts of murder, one count of attempted murder and robbery with firearms, committed on 1 June 2009 in Austria, and sentenced to life imprisonment. On 13 December 2007 the applicant was expelled to Bulgaria in accordance with the deportation order issued by the city of Munich on 16 April 1997 (2 BvR 1676/05) and served his sentence in Bulgaria. The judgment was upheld on appeal.

Orlikowska-Wrońska, a lawyer practising in Sopot. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The court based its detention order on a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences and on the severity of the likely penalty. The applicant was charged with twelve offences, including aggravated robbery, kidnapping and illegal possession of a weapon. The first hearing planned for 10 April 2000 was adjourned. The next hearings took place on 27 December 2001, 7 January 2002, 14 January 2002 and 21 January 2002. On 28 January 2002 the Gdańsk Regional Court convicted the applicant of nine offences, acquitted him of the remaining three and sentenced him to 15 years’ imprisonment. The applicant and other accused appealed. The hearing of 6 April 2004 was postponed due to the absence of a lawyer representing one of the accused. The hearings of 22 August 2003, 7 October 2003, 18 November 2003 and 19 December 2003 were adjourned since the applicant had so requested. Hearings were held on 6 July 2004, 28 July 2004 and 6 August 2004. The Court of Appeal found that the length of proceedings had been excessive in the applicant’s case and awarded him compensation. In its reasoned grounds the court stated that as a result of the fact that the trial court had exceeded the permissible length of time between the hearings of 26 March 2001 and 6 June 2001, the proceedings had to be conducted anew. On 27 December 2005 the Gdansk Regional Court sentenced the applicant to 15 years’ imprisonment. The applicant expressed his intention to lodge an appeal. The reasoned grounds for this judgment are being drawn up. The decision is expected to be announced later in the year. It is unclear whether the applicant will be able to appeal the decision.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5786/08) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It unanimously declared it admissible, holding, by four votes to three, that there had been no violation of that provision. The applicant was born in 1987 and lives in Ludvika. She discovered that her stepfather had hidden a video-camera in the laundry basket in the bathroom, which was in recording mode and directed towards the spot where she had undressed. Immediately after the incident, the film was burned without anyone seeing it. In 2005, the public prosecutor indicted the applicant’s stepfather for sexual molestation (sexuell) The Court heard addresses by Mr Crafoord, Mr Lewis, Mr Södergren and Mr Rönquist, as well as their replies to questions put by Judges Ziemele, Sicilianos, Pinto de Albuquerque and Zupančič. The applicant, her stepfather, her mother and her cousin gave evidence before the District Court of Falun (Falu Tingsrätt) The applicant’s stepfather explained that he had lived with her mother from 1997 until the autumn of 2003. They had separated on account of the incident in question, among other things. He had wanted to try to film with a hidden camera, but it had been an impulsive act. He was not sure whether the camera had been in recording mode or whether a film had been recorded. The applicant's mother had burned the film. On 20 January 2006 the applicant submitted a claim for damages of 25,000 Swedish kronor (SEK) The applicant’s stepfather was given a suspended sentence combined with seventy-five hours’ compulsory community service. He was also ordered to pay the applicant damages in the amount of SEK 20,000. The Court of Appeal acquitted him on the counts of sexual molestation allegedly committed against the applicant. It was apparent, the court continued, that his motive had been to film the applicant covertly for a sexual purpose. In assessing whether the act legally constituted sexual molesting within the meaning of Chapter 6, Article 7 § 3, of the Penal Code, the Court of appeal referred to a case in which the stepfather filmed his cousin while she was naked. A man was acquitted of sexual molestation because he had not intended his girlfriend to find out about the filming. The isolated act of filming was not a crime in itself, as in Swedish law there was no general prohibition against filming an individual without his or her consent. The Court of Appeal went on to point out that the act might, at least theoretically, have constituted the crime of attempted child pornography (försök till barnpornografibrott) considering the applicant’s age. The Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused leave to appeal and the applicant's claim for damages was dismissed.

name: Eser Ceylan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 14166/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant claims to have been insulted and beaten, in particular, hit with truncheons on the legs, and that one of the policemen sexually harassed her. The same police officer punched the applicant in her right eye after she had been placed in the police vehicle. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. Eser Ceylan was charged with taking part in an unauthorised demonstration. A forensic expert found no traces of battery on the applicant's body. The public prosecutor decided not to prosecute the police officers who had been on duty at the relevant time. The applicant filed an objection with the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance on 18 June 2001. The court ordered the applicant to be released on bail. She has written to the public prosecutor’s office to ask that her case be investigated again and that the charges against her be dropped. She writes that she was beaten and sexually harassed during her arrest. She says that she has been unable to work for seven days because of her injuries. The Ministry of the Interior lodged an action for compensation against the applicant and the other co-accused and requested the reimbursement of the amount of compensation paid to the injured police officers. The court's reasoned decision refers to evidence such as eye-witness reports, video recordings of the Security Directorate and other national television channels. According to the information available in the file, the compensation proceedings were apparently still pending on the date on which the present judgment was adopted. On 22 January 2004 the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance acquitted the applicant on account of lack of evidence. The case was referred to the closest assize court, against the decision of 30 January 2001.

Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) by a Turkish national, Ms Eser Ceylan (‘the applicant’), on 19 October 2001. The applicant claims that she had been on her way to her sister's law office when she saw armoured police vehicles firing high pressure water jets and a group of people throwing stones at others in the vicinity. She had had to enter the ÖDP (Liberty and Solidarity Party) building in order to protect herself from the police and the demonstrators. She claims to have been insulted and beaten, in particular, hit with truncheons on the legs, and that one of the policemen sexually harassed her. Eser Ceylan was charged with taking part in an unauthorised demonstration. She claimed she had been beaten and sexually harassed during her arrest. The judge of the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance sent a letter to the Ankara public prosecutor's office. The public prosecutor decided not to prosecute the police officers who had been on duty at the relevant time. He maintained that the complainants had taken part in a demonstration against F-type prisons. Although before intervening and making arrests the police had given the demonstrators a warning and had ordered them to disperse, the demonstrators had resisted the police and thrown stones at them. name: Marie-Patrice Guillot
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 29 May 1995. It originated in an application (no. 22500/93) against the French Republic lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by two French nationals. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8 of the Convention. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings. The President gave the applicants leave, as lawyers, to present their own case. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr L.-E. Pettiti, the elected judge of French nationality. The case was brought by the parents of a child born on 7 April 1983. The couple gave their daughter the forenames “Fleur de Marie, Armine, Angèle’. The Court heard addresses by Mr Martínez, Mr Guillot and Mrs Dubrocard. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 April 1996. The case was dismissed by the Nanterre tribunal de grande instance on 7 February 1984. The appeal was heard by the Strasbourg Court of Human Rights on 6 July 1996. It was decided not to grant the parents the right to have their daughter heard in court. 'Fleur de Marie' is composed of two forenames recognised by French law, which when linked by the preposition 'de' form the name of the heroine of Eugène Sue's Mystères de Paris. Although a forename may be composed of up to two names already in use, it cannot, as in the present case, consist of a combination of two names linked by a preposition since it would cease to be a mere reuse of a traditional boy's or girl's name. The main claim in the application must be dismissed but there is no reason not to grant the claim made in the alternative relating to the forename 'Fleur-Marie' The Court of Cassation (First Civil Division) dismissed the appeal on 1 October 1986. The Court of Appeal held that the chosen forename, because it was eccentric and excessively whimsical, was likely to harm the interests of the child. The case was decided on the grounds that the provisions of section 1 of the Law of 11 Germinal Year XI are not contrary to Articles 8, 9 and 14 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The court upheld the previous decision in the case of 'Fleur de Marie' against the Government of France. The appeal was dismissed on the following grounds: “(...) the provisions ... are not contradictory to ... Articles [8, 9] and 14”.

But the court held that it would cease to be a mere reuse of a traditional boy's or girl's name and become an image invented at the whim of individuals, for all that they might possess an imagination as Eugène Sue. The applicants appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation. Case-law is tending towards a more liberal approach in order to take account of changes in social mores, local customs and family traditions. It is necessary to prevent parents from choosing forenames which are excessively whimsical and so eccentric that the child is likely to be the first victim. This is the case with the forename 'Fleur de Marie', notwithstanding that it was the name of the heroine of a famous literary work. On the other hand, there is no reason not to allow the claim made in the alternative that the fore Name should consist of the two forenames 'Fleer' and 'Marie' juxtaposed.

There was, however, no indication that the teachers had used unlawful and unobjective means, such as, for example, the use of their authority to assign marks. It was, on the contrary, because of the teachers' unbending attitude that pupils and parents had finally resigned and agreed to the compromise. The Wels Regional Court dismissed the appeal. It noted that the statement at issue constituted a statement of fact susceptible of proof. The injunction at issue did, therefore, not violate the applicant's right to freedom of expression.

name: Henryk Kreuz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46245/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his case had not been heard within a reasonable time in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 14 January 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was heard by a Chamber that would consider the case under former Article 25 of. the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’s” Article 27). The Chamber was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court. Unirol Ltd. was sued in Płock Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) in 1994. The applicant applied for an exemption from court fees. The trial court dismissed the applicant’s challenge of the presiding judge on 4 November 1996. On 5 March 1997 the court decided that it would not deliver the final decision and resumed the proceedings. On 9 June 1999 the court held a hearing and ordered the parties to specify their claims. On 15 October 1999 the hearing listed for 10 July 1998 was cancelled. On 27 August 1998 the Regional Court ordered that the lost case-file be reconstituted. Unirol Ltd. asked the court to appoint an expert. An expert submitted the relevant opinion to the court. The Płock Regional Court delivered a judgment on 22 November 2000. Both parties appealed. On 27 June 2003 the Supreme Court dismissed both cassation appeals. The case was settled out of court in 2002, but the parties have appealed the decision to the Warsaw Court of Appeal. The parties are still appealing the decision of the Polish Supreme Court to the Polish High Court of Justice. The appeal was dismissed on 29 June 2003. The court ruled that the ruling was not justified by the facts of the case, and that the parties had no right to appeal the decision.

name: Sandro Nerva
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42295/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, in particular, that their rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and under Article 14 of the Convention had been breached given that the domestic courts of the respondent State had ruled that money which was left to them as tips by customers passed to their employer to be used as it wished. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it admissible on 11 September 2001. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). In 1979, following an inspection from the tax authorities, the applicants’ employer was required to treat tips left by cheque or credit card within the ‘Pay-As-You-Earn’ (‘PAYE’) system. The applicants submitted that the staff agreement to the new system was not intended to alter the fact that the gratuities were to be paid in full to employees. The employer bore the charges of the credit card companies, varying at the time from 3% to 5% on the amount of the gratU. It would appear that the method of distribution was the same as the method hitherto applied to tronc money. Employer did not seek to recover any sums distributed to waiters in respect of any gratuity included on the voucher. It does not appear either that the employer sought to recover from the waiters any sums which it did not receive as a result of dishonoured cheques. The applicants highlighted their view that this was not a new practice, but that it applied before 1979. In his judgment, the employer obtained the legal title to a tip paid by credit card or cheque, with the result that it became the employer’s property. By the time of the hearing before the Court of Appeal, the applicants had accepted that property in the cheque and credit card tips passed to their employer. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. Lord Justice Staughton observed that the relevant legislation embodied the rule that what was paid by the employer and not by any other person counted as remuneration for the purpose of that legislation. In his opinion, it was decisive that the employer was paying the tips with its own money even if they had beenpaid by the customers to the employer in the belief that the latter would pass the tips on to the waiters and on the understanding that it would do so. As to the issue of the customers’ intention when adding the tip to the cheque or credit card payment, Mr Justice Douglas Brown stated that the intention of different customers could only be the subject of speculation. Lord Justice Aldous said there was no difference in principle between tips paid in cash and tips paid by cheque or credit card. In the latter cases the employer acted as agent for the customer and, when doing so, had to carry out its duties under the relevant tax legislation to ensure that tax was levied on the tips. However, the fact that tax on cheque and credit card tips was deducted under the PAYE system, instead of being paid by the waiters, did not affect the relationship between the customer. and the employee. The applicants’ counsel was given the opportunity to speak to the petition for leave and to address the employer’s written objections.

The case originated in an application (no. 42295/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that their rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and under Article 14 of the Convention had been breached given that the domestic courts of the respondent State had ruled that money which was left to them as tips by customers passed to their employer to be used as it wished. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it admissible on 11 September 2001. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicants were employed as waiters at the material time. When the applicants received a tip in cash directly from a customer, the money was placed in a box called a ‘tronc’ In 1979, following an inspection from the tax authorities, the applicants’ employer was required to treat tips left by cheque or credit card within the ‘Pay-As-You-Earn’ system. Under the PAYE system an employer had to ensure that employees’ income tax and national insurance contributions were deducted from the sums paid. The applicants submitted that the staff agreement to the new system was not intended to alter the fact that the gratuities were to be paid in full to employees. Waiters sued their employer for breach of contract. They challenged the employer’s right to count the tips included in cheque or credit card payments as part of their statutory minimum remuneration. In 1994 a High Court judge, Mr Justice Mance, held on a preliminary point that tips included on cheque and credit card transactions did count against the minimum. By the time of the hearing before the Court of Appeal, the applicants had accepted that property in the tips passed to their employer and no longer relied on the argument that they were to be held in trust for them by the employer. In his judgment, the employer obtained the legal title to a tip paid by credit card or cheque, with the result that it became the employer's property. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. Lord Justice Staughton observed that the relevant legislation embodied the rule that what was paid by the employer and not by any other person counted as remuneration for the purpose of that legislation. He considered that the same reasoning could not apply to tips which were built into payments made by cheque or credit card to their employer since the amounts became the latter’s property. The employer thereafter paid an equivalent amount to the applicants. In his view, tips paid in this manner should count against the minimum remunerations requirement. As to the issue of the customers’ intention, Mr Justice Douglas Brown stated that the intention of the different customers could only be the subject of speculation. In either case, the customer had no intention of giving anything to the employer. Lord Justice Aldous observed that there was no difference in principle between tips paid in cash and tips paid by cheque or credit card. In his opinion, the only difference was that in the latter cases the employer acted as agent for the customer. However, the fact that tax on cheque and credit card tips was deducted under the PAYE system, instead of being paid by the waiters, did not affect the relationship between the customer and the employee. The applicants’ counsel was given the opportunity to speak to the petition for leave and to address the employer’s written objections.

name: J. Peter
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68919/10) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Lenz, a lawyer practising in Stuttgart. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mr H.-J. Behrens, Ministerialrat, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. On 3 June 2013 the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court and the lack of an effective remedy was communicated to the Government. On the same day the President of the Section sitting in a single-judge formation declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The applicant's civil partnership had not lasted longer than a year, which would have led to statutory exclusion from the benefit even for married couples. The remaining leapfrog appeal on points of law (Sprungrevision) was dismissed on 13 December 2005 by the Federal Social Court. On 20 January 2006 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (no. 1 BvR 170/06) with the Federal Constitutional Court. The complaint did not raise a pressing constitutional question as the relevant provision of the social security legislation had meanwhile been amended. The Government informed the Court that in response to the pilot judgment in Rumpf v. Germany an Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations ( no. 46344/06, 2 September 2010) was to be introduced. The applicant complained that constitutional court proceedings that lasted four years, six months and one day were excessively long. The judge rapporteur conceded that the applicant’s submissions were sufficiently substantiated for his constitutional complaint to indeed have been dealt with earlier on the basis of the actual reasoning given. Subsequently, it became clear that the 2007 case did not pose a problem of retroactivity and therefore did not affect the outcome of the applicant's constitutional complaint. The applicant's complaint concerned the retroactive application of a legislative amendment. It would have been obvious even from a cursory examination of the constitutional complaints that his complaint was not given any attention whatsoever after it was lodged. On 1 October 2012 the complaints panel of the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. Citing Gast and Popp v. Germany (no. 29357/95, ECHR 2000‑II), the court noted that a chronic backlog of cases in the constitutional courts could not justify the excessive length of proceedings. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution and served further purposes beyond the administration of individual justice. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. decisions and judgments of the Constitutional Court had binding inter omnes legal effect and for this reason had to be drafted with the utmost diligence. The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. – on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. The Act introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 97b (1) A decision on compensation and reparation shall be rendered, and the compensation amount must amount to €1,200 for every year of delay. Complaint of undue delay must be lodged by 3 June 2012 at the earliest. Complaint must set out circumstances purported to establish the unreasonableness of the length of the proceedings. In the event of a tie the complaint of undue delays shall be dismissed. The complaints panel shall render its decision without an oral hearing. The decision is not subject to appeal. The complaint is not required to be made before the end of the trial. The complainant does not need to make a claim for compensation before the complaint is heard. The panel will decide by a majority. It is not necessary to raise the complaint before filing a complaint claiming compensation. If the complaint was made before filing the compensation claim, the complaint would not be heard.

The case originated in an application (no. 68919/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr J. Peter, entered into a civil partnership with Mr Peter, né V., on 5 October 2001. In September 2002 the applicant applied for a survivor’s pension to the German Pension Fund (Bundesversicherungsanstalt für Angestellte), a public-law corporation. He argued that the term “widow or widower” in Article 46. 1 and 2 of the Social Security Code, Book VI (Sozialgesetzbuch Nr. VI) should be construed as encompassing the surviving partner in a civil. partnership. On 3 June 2013 the President of the Section sitting in a single-judge formation declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. An applicant's civil partnership had not lasted longer than a year, which would have led to statutory exclusion from the benefit even for married couples. The remaining leapfrog appeal on points of law (Sprungrevision) was dismissed on 13 December 2005 by the Federal Social Court. A three-judge panel of the Federal Constitutional Court decided not to review the applicant’s constitutional complaint. The Government informed the Court that in response to the pilot judgment in Rumpf v. Germany (no. 46344/06, 2 September 2010) an Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was passed in December 2011. The applicant filed a complaint under the new Act, claiming compensation in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. He complained that constitutional court proceedings that lasted four years, six months and one day were excessively long. The judge rapporteur conceded that the applicant’s submissions were sufficiently substantiated for his constitutional complaint to indeed have been dealt with earlier on the basis of the actual reasoning given. However, the judge maintained that it had been in the applicant's best interest to wait for the court's ruling in the 2007 case. Subsequently, it became clear that the2007 case did not pose a problem of retroactivity and therefore did not affect the outcome of the constitutional complaint. On 1 October 2012 the complaints panel of the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. Citing Gast and Popp v. Germany (no. 29357/95, ECHR 2000‑II), the court noted that a chronic backlog of cases in the constitutional courts could not justify the excessive length of proceedings. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. decisions and judgments had binding inter omnes legal effect and for this reason had to be drafted with the utmost diligence, the court said. The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. – on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. It introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 2 amended the Federal Constitutional Court Act as follows: “Any person who, as the result of the unreasonable length of proceedings, experiences a disadvantage as a participant in those proceedings, shall be afforded reasonable compensation” Complaint of undue delay must be lodged in writing. Complaint must set out circumstances purported to establish the unreasonableness of the length of the proceedings. Complaints must be made by 3 June 2012 at the earliest. The complaints panel shall decide by a majority. In the event of a tie the complaint of unduedelay shall be dismissed. The decision is not subject to appeal. The complaint is not required to be made within 12 months after the case has been lodged with the Federal Constitutional Court (Verzögerungsrüge) The complaint must not require a reasoned notification. It is not necessary to make the complaint before the court before filing a complaint claiming compensation.

In its reasoning the panel explained that the complaint did not raise a pressing constitutional question as the relevant provision of the social security legislation had meanwhile been amended. The applicant complained that constitutional court proceedings that lasted four years, six months and one day were excessively long. The applicant informed the Court that he intended to file a complaint under the new domestic provisions. Subsequently, it became clear that the 2007 case did not pose a problem of retroactivity and therefore did not affect the outcome of the applicant’s constitutional complaint. The judge rapporteur conceded that the applicant's submissions were sufficiently substantiated for his constitutional complaint to indeed have been dealt with earlier on the basis of the actual reasoning given. However, the judge maintained that it had been in the applicant ‘best interest’ to wait for the court's ruling in the 2007 cases. The Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint under section 97a of the Federal Constitutional court Act. The court noted that the actual duration of the proceedings – four and a half years – was unusually long, but not excessive. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution and it served further purposes beyond the administration of individual justice. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. The decisions and judgments of the Constitutional Court had binding inter omnes legal effect and for this reason had to be drafted with the utmost diligence, according to the court's decision. The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. – on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. The Act introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 97b (1) A decision on compensation and reparation shall be rendered. If the sum thus calculated is not equitable, the Federal Constitutional Court shall assess a higher or lower sum. Such compensation shall amount to €1,200 for every year of delay. Complaint of undue delay must be lodged by 3 June 2012 at the earliest. Complaint must set out circumstances purported to establish the unreasonableness of the length of the proceedings. Complaints panel will decide by a majority, and decision is not subject to appeal. In the event of a tie the complaint of undue Delay shall be dismissed. The complaints panel shall render its decision without an oral hearing. Reasons need not be given in the case of such a complaint. The complaint must be made before the end of the current financial year. It must also be made at least 12 months before the next year's budget is due to be voted on.

name: Ferman Ayçoban
train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were detained in Elazığ Prison in Turkey. They were arrested by police officers from the anti-terror branch of the Diyarbakır Security Directorate on suspicion of being members of Hezbollah. On 14 March 1999 the police raided a flat which was used as a cell by Hezbollah in Mardin. The police officers seized, among other things, three computer hard disks during the operation. The applicant's names were recorded on these hard disks as members of Lebanon's terrorist organisation Hezbollah. The applicants were accused of being members of Hezbollah. They were convicted of the offence as charged and sentenced to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. The applicants appealed the decision of the Diyarbakır State Security Court. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision on 27 May 2002, after the applicants appealed to the Supreme Court of Justice. They claim their police statements were taken under duress and that they had no idea how their names appeared on the hard disks found during the raid in Mardin. The court read out the police statements that were taken from M.Ç., M.P. and A.Y. to the applicants and asked the latter to comment on them.

The applications were dismissed on the grounds of lack of prompt and detailed information on the nature and cause of the accusations. The decision was made on a unanimous vote of the Court of Cassation. The case was dismissed on a majority of votes. The application was dismissed and the appeal was dismissed. The applicants were accused of being members of Hezbollah. They were convicted and sentenced to 12 years and 6 months in prison. The applicants appealed and the decision was upheld by the Court of Cassation in May 2002. The convictions were upheld after a re-trial in November 2003. The court read out the police statements that were taken from M.Ç., M.P. and A.Y. – who were also members of the same organisation – to the applicants and asked the latter to comment.

name: Türkan Yavuz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 67137/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The Court will decide on both the admissibility and merits of the application. The application was filed by a Turkish national, Ms Türkan Yavuz (“the applicant”), on 8 February 2001. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). The applicant was brought before the public prosecutor at the İstanbul State Security Court on 21 May 1997. She acknowledged the contents of her police deposition. She stated that during her custody, four or five police officers had sexually harassed her by touching her breasts and buttocks. She claimed that she was also punched. The report drafted by the doctor concluded that, apart from these findings, there were no other signs of injury attributable to ill-treatment. On the same day, the applicant was released and no criminal proceedings were brought against her. The applicant signed her deposition saying she would be able to recognise the police officers if she were to meet them again. The applicant, her husband, Mr E.Y. and the accused police officers. claimed that she was attacked by police officers who pulled her hair and hit her, particularly between her shoulders. She maintained that they stripped her naked in front of her husband. She claimed that, during her interrogation, one of the police officers threatened her with rape, while all the officers insulted her verbally and also threatened to accuse her of murder if she refused to co-operate. The applicant stated that it was impossible for her to provide witnesses since she was in custody, incommunicado, away from all eyewitnesses. The officers all refuted the accusations against them, claiming that both the applicant and Mr E Y. had resisted arrest and that, as a result, they could have sustained some injuries. The applicant’s husband testified in favour of the applicant. He submitted that they were all subjected to systematic torture whilst in police custody. He claimed that their clothes were ripped, their feet were squeezed, they were hosed with pressurised water and that their heads were pushed into a pool of water. had taken place during her arrest. The court concluded that, apart from the findings in the medical reports, there were no other signs of injury and that those mentioned in these reports could have been sustained during the arrest of the complainants. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Assize Court on 4 October 2000.

train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of two sets of proceedings concerning custody of his children had been excessive. On 9 December 2009 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the cases at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The court ruled in favour of the applicant and he was granted contact with his children every second and fourth weekend of the month from 6 p.m. Friday to 6p.m Saturday. The proceedings concerning custody of the children and the applicant's contact rights began in 1998. The parties agreed to the commissioning of an expert opinion on a possible regulation of custody and contact rights. They further agreed that until the completion of the expert opinion the contact of the applicant with his children should be provisionally regulated by the acting judge in cooperation with the Kleve child protection agency (Kinderschutzbund). On 28 April 1999 the parties agreed that the contact with the applicant would be Provisionally regulated until such time as the expert's opinion had been completed. The application was settled on 9 September 2002, but the applicant later challenged it. The applicant was granted custody of his children by a judgment dated 29 November 2001. In the meantime the applicant had supervised contact in cooperation with the Kleve child protection agency. He revoked his approval of the supervised contacts and applied to the District Court for contact in accordance with the regulations set out in the court's decision of 23 July 1998. The mother requested sole custody of the children for the duration of the separation of the spouses. The expert opinion was finalised on 31 August 2000. The parties agreed that from 15 October 1999 the applicant would be entitled to visit his children every fortnight and have telephone contact with the children every two weeks at a set time. Nevertheless, it appears that regular contact between the father and the children ceased temporarily during the year 2000. The applicant asked to be granted contact rights in accordance with his request as reformulated on 18 October 2000. The curator ad litem emphasised, in particular, that the son's apparent rejection of his father was due to the influence of the mother and the grandparents. The applicant appealed against the attribution of sole custody to the mother. The Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's request for legal aid in the appellate proceedings on the ground that his claim was devoid of any prospect of success. By transferring the right to determine the children's place of residence to the Kleve District Youth Welfare Office, the District Court had set the stage for implementing regular contact between the father and his children. The wife's petition for divorce and custody of the children was granted on 29 November 2001. The applicant appealed on 18 February 2002 and requested to be granted joint custody with the mother. On 10 May 2002 a hearing took place before the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal to which the children had also been summoned. The children attended the hearing but were not heard by the Court of appeal. By a decision of 26 June 2002 the D Düsseeldorf Court of Appeal partially partially overturned the decision of 27 August 2001 regarding the provisional regulation of custody. The court again found that, in view of the lack of cooperation between the parents on matters concerning their children, joint custody was not an option. The applicant and his former wife entered into a court settlement (Prozessvergleich) stipulating that the applicant should have contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 2 p.m. in the mother's presence. The parties further agreed that with effect from 2003 they would plan at least one holiday per year. The applicant was further granted the right to visit the children at their mother's house on the occasion of the Iranian public holidays at a time to be previously agreed with the mother. On 2 April 2004 the Düsseldorf Court of. Court of Appeal ruled that the settlement constituted a binding agreement between the parties. The father applied to extend his contact rights with his children at his home in Heidelberg. Appeal dismissed the appeal and confirmed that the settlement was neither invalid nor void. For the period until finalisation of the expert opinion the applicant was granted unaccompanied contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 10.00 a.m. to 6.00 p.m.;. The children had objected to spending holidays alone with their father;. The court further found that there was no evidence that the children had been manipulated by their grandparents;. It specified that in reaching its conclusion it could not rely on an expert opinion because the father had refused to be examined by the appointed expert. The case was heard at the D. sseldorf Court of Appeal on 2 March 2007, during which the parties, the children and their guardian were heard. The curator ad litem could not attend. On 20 March 2007 the applicant's appeal was dismissed. In February 2008 the applicant filed a request to spend summer holidays with his children at his home in Heidelberg from 23 July to 3 August 2008. By a decision of 6 June 2008 the District Court rejected the request since the children had objected to spending the holidays with him; the request therefore could not be regarded as being in their interest. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the constitutional complaint concerning the separate custody proceedings. The Federal Constitutional Court held that the applicant's parental rights as guaranteed by the Basic Law included an obligation for the courts to conduct custody proceedings in such a way as to obtain a reliable basis for a decision founded on the child's wellbeing. A decision in line with the child’s concerns could only be taken after the child had been given the opportunity to disclose its personal relations with the other family members during the proceedings. The lower courts had not given any convincing reasons why the children had not been heard. The applicant could not claim to have suffered a particularly serious disadvantage since his complaint did not have any prospect of success even if remitted to the lower courts. The applicant lodged a separate application with the Emmerich District Court on behalf of and in the name of his children for the regulation of the children's contact rights with respect to their father. The applications were rejected by the District Court and the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint (File no. 1 BvR 2127/01) in December 2005. The applicant had already lodged a similar application in previous proceedings (5 F 155/99), which had been rejected by a decision of the District court dated 9 November 2000. The proceedings regarding the grandparents' contact rights were also dismissed. Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 3 June 2002. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint that his parental rights had been violated by the decisions of the lower courts. It held that the right to determine the contact of the children with third persons was part of the right of custody which had been awarded solely to the mother. However, a limitation on the contact rights of third persons with the children could not entail any binding regulation of the applicant’s contact with his children and he could thus not claim that his own rights were affected. The Court held that even though the grandparents might have a negative impact on the children's relations with their father, a complete ban on their contact was neither practicable, owing to the proximity of their respective homes, nor in their best interest.
