The proceedings for the regulation of the father's contact rights, instituted under file no. 5 F 272/98 and fileNo. 5F 271/04, were settled in the fall of 2005. A court in Düsseldorf found that a ban on contact with the grandparents was neither practicable nor in the children's best interest. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint that his parental rights had been violated by the decisions of the lower courts. It held that the right to determine the contact of the children with third persons was part of the right of custody which had been awarded solely to the mother. The court found that preventing contact between the children and their grandparents could in no way help to ensure regular contact. The applicant's own contact rights could be affected only indirectly by his children's contact with their grandparents.
eval_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of two sets of proceedings concerning custody of his children had been excessive. The application was made by Mr Iradj Kuhlen-Rafsandjani, who had been granted legal aid. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, Federal Ministry of Justice. The case was decided on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time. The applicant filed an application with the Emmerich District Court to be granted contact with his children. The proceedings were instituted under file no. 5 F 272/98. At approximately the same time custody proceedings were opened before the same court. The parties agreed to the commissioning of an expert opinion on a possible regulation of custody and contact rights. They further agreed that until the completion of the expert opinion the contact of the applicant with the children should be provisionally regulated by the acting judge in cooperation with the Kleve child protection agency (Kinderschutzbund). On 28 April 1999 the judge ruled that the applicant's contact rights should be Provisionally regulated. The father applied to the District Court for contact in accordance with the regulations set out in the court's decision of 23 July 1998. The mother requested sole custody of the children for the duration of the separation of the spouses. The parties agreed that from 15 October 1999 the applicant would be entitled to visit his children every fortnight, accompanied by a representative of the Kleve child protection agency. The expert opinion was finalised on 31 August 2000. Nevertheless, it appears that regular contact between the father and the children ceased temporarily during the year 2000. The judge ruled that the mother should have sole custody and awarded it to her. The father appealed the decision and the case was decided in favour of the mother. The applicant requested contact rights in accordance with his request as reformulated on 18 October 2000. The curator ad litem emphasised, in particular, that the son's apparent rejection of his father was due to the influence of the mother and the grandparents. The applicant appealed against the attribution of sole custody to the mother. The Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's request for legal aid in the appellate proceedings on the ground that his claim was devoid of any prospect of success. In view of the tensions and. lack of cooperation between the parents, the transfer of sole Custody to the. mother was in the children's best interest. The District Court had set the stage for regular contact between the father and his children. The applicant appealed against the decisions of the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal and the Emmerich District Court. By a joint judgment (Verbundurteil) of 29 November 2001 the District Court granted the wife's petition for divorce and transferred sole custody of the children to her. The applicant appealed on 18 February 2002 and requested to be granted joint custody with the mother and to leave the right to determine the children's place of residence with the District Youth Welfare Office. The children attended the hearing but were not heard by the Court of appeal. On 10 May 2002 a hearing took place. to which the children had also been summoned. The parties continued to argue about the applicant's contact rights following the divorce. The parties entered into a court settlement stipulating that the applicant should have contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 2 p.m. in the mother's presence and by prior agreement with her. The applicant was further granted the right to visit the children at their mother's house on the occasion of the Iranian public holidays at a time to be previously agreed with the mother. On 2 April 2004 the Düsseldorf Court of Court of Appeal ruled that the settlement constituted a binding agreement between the parties in this regard. The application for a decision on his contact rights was rejected on 28 August 2003. The applicant filed an application with the Emmerich District Court to extend his contact rights with a view to enabling him to spend holidays with his children at his home in Heidelberg. Appeal dismissed the appeal and confirmed that the settlement was neither invalid nor void and had therefore effectively terminated the proceedings. For the period until finalisation of the expert opinion the applicant was granted unaccompanied contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 10.00 a.m. to 6 p.m., with no restrictions on his contact with them. The court further found that there was no evidence that the children had been manipulated by their grandparents. Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal on 20 March 2007. The children had objected and thus it could not be in their interest to extend contact rights with the father. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against the decision of the Emmerich District Court of 29 March 2006. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the constitutional complaint concerning the separate custody proceedings (5 F 283/98) in which the applicant challenged the provisional attribution of sole custody to the mother. The decision was served on the applicant on 7 December 2005. The court dismissed an appeal against that decision on 19 August 2008, since because of the passage of time a decision was no longer required. The Federal Constitutional Court held that the applicant's parental rights as guaranteed by the Basic Law included an obligation for the courts to conduct custody proceedings in such a way as to obtain a reliable basis for a decision founded on the child's wellbeing. The court said that the lower courts had not given any convincing reasons why the children had not been heard. A decision in line with the child’s concerns could only be taken after the child had been given the opportunity to disclose its personal relations with the other family members during the proceedings. The applicant could not claim to have suffered a particularly serious disadvantage since his complaint did not have any prospect of success even if remitted to lower courts. The applicant's contact rights with respect to his children are under the German Civil Code. The proceedings for the regulation of his contact rights were instituted under file no. 5 F 272/98 and file no., 5 F 271/04. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court against the decisions of the District Court and Court of Appeal. The Federal Constitutional court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint (File no. 1 BvR 2127/01) by a decision of 7 December 2005, served on the applicant on 20 December 2005. The judge ruled that the application was not inadmissible because the power of representation was part of the right to custody which in proceedings no.5 F 283/98 was transferred solely to the mother. Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal since there was nothing to establish that contact with their grandparents was contrary to the children's wellbeing. Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint that his parental rights had been violated by the decisions of the lower courts. It held that the right to determine the contact of the children with third persons was part of the right of custody which had been awarded solely to the mother. However, a limitation on the contact rights of third persons with the children could not entail any binding regulation of the applicant’s contact with his children and he could thus not claim that his own rights were affected.

name: Yash Pal Kansal
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the statements obtained under compulsion in bankruptcy proceedings should not have been admitted in criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The applicant but not the Government filed observations on the merits. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merit of the case was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The Court declared the rest of the application admissible on 23 September 2003. A building society advanced 150,000 pounds sterling (GBP) and GBP 116,250 respectively to the applicant. On 23 March 1988, the applicant's wife collected part of the advance, GBP 104,000, and took it to India in a bin liner. The applicant was subsequently charged with two offences of obtaining property by deception and failing to account for the loss of property while bankrupt. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal deciding that the transcript of the bankruptcy examination was admissible under section 433 of the Insolvency Act 1986 which abrogated the privilege against self-incrimination. In 1995, the Royal Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain decided to remove his licence to practise as a pharmacist on the grounds of unfitness. The Court of Appeal ruled that the answers given to the official receiver were in breach of Article 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998. The case was appealed to the House of Lords, who ruled in favour of the applicant. The court found that the act could not apply retrospectively to cases brought after the Act came into force. The application was dismissed and the case was heard again by the Court of Appeals in May 2001. The appeal was rejected and the appeal was dismissed again on the grounds that the answer given by the receiver had been given under compulsion, which was a breach of the human rights law. The decision was upheld on appeal by the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom.

The applicant alleged that the statements obtained under compulsion in bankruptcy proceedings should not have been admitted in criminal proceedings against him. In 1995, the Royal Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain decided to remove the applicant's licence to practise as a pharmacist on the grounds of unfitness due to his involvement in the deception connected with his bankruptcy proceedings. Leave to appeal was refused by the Court of Appeal and by the House of Lords. On 27 April 1998, the Criminal Cases Review Commission (“CCRC”) referred the applicant to the High Court. The European Court of Human Rights ruled that the answers given by the official receiver were in breach of Article 6 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal overturned the conviction on the grounds that the answer had been wrongly admitted at trial. The House of Lords ruled in favour of the applicant. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court of England and Wales, which is expected to make a decision by the end of the year or early in the next year, depending on the outcome of the appeal. The decision is likely to be appealed on the basis that the decision was made on the ground that the admission of the answers was unlawful. The Supreme Court has the power to reverse the decision if it finds that it was unlawful to admit the answers.

The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal deciding that the transcript of the bankruptcy examination was admissible under section 433 of the Insolvency Act 1986. The Court of Appeal ruled that the answers given by the official receiver were in breach of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The House of Lords ruled in 2001 that the Human Rights Act 1998 could apply retrospectively to the case. The case was dismissed by the Supreme Court in 2004. The appeal was brought again in 2008, this time by the Attorney General for England and Wales. The Supreme Court again ruled in favour of the applicant, and the case was thrown out of court. It was the first time a case had been dismissed by a high court on the grounds of the breach of the Convention.

name: Derek Edwards
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 13 September 1991 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 13071/87) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 29 September 1986. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 June 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mr Pannick for the Government, by Mr Ermacora for the Commission and by Mr Clarke and Mr Campbell for the applicant. Various documents were filed by the applicant in the course of the hearing. The evidence against the applicant consisted of detailed oral admissions that he had allegedly made to the police concerning his involvement in the three offences. He received a sentence of ten years for the robbery, and two sentences of eight years each for the burglary offences. All three sentences were to be served concurrently. The trial and appeal proceedings began on 9 November 1984. The jury’s decision was by a majority verdict of ten to two. The victim of the robbery (Miss Sizer) was awakened from her sleep to find a man standing over her. She remained tied up until she was freed the next morning. The only witnesses called by the defence were the two police officers who had given evidence in the trial. The Director of Public Prosecutions decided that there was insufficient evidence to support criminal charges against the police officers. The case was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 15 June 1988. The decision was taken on the grounds of public interest immunity for the officers involved in the case. The appeal was eventually settled out of court in a settlement of around £1.2 million. The case was referred to the Court of Appeal under section 17 (1)(a) of the Criminal Appeal Act 1968 (“the 1968 Act’) The reference was heard on 18 July 1986 and judgment delivered on the same date. The applicant argued that the police officer had told lies and that his veracity as regards the admission statements was thus called into question. We do not think, had the matter been carried further, it would have been demonstrated that Detective Sergeant Hoyland was a person who to that extent could not be believed on his own. We think quite plainly what he was indicating there and intended to indicate was that no fingerprints relating to either of the two alleged burglars were discovered at the scene: neither the fingerprints of Rose nor the fingerprint of Edwards. Court of Appeal examined other impugned shortcomings which it did not consider to cast any doubt on the verdict. It was of the opinion that, even if these matters had been investigated, it would have made no difference to the outcome. The court concluded as follows: “It is clear that there was some slipshod police work in the present case’. He is currently serving a sentence of two years’ imprisonment following his conviction on 26 March 1992 at Sheffield Crown Court on three counts of burglary. The Court of Appeal also rejected this argument: ‘The fact that Miss Sizer had a fleeting glimpse of her assailant, and that such identification as she did make was largely directed to other matters of identification rather than his features, leads us to believe that the jury would not have been influenced to act other than they did'

The case was referred to the Court on 13 September 1991 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 13071/87) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On 28 September 1991 the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members of the Chamber. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 June 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mr Pannick for the Government, by Mr Ermacora for the Commission and by Mr Clarke and Mr Campbell for the applicant. The evidence against the applicant consisted of detailed oral admissions that he had allegedly made to the police concerning his involvement in the three offences. The jury’s decision was by a majority verdict of ten to two. He received a sentence of ten years for the robbery, and two sentences of eight years each for the burglary offences. All three sentences were to be served concurrently. The victim of the robbery (Miss Sizer) was awakened from her sleep to find a man standing over her. She remained tied up until she was freed the next morning. In a statement to the police she gave a description of the man and stated that she thought she would recognise him again. She was not called as a witness during the trial but her written statement was read to the jury. On 3 December 1985, the man applied for leave to appeal against conviction out of time. The Director of Public Prosecutions decided that there was insufficient evidence to support criminal charges against the police officers. At the disciplinary hearing, on 13 to 15 June 1988, the tribunal decided there was no case to answer and dismissed the charges. The applicant submitted to the Court of Appeal that the verdict should be set aside as unsafe and unsatisfactory because of certain shortcomings in the prosecution case. At the trial one of the police witnesses had stated under cross-examination that no fingerprints were found at the scene of the crime. In fact two fingerprints had been found which later turned out to be those of the next door neighbour who was a regular visitor to the house. The applicant had not been informed of this by the prosecution before his trial. A further shortcoming complained of by the applicant related to the fact that the police had shown two volumes of photographs of possible burglars (including a photograph of the applicant) to the elderly victim of the robbery who said that she had caught a fleeting glimpse of the burglar. Court of Appeal examined other impugned shortcomings which it did not consider to cast any doubt on the verdict. It was of the opinion that, even if these matters had been investigated, it would have made no difference to the outcome. The court concluded as follows: “It is clear that there was some slipshod police work in the present case’. “We do not think in the circumstances there was anything unsafe or unsatisfactory in the end about these convictions. Consequently, treating this matter as we have to according to section 17 of the Act, we think this appeal fails and must be dismissed.”

The Appeal Court heard that the police had withheld information that could have cast doubt on the confession statements given to the jury by the applicant. The application was rejected on the basis that the evidence was not sufficient and that the verdict was unsafe. The Court of Appeal examined other impugned shortcomings which it did not consider to cast any doubt on the verdict. It was of the opinion that, even if these matters had been investigated, it would have made no difference to the outcome. The court concluded as follows: “It is clear that there was some slipshod police work in the present case’. He is currently serving a sentence of two years’ imprisonment following his conviction on 26 March 1992 at Sheffield Crown Court on three counts of burglary. The applicant took advice concerning the possibility of appealing to the House of Lords but was informed, in an opinion of counsel dated 8 September 1986, that there were no grounds on which an appeal could successfully be pursued.

The Court of appeal rejected this submission as follows: “We do not accept that interpretation of Detective Sergeant Hoyland’s evidence. We think quite plainly what he was indicating there and intended to indicate was that no fingerprints relating to either of the two alleged burglars were discovered at the scene.“ The Court of Appeal examined other impugned shortcomings which it did not consider to cast any doubt on the verdict. The court concluded as follows: “It is clear that there was some slipshod police work in the present case, no doubt because they took the view that here was a man who had admitted these crimes fully, and consequently there was very little need for them to indulge in a further verification of whether what he said was true’‘We do not think in the circumstances there was anything unsafe or unsatisfactory in the end about these convictions. Consequently, treating this matter as we have to according to section 17 of the Act, we think this appeal fails and must be dismissed.’

Under French law, simple or full adoption creates a legal parent-child relationship for the benefit of the adopters. Under Article 370-3 of the French Civil Code, a child could not be adopted if the law of his or her country prohibited adoption, which it did in the case of Hind. Convention of 26 January 1990 [adopted on 20 November 1989] on the Rights of the Child, as preserving, on a par with adoption, the. child's best interests.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Zina Hind was born on 3 November 2003 in Algeria and was abandoned immediately by her biological mother, who gave birth anonymously. She became a ward of the Algerian State on 3 December 2003. On 13 January 2004 the President of the court of Boumerdès granted the applicant, then aged 42 and unmarried, the right to take the child into her legal care (kafala) Since then she has been living with the applicant and the applicant’s mother. On 8 November 2006 the applicant applied for the full adoption of Hind. Kafala gave the child the protection to which all children were entitled under the international conventions. Under French law, simple or full adoption creates a legal parent-child relationship for the benefit of the adopters. The Algerian Family Code does not provide for any exception to the prohibition of adoption where the child has no established parentage. The executive decree of 13 January 1992 on changes of name does not establish parent-Child relationships, as the holder of the right of kafala retains the status of guardian. The kafalan system preserves the child’s right to an adoption. The French Civil Code states that adoption of a foreign minor may not be ordered where his or her personal law prohibits that institution, unless the minor was born and resides habitually in France. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. Under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention, she relied on Hind’s right to respect for her family life. The Court of Appeal did not establish any difference in treating the child in the same way as a child born in countries which did not prohibit adoption could be adopted in France. In a judgment of 25 February 2009 the Court of Cassation dismissed her appeal on Points of Law.

The applicant continued to see him and to have sexual relations with him. In November 1997 the applicant entered Turkey illegally. name: Jean-Claude Gacon
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1092/04) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the additional time granted to the Principal Public Prosecutor for appealing against a judgment of the Criminal Court amounted to a breach of the principle of equality of arms. On 16 October 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application. It also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of. the Convention). The application was brought by a French national, Mr Jean-Claude Gacon (“the applicant”), on 23 December 2003. In 2000 the applicant and his brother were committed to stand trial in the Lyons Criminal Court. They were charged with having deceived the social security scheme and the relevant health insurance offices through fraudulent practices. The Lyon Criminal Court held that the prosecution had lapsed as the offence of professional collusion was covered by an automatic amnesty, and that it lacked jurisdiction to examine the claims of the civil parties. The applicant was accordingly acquitted. The Principal Public Prosecutor lodged an appeal against the judgment on 20 April 2001, availing himself of the two-month time-limit granted to him for that purpose by Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that it was incompatible with the guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention. The applicant was sentenced to a suspended term of two years’ imprisonment, ordered to pay a fine of 120,000 euros (EUR) and stripped of his civic, civil and family rights for five years. He was also ordered, jointly and severally with his brother, to pay the sum of EUR 442,573.13 in compensation for all the damage found to have been sustained by the civil parties. The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing in particular that the time available to the Principal Public Prosecutor for lodging an appeal under Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was incompatible with Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

name: Jean-Marie Colombani
train_texts: Two French nationals, Mr Jean-Marie Colombani and Mr Eric Incyan, and the company Le Monde (“the applicants’) filed an application against the French Republic under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on 19 April 1999. The applicants alleged, in particular, a violation of their freedom of expression. The case was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case. The Government, but not the applicants, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59): the case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The decision of 4 September 2001 declared the application partly admissible. Report contained names of people implicated in drug trafficking in Morocco. Commission asked the Observatory for a revised version of the report, with the names of the drug traffickers deleted. Report contained twelve chapters with the following titles: “Cannabis in Morocco – the historical background”, “The characteristics of cannabis growing” and “Drug money”. It related how, over a period of ten years, there had been a tenfold increase in the area of land that had historically been used for cannabis production in the region of Er Rif. Current levels of production made ‘the sharif kingdom a serious contender for the title of the world’s leading exporter of cannabis’ Le Monde obtained a copy of a confidential report sent to the European Union in 1994. The report casts doubt on the sharif authorities’ determination to put an end to the trafficking, despite the ‘war on drugs’ they declared in a blaze of publicity in the autumn of 1992. Corruption guarantees the drug-trafficking rings the protection of officials ‘ranging from the humblest customs officer to the King’s inner circle ...’ Le Monde editor-in-chief and author of article were summoned to appear in the Paris Criminal Court on charges of insulting a foreign head of State. The Court of Appeal noted that the journalist had not shown that he had “contacted any Moroccan dignitaries, officials, public authorities or services for an explanation for the failure to match words with deeds” The applicants were therefore found guilty of insulting a foreign head of State and sentenced to fines of 5,000 French francs (FRF) each. name: Eleonor Levin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35141/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged a breach of Article 8 of the. Convention in relation to the contact restrictions following the. taking into public care of her three children. On 20 January 2009 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the contact. restrictions to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) On 1 February 2011 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section. On 3 May 2005 the applicant contacted BUP in a state of despair and, in response, a social emergency unit (social beredskap) went to the applicant’s home. The authorities found the interior of the home completely destitute; there was hardly any furniture and there was no electricity or running water. On the following day, the applicant was committed to compulsory psychiatric care in accordance with the Act on Compulsory Psychiatric Care (Lagen om psykiatrisk tvångsvård, 1991:1128). The applicant claimed that she was not ill but agreed to the placement of the children in the temporary family home. A week later, she was released from psychiatric care and returned to her home. All three children had worn nappies when they arrived at the temporary family home. T. had no limits towards adults and wanted to control everything and everyone around her. S. had nightmares and had been afraid of sudden movements. D. had been late in her speech and motor development. The applicant disputed the measure and claimed that she was capable of caring for her children, who suffered from being separated from her. The Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in Sundsvall upheld the lower court’s judgment in full on 9 January 2006. Since the applicant did not agree to voluntary care it was necessary to take the children into public care on a permanent basis. The children were placed in three different family homes, all within approximately 50 km of Skellefteå, as one family was not able to provide the care and support that each child needed. The applicant, through her legal counsel, requested the Social Council to allow her more time with her children as she felt that the children were being deprived of contact with her. The Social Council decided to restrict the applicant’s contact rights to all three children. This meant that each parent should meet with the children once every three months in a neutral environment where the family home parents and the social worker responsible for the file should be present. The decision was based on an investigation carried out by the Social Council, in consultation with BUP, into the children’s situation. The Social Council concluded in its investigation report that the children had a right to contact with their mother but that their best interests required that the contact be limited in order to ensure their secure and positive development. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court and requested that she be granted contact rights to her children much more often than only twice a year. In the summary, the court ruled that the applicant would meet her children once every six months and the children would be allowed to visit their father once every two months. The Social Council contested the appeal. It submitted that the children were currently in the process of developing and learning things that they had not had the opportunity to learn before. Consultation had taken place with BUP, which agreed with the Social Council that contact restrictions were necessary in order to ensure a positive development for the children. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Administrative Court of Appeal, maintaining her claims and adding that she wished to see her children at least once a month. name: Filiz Uyan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7496/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Ms Filiz Uyan, had been convicted of being a member of a terrorist organisation and sentenced to twenty-two years’ imprisonment. She was taken to a hospital to undergo an ultrasound scan by a gynaecologist. The bottom of the consulting room windows was only 50 cm above floor level and the windows were unprotected. The male security officers refused to leave the consultation room for security reasons. They stated that they would wait behind a folding screen. The. applicant refused to be examined in such conditions. The proceedings against the male prison guard were dropped on 3 December 2001. On 23 January 2002, the applicant’s lawyer filed a complaint with the İzmir Medical Association against the doctor who had not asked the male security officers to leave the room. The applicant objected and on 5 October 2002 the Turkish Medical Association (Türk Tabipleri Birliği) quashed that decision. The doctor was issued with a warning for professional misconduct on 23 January 2003 for not taking the initiative to request the malesecurity officers to leaving the consultation room or remove the applicant's handcuffs, as required by ethical rules. On 29 July 2002 the Karşıyaka Assize Court dismissed the applicants appeal.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20315/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The applicant, Mr Sławomir Wierzba (“the applicant”), was born in 1980 and lives in Gdańsk. The case was brought before the Gdańsk District Court. The bill of indictment concerned five defendants and, in all, twelve charges were brought against them. Hearings scheduled for 9 October and 11 December 2003 were cancelled due to, among other things, the failure to bring the applicant to trial from prison. The applicant was convicted in July 2004 and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. His detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. The appellate hearings scheduled for 12 October and 12 December 2005 and 2 February 2006 were cancelled for various reasons, such as the fact that a trial judge was on mission. The case was decided in the summer of 2006 at the Sąd Apelacyjny. The first-instance judgment was upheld by the Gdańsk Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) on 11 July 2007. In the meantime, between 3 October 2002 and 5 January 2005 the applicant served prison sentences which had been imposed on him in other criminal proceedings. The applicant lodged a complaint under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. He sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the GDAńska District Court had been excessive and an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 Polish zlotys.

It found that, despite its request for a detailed business plan, the applicant failed to provide one. The applicant alleged, in particular, a violation of his right to freedom of assembly. The purpose of the meeting was to be to commemorate the Salzburg Jews killed by the SS during the Second World War. The parties did not submit further observations on the merits (Rule 59): The Court declared the application admissible on 24 March 2005. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26: The Salzburg Federal Police Authority prohibited the meeting on the ground that it would endanger public order and security. It noted that Comradeship IV was a registered association whose members were mainly former members of the SS. For more than forty years they had commemorated SS soldiers killed in the Second World War by gathering on All Saints’ Day and laying a wreath in front of the war memorial. The disruption of this and other commemoration ceremonies was likely to offend the religious feelings of members. of the public visiting the cemetery and would indisputably be regarded as disrespectful towards the dead soldiers of both world wars. Accordingly, the demonstration could not take place. The Constitutional Court observed that the authorities deciding on the prohibition of an assembly had to weigh the applicant’s interest in holding the meeting against the public interests enumerated in Article 11 § 2 of the Convention. The authorities had also had regard to the fact that the gathering of Comradeship IV had in previous years been the target of activities aimed at disrupting it which had caused considerable nuisance to other visitors of the cemetery. As a religious tradition, the commemoration of the dead was protected by Article 9, which contained a positive obligation for the State to protect persons manifesting their religion against deliberate disturbance by others. It followed that it did not violate any other Convention right relied on by the applicant.

name: Ewa Biskupska
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39597/98) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Drzewicki, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the proceedings in her case had exceeded a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 26 March 2002 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant was ordered to indicate the value of her claim (wartość przedmiotu sporu) in her letter of 16 October 1995. On 27 February 1996 the Warsaw Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) dismissed her appeal. On 9 October 1996 the defendant co-operative lodged a counter-claim against the applicant. The applicant appealed against that decision and requested exemption from the court fees relating to that appeal. The court dismissed that appeal on 19 July 1996. On 17 February 1999 the applicant submitted a request for legal assistance, stating that she had not been able to contact a lawyer chosen by her. In June 1999 the court ordered an expert opinion concerning the construction costs. The applicant had requested documentation on the financing of the construction of her house. The Ministry of Justice told the court that they did not possess any such documentation. The applicant requested exemption from court fees but the court refused her request. She appealed the decision but the Court of Appeal quashed that decision on 9 December 2002. On 27 January 2003 the Regional Court rejected the applicant's additional claim of 10 April 2002, since she had not paid the due fee. On the same day it ordered an expert opinion. On 10 April 2003 the court granted the applicant partial exemptions from court costs. The proceedings are still pending. The application was dismissed on 30 August 2001, but the applicant appealed against that decision.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32849/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 13 September 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the unreasonable length of the applicant's pre-trial detention to the Government. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The court considered the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. It found that Article 258 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure established a presumption to the effect that the applicant was a member of an organised gang. The applicant and 15 co-accused were indicted before the Bielsko-Biała Regional Court. The first hearing was held on 13 November 2003. In total, the trial court held 36 hearings. The application was granted on 6 August 2003. The trial court had not yet started to examine the merits of the case. The applicant's request of 5 May 2003 to lift his pre-trial detention was dismissed on 9 June 2003. On 17 December 2003 the Court of Appeal granted the application to extend the applicant's detention beyond the statutory time-limit of 2 years laid down in Article 263 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant appealed against this decision, but it was dismissed on 21 July 2004. The Bielsko-Biała Regional Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to 8 years' imprisonment. The applicant lodged an appeal. On 26 January 2006 the Katowice Court of Appeal upheld the judgment. It appears that the applicant did not lodge a cassation appeal. The judgment is final. The court pointed to the complexity of the case and the advanced stage of the proceedings before the trial court. The judge ruled that the application could not be successful. The appeal was dismissed and the applicant was sentenced to eight years in prison.

Berlin Court of Appeal repeatedly ordered the applicant’s continued detention on remand. name: Yaşar Kanbur
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 8 May 2003 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that decision. On 1 February 2005 the Van Criminal Court found that it lacked jurisdiction and transferred the case to the Van Assize Court, holding that the accused policeOfficers should be tried under Article 452 of the former Criminal Code, which governed unintentional homicide. The Assize Court also heard the statements of twelve witnesses who had been eyewitnesses to the incident. Nine of the witnesses, who were also pedlars, stated that on the day of the incident two police officers had knocked down their stands and chased them. They all stated that one of the officers had kicked him, causing him to fall down and hit his head on the edge of the pavement. name: Wiesław Chodecki
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49929/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. On 9 October 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand to the Government. The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Sosnowiec. On 12 June 1994 he was arrested on suspicion of murdering his common-law wife. The prosecutor considered that, given the serious nature of the offence in question, keeping the applicant in custody was necessary to ensure that the process of obtaining evidence followed its proper course. The applicant was arrested in July 1994. The Sosnowiec District Court ordered that two psychiatric reports be obtained in order to establish the applicant’s criminal responsibility. The prosecutor asked the court to hear evidence from 38 witnesses. The trial court held hearings on 12 January, 16 March, 21 March, 28 March, 1 June, 8 June, 20 June, 12 October and 12 December 1995, as well as on 28 March 1996. The court convicted the applicant as charged, and sentenced him to twelve years’ imprisonment. On 30 May 1996 the applicant appealed. The Katowice Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case for re-examination. The applicant was convicted of homicide and sentenced to ten years' imprisonment in 1998. The Katowice Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention on remand until 29 January 1999 in view of the applicant's conviction and sentence the month before. The applicant challenged that decision before a court which did not have the necessary jurisdiction. The matter was transferred to the KatowICE Court of Appeal, which on 25 February 1999 dismissed both of his appeals. On 6 March 2000 the Supreme Court dismissed that appeal. The case is still pending at the European Court of Human Rights and Human Rights Commission (ECHRC), with a verdict expected by the end of the year.

name: Tevfik Kalaylı
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43654/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Tevfik Kalaylı. The applicant was born in 1963 and lives in Izmir. On 12 December 2003 the Izmir Magistrates’ Court issued an arrest warrant for the applicant on suspicion of assault and attempted murder. On 6 October 2004 the applicant was arrested. On 1 December 2005 the IzMir Assize Court sentenced the applicant to six years and two months’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment on 6 June 2007.

name: Paweł Kurczewski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18157/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 4 May 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the excessive length of the applicant's detention to the Government. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The court ruled that the application should be allowed to stand. The applicant was indicted before the Gdańsk District Court on 25 March 2003. He was charged with robbery and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. The trial court held the first hearing on 5 June 2003. It subsequently scheduled sixteen hearings in the case. Four of them were cancelled for various reasons. On 28 July 2004 the judge convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to four years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed on 7 December 2004. His detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. In all those decisions the courts stated that the grounds originally given for the applicant's detention were still valid. They repeated the grounds previously given for his continued detention. Appeals hearings were cancelled for various reasons, such as illness or absence of defence lawyers, and the need to obtain evidence. On 3 February 2006 the Gdańsk Regional Court quashed the applicant's detention order. He was released on the same date. It appears that the first-instance judgment was upheld on 11 July 2007. It is not known if he is still in prison, and has not been charged with any crime. He has been in prison since 2005, and was convicted of two counts of attempted murder and one of attempted kidnap. He is currently in prison in Poland, awaiting trial on all charges, but has been released on bail.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the obligation imposed on him as a man in employment over age 60 to pay national insurance contributions, which did not apply to a woman in work of over that age, was in violation of Article 14. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 16 March 2004, the Court declared the application admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant and the Government submitted further observations. The applicant wrote to his Member of Parliament and the Paymaster General complaining about the difference in treatment for men and women. Both replied stating that since liability to pay national insurance contributions is linked to the state pension age, the treatment of men andWomen would equalise in 2020 when the state Pension age will equalise. The applicant will be required to pay National Insurance contributions from his earnings until he reaches the age of 65. A woman of 60 years or more who continued to work would not be needed to pay any NICs on her earnings. A man who worked until he was 65 would not have to pay NICs at all. train_texts: The case of Klass and others was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights. The case originated in an application against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission on 11 June 1971 under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 28 July, the President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges called upon to sit as members of the Chamber. The five judges thus designated were Mr. J. Cremona, Mr. W. Ganshof van der Meersch,. Mr. D. Evrigenis and Mr. G. Lagergren. The Government filed their memorial on 28 November. On 27 January 1978, a memorial by the Principal Delegate of the Commission was received at the registry. At that meeting the Court, granting a request presented by the Government, decided that their Agent and counsel would be authorised to address the Court in German. The Court also authorised Mr. Pohl to speak in German (Rules 29 para. 1 in fine and 27 para. 3). The oral hearings took place in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 10 March. There appeared before the Court: Mrs. I. MAIER, Ministerialdirigentin at the Federal Ministry of Justice, Agent, Mr. H. G. MERK, Regierungsdirektor. The applicants, who are German nationals, are Gerhard Klass, an Oberstaatsanwalt, Peter Lubberger, a lawyer, Jürgen Nussbruch, a judge, Hans-Jürgen Pohl and Dieter Selb, lawyers. They claim that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law (Grundgesetz) and a statute enacted in pursuance of that provision, namely the Act of 13 August 1968 on Restrictions on the Secrecy of the Mail, Post and Telecommunications, are contrary to the Convention. They do not dispute that the State has the right to have recourse to the surveillance measures contemplated by the legislation. They challenge this legislation in that it permits those measures without obliging the authorities in every case to notify the persons concerned after the event. The applicants claimed before both the Constitutional Court and the Commission that they were being subjected to surveillance measures. However, as a precautionary measure, the applicants did not know whether the G 10 had actually been applied to them. The Government of the Federal Republic of Germany were prompted by this judgment to propose amendments to the G10, but the parliamentary proceedings have not yet been completed. The Court held: “In order to be able to enter a constitutional application against an Act, the applicant must claim that the Act itself ... constitutes a direct and immediate violation of one of his fundamental rights ...” (ibid, pp. 16-17) After the end of the Second World War, the surveillance of mail, post and telecommunications in Germany was dealt with by the occupying powers. The Government wished to substitute the domestic law for the rights exercised by the Three Powers and to place under legal control interferences with the right, guaranteed by Article 10 of the Basic Law, to respect for correspondence. The two Acts, having been adopted by the federal legislative assemblies, were enacted on 24 June and 13 August 1968 respectively. in such cases the person concerned is notified of the surveillance measure.“ The contested legislation is being debated by the Bundestag and is expected to be voted on next week. Law guaranteed secrecy of mail, post and telecommunications. Restrictions could be ordered only pursuant to a statute. Legal remedy through the courts shall be replaced by a system of scrutiny by agencies and auxiliary agencies appointed by the people’s elected representatives.“The G 10, adopting the solution contemplated by the second sentence of paragraph 2 of the above-quoted Article 10, specifies (in Article 1 para. 1) the cases in which the competent authorities may impose the restrictions provided for in that paragraph, that is to say, may open and inspect mail and post, read telegraphic messages, listen to and record telephone conversations.” The measures ordered must be immediately discontinued once the required conditions have ceased to exist or the measures themselves are no longer necessary. Measures are ordered, on written application giving reasons, either by the supreme Land authority in cases falling within its jurisdiction or by a Federal Minister empowered for the purpose by the Chancellor. The measures remain in force for a maximum of three months and may be renewed only on fresh application. The G 10 Commission may direct the Minister to inform the person concerned that he has been subjected to surveillance measures. The person concerned is not to be notified of the restrictions affecting him. However, since the Federal Constitutional Court’s judgment of 15 December 1970 (see paragraph 11 above), the competent authority has to inform him as soon as notification can be made without jeopardising the purpose. The G 10 Commission decides, ex officio or on application by a person believing himself to be under surveillance, on both the legality of and the necessity for the measures. If it declares any measures to be illegal or unnecessary, the Minister must terminate them immediately. The Commission members are appointed for the current term of the Bundestag by the above-mentioned Board of five Members of Parliament after consultation with the Government. They are completely independent in the exercise of their functions and cannot be subject to instructions. For the Länder, their legislatures lay down the parliamentary supervision to which the supreme authorities are supreme authorities. The G 10 draws up its own rules of procedure which must be approved by the Board; before taking this decision, the Board consults the government. The surveillance of the post and telecommunications of a certain person can serve a useful purpose only if the person concerned does not become aware of it. For this reason, notification to this person is out of the question. A person who intends to commit, or who has committed, the offences enumerated in the Act can, by using a legal remedy, inform himself whether he is under surveillance. The Bill presented during the 4th legislative session ... provided for the ordering (of such measures) by an independent judge. The Federal Government abandoned this solution in the Bill amending Article 10 of the Basic Law, introduced as part of the Emergency Legislation. The person concerned is notified, after the measures have been discontinued, that he has been subject to surveillance. Several legal remedies against the interference with his rights become available to him. If none of these remedies is successful, apply to the Federal Constitutional Court for a ruling as to whether there has been a breach of the Basic Law. In urgent cases, the decision may be taken by the public prosecutor’s department but to remain in effect it must be confirmed by a court within three days. The persons concerned are informed of the measures taken in their respect as soon as notification can be made without jeopardising the purpose of the investigation (Article 101 para. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure). The applicants alleged that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law and the G 10 violate Article 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. The Commission declared the application admissible on 18 December 1974. Some of the applicants are barristers and it is theoretically excluded that they are in fact subject to secret surveillance in consequence of contacts they may have with clients who are suspected of anti-constitutional activities. In view of this particularity of the case the applicants have to be considered as victims for the purpose of Article 25 (art. 25) of the convention, the Commission ruled in March 1977. The applicants relied on the notion “civil rights’; the present case did not disclose any breach of this notion. The case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) in so far as the applicants relied on the notion “criminal charge’. The Delegates of the Commission made the following concluding submissions to the Court: “May it please the Court to say and judge whether the applicants could claim to be ‘victims’ of a violation of their rights by reason of the system of surveillance established by the so-called G 10 Act’“ The application was inadmissible. After the end of the Second World War, the surveillance of mail, post and telecommunications in Germany was dealt with by the occupying powers. Neither the entry into force on 24 May 1949 of the Basic Law nor the foundation of the State of the Federal Republic altered this situation which continued even after the termination of the occupation régime in 1955. On 13 June 1967, the Government introduced two Bills as part of the Emergency Legislation. The first sought primarily to amend Article 10 para. 2 of thebasic Law; the second was designed to limit the right to secrecy of the mail,Post and telecommunications. The two Acts, having been adopted by the federal legislative assemblies, were enacted on 24 June and 13 August 1968. Law guaranteed the secrecy of mail, post and telecommunications with a proviso that restrictions could be ordered only pursuant to a statute. As amended by the Act of 24 June 1968, it now provides: “(1) Secrecy of the mail,Post and telecommunications shall be inviolable. (2) Restrictions may be orderedOnly pursuant to the law.” The statute may provide that the person concerned shall not be notified of the restriction and that legal remedy through the courts shall be replaced by a system of scrutiny by agencies and auxiliary agencies appointed by the people’s elected representatives.“The G 10, adopting the solution contemplated by the second sentence of paragraph 2 of the above-quoted Article 10, specifies (in Article 1 para. 1) the cases in which the competent authorities may impose restrictions. The Act provides that an application for surveillance measures may be made only by the head, or his substitute, of one of the following services. The measures are ordered, on written application giving reasons, either by the supreme Land authority in cases falling within its jurisdiction or by a Federal Minister empowered for the purpose by the Chancellor. Measures ordered must be immediately discontinued once the required conditions have ceased to exist or the measures themselves are no longer necessary (Article 1 para. 7, sub-paragraph 2). The measures remain in force for a maximum of three months and may be renewed only on fresh application. The person concerned is not to be notified of the restrictions affecting him. However, since the Federal Constitutional Court’s judgment of 15 December 1970, the competent authority has to inform the person concerned as soon as notification can be made. The competent Minister must, at least once every six months, report to a Board consisting of five Members of Parliament on the application of the G 10. The G 10 Commission decides, ex officio or on application by a person believing himself to be under surveillance, on both the legality of and the necessity for the measures. If it declares any measures to be illegal or unnecessary, the Minister must terminate them immediately. The Commission members are appointed for the current term of the Bundestag by the above-mentioned Board of five members of Parliament after consultation with the Government. They are completely independent in the exercise of their functions and cannot be subject to instructions. For the Länder, their legislatures lay down the parliamentary supervision to which the supreme authorities are. According to Article 1 para. 9, sub-paragraph 5, of the G 10: “... there shall be no legal remedy before the courts in respect of the ordering and implementation of restrictive measures.” “The surveillance of the post and telecommunications of a certain person can serve a useful purpose only if the person concerned does not become aware of it. For this reason, notification to this person is out of the question.“ “A person who intends to commit, or who has committed, the offences enumerated in the Act can, by using a legal remedy, inform himself whether he is under surveillance” The Constitutional Court may reject the application on the ground that the applicant is unable to adduce proof to substantiate a complaint. It may also request the Government concerned to supply it with information or to produce documents to enable it to verify for itself the individual’s allegations. The authorities are bound to reply to such a request even if the information asked for is secret. It is then for the Constitutional Court to decide whether the information and documents so obtained can be used; it may decide by a two-thirds majority that their use is incompatible with State security and dismiss the application. The Agent of the Government admitted that this remedy might be employed only on rare occasions. The applicants alleged that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law and the G 10 violate Article 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. On 18 December 1974, the Commission declared the application admissible. The Commission then expressed the opinion:by eleven votes to one with two abstentions, that the present case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) The applicants relied on the notion “civil rights’;. The applicants say that they may be or may have been subject to secret surveillance, for example, in course of legal representation of clients who were themselves subject to surveillance. The application was inadmissible; in the alternative, to find that the Federal Republic of Germany has not violated the Convention. case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) in so far as the applicants relied on the notion ‘criminal charge’. The report contains various separate opinions. by twelve votes in favour with one abstention, that the present case didn't disclose any Breach of Article 8 or Article 13. The applicants could claim to be ‘victims’ of a violation of their rights guaranteed by the Convention by reason of the system of surveillance established by the so-called G 10 Act.

name: Halil Kaya
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22922/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the lack of legal assistance to the applicant during his police custody. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was convicted of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation and sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment. The court had regard to the. applicant’s statements to the police and the public prosecutor, which were taken in the absence of a lawyer. The case was re-opened by the Adana Criminal Court in view of recent legislative amendments. The applicant was sentenced to three months and ten days’ imprisonment and his sentence was converted to a fine. The court further converted the sentence to a. fine and, pursuant to Law no. 5395 on Juvenile Protection, it decided to defer adjudication of the sentence. This decision was upheld by the. Adana Assize Court on 20 June 2007. The case file was remitted to the Court of Cassation on 19 December 2005. The prosecutor referred to new legislation which had entered into force on 12 October 2004, amending the Criminal Code once again.

name: Martin Zumtobel
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 1 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12235/86) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by the firm of F.M. Zumtobel. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 ( art. 6-1) The Court was established on 26 September 1992, in the presence of the Registrar, and included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President. The case concerns expropriation proceedings instituted with a view to the construction in the province of Vorarlberg of a provincial highway, the L 52. It appears that the scheme in question dated back to 1960, but that opposition from local landowners had prevented its realisation. The authorities conducted an investigation into inter alia whether the projected road was compatible with the requirements of environmental protection (Landschaftsschutz). The proposed route was published (zur öffentlichen Einsichtnahme aufgelegt) and the file made available for consultation at the Rankweil council offices from 1 to 31 October 1984.  expropriation proceedings relating to a parcel of land of 2,140m2 belonging to the Zumtobel partnership were opened on 28 February 1985. The authorities consulted several experts. According to the highways expert and the road traffic expert, the proposed section of highway was important because it would improve traffic links between Rankweil and Feldkirch. The first applicant repeatedly but unsuccessfully requested to be allowed to study various documents in the file. On 13 February 1986 the Office made an order for expropriations and fixed compensation at 620 schillings per square metre. It claimed that the proceedings, which were subject to final review, had violated its right of access to a court with full jurisdiction, guaranteed inter alia by Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6) The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 22 September 1989, after a purely written procedure; the applicants had not asked it to hold a hearing. In the court’s opinion, the complaint that the scheme objected to was not based on any reasonable overall plan. The court held that the applicant partnership had also failed to cast doubt on the official experts’ reports such as could disclose a procedural irregularity capable of affecting the road network.“ As can be seen from the findings of fact in the contested decision, the respondent authority took the view that it was in the interests of road users to divert through- traffic from the built-up area.” The Government Office had not made the commencement of construction work for the L 52 subject to a final decision on the length of the route. The court also rejected the complaints relating to the hearing of the official experts. The fact that such an expert took part in proceedings to which the Province was a party did not, unless there were special circumstances, constitute a serious reason within the meaning of the 1950 Law to doubt his complete impartiality. As the applicant partnership had not been a party to the environmental protection proceedings (Landschaftsschutzverfahren), it could not claim a right to compensation in kind or an exchange of land. Administrative Court also found that there had been no breach of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention and declined to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. The first applicant had meanwhile applied to the Feldkirch District Court (Bezirksgericht) to determine the amount of compensation. On 17 December 1987 this was set at 9,963,032.50 Austrian schillings (ATS) On 28 May 1988, on appeal (Rekurs), the amount was reduced to ATS 4,560,000.50 (ATS). On 6 November 1988, the court ruled that the compensation was not to be awarded. The first applicant’s appeal on points of law (Revisionsrekurs) against this decision was dismissed by the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) October 1988 the first applicant's appeal onPoints of Law against this Decision was dismissed. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 1 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12235/86) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by the firm of F.M. Zumtobel. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 ( art. 6-1). The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them. The case concerns expropriation proceedings instituted with a view to the construction of a provincial highway. It appears that the scheme in question dated back to 1960, but that opposition from local landowners had prevented its realisation. The authorities conducted an investigation into inter alia whether the projected road was compatible with the requirements of environmental protection (Landschaftsschutz). The proposed route was published (zur öffentlichen Einsichtnahme aufgelegt) and the file made available for consultation at the Rankweil council offices from 1 to 31 October 1984. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 March 1993. The Court heard addresses by them and also their replies to its questions. Expropriation proceedings relating to a parcel of land of 2,140m2 belonging to the Zumtobel partnership were opened on 28 February 1985. The authorities consulted several experts. The first applicant repeatedly but unsuccessfully requested to be allowed to study various documents in the file. According to the highways expert and the road traffic expert, the proposed section of highway was important because it would improve traffic links between Rankweil and Feldkirch, which went through densely populated built-up areas. On 13 February 1986 the Office made an order for expropriation and fixed compensation at 620 schillings per square metre. The first applicant also challenged the decision of 13 February 1986 (see paragraph 10 above) in the Administrative Court. Relying on substantially the same arguments as in the Constitutional Court, it now complained of breaches of procedural and substantive law. The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 22 September 1989, after a purely written procedure; the applicants had not asked it to hold a hearing. In the court’s opinion, the complaint that the scheme objected to was not based on any reasonable overall plan was not enough to establish that the contested decision had been unlawful. The court held that the applicant partnership had also failed to cast doubt on the official experts’ reports. The court rejected the complaints relating to the hearing of the official experts. It noted to begin with that the Office was obliged to consult them, under the General Administrative Procedure Law of 1950. The fact that such an expert took part in proceedings to which the Province was a party did not, unless there were special circumstances, constitute a serious reason within the meaning of the 1950 Law to doubt his complete impartiality. There was nothing to prevent a written record being made of an orally delivered expert report, without the expert having to supplement it in writing. As the applicant partnership had not been a party to the environmental protection proceedings (Landschaftsschutzverfahren), it could not claim a right. The Administrative Court also found that there had been no breach of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention and declined to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. The first applicant had meanwhile applied to the Feldkirch District Court (Bezirksgericht) to determine the amount of compensation. On 17 December 1987 this was set at 9,963,032.50 Austrian schillings (ATS). On 28 May 1988, on appeal (Rekurs), the amount was reduced to ATS 4,560,000. 50 Austrianschillings. On 6 December 1987, the court set the compensation at ATS 8,000,000 (8,500,000 AustrianSchillings) The first applicant’s appeal on points of law (Revisionsrekurs) against this decision was dismissed by the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) in October 1988. In October 1988 the first applicant's appeal onpoints of law was dismissed. In. October 1988, the first appeal on points of law ( revising the laws of the law was dismissed by the Supreme Court. The appeal was dismissed in October 1988, and in. October 1989, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal again, this time in favor of the original decision. In 1991, the appeal was finally dismissed.

name: Marta Döry
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28394/95) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that her rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated on account of the lack of an oral hearing in judicial proceedings concerning social security benefits. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. By a decision of 23 May 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice (ECJ). The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Stockholm. She claimed that she was entitled to continued benefits after 27 April 1990. The court’s assessment was based on medical certificates from three different physicians who all stated that the applicant was able to work and was not entitled to the benefits in question. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Supreme Social Insurance Court (Försäkringsöverdomstolen). She complained about the lack of oral hearings in the lower courts. In that respect, she maintained that the case had not been adequately investigated and that an oral hearing had been necessary for her to explain. The applicant was on sick-leave between 1 May and 30 June 1991, during which period she received per diem sickness benefits under the Social Insurance Act. However, by a decision of 7 August 1991 the Office found that she was no longer entitled to such benefits. At the applicant’s request, the Office reviewed its decision on 10 June 1992 but did not change it. The applicant appealed to the Administrative Court of Appeal. She requested also in this case that the appellate court hold an oral hearing and, moreover, asked it to obtain further medical evidence. On 8 June 1995 the Supreme Social Insurance Court refused the applicant leave to appeal.
