name: Uli Lutz
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 28 January 1986. It originated in an application (no. 9912/82) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr. Uli Lutz, on 14 June 1982. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Englert and Nölkenbockhoff cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality. The Government’s memorial was lodged with the registry on 13 November 1986. The applicant informed the Registrar on the same day that he would not be filing a memorial. On 29 November, the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government, by Mr. Weitzel for the Commission and by. Mr. Wingerter and Mr. Hohbach for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. Uli Lutz, a German national born in 1959, lives in Heilbronn-Horkheim. On 10 October 1980, he was riding a motor cycle and was involved in a road accident. According to the police report (Verkehrs-Ordnungswidrigkeiten-Anzeige), he had attempted to overtake a car, although the traffic situation was unclear. The result had been a collision which caused damage to both vehicles. Mr. Lutz was fined DM 125, to which were added costs of DM 14, for “joint responsibility for a road. accident due to overtaking in an unclear traffic situation such that a collision was. The decision was based on section 24 of the Road Traffic Act (Strassenverkehrsgesetz) and Regulations 1(2), 5 and 49. The driver of the car was likewise fined for a “regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) on 9 December 1980. Heilbronn District Court stayed the proceedings on the ground that they were time-barred. On 12 August 1981, Mr. Wingerter replied that his client naturally agreed to the stay of proceedings, but not to an order requiring him to bear his own necessary costs and expenses (notwendige Auslagen) The costs of the proceedings shall be borne by the Treasury. The defendant shall bear his own necessary costs and expenses. The decision on costs is based on Article 467 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, taken together with section 46 of the Act on ‘regulatory offences’. As the file stands, the defendant would most probably have been convicted of an offence against the Road Traffic Regulations. That being so, it would be unjust (unbillig to award his necessary costs) to award the defendant’s necessary costs against the treasury. The court held that Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) of Article 6 (1) of the German Criminal Procedure Code was not a violation of the law. The court ruled that Article 6 (art. 6) protected the individual only from possible hazards in civil or criminal trials. Mr. Lutz had himself admitted to the police that he was not expecting the car which was moving out to the left onto the road in front of him to make a U-turn. The court held that in such circumstances it would have been unjust to award the defendant’s necessary costs and expenses against the Treasury. The decisions of the District Court and the Regional Court did not offend the presumption of innocence, which was founded on the principle of the rule of law and was embodied in Article 6 of the Convention. The presumption of innocence precluded taking measures against a defendant that amounted in effect to a penalty (Strafe) in anticipation of a penalty. This rule was not infringed where the necessary costs and expenses of a party who had been proceeded against in respect of a ‘regulatory offence’ were not awarded against the Treasury in the event of the proceedings being discontinued. ‘The decision not to order the Treasury to pay the costs and. expenses of the party concerned obviously cannot be regarded as a punishment (Bestrafung) or. even be equated with such,’ said the court in a judgment. the Convention.

It also heard replies from Mr. Weitzel, Delegate for the Commission and by Mr. Wingerter, Rechtsanwalt for the applicant. Uli Lutz, a German national born in 1959, lives in Heilbronn-Horkheim. The result had been a collision which caused damage to both vehicles. Mr. Lutz was fined DM 125, to which were added costs of DM 14, for “joint responsibility for a road crash due to overtaking’ The decision was based on section 24 of the Road Traffic Act (Strassenverkehrsgesetz - see paragraph 38 below) The driver of the car was likewise fined for a “regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) The court informed the applicant that it intended to discontinue the proceedings as they were time-barred and order costs against the Treasury (Staatskasse) The applicant would have to bear his own necessary costs and expenses (notwendige Auslagen) The District Court stayed the proceedings on the ground that they wereTime-Barred. Its decision read as follows: “In the ‘regulatory offences’ matter (B), the driver was found guilty of contravening Regulations 1(2) and 5(1) to (3“ Heilbronn Police Authority took a decision to impose a fine (Bussgeldbescheid) on the defendant for a breach of the Road Traffic Regulations. The costs of the proceedings shall be borne by the Treasury. The defendant shall bear his own necessary costs and expenses. The decision on costs is based on Article 467 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, taken together with section 46 of the Act on ‘regulatory offences’ (Gesetz über Ordnungswidrigkeiten) The court declines to order the Treasury to bear the defendant’s necessary costs. The case was dismissed as being unfounded. Mr. Lutz then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) but on 2 February 1982 a bench of three of that court’s judges refused to entertain the application. Mr Lutz had thus broken the basic rule in Regulation 1(2) of the Road Traffic Regulations and, in particular, had disregarded his duty under Regulation 5(3)(1) not to overtake where the traffic situation was unclear. The court held that in such circumstances it would have been unjust to award the defendant's necessary costs and expenses against the Treasury, especially as the prosecution had become time-barred only during the court proceedings. The presumption of innocence precluded taking measures against a defendant that amounted in effect to a penalty. This rule was not infringed where the necessary costs and expenses of a party who had been proceeded against in respect of a ‘regulatory offence’ were not awarded against the Treasury in the event of the proceedings being discontinued. The decision not to order the Treasury to pay the costs and. expenses of the party concerned obviously cannot be regarded as a punishment (Bestrafung) or even be equated with. such. The reasons for the order as to costs in the impugned decisions are therefore rightly confined to the finding that the defendant would most probably have been found guilty.

name: Halil Kızılöz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32962/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” and that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. The Court declared the remainder of the applicant’s complaints inadmissible. The case was heard by the First Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) The applicant was suspected of membership of an illegal organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) The applicant admitted that the weapons and bullets found in his possession belonged to him. He was found guilty as charged and sentenced to 13 years and 4 months’ imprisonment. The judge also permanently debarred him from working in Turkey. The case was decided by a court of the Ankara Martial Law Court (sıkıyönetim mahkemesi) The judge. filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The judge found the applicant guilty of the charges against him and sentenced him to 13. years and four months imprisonment. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) following promulgation of the Law of 27 December 1993, which abolished the jurisdiction of the martial law courts. The case was reviewed on 27 December 1995 and the applicant’s sentence was reduced to ten years’ imprisonment. The applicant was sentenced to 10 years' imprisonment for. employment in the civil service for offences under Article 168 § 1 of the Criminal Code and. Article 17 of Law no. 1402. The judge found the applicant guilty of the offences and sentenced him to a year in prison. The sentence was later reduced to five years.

On 27 May 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the Application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant was born in 1968 and lives in Trabzon. The applicant's appeal could be examined as an “objection” and forwarded to the prosecutor for the necessary action to be taken. The applicant and his two colleagues brought a case against the bank before the Trabzon Labour Court, claiming compensation for their dismissal. The applicant appealed against the decision, submitting that the criminal proceedings against him had been suspended by the Istanbul Assize Court. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision in so far as it concerned the applicable rate of interest. In July 2004 the bank brought proceedings to enforce the decision with a view to recovering the money. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29281/95) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a ‘reasonable time’ He also alleged that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. The Chamber retained the applicant’s complaints concerning his rights to fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible. The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights (ECHR) on 11 January 2000. The Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) was a Marxist-Leninist organisation. It was formed to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist regime. In 1981 the applicant was brought to Sivas to explain his role in the organisation. In 1982 the Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Martial Law Court against the applicant and 722 other defendants. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In 1987 the Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s release pending trial. In 1989 the judge convicted the applicant of membership of an illegal organisation, the Dev- Yol, and of of other charges. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) The court acquitted the applicant of the other charges and sentenced him to 13 years and 4 months' imprisonment. It held that the Martial Law Court had wrongly applied Article 17 of Law no. 1402 to the applicant’s case. It considered however that this error did not require the re-trial of the applicant. The court revised the judgment and sentenced the applicant to 10 years’ imprisonment. The case was quashed on 27 December 1995 and the applicant was acquitted of all charges. The application was dismissed.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, among other things, that he had been dismissed on account of his political views and membership of a political party. The application was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1) The Court ruled that the application was not in breach of Article 34 and upheld the dismissal of the applicant. The case was heard on 9 February 2009 and the jury returned a verdict of not guilty on 15 February 2009. The ruling was quashed on 8 February 2010 and the case is now being appealed. The BNP’s overt and racist/fascist agenda was a ‘significant cause for concern’ for public sector workers’ trade union UNISON. The applicant claimed that he had been unlawfully discriminated against as his dismissal constituted less favourable treatment on racial grounds. Serco cited potential health and safety risks as the applicant's continued employment would give rise to considerable anxiety among passengers and their carers. The Employment Tribunal gave judgment on 2 February 2005 in favour of the BNP in a case brought by the applicant against Serco. The tribunal ruled that the applicant lacked sufficient continuous service to bring an action for unfair dismissal. Employment Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not on racial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. Tribunal also dismissed claim of indirect discrimination on the ground that the applicant’s dismissal was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. Court of Appeal allowed Serco's appeal and restored the order of the Employment Tribunal. Mummery LJ found the applicant's submission that he had been subjected to direct race discrimination to be wrong in principle and inconsistent with the purposes of the legislation. The dividing line of colour or race was not made by Serco, but by the BNP which defines its own composition by colour and race. The BNP cannot make a non-racial criterion (party membership) a racial one by the terms of its constitution limiting membership to white people. Mr Redfearn’s complaint is of discrimination on political grounds, which falls outside the anti-discrimination laws. The employment tribunal appears to have attempted itself a version of a ‘provision, criterion or practice’ in paragraph 5.6 of its decision (see paragraph 28 above) However, it is formulated too narrowly (membership of the BNP) to be meaningful. A more general and meaningful provision along similar lines would be one applying to membership of a political organisation, which existed to promote views hostile to members of a different colour. The applicant was refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. 1976 Act are incompatible with the Convention rights. As for justification under the 1976 Act I have already explained that it does not arise, as no case of indirect discrimination has been made out.” The judge ruled that the applicant was not entitled to an appeal against his decision. The hearing was adjourned until September 17, and the case will be heard again on September 20, when the judge will make a further decision on the appeal. The case was referred to the Court of Appeal by the European Court of Human Rights on September 14, 2012. name: Piotr Rachwalski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47709/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows. The Court will decide on the merits of the applicants' case in the future. Policemen, armed with truncheons and guarded by police dogs, entered the house, woke up the other occupants and ordered them to stand against the wall. During this time the police showered abuse on the students. It was established that the first applicant had two long bruises on his left arm, and other bruises on the palm of his hand. The second applicant had a blue mark on her bottom (13 by 9 cm) It was stated that these bruises could have been caused by the use of police trunchetons. The applicants requested to be examined by a forensic medicine specialist. No information was provided about the grounds, purpose or legal basis for the search. The applicants requested the Wrocław District Prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. On 23 December 1997 the prosecutor refused to do so. He found that no criminal offence had been committed. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. The further developments had certainly come as a surprise to both the police and other persons involved in the incident. The applicants talked to the police with raised voices and took a very active part in the struggle with the policemen. After that, the intervention was terminated. The prosecutor concluded that the measures taken by the police had been proportionate to the situation. The first applicant appealed. He argued that the police brutality and aggression had been totally unjustified. Nothing in the behaviour of the persons present had justified the use of force. The police had entered private property and effected a search. The applicants had been hit as they had ignored the order to let D. S. go so that he could be taken to the car. It was finally noted that the accounts of the facts given by the persons. present at the scene, other than the police, were highly divergent, making it. impossible to establish the facts of the case. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. He had not given any reason to be beaten, verbally insulted and humiliated just at the whim of the police. The police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. He considered that the police intervention had been justified in so far as they wanted to verify the identity of the owner of the car. Regardless of whether he had intended to hit A. C. in the face or not, his behaviour could have been perceived as an intentional assault.

The case originated in an application (no. 47709/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicants tried to argue with the policemen, to no avail. They produced their identity cards and the registration card of the car, whose owner was asleep in the house. The police were not satisfied with their explanation and the dispute became more intense. In reaction to the opinions expressed about the intervention, in particular by D. S., the policemen used truncheons. The applicants were ordered to stand against a fence. They were pushed and jostled and the policemen insulted them referring to them as ‘scum’, ‘slobs’ and ‘queers’ (hołota, brudasy, pedały) The prosecutor found that no criminal offence had been committed. The applicants asked the Wrocław District Prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. The further developments had certainly come as a surprise to both the police and other persons involved in the incident. The applicant was most probably hit once. The second applicant had objected in a pretentious tone (“pretensjonalny ton głosu”) to having been woken up and to the check on the car taking place at night. D. S. had objected in a loud voice to the police intervention. He had insisted that the intention of the police was to harass the persons in the house. As he had not obeyed the police requests to calm down and the verbal exchange between him and the police officer A. C. had become increasingly heated, it had been decided that he should be taken to a police car. The first applicant appealed. He argued that the police brutality and aggression had been totally unjustified. Nothing in the behaviour of the persons present had justified the use of force. The prosecutor concluded that the measures taken by the police had been proportionate to the situation. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen. He had not given any reason to be beaten, verbally insulted and humiliated. The police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. He considered that the intervention of the police had been justified in so far as they wanted to verify the identity of the owner of the car. Regardless of whether he had intended to hit A. C. in the face or not, his behaviour could have been perceived as an intentional assault. The identity check of the persons present in the house had been necessary.

The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows: The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicants were asked to produce their identity cards and the registration card of the car, whose owner was asleep in the house. The police were not satisfied with their explanation and the dispute became more intense. In reaction to the opinions expressed about the intervention, in particular by D. S., the policemen used truncheons. The applicants were ordered to stand against a fence. They were pushed and jostled and the policemen insulted them referring to them as “scum’, “slobs”, ‘queers’ (hołota, brudasy, pedały). The police left the house and warned the students that some of them were in an illegal situation as they were not registered as inhabitants. The applicants requested the Wrocław District Prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. On 23 December 1997 the prosecutor refused to do so. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. The further developments had certainly come as a surprise to both the police and other persons involved in the incident. The applicant was most probably hit once. The atmosphere was tense. The owner of the car gave the police the keys and documents to the car. As D. S. was unruly and continued to express objections, the policemen decided to arrest him. Thereupon truncheons were used against him. D. S. had objected in a loud voice to the police intervention. He had insisted that the intention of the police was to harass the persons in the house. The prosecutor considered that this had been justified in the light of D. S’s aggressive behaviour. It was clear that, in the face of his resistance, it had been necessary to use such force in order to take D.S. to the car. The accounts of the facts given by the persons present at the scene, other than the police, were highly divergent, making it impossible to establish the facts of the case. The submissions of the other persons could not be considered credible and had to be assessed critically. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen. The police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. The outcome of the appeal was not made public until after the case had been settled by the Supreme Court of Poland on 20 May 1998. The court ruled that the police had been justified in so far as they wanted to verify the identity of the owner of the car. It also ruled that police had not established that the students had been insulted verbally by the police, as they consistently denied this.

name: Zbigniew Majchrzak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1524/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Zbigniew Majchrzak (‘the applicant’) made the application on 23 June 2001. The applicant was born in 1943 and lives in Poznań, Poland. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was sent to the President of the Fourth Section on 1 September 2005. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant appealed against the District Court’s decision. The Poznań Regional Court quashed the decision and remitted the case. On 2 January 2001 the Poznan District Court held the first and the only hearing. On the same day it held in a decision that the only person entitled to inherit from P.M. was M.M (the applicant's daughter) in accordance with the will made in 1988. It appears that none of the parties appealed against that decision. It is not known whether the case will be heard in the Polish Supreme Court or the Polish Court of Cassation in Strasbourg.

It also decided to join the application to other applications. The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in London. His wife died on 12 September 1999 leaving two children, born in 1995 and 1998. On 30 March 2000 the applicant applied for benefits equivalent to those to which a widow, whose husband had died in similar circumstances to those of his wife, would have been entitled. On 12 October 2000 he was informed that his claim could not be accepted because there was no basis in domestic law allowing widowers to claim this benefit. The applicant receives child benefit in the sum of GBP 100 every four weeks.

name: Torsten Leander
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9248/81) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission on 2 November 1980 under Article 25. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Sweden recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed violations by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 10 and 13. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality and Mr. R. Ryssdal. President of the Chamber ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Swedish Government (“the Government“), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant regarding the need for a written procedure. On 12 December 1985, he directed that the lawyer and, should he so decide, the Agent should each have until 4 February 1986 to file a memorial. The applicant’s memorial was received at the registry on 3 February. On 21 March, the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegates would present their observations at the hearing. On 28 April, the Commission communicated to the Registrar a number of documents whose production he had requested on the instructions of the President. The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. Torsten Leander was employed as a temporary technician at the Naval Museum at Karlskrona in the south of Sweden. He claimed he was told to leave his work pending the outcome of a personnel control which had to be carried out on him in accordance with the Personnel Control Ordinance 1969 (personal-kontrollkungörelsen 1969:446 - see paragraphs 18-34 below) The Government submitted that the applicant was employed only from 20 August to 31 August 1979. They further contended that in employing Mr. Leander the Director had committed two mistakes. The Museum possesses several storage rooms and historical objects within the area for the security of which the Chief of the Naval Base is responsible. The applicant complained to the Government and requested that the assessment of the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy be cancelled. He pointed out in particular that he had left a permanent position in Dalarna, in the North of Sweden, on being told that he was accepted for employment at the Naval Museum. In his original complaint, and also in a letter of 4 December 1979, Mr. Leander further requested that he be given information about the reasons for his not being accepted. The Government requested the opinion of the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces (överbefälhavaren), who in turn consulted the Commander in Chief of the Navy. The employment of Mr. Leander during this time, 15 August - 1 September 1979, did not involve any access to the Naval Base. The Commander-in-Chief of the Navy has said that he does not oppose such employment. The Director of the Naval Museum has, however, affirmed the requirement that Mr Leander should have access to. the Naval base. In view of the above and the fact that, if Mr.Leander was given access to  Naval Base, he would have access. to secret installations and information, the Commander-In-Chief. of the navy decided not to accept the applicant. The opinion of the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces was accompanied by a secret annex, containing the information on Mr. leander released by the National Police Board (rikspolisstyrelsen). This annex was never communicated to the applicant and has not been included in the material submitted to the Court. Government rejected the whole of the applicant’s complaint. No special reasons were found for not giving Leander access to the information. The Government do not examine Leander's request for a revised assessment of his person. Leander has lodged no appeal with the Government in respect of appointment. His request that the Government should declare him acceptable for the provisional employment concerned cannot therefore be examined. The remainder of Leander’S petition is a request to be given an extract from, or information about the contents of, a police register. At the relevant time, he had not belonged to any political party since 1976. Earlier he had been a member of the Swedish Communist Party. He had also been a. member of an association publishing a radical. He had been active in the soldiers’ union and a representative at a conference in 1972 which, according to him, had been infiltrated by the security police. His only criminal conviction stems from his time in military service and consisted of a fine of 10 Swedish Crowns for having been late for a military parade. The applicant asserted however that according to unanimous statements by responsible officials, none of the above-mentioned circumstances should have been the cause for the unfavourable outcome of the personnel control. He also had travelled a couple of times in Eastern Europe and was active in Swedish Building Workers’ Association and the Swedish Firefighters Association.

The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Sweden recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Art. 46) The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed violations by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 10 and 13. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality, and Mr. R. Ryssdal. President of the Chamber ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Swedish Government (“the Government’), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant regarding the need for a written procedure. He directed that the lawyer and, should he so decide, the Agent should each have until 4 February 1986 to file a memorial. The applicant’s memorial was received at the registry on 3 February. On 21 March, the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegates would present his observations at the hearing. On 28 April, the Commission communicated to the Registrar a number of documents whose production he had requested on the instructions of the President. On 12 May, certain additional documents furnished by the applicant were received. Torsten Leander is a Swedish citizen born in 1951 and a carpenter by profession. On 20 August 1979, he started to work as a temporary replacement in a post of museum technician (vikarierande museitekniker) at the Naval Museum at Karlskrona in the south of Sweden. The museum is adjacent to a restricted military security zone. The applicant maintained before the Court that the intention was that he should work for ten months in this post, while its ordinary holder was on leave. He alleged that on 3 September he was told to leave his work pending the outcome of a personnel control which had to be carried out on him. “On 22 October 1979, the applicant complained to the Government and requested that the assessment of the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy be cancelled. He pointed out in particular that he had left a permanent position in Dalarna, in the North of Sweden, on being told that he was accepted for employment at the Naval Museum’s premises” “The decision whether or not to employ you is taken in a procedure distinct from the present one,” the Navy commander said. “According to his information, the Director of the Museum required the person employed in the post in question to have free access to, and freedom to circulate in, the Naval Base’” The Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces considers that Mr. Leander may properly be employed by the Naval Museum provided that the. holder of the appointment does not require access to the Naval Base. The Commander-in-Chief of the Navy has said that he does not oppose such employment. The applicant requested that the Government should, before taking a decision on his request of 22 October 1979, give him the right to be apprised of and to comment upon the information thus released by the National Police Board. The Government sought the opinion of the Board. In its reply of 22 February 1980, the Board proposed that the applicant’s complaints be dismissed. ‘Under section 13 of the Personnel Control Ordinance, the person whom the information concerns ought to be given the opportunity to submit observations on the matter. However, the National Police Board did not see any cause to apply this provision in the case of the applicant as no special reasons were found, and also as the registering had been effected in accordance with the secret Royal Decree.’ ‘The Government do not examine Leander’s request for a revised assessment of his person and take no measure in regard to any other part of his petition' ‘Leander has lodged no appeal with the Government in respect of appointment. His request that the Government should declare him acceptable for the provisional employment concerned cannot therefore be examined’ During his military service, in 1971-72, he had been active in the soldiers’ union. His only criminal conviction stems from his time in military service and consisted of a fine of 10 Swedish Crowns for having been late for a military parade. The applicant asserted however that, according to unanimous statements by responsible officials, none of the above-mentioned circumstances should have been the cause for the unfavourable outcome of the personnel control. He also claimed that he had travelled a couple of times in Eastern Europe and had been involved in the Swedish Building Workers’ Association. He was found guilty of misconduct in a public office.

Leander argued that the Board should have communicated to him, at least orally and subject to a duty of confidentiality, the information kept on him. name: Fahriye Çetinkaya
train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants were arrested on suspicion of having participated in an illegal demonstration which took place in Ümraniye. The Court declared the applications partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicants’ alleged ill-treatment in police custody, the right to an effective remedy in this regard, and the length of their detention in police. custody. The applicants also complained about the alleged deprivation of their right to challenge the lawfulness of their. detention, and to compensation in this respect. The applicants were taken to the Forensic Medicine Institute for medical examinations both in the evening of 3 August 2001 and in the morning of 4 August 2001. The medical reports drafted on these dates concluded that there were no signs of blows on the applicants’ bodies. On 7 August 2001 the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court filed an indictment, charging the applicants with aiding and abetting the PKK under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. The applicants denied all the allegations made against them. They contended that they had been forced to sign police statements without reading their contents. The court ordered their detention on remand. The first applicant contended that, although there was no marks on her body, she had been tortured in police custody. The second applicant maintained that police officers had hit him, pulled his hair and insulted him. The applicants' lawyer filed two separate petitions with the Fatih public prosecutor, complaining about the applicants’ ill-treatment during their arrest and detention in police custody. November 2001 the first hearing was held before the Istanbul State Security Court. The court gave a decision of non-jurisdiction and transferred the case file to the Ümraniye Criminal Court of First Instance. The applicants were acquitted on account of lack of evidence in February 2004. The investigation against the police officers was closed in May 2002. The case is now pending at the Istanbul High Court of Human Rights and Human Rights Arbitration, which will decide whether or not the applicants should be charged with a crime.

The applicants were represented by Mrs F. Karakaş Doğan, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applications were brought by two Turkish nationals, Ms Fahriye Çetinkaya and Mr Akın Çağlayan, on 23 October 2001, 13 July 2002 and 6 May 2003. The applicants were taken to the Forensic Medicine Institute for medical examinations both in the evening of 3 August 2001 and in the morning of 4 August 2001. The medical reports drafted on these dates concluded that there were no signs of blows on the applicants’ bodies. On 7 August 2001 the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court filed an indictment, charging the applicants with aiding and abetting the PKK under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. The court ordered their detention on remand. The applicants denied all the allegations made against them. They contended that they had been forced to sign police statements without reading their contents. The first applicant contended that, although there was no marks on her body, she had been tortured in police custody. The second applicant maintained that police officers had hit him and pulled his hair. The applicants' lawyer filed two separate petitions with the Fatih public prosecutor, complaining about the applicants’ ill-treatment during their arrest and detention in police custody. The first hearing was held before the Istanbul State Security Court in November 2001. The court gave a decision of non-jurisdiction and transferred the case file to the Ümraniye Criminal Court of First Instance. On 16 February 2004 the court acquitted the applicants on account of lack of evidence. The investigation against the police officers against the applicants was later dropped. The applicants were acquitted of all charges against them and their release pending trial was ordered by the court.

name: William Faulkner
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37471/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the prison authorities had interfered with a letter from him to the Scottish Minister of State. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. It was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it partly admissible on 18 September 2001. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and the application was allocated to a new Second Section. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required.

name: Cahit Demirel
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18623/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to release pending trial, to take proceedings to challenge the lawfulness of his detention and to a fair hearing within a reasonable time. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant, Mr Cahit Demirel, was convicted as charged and sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment. The case against the applicant was transferred to the Diyarbakır Assize Court in 2004. The case was terminated in 2005 on the ground that the statutory time limit under Article 102 of the Criminal Code had expired. The applicant was convicted under Article 168 of the former Criminal Code and sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment. He was released from prison in 2003 pending trial. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on 9 October 2002. On 23 March 2004 the State Security Court once again convicted the applicant and sentenced him to 12 years and 6 months' imprisonment. On 19 October 2004 the Court ofCassation quashes the judgment. On 2 May 2005 the Assize court decided that the proceedings should be terminated as the applicant had not appealed.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to release pending trial, to take proceedings to challenge the lawfulness of his detention and to a fair hearing within a reasonable time. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment in 2001. The case was heard by the Diyarbakır State Security Court on 11 September 2007. The court ruled on the merits of the case on 25 December 2001 and sentenced the applicant to 12 years and 6 months' imprisonment. The case against the applicant was transferred to the Diyarbakır Assize Court. The applicant was sentenced to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 23 March 2004. On 2 May 2005, the judge decided that the proceedings should be terminated as the statutory time limit under Article 102 of the Criminal Code had expired. This decision to terminate the case became final as neither the applicant nor the public prosecutor appealed. The case was dismissed on 8 June 2007 and the case was dropped. The application was dismissed again on 8 January 2008. The judge dismissed the application on 8 February 2008 and the judge's decision was overturned on 9 February 2008.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26718/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who was born in 1985 and lives in İzmir, was a student at a military academy. He was expelled from the academy following a secret security investigation conducted by the Ministry of Defence into him and his family. The court acknowledged that the security investigation had revealed that his father had previously been convicted of forgery. It further held that this information justified the applicant's expulsion under the relevant laws and regulations. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 17350/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. The first two applicants, a married couple, were born in 1935 and 1944 respectively and live in Klippan. The third applicant was a limited liability company wholly owned by the first two applicant. The court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The case was decided in favour of the applicants on 26 September 2006. The company was declared bankrupt on 7 September 1994. The bank paid the company the remainder of the loan on 28 June 1993. The company tried to find other customers and reiterated its request to the bank to receive the remainder. The court rejected the bank's request for the company's and Boket Konsult AB's action to be dismissed due to lack of standing. The parties asked the court to rule on the alleged breach of contract in a partial judgment in February 1997. An oral preparation was held on 7 April 1998. On 29 September 1998 the court sent a summary of the cases to the parties and, by a decision of 30 September 1998, it rejected the request for apartial judgment. Boket's action was struck out of the court's list on 17 January 2000. The applicants appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) On 5 February 2002, following a hearing, the appellate court agreed with the District Court's reasoning and upheld its judgment. On 29 November 2002, after the applicants had been granted several respites to complete their submissions, the Supreme Court refused the applicants leave to appeal. By a judgment of 27 April 2001, the district court found in favour of the bank. It noted that 2 million SEK of the loan had been pledged by the company at the time when the loan contract had been concluded.

name: Maciej Maksym
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 14450/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. name: Laleş Çeliker
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that she had been denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was brought by a Turkish national, Ms Laleş Çeliker (‘the applicant’), on 25 June 2001. She was charged with carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. Diyarbakır State Security Court held nineteen hearings and heard a number of witnesses. The applicant renounced her statements taken during her detention in police custody. Witnesses heard by the court stated that the applicant was an active member of the PKK and that she had been involved in armed clashes with the security forces. Taking into account her confessions before the court, the death penalty was commuted to a life sentence of imprisonment. On 19 December 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the first instance court. It reasoned that the decision was justified as the evidence in the case file was capable of proving the applicant's membership of an illegal organisation.

name: Alan Wainwright
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that they had been strip-searched when seeking to visit a relative in prison. The applicant, but not the Government, filed further observations (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The Government made comments on just satisfaction of the applicants' case. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Chamber declared the application admissible in December 2005. The applicants were taken to the north gatehouse at HMP Armley, Leeds. They were told they would be strip-searched and if they refused would be denied their visit to Mr O’Neill. The first applicant was told to take off her jumper and vest. She was then instructed to remove her shoes, socks and trousers, which she did. The second applicant was then taken to separate rooms for the searches. The search of the first applicant took place in a small room overlooking the road in front of the prison and the administration block beyond it. The application was denied on the grounds that the room was too dark. The applicants were told that they would not be able to return to the prison until the search was complete. The first applicant was standing naked apart from her underwear. She was told to pull down her underwear and then told to spread her legs. Her sexual organs and anus were visually examined. By this time she was crying. On her request, she was returned her vest and allowed to put it back on. After she had been told to put her clothes back on, one of the officers approached the first applicant and asked her to sign the form to consent to a strip-search (F2141) The first applicant told the officers that she might as well sign it as there was by that stage nothing else the officers could do to her and she then did so without reading it. The applicants were led back to the prison to proceed with their visit. During the visit, the first applicant told Mr O’Neill what had happened. The first applicant went into the toilet where she cried and vomited about four times. The second applicant felt shaken and nervous and was upset. On returning home, she removed her clothes and bathed because she felt upset, angry and dirty. Because of her experience, she did not visit Mr O'Neill for a further four months. In October 1998, in the context of the civil proceedings, she was examined by Dr Sims, Professor of Psychiatry. Dr Sims considered that the severe upset that she had experienced in the prison made her existing depression (for which she was receiving medication at the time of the visit) worse. The first applicant had intrusive recollections of her time at the prison and psychological distress at anything that resembled her experience. For about five weeks after the incident, he would not see his girlfriend, baby son, friends or anyone else and spent large amounts of his time in his bedroom. He was also examined by Dr Sims in October 1998. Dr Sims concluded that the second applicant was suffering from PTSD (scoring 15 on the DSM-IV scale) and had a depressive illness. He predicted some improvement, with appropriate treatment, within one to two years. The County Court upheld the applicants’ civil claims against the Home Office, holding that the searches constituted a trespass. The Home Office claimed the strip-search was an invasion of privacy. The trial judge held that the prison authorities had not adhered to their own rules. The court disagreed that trespass to the person could be extended to fit these circumstances and found that no wrongful act had been committed. Lord Chief Justice Woolf noted that there were numerous ways in which drugs could be smuggled into prison and that the most vigorous regime of searching prisoners would not in itself suffice. He found therefore that a search of Mr O’Neill would have been inadequate. He awarded the first applicant a total of 2,600 pounds sterling (GBP) and the second applicant 4,500 (comprising GBP 3,500 basic damages and GBP 1,000 aggravated damages) The court set aside the first-instance judgment and substituted an award of a total of GBP 3,750 to the second applicant for battery. The Wainwrights were upset about having to be searched but made no complaint about the manner of the search. The court found that the prison officers acted in good faith and that there had been no more than ‘sloppiness’ in the failures to comply with the rules. The only inexplicable act was the search of Alan’s penis, which they were unable to explain because they could not remember having done it. But this has been fully compensated. Although Article 8 guarantees a right of privacy, I do not think that it treats that right as having been invaded and requiring a remedy in damages. The applicants said the House of Lords should find that there was (and in theory always had been) a tort of invasion of privacy under which the searches of the applicants were actionable and damages for emotional distress recoverable. Lord Hoffmann stated that a merely negligent act should, contrary to general principle, give rise to a claim for damages for distress because it affects privacy rather than some other interest like bodily safety. The European Court is concerned only with whether English law provides an adequate remedy in a specific case in which it considers that there has been an invade of privacy contrary to Article 8. The court expressed some impatience, at paragraph 103, at being given a tour d’horizon of the remedies provided and to be provided by English law to deal with every imaginable kind of privacy. The coming into force of the Human Rights Act 1998 weakens the argument for saying that a general tort of invasion of privacy is needed to fill gaps in the existing remedies. Sections 6 and 7 of the Act are in themselves substantial gap fillers. This is an area which requires a detailed approach which can be achieved only by legislation rather than the broad brush of common law principle.” For these reasons I would reject the invitation to declare that since at the latest 1950 there has been a previously unknown tort of invaded privacy’. The creation of a general Tort will pre-empt the controversial question of the extent, if any, to which the Convention requires the State to provide remedies for invasions of privacy by persons who are not public authorities.

The case was brought by two British nationals, Mary and Alan Wainwright, on 2 April 2004. The applicants complained that they had been strip-searched when seeking to visit a relative in prison, relying on Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. By a decision of 13 December 2005, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The applicant, but not the Government, filed further observations (Rule 59 § 1), but the Chamber decided there was no need for them. The Government made comments on just satisfaction of the applicants' claims. Governor ordered all Mr O’Neill’s visitors to be strip-searched before visits. The applicants were told they would be denied their visit if they did not comply. They were then taken to separate rooms for the searches. The first applicant was told to take off her jumper and vest. One of the officers searched them whilst the other officer walked around her, examining her naked upper body. The second applicant was then instructed to remove her shoes, socks and trousers, which she did. The search of the first applicant continued until she was naked. The application was accepted and the applicants were returned to prison. The first applicant was told to pull down her underwear and spread her legs. She was then told to bend forward and her sexual organs and anus were visually examined. The officer inspecting her body then asked the first applicant to pull her vest up again, asking for it to be raised higher and higher until it was above her breasts. The first applicant asked why that was necessary since they had already inspected her top half, but the officer ignored her and continued walking around her body. By this time she was crying and was standing naked apart from her underwear. On her request, she was returned her vest and allowed to put it back on. The second applicant was taken to a separate room by two male officers. The applicants were led back to the prison to proceed with their visit. During the visit, the first applicant told Mr O’Neill what had happened. The first applicant went into the toilet where she cried and vomited about four times. The second applicant felt shaken and nervous and was upset. On returning home, she removed her clothes and bathed because she felt upset, angry and dirty. Because of her experience, she did not visit Mr O'Neill for a further four months. In October 1998, in the context of the civil proceedings, she was examined by Dr Sims, Professor of Psychiatry. Dr Sims considered that the severe upset that she had experienced in the prison made her existing depression (for which she was receiving medication at the time of the visit) worse. The first applicant had intrusive recollections of her time at the prison and psychological distress at anything that resembled her experience. For about five weeks after the incident, he would not see his girlfriend, baby son, friends or anyone else and spent large amounts of his time in his bedroom. He was also examined by Dr Sims in October 1998. He concluded that, as a result of her aversive experience in the prison, the first applicant would be more vulnerable to future traumatic events and more prone to depressive reaction. Dr Sims concluded that even after recovery the second applicant would remain vulnerable to further symptoms with lesser provocation than previously. The County Court upheld the applicants’ civil claims against the Home Office, holding that the searches constituted a trespass. Court of Appeal allowed the Home Office’s appeal. The court disagreed that trespass to the person could be extended to fit these circumstances and found that no wrongful act had been committed. He found therefore that a search of Mr O’Neill would have been inadequate. The judge rejected the applicants’ submission that Article 3 was relevant, holding that although strip-searches were unpleasant they did not amount to inhuman or degrading treatment. He awarded the first applicant 2,600 pounds sterling (GBP) and the second applicant a total of GBP 4,500 (comprising GBP 3,500 basic damages and GBP 1,000 aggravated damages) The court set aside the first-instance judgment and substituted an award of a total of GBP 3,750 to the second applicant for battery. The House of Lords upheld the judgment of the Court of Appeal and dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Wainwrights were upset about having to be searched but made no complaint about the manner of the search. The only inexplicable act was the search of Alan’s penis, which the prison officers were unable to explain because they could not remember having done it. Although Article 8 guarantees a right of privacy, I do not think that it treats that right as having been invaded and requiring a remedy in damages. Lord Hoffmann said there was no reason to adopt a high level principle of privacy. The European Court is concerned only with whether English law provides an adequate remedy in a specific case, he said. The court expressed some impatience, at paragraph 103, at being given a tour d’horizon of the remedies provided and to be provided by English law to deal with every imaginable kind of invasion of privacy, Lord Hoffmann added. But in my opinion it shows no more than the need, in English law, for a system of control of the use of film from CCTV cameras which shows greater sensitivity to the feelings of people who happen to have been caught by the lens. Human Rights Act 1998 weakens the argument for saying that a general tort of invasion of privacy is needed to fill gaps in the existing remedies. Sections 6 and 7 of the Act are in themselves substantial gap fillers. This is an area which requires a detailed approach which can be achieved only by legislation rather than the broad brush of common law principle. The applicants complained that they had been strip-searched when seeking to visit a relative in prison. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The Government made comments on just satisfaction of the application. Governor ordered that all Mr O’Neill’s visitors be strip-searched before visits. Neither of the applicants had ever been to a prison before. They were taken across the courtyard from the south gatehouse by four or five prison officers. One of the officers stated that they had reason to believe that the applicants were carrying contraband. When the first applicant asked what this meant, she was told that he was referring to drugs. The first applicant was taken by two female officers into a small room which had windows overlooking the road in front of the prison and the administration block beyond it. Although there were roller blinds on the windows, they were not pulled down. The first applicant was crying and visibly distressed. She believed that anyone outside the prison looking at the windows in the room where she was being strip-searched could have seen her in a state of undress. She was worried that if she protested too much she would not be allowed in to visit Mr O’Neill. Although none of the officers touched her, she felt threatened by their actions and considered that she had no alternative but to comply with their instructions. The first applicant told the officers that she might as well sign it as there was by that stage nothing else the officers could do to her and she then did so without reading it. The first applicant went into the toilet where she cried and vomited about four times. The second applicant felt shaken and nervous and was upset. The applicants did not stay for the full length of their visit. The first applicant stated that she still thought about the strip-search about once a week, continued to get upset about it, remained angry about what had happened and had difficulty sleeping. In October 1998, in the context of the civil proceedings, she was examined by Dr Sims, Professor of Psychiatry. Dr Sims considered that the severe upset that she had experienced in the prison made her existing depression (for which she was receiving medication at the time of the visit) worse. The first applicant had intrusive recollections of her time at the prison and psychological distress at anything that resembled her experience. For about five weeks after the incident, he would not see his girlfriend, baby son, friends or anyone else and spent large amounts of his time in his bedroom. He was also examined by Dr Sims in October 1998. He concluded that, as a result of her aversive experience in the prison, the first applicant would be more vulnerable to future traumatic events and more prone to depressive reaction. Dr Sims concluded that even after recovery the second applicant would remain vulnerable to further symptoms with lesser provocation than previously. The trial judge found that the strip-searches were an invasion of their privacy exceeding what was necessary and proportionate to deal with the drug smuggling problem. The court disagreed that trespass to the person could be extended to fit these circumstances and found that no wrongful act (save for the battery against the second applicant) had been committed. On 20 December 2001 the Court of Appeal allowed the Home Office’s appeal. Lord Chief Justice Woolf noted that there were numerous ways in which drugs could be smuggled into prison and that the most vigorous regime of searching prisoners would not in itself suffice. He found therefore that a search of Mr O’Neill would have been inadequate. The Wainwrights were upset about having to be searched but made no complaint about the manner of the search. The only inexplicable act was the search of Alan’s penis, which the prison officers were unable to explain because they could not remember having done it. Although Article 8 guarantees a right of privacy, I do not think that it treats that right as having been invaded and requiring a remedy in damages, irrespective of whether the defendant acted intentionally, negligently or accidentally. It is one thing to wander carelessly into the wrong hotel bedroom and another to hide in the wardrobe to take photographs. Lord Hoffmann said there should be a tort of invasion of privacy under which searches of applicants were actionable. He added that the European Court of Human Rights is not concerned with whether English law provides an adequate remedy in a specific case. In Earl Spencer v United Kingdom 25 EHRR CD 105 it was satisfied that the action for breach of confidence provided an adequate. remedy for the Spencers’ complaint and looked no further into the rest of the armoury of remedies available to the victims of other invasions of privacy. But the court expressed some impatience, at paragraph 103, at being given a tour d’horizon of the remedies provided and to be provided by English law to deal with every imaginable kind of invasion. The coming into force of the Human Rights Act 1998 weakens the argument for saying that a general tort of invasion of privacy is needed to fill gaps in the existing remedies. Sections 6 and 7 of the Act are in themselves substantial gap fillers. This is an area which requires a detailed approach which can be achieved only by legislation rather than the broad brush of common law principle. The creation of a. general tort will pre-empt the controversial question of the extent, if any, to which the Convention requires the State. to provide remedies for invasions of privacy by persons who are not public authorities.” For these reasons I would reject the invitation to declare that since at the latest 1950 there has been a previously unknown tort of invade of privacy’

train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented by Mr H. Graupner, a lawyer practising in Vienna. The Austrian Government (“the Government’s Agent”) was represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The first applicant was convicted under section 209 of the Criminal Code of having committed homosexual acts with an adolescent and sentenced to a fine of ATS 4,500 (approximately EUR 330) with 75 days’ imprisonment in default. The second applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Austria. The second applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed homosexual acts with an adolescent contrary to section 209 of the Criminal Code. He was sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment, 14 of which were suspended on probation. On appeal the Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the second applicant’s appeal on points of law. On 7 July 2002 he requested a pardon and a further stay of execution pending the decision on his request for pardon. On 23 September 2002 the Federal President granted him a remission of the remaining sentence. His sentence was later reduced to ten out of fifteen months of imprisonment. The second applicant has since been released from detention on remand.

name: Ronald Easterbrook
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his tariff as a discretionary life prisoner had not been set at trial by a judge but had been fixed by the Secretary of State after a long delay and without an oral hearing. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case. The Court declared the application admissible in a decision of 26 September 2002. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59: 3 in fine). The applicant fired six shots, wounding one police officer in the leg. The applicant received a superficial wound to his shoulder. He was arrested and immediately detained. The Court of Appeal also rejected the applicant’s appeal against sentence. At this hearing the applicant was again not represented. On 5 February 1998, the Home Secretary agreed to certify that the applicant should be subject to the arrangements for the release of discretionary life prisoners, despite having previously qualified the applicant as someone serving a mandatory life sentence. The decision also set the tariff of the applicant's sentence at 16 years, expatriate. The first review of the case by the Parole Board would be in November 2004. The applicant’s solicitors made written submissions as to the appropriate length of the tariff and submitted that the applicant should be entitled to an oral hearing before the Lord Chief Justice. On 27 November 1998, the Prison Service informed the applicant's solicitor that the Home Secretary had decided on a tariff of 12.5 years, to expire in May 2000. On 8 January 1999, the applicant made an application for judicial review. The application was dismissed on 11 February 1999. The applicant became eligible for Parole Board review procedures. He has stated however that he has decided not to participate in the procedures due to his continuing belief that the Government have breached his human rights and still refuses to acknowledge those breaches.

name: Jadwiga Hulewicz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35656/97) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her case had not been heard within a reasonable time in breach of Article 6 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. By a decision of 12 November 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. In 1994 the Słupsk Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) amended the first-instance judgment. The applicant twice requested the Minister of Justice to grant her leave to file an extraordinary appeal with the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court quashed both judgments given in the applicant’s case and remitted the case to the court of first instance. It held that the lower courts had committed serious errors of fact and law. The Lębork District Court joined the applicant's case with similar proceedings against seven other members of the co‑operative. In 2002 the applicant appealed against this judgment.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 473/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 29 April 2008 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application. On 21 July 2006 the Gdynia District Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to one year and six months’ imprisonment and a fine of 800 Polish zlotys (PLN) The applicant appealed. On 11 December 2006 his appeal was dismissed by the Gdańsk Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). The Regional Court found that there were no delays for which the District Court could be held responsible. Pointing to the complexity of the case and the voluminous documentation gathered in the proceedings it held that the proceedings had been conducted with due diligence and within a reasonable time.

name: Karin Andersson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29878/09) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway. The applicants own property close to Umeå, in the vicinity of a Natura 2000 area, the European network of nature protection areas established under the EU Habitats Directive of 1992. Most of them live there (permanently or on a part-time basis) The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. The property owners claimed that the decision contradicted Swedish law as well as applicable European Union law, including the Habitats Directive. The distance from their properties to the “corridor” or the specific stretch of the railway fixed in later proceedings vary; the houses appear to be situated 300 – 2500 metres away. The closest piece of land is located about 50 metres from the ‘cor Corridor’. The court ruled that the Government’s decision should be quashed. NRA applied to the County Administrative Board in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. They also asked the Environmental Court in Umeå for permits to build two bridges. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the petitions for a judicial review because it was not possible to determine who should be considered an interested party at that stage of the railway planning. The Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, considering itself bound by the Government’s decision of 12 June 2003, the court decided to grant all permits requested by the NRA. On 21 June 2005 the NRA adopted a railway plan for the area in question. On 26 April 2007 the Environmental Court decided anew to grant the permits requested by the NRA. The Environmental Court of Appeal affirmed the binding nature of the Government’s permissibility decision and approved the construction of the railway and the bridges with certain added conditions. On 9 May 2008 the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused leave to appeal. The Supreme Administrative Court, after having held a hearing in the case, rejected the petition, finding that the railway plan was in line with the EU Habitats Directive. The court considered itself bound by the Government's decision. Government had not been obliged to review its decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissibility of the railway project and the designation of the ‘corridor’ in which the railway could be located.
