Case originated in an application (no. 29878/09) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway, in violation of their rights under Articles 6 and 8. The applicants own property close to Umeå, in the vicinity of a Natura 2000 area, the European network of nature protection areas established under the EU Habitats Directive of 1992. The NRA applied to the Government for permission, under the Environmental Code (Miljöbalken), to construct a 10 km long railway section. The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. The property owners claimed that the decision contradicted Swedish law as well as applicable European Union law, including the Habitats Directive. A number of individual property owners, including three of the applicants in the present case, petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) for a judicial review of the case and requested that the Government’s decision be quashed. The case was settled in January 2011. The NRA applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. The Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, considering itself bound by the Government’s decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissibility of the railway project, the court decided to grant all the permits requested by the NRA. On 15 June 2006 the Environmental Court of Appeal (Miljööverdomstolen) in Stockholm quashed the judgments and referred the cases back to the latter instance. Twelve applicants – all but Ms Holmström, Mr Härestål and Mr Höjer – appealed to the Government against the railway plan. They essentially complained of the specific stretch of the railway, invoking, inter alia, nuisance such as noise and vibrations affecting the enjoyment of their property. The Supreme Administrative Court, after having held a hearing in the case, rejected the petition, finding that the railroad plan was in line with the European Convention on Human Rights and the EU Habitats Directive. The court considered itself bound by the Government’s decision as to the permissibility of the project and thus limited its examination to the environmental compensation measures. The Government’s permissibility decision was binding for the subsequent proceedings in that courts and other decision-making bodies could not examine issues that had been determined by that decision. The Government had not been obliged to review its decision of 12 June 2003. The adoption of a railway plan had direct consequences for the individual as it entailed a right for the railway company, under certain conditions, to expropriate land. According to the dissenting judge, a full judicial review had also been foreseen by the court in its earlier decision. At least ten of the applicants have received some form of compensation as a consequence of the railway construction. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values. name: Jan-Åke Andersson
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden on 8 and 28 June 1990 respectively. It originated in an application (no. 11274/84) against Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Jan-Åke Andersson, a Swedish national, on 16 October 1984. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). On 30 June 1990 the President of the Court decided under Rule 21 para. 6 and in the interest of sound administration of justice, that a single Chamber should be constituted to consider both the instant case and the Fejde case. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government, Mrs Thune for the Commission and Mr Arnewid for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. On 23 November 1990 the Chamber decided unanimously, under Rule 51, to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. At the final deliberations Mr Cremona, the Vice-President of the Court, replaced Mr Ryssdal as President, the latter being unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rule 9). Mr Andersson refused to pay a fine for driving a. tractor on a highway (motortrafikled), on which this was prohibited under the Traffic Ordinance of 1972. He maintained that he had not seen any road sign indicating the category of the road or the prohibition in question. The applicant's appeal against this decision was dismissed by the Court of Appeal (hovrätten) of Skåne and Blekinge on 15 June 1983, with no possibility of further appeal. On 21 September 1983 the District Court held a hearing (huvudförhandling) during which both the applicant and police inspector B. were heard. It did not, however, order the production of the relevant meteorological records. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal of Skåne and Blekinge. He claimed that the proceedings before the District Court had been ‘unbalanced’ and that numerous ‘interruptions’ by the judge had prevented him from following the arguments and from presenting his case in a satisfactory manner. He also applied for a public hearing to be held in Karlskrona, for police inspector B. to be heard as a witness and for the relevant meteorological records to be examined. In its judgment of 10 February 1984, upholding the findings of the District. Court, it stated: ‘The fact that the weather was misty does not relieve him from his obligations as a driver. He shall therefore be convicted in accordance with the charge against him’ Mr Andersson applied for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (högsta domstolen), claiming that the appeal proceedings had been very “unbalanced’ and had not complied with human-rights standards. The Supreme Court refused the application on 26 April 1984. “From the photos which have been referred to, it appears that the fact that the road in question was a ‘motortrafikled’ did appear from appropriate and visible road signs at Stensnäs. For this reason and since [the applicant] nevertheless drove the tractor on [the road] he committed the offence with which he has been charged by the prosecution.”

name: Dariusz Pasiński
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The charges against the applicant included leading an organised criminal group, leading participation in several robberies and illegal possessing of firearms. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was born in 1968 and is presently detained in the Koszalin Detention Centre. The bill of indictment was directed against twenty‑two co‑accused. The trial court prolonged the applicant’s detention relying on the strong probability that the applicant and 13 co‑accused had committed the offences with which he had been charged. The court also considered that, given the severity of the penalty that might be expected, the applicant might obstruct the proceedings. That decision was upheld on appeal on 13 January 2004. On 16 April 2004 the court granted the application while noting the prolonged application of preliminary detention with respect to the applicant. At the hearing held on 2 June 2004 the trial court further prolonged the detention of the applicant, and other accused. The application for release was dismissed on 22 October 2003. The trial court held 43 hearings during which it heard 86 witnesses and the depositions of 130 other witnesses were read at the hearings. On 21 July 2004 the Opole Regional Court gave judgment. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to twelve years’ imprisonment. On 19 April 2005 the Wroclaw Court of Appeal partly dismissed the applicant’s appeal and lowered the sentence against him to eleven years' imprisonment. However, it is not clear whether a cassation appeal had actually been lodged. It appears that the applicant was appointed for the applicant a legal-aid lawyer with the purpose of lodging on his behalf a cassated appeal.

name: Vereinigung Bildender Künstler
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68354/01) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant association alleged that the Austrian courts' decisions forbidding it to continue exhibiting a painting by Otto Mühl had violated its right to freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26: 1. By a decision of 30 June 2005 the Court declared the application admissible. The decision was published in the current issue of the Vienna-based International Court of Justice. Former general secretary of the FPÖ (FPÖ) was shown in sexual positions with Bishop Groer and Mother Teresa. Mr Meischberger sought an injunction against the exhibition after a visitor covered his face and body in red paint. He argued the painting debased him and his political activities and made statements as to his allegedly loose sexual life. The Vienna Commercial Court dismissed his action and ordered the painting to be removed from the exhibition. It noted that it had initially been intended to show a different group of people, and that the original intention was to show the same people in a different way. The painting has since been restored to its original form. Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) issued an injunction against the applicant association prohibiting it from continuing to display the painting at exhibitions. It noted that Mr Meischberger's picture was only partly covered by red paint, so that part of his face, the shape of his head and his hairstyle were still recognisable. The court further added that there appeared to be no danger of recurrence (Wiederholungsgefahr) as the painting had been partly covered with red paint and MrMeischberger was therefore no longer recognisable on it. The limits of artistic freedom were exceeded when the image of a person was substantially deformed by wholly imaginary elements. The applicant association could not justify the exhibition of the painting under the artistic freedom protected by Article 17a of the Basic Law (Staatsgrundsgesetz) The painting in the present case was not intended to be a parable or even an exaggerated criticism conveying a basic message, such as, for example, the statement that Mr Meischberger had disregarded sexual decency and morals. It therefore did not fall within the scope of Article 10 of the Convention, but in fact constituted a debasement of Mr Meischerberger's public standing (Entwürdigung öffentlichen Ansehens)

The case originated in an application (no. 68354/01) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant association alleged that the Austrian courts' decisions forbidding it to continue exhibiting a painting by Otto Mühl had violated its right to freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared the application admissible by a decision of 30 June 2005. The case was decided in favour of the applicant association and against the Austrian Government. The decision was made by a jury of three judges. The painting showed members of the Austrian National Assembly in sexual positions. The eyes of some of the persons portrayed were hidden under black bars. The painting was damaged by a visitor, who covered with red paint the part which showed, among others, Mr Meischberger. He sought an injunction prohibiting it from exhibiting and publishing the painting. The Vienna Commercial Court (Handelsgericht) dismissed this action on 6 August 1999. It noted that it had initially been intended to show a group of politicians in sexual situations with Bishop Groer and Mother Teresa. After the incident of 12 June 1998, which had further increased the publicity given to the painting, the painting was shown at another exhibition. The Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), after having held an oral hearing, granted an appeal on points of law and fact by Mr Meischberger. The court issued an injunction against the applicant association prohibiting it from continuing to display the painting at exhibitions. It ordered it to pay the costs incurred by the claimant in the proceedings and ATS 20,000 (EUR 1,453.46), plus 4% interest with effect from 8 July 1998, in compensation. The limits of artistic freedom were exceeded when the image of a person was substantially deformed by wholly imaginary elements without it being evident, the court said. The applicant association could not justify the exhibition of the painting under the artistic freedom protected by Article 17a of the Basic Law (Staatsgrundsgesetz) The Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) rejected an appeal by the applicant association as it did not concern a legal question of considerable interest. The Court of Appeal had not questioned the. fact that the painting fell within the scope of protection provided by Article. 17a but, weighing the guarantee of artistic freedom enshrined in. that provision against Mr Meischberger's personal rights as protected by section 78. of the Copyright Act, had considered that the latter prevailed over the. former because a picture of Mr Meischerberger had been used in a degrading and insulting manner.

The court found that it could be ruled out that the painting had adversely affected the claimant or divulged information about his private life. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5989/03) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that civil proceedings initiated by her had not been determined within a reasonable time. The case was assigned to the newly constituted Fifth Section of the Court on 1 April 2006. The circumstances of the case can be summarised as follows: The applicant was born in 1948 and lives in Hundested. She suffered severe problems with her jaw, resulting in her being able to open her mouth only 5 millimetres. In April 1990 she had Teflon implanted in both her jaw-joints. In February 1992, alleging mal‑practice, she complained to the National Patients' Complaints Board. The applicant claimed compensation for her medical costs, loss of working capacity and disablement. The applicant instituted proceedings before the City Court of Hillerød against the County of Frederiksborg (Frederiksborg Amt) The case was re-submitted to the Medico‑Legal Council on 17 June 1994 with further questions. The National Board of Health issued their opinion on 10 October 1994. At some time during 1994, the applicant was awarded anticipatory pension. The City Court requested that the parties inform it of what was holding up the case, and indicated that it would be set down for trial should it go ahead. The City Court ordered the parties to file their pleadings within three weeks. The parties requested an adjournment of the proceedings in October 1996. In December 1996 the City Court agreed to obtain the applicant's patient files from three hospitals and to draft questions to the Medico-Legal Council, when the material was available. The City Court ruled that the parties could proceed with their pre-trial proceedings without the assistance of the court. name: Steven Phillips
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41087/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the statutory assumption made against him by the court which issued a confiscation order following his conviction for a drug offence violated his right to the presumption of innocence. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). It was declared partly admissible on 30 November 2000. The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry [Note by the Registry]. An inquiry was conducted into the applicant’s means, pursuant to section 2 of the Drug Trafficking Act 1994 (‘the 1994 Act’ – see below) The applicant had previous convictions, but none in respect of a drug-related offence. The investigation officer concluded that the applicant had benefited from drug trafficking and that the total benefit was GBP 117,838.27. On 12 July 1996 he was sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment in respect to this offence. the Customs and Excise Management Act 1979. The applicant was found to have become a director of a newsagents business in July 1992 of which his parents were the sole shareholders. He was the registered owner of five cars of an estimated total value of approximately GBP 15,000. The applicant filed a written statement in response, in which he denied having benefited from drug trafficking. He explained that in 1990-91 he had been convicted of car theft and required to pay GBP 25,000 to the insurance company which had indemnified the victims. The investigation officer filed a second statement in accordance with section 11(1) of the 1994 Act. The applicant filed documentary evidence and affidavits in support, primarily, of his claim no longer to own the house. The judge observed: “It is for the prosecution to establish, of course, on a balance of probabilities that he has benefited from drugs trafficking’ The judge held that the applicant had failed to take obvious, ordinary and simple steps which would clearly have been taken if his account of the facts had been true. Instead of calling as witnesses the alleged purchaser of the house, X, and other individuals for whom he claimed to have bought and sold cars, the applicant called only himself, his father and a solicitor. The judge also held that X’s purported purchase payment of GBP 50,000 had in fact been a benefit of drug trafficking. There are real indications on the civil basis of proof that [X] was complicit in the crime of which the accused was convicted. The judge said it was impossible, in his judgment, to see any sensible reason other than that he did not cash a cheque. The judge assessed the applicant to have benefited from drug trafficking to the extent of GBP 91,400. ‘I have seen what must have been a fraction of his dealings, and I am satisfied that the GBP 11,400 must be treated as a benefit,’ said the judge. The jury were told the applicant was a ‘general wheeler-dealer, having specialised at one stage in cars, more recently in mobile telephones, but willing to deal in anything which would offer a profit' The judge allowed him three years in which to pay the confiscation order, with a period of two years’ imprisonment to be served in default of payment. The applicant was refused leave to appeal against conviction and sentence (including the imposition of the confiscations order) His application to renew leave to launch an appeal against his conviction was refused on 22 January 1998 after a full hearing before the Court of Appeal. In view of the difficulties inherent in realising the applicant’s share of the family business, the judge allowed the applicant to pay just over £100,000. He was sentenced to two years in prison and a confiscation of more than £90,000, plus a fine.

The application was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that the statutory assumption made against him by the court which issued a confiscation order following his conviction for a drug offence violated his right to the presumption of innocence. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court and was declared partly admissible on 30 November 2000. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 February 2001 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Ms H. Fieldsend, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr D. Perry, Counsel, Ms M. Dyson, Home Office, Mr P. Vallance, Advisers. The Court heard addresses by Mr Pearse Wheatley and Mr Perry. An inquiry was conducted into the applicant’s means, pursuant to section 2 of the Drug Trafficking Act 1994 (“the 1994 Act’ – see below) The applicant had previous convictions, but none in respect of a drug-related offence. The investigation officer concluded that the applicant had benefited from drug trafficking and that the total benefit was GBP 117,838.27. On 12 July 1996 he was sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment inrespect of this offence. the Customs and Excise Management Act 1979. The applicant declined to take part in the interview. He was also found to have become a director of a newsagents business in July 1992. The applicant denied having benefited from drug trafficking. He claimed that he had sold the house for GBP 50,000 to X in order to clear this debt. He denied owning any part in the newsagents business. He alleged that his only realisable assets were some GBP 200 in a building society account and the fittings of a garage rented from the local authority. The judge observed: “It is for the prosecution to establish, of course, on a balance of probabilities that he has received any payment or reward in connection with drug trafficking” The judge ordered the house to be confiscated on 24 December 1996. The case was heard at the Crown Court and the judge ruled that the house should be confiscated. The judge found the prosecution’s allegation that the applicant still owned the house to be correct. He held that the purported purchase payment of GBP 50,000 had in fact been a benefit of drug trafficking. The judge stated: “The assumption to be made is plain, and the accused has neither shown that it is incorrect nor demonstrated a risk of injustice. Just as the jury did not believe Mr Phillips, neither do I. What has happened here, in my judgment, is a device of just the sort providing a cover to explain the transfer of money which one would expect to find in concealing benefit from drug trafficking” The judge said it was impossible, in his judgment, to see any sensible reason other than that he did not cash a cheque; that it was a simple payment. The judge assessed the applicant to have benefited from drug trafficking to the extent of GBP 91,400. He next calculated the value of the realisable property held by the applicant as follows: “For the reasons that I have given above I am satisfied that [the applicant] is in fact the drug trafficker’s son.” The judge concluded: ‘Even within a family I find the purchase of a share of a business for GBP 50,000 entirely without documentation simply unbelievable.’ The judge allowed him three years in which to pay the confiscation order, with a period of two years’ imprisonment to be served in default of payment. The judge said that the applicant still has a one-third interest with his parents in the [newsagents business]. He and his father said the business was worth GBP 150,000 in 1993. There is no evidence that it is worth any less now, and I therefore find his realisable share in the equity in that business to be worth £50,000. Since I am satisfied as to GBP 100,000 realisable sums, that figure exceeds the GBP 91,400 and under section 5 I find the amount to be recovered to be that figure.

The judge stated: “The assumption to be made is plain, and the accused has neither shown that it is incorrect nor demonstrated a risk of injustice. Just as the jury did not believe Mr Phillips, neither do I. What has happened here, in my judgment, is a device of just the sort providing a cover to explain the transfer of money which one would expect to find in concealing benefit from drug trafficking” The judge described the defendant as a 'general wheeler-dealer' who specialised in cars and mobile telephones. He said that it was impossible, in his judgment, to see any sensible reason other than that he did not cash a cheque. The judge assessed the applicant to have benefited from drug trafficking to the extent of GBP 91,400. He next calculated the value of the realisable property held by the applicant as follows: “For the reasons that I have given above I am satisfied that [the applicant] is in fact the applicant’s property.” The judge concluded by saying: ‘I think family loyalty has overcome his honesty.’ The judge allowed him three years in which to pay the confiscation order, with a period of two years’ imprisonment to be served in default of payment. In view of the difficulties inherent in realising the applicant’s share of the family business, the judge allowed the applicant three years to pay. On 28 January 1997 the applicant was refused leave to appeal against conviction and sentence (including the imposition of the confiscating order) His application to renew leave to Appeal against conviction was refused on 22 January 1998 after a full hearing before the Court of Appeal. He was sentenced to two years in prison and a fine of GBP 91,400. The judge ruled that the amount to be recovered was that figure.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of the Republic of Austria. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Türk, Mrs Bernegger and Mrs Gartner for the Government, Mr Frowein for the Commission and Mr Blum for the applicant, as well as their answers to its questions. Mr Obermeier, who resides at Linz, was formerly employed by a private insurance company (‘the company’) as the director of their regional branch office for Upper Austria. Court decided not to have regard to them on account of the lateness of their submission of documents, whose production had not been requested. In 1974 a dispute arose between the applicant and the company concerning various paid activities which it proposed to withdraw from him. On 10 March 1978, the day following the first hearing, he was suspended from his duties by his employer. The company considered that it was entitled to take such a decision at any time without giving reasons. The applicant alleged in particular that the measure in question was designed to penalise him for having instituted legal proceedings against the company and was therefore unjustified. On 23 April 1981 the Linz Labour Court dismissed the applicant’s claims. The case was therefore remitted to the Labour Court. The court dismissed the remainder of the appeal, finding that, under Article 228 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Zivilprozessordnung), a declaratory judgment may bear only on the existence of a legal relationship. On 21 May 1980 Mr Obermeier had been declared disabled for the purposes of that Act. On 8 May 1981, the company had sought the authorisation of the Disabled Persons Board for the applicant’s dismissal. Following a hearing, the Board gave its consent to the dismissal on 8 July 1981, finding that the relationship of trust between the parties had been irremediably undermined. The Provincial Governor (Landeshauptmann) for Upper Austria confirmed this decision on 16 October 1981. The applicant then appealed to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) which dismissed his appeal on 9 March 1983. The application to the European Commission of Human Rights was declared inadmissible on 12 March 1986. The company pleaded Mr Obermeier’s lack of a legal interest (Rechtsschutzbedürfnis) in the revocation of his suspension, since in the meantime he had been dismissed. The applicant, for his part, challenged the lawfulness of his dismissal. He stressed in particular that it had been pronounced before the authorisation from the Disabled Persons Board had become final, as the case was still pending before the Administrative Court. The company sent to the applicant, on 21 December 1984, a further notification of dismissal, which was to take effect on 30 June 1985. On appeal, the applicant appealed on points of law to the Supreme Court which quashed the decisions of the labour courts. The case was brought by Mr Obermeier against the company. The company had dismissed him before the authorisation had become final. The Provincial Governor gave retroactive consent to the applicant’s first dismissal. The Board and the Provincial Governor found, on 10 February 1986 and 12 January 1987 respectively, that they lacked jurisdiction to make such a declaration. The applicant then asked the Board to declare, pursuant to sections 8 to 12 of the Disabled Persons (Employment) Act, that his employment contract subsisted. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on points of law lodged on 7 October 1985. The third round of proceedings concerning the suspension of his employment began on 1 June 1986. The case was heard by the Administrative Court and the Constitutional Court. The Supreme Court did not take into account the applicant’s appeal to the Constitutional Court and the Administrative Court. The Supreme Court stated that it was not for the civil courts to review the decisions of the administrative authorities. The company had not waited until the authorisation given by the Disabled Persons Board had become final in law and had in addition failed to inform the works council, as it was required to do under section 105 § 1 of the Industrial Relations Act (Arbeitsverfassungsgesetz, see paragraph 46 below) The parties did not appeal from this decision. The Labour Court found that Mr Obermeier had never been validly dismissed. It took the view that the effects of the prior authorisation giving by the Board were not permanent. The case involves the dismissal from employment of a disabled man in 1984. The company appealed the dismissal, which was set aside on 15 March 1988. The applicant appealed on a point of law against the Court of Appeal’s judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 29 June, holding that section 105 of the Industrial Relations Act did not apply to a disabled person. In September 1988 the applicant instituted new proceedings in the Linz Regional Court, sitting as a social and labour court. He relied on the judgment delivered by the Administrative Court on 21 May 1986. name: María Iglesias Gil
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56673/00) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr J. Thomas Mulet, of the Palma de Mallorca Bar. The Spanish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. J. Borrego BorreGo, Head of the Legal Department for Human Rights at the Ministry of Justice. The Court heard addresses by the above-mentioned representatives. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. By a decision of 5 March 2002 the Chamber declared the application admissible. María Iglesias Gil, born in 1961, lives in Vigo. She is the mother of the second applicant, A.U.I., who was born in 1995. The first applicant lodged a criminal complaint with Vigo investigating judge no. 5 alleging child abduction. On 1 February 1997 A.u.A. abducted his son during an access visit and left Spain with him. After passing through France and Belgium, he travelled with the child by air to the United States. In a decision of 20 December 1996, the Vigo Family Court awarded the first applicant custody of A. U.I. and the father access. On 4 February 1997 the investigating judge made orders for a nationwide search to be made. A wanted notice was issued for A.U.A. U.S.A., but in an order of 29 May 1997, he declined, stating that the offences of coercion and extortion have not been made out. It is debatable whether there has been an offence of criminal contempt, since it has not been proved that the person concerned was ordered to comply with the judgment of the family court. An international search and arrest warrant is not justified, as the conduct complained of appears to come within Article 622 of the Criminal Code, which characterises it as a minor offence. A wanted notice has been issued for U.N.A.: As soon as he has been traced, final provision 19 of Institutional Law no. 1/1996 of 15 January 1996 on legal protection of minors can be applied. The first applicant sought amparo relief under Articles 24 (right to a fair hearing) and 15 ( right to life and mental and physical integrity) of the Constitution. An appeal by the first applicant was dismissed by the Pontevedra Audiencia Provincial on 9 November 1998. In a decision of 2 June 1999, the Constitutional Court dismissed her appeal as manifestly ill-founded, holding that she had not stated why she disagreed with the reasoned decisions of the lower courts. The first applicant lodged a second appeal in May 1999. A.U.A. was charged with child abduction, but the charges were dismissed in July 1998. The mother of a missing child in Spain filed an amparo appeal against the decisions of the criminal courts. She alleged violations of Article 17 (right to liberty and security) of the Constitution. She also relied on Articles 5 and 8 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child of 1989. In a decision of 17 June 1999, the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal as unfounded, holding that the first applicant had confined herself to contesting the criminal court's decisions. The case is still ongoing and the mother of the missing child is still waiting for her son to be returned to her after the family court allowed him to leave the country. Vigo Family Court withdrew parental responsibility from A.U.A. of 22 February 1999. An application for the proceedings to be declared null and void was likewise dismissed. On 18 April 2000 the first applicant saw her son for the first time since his abduction in February 1997. The first applicant lodged a criminal complaint alleging threatening behaviour and coercion. On 30 September 2000 Vigo investigating judge no. 6 made a provisional discharge order. That order was quashed by the Pontevedra Audiencia Provincial in a decision of 15 May 2001. Renewal of contact between first applicant and her son, the return of the child and further criminal complaints were all successful. The first applicant was able to recover her child with police assistance on A.U.A.’s return to Vigo with the child. She said that for a time she was forced to go into hiding with her son in a shelter for women. The relevant provisions of the Constitution read as follows: Article 10 § 2 “Provisions relating to the fundamental rights and the freedoms recognised by the Constitution shall be construed in accordance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights ...” Article 39 § 4 “Children shall enjoy the protection provided for in the international agreements safeguarding their rights.”Article 96 § 1 “Once officially published in Spain, international treaties that have been validly concluded shall be part of the domestic legal order” “The removal or the retention of a child. is to be considered wrongful where: (a) it is in breach of. rights of custody attributed to a person, an institution or any other body, either jointly or alone, under. the law of the State in which the child was habitually resident immediately before the removal or retention.” “A Contracting State shall designate a Central Authority to discharge the duties which are imposed by the Convention upon such authorities. ...” Article 7 “Central Authorities shall cooperate with each other and promote cooperation amongst the competent authorities in their respective States to secure the prompt return of children” Article 8: Any person, institution or other body claiming that a child has been removed or retained in breach of custody rights may apply to the Central Authority of the child’s habitual residence. Article 11: The judicial or administrative authorities of Contracting States shall act expeditiously in proceedings for the return of children. Article 12: If a child is wrongfully removed, a period of less than one year has elapsed from the date of the wrongful removal or retention, the authority concerned shall order its return forthwith. Article 13: The authority concerned is not bound to order a child's return if the person opposing its return establishes that the person is not actually exercising custody rights. The law is based on a law passed in 1996 on the legal protection of minors in Spain. The law is in line with the U.N. Convention on the Rights of the Child, which was signed by Spain in 1989. A court can order the return of a child if it finds it is in an intolerable situation. It can also refuse to order the child's return if the child objects to being returned and has attained an age and degree of maturity at which it is appropriate to take account of its views. The public authorities shall guarantee compliance with the rights of minors and shall ensure their decisions comply with this law and the aforementioned international instrument, the law says. The Spanish courts have refused to characterise a failure by a person with parental responsibility for a minor to return the child as false imprisonment or kidnapping. Under the case-law, a person guilty of such conduct may only be prosecuted for criminal contempt or extortion under Article 556 of the Criminal Code, for which the punishment is six months’ to one year’s imprisonment. A parent who, without any justification, abducts his or her minor child shall be liable on conviction to between two and four years’ imprisonment and shall forfeit his/her parental responsibility. The Law inserted a new Article 225 bis in the Criminal code, worded as follows: “1. transferring a minor from his place of residence without the consent of the parent ...” The penalty for failing to return a minor in material breach of an obligation arising under a judicial or administrative decision will be in the upper half of the range set out in paragraph 1. The penalties stated in this Article shall also apply to any person from whom the minor is descended or any relative of the parent by blood or marriage up to the second degree who has committed the aforementioned acts. The penalty for not returning a minor to Spain will be the same as the penalty for neglecting to return him or her to a foreign country when he or she is under the age of 18. The sentence for neglect will also apply if the child is removed from Spain or a condition is imposed for its return.

name: Andrzej Pakos
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time’ within the meaning of Article 5:3. The court considered that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings given the risk that he might obstruct them. In their decisions, the courts repeatedly relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged, the serious nature of the offences, and the severity of the likely sentence. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant. The prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment with the Katowice Regional Court against the applicant and 32 other co-accused. The prosecutor requested 22 witnesses to be heard. After 15 March 2006 the applicant’s detention was extended three more times and the measure has still not been lifted. The applicant has appealed against all those decisions, apart from the one given on 24 October 2007, and on 6 February 2008, he is still in detention. The judge in the case has ruled that the applicant can be treated in detention due to his health and his family situation. He is being held in a prison in the city of Krakow, Poland. The applicant is still detained and the proceedings before the first-instance court have not yet been terminated. The suspicion was justified, in the court’s view, by the charge of acting in an organised criminal group. The applicant was detained on suspicion of the serious nature of the offences with which he had been charged, the severity of the penalty to which he was liable and the risk that he might obstruct the proceedings. The first-institution court has ruled in favour of the applicant but the Court of Appeal has ruled against him and ordered him to be released on bail while the appeal is heard. The appeal was upheld on the same grounds as the first court.

The case originated in an application (no. 3252/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. He is currently detained in the Katowice Remand Centre. In their decisions, the courts repeatedly relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged, the serious nature of the charges and the severity of the likely sentence. The Court will examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). In December 2004 the prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment with the Katowice Regional Court against the applicant and 32 other co-accused. The prosecutor requested 22 witnesses to be heard. The applicant appealed against the decision to extend his detention. After 15 March 2006 the applicant’s detention was extended three more times and the measure has still not been lifted. In January 2007 the applicant's lawyer requested the court to vary the preventive measure. The court refused the request, again invoking the serious nature of the offences with which the applicant had been charged and the risk that he would obstruct the proceedings. The judge in the case found that the applicant can be treated in detention. The applicant is still detained and the proceedings before the first-instance court have not yet been terminated. The suspicion was justified, in the court’s view, by the charge of acting in an organised criminal group. The applicant is currently being held in a Polish detention centre. He is being held on suspicion of aggravated membership in a criminal group and acting in an organised criminal group. The appeal was successful on the grounds of the serious nature of the offences with which he had been charged and the severity of the penalty to which he was liable. He was also accused of obstructing the proceedings.

name: Anthony White
train_texts: The applicant lives in Beira, Mozambique. He brought a private prosecution against the newspapers through their legally responsible editors (ansvariga utgivare) He claimed that the editors were responsible for gross defamation, or alternatively defamation of a normal degree. He also joined an action for damages to the private prosecution and sought compensation for mental suffering and pecuniary damage. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the right to respect for private and family life to the Government. In accordance with Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The District Court put to the jury 66 questions relating to the articles published in Expressen. The jury answered all but six questions in the negative. In accordance with the applicable rules, the jury’s finding of ‘no guilt’ was final. The court then had to make a re-assessment of liability. The contravening statements or pictures were the following: “He is pointed out as PALME’S MURDERER” [“Han pekas ut som PALMES MÖRDARE”] together with a picture of the applicant. “In addition to Long reach, Williamson and White had several companies together, some with links to the Mafia.” Anthony White is one of southern Africa’s biggest poachers, tells a source. It is to a large degree his fault that the elephants in Mozambique are all but extinct. Together with Williamson, Anthony White appropriated the ivory. By a judgment of 24 February 2000, the District Court acquitted the editors in all respects and rejected the applicant's claims for damages. It found the editors had acted in good faith and had not intended to injure the reputation of Anthony White or any of the elephants they had been involved in poaching. The court also found that the editors’ conduct had not been ‘grossly negligent’ or ‘reckless’. The Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s judgment in 2002. A balance has to be struck between the protection against offensive statements and the demands of freedom of speech. In certain situations the interest of protecting someone against offensive statement has to yield to the public interest. If the information is correct it may as a rule be communicated even if it is deprecatory, if this is justifiable. However, there is no general right always to speak the truth if the statements are offensive. The court found that it had been justifiable to publish the relevant statements and pictures. It further considered that the newspapers had had a reasonable basis for the published information. The Court of Appeal agrees with the District Court’s assessment that it was obviously legitimate to write about the so-called “South Africa trail’ The question is whether it was justified to identify the plaintiff by name and picture in the manner employed and to publish statements to the effect that he was supposed to be guilty of large scale, serious criminality. The information in the case reveals that Anthony White has been much better known than he has wished to admit in southern Africa and among representatives of various organisations for the protection of animals and the conservation of nature. In view of the above, and for the reasons given by the District. Court in this respect, the Court of. Appeal finds that itwas justifiable in the circumstances to publish Anthony White’‘s name and pictures in Expressen and to. publish information about the person Anthony White in Aftonbladet. Expressen and Aftonbladet have asserted that Anthony White’s name and picture have been published in international news media and on Swedish television. In their defence, [the responsible editors] have also pointed out that, despite time constraints, they had careful checks made which gave an unequivocal picture of Anthony White. The fact that the information had already been published by other media shows, however, that these news services might have considered that there was a reasonable basis for the information. ... Having regard to the above, in particular the checks made, and the informant Dirk Coetzee has given the impression of being a credible person, the Court of Appeal considers that the communication of the identifying information does not appear unjustified. Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused the applicant leave to appeal. The Court of Appeal further considers that Aftonbladet, in the circumstances, must be considered to have performed the checks that were called for. Having regard to this and the reasons. given with respect to the publication in Expressen, the Court of. Appeal finds that there was also a reasonable basis for the assertions in Aft on. the assertion and the reproduction of the picture in. Expressen’s. “Afton Bladet’.” It was published on 29 May 2002.

The case originated in an application (no. 42435/02) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant lives in Beira, Mozambique, and was represented by Mr E. Kalman, a lawyer practising in Stockholm. The Swedish Government were represented by their Agent, Ms I. Kalmerborn, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The District Court put to the jury 66 questions relating to the articles published in Expressen. The jury found that certain published statements or pictures amounted to defamation of a normal degree. The court then had to make a re-assessment of liability. The contravening statement or pictures were the following: The heading on the front page stating “He is pointed out as PALME’s MURDERER” [“Han pekas ut som PALMES MÖRDARE”] together with a picture of the applicant. The text on page 6: “In addition to Long reach, Williamson and White had several companies together, some with links to the Mafia.” Anthony White is one of southern Africa’s biggest poachers, tells a source. It is to a large degree his fault that the elephants in Mozambique are all but extinct. The District Court acquitted the editors in all respects and rejected the applicant's claims for damages. By a judgment of 24 February 2000, the District Court found the editors were not responsible for the actions of Anthony White and his associates and acquitted them of any wrongdoing. The judge also found that the editors had not broken any laws or regulations in connection with the use of ivory. The editors were also acquitted of any wrong-doing in relation to the sale of ivory by White, and of any of his associates. The Svea Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s judgment. A balance has to be struck between the protection against offensive statements and the demands of freedom of speech. If the information is correct it may as a rule be communicated even if it is deprecatory, if this is justifiable with reference to the public news interest. However, there is no general right always to speak the truth if the statements are offensive. The information has been liable to expose him to the contempt of others and consequently, as such, constitutes defamation. The question then is whether there are grounds for excluding liability. Expressen has claimed that, on account of the public interest, it was justifiable to name and show a photograph of Anthony White in the newspaper. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his pre-trial detention had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3. The court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The case was decided on 9 February 2009 by the President of the Fourth Section of the Court. The decision was made to rule in favour of the applicant and to order his release. The case has been adjourned until the end of May 2010. On 5 December 2006 a bill of indictment was lodged with the Gdańsk Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). The applicant was charged with drug trafficking. The bill of indicted comprised numerous charges of drug trafficking brought against twenty-one defendants. Although several defendants were charged with acting as part of an organised criminal group, the applicant himself was not charged with being a member of such a group. The courts underlined the unique nature of the proceedings involving drug-trafficking, which often took more time because offences and suspects emerged gradually. Finally, referring to Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, they referred to the severity of the penalty to which the applicant was liable. The applicant's detention had reached the statutory two-year time limit. The Gdańsk Regional Court applied to the Court of Appeal, asking for his detention to be extended beyond that term. The court extended his detention on 20 February 2008 (to 31 March 2008) and 19 March 2008 ( to 30 June 2008). The applicant appealed against the decision of 20 Feb 2008 but the appeal was dismissed on 11 March 2008. The applicant lodged an interlocutory appeal against the above‑mentioned decision, arguing that, before being arrested, he had lived and worked in Denmark and that, by prohibiting him from leaving Poland, he was being prevented from joining his family and taking up his former job. The criminal proceedings against the applicant are still pending. Gdańsk Court of Appeal dismissed his complaint as unfounded. It found that, out of about eighteen hearings scheduled in the case, only a few had been adjourned. The court further stated that, in December 2007, no hearing could be scheduled because the applicant had dismissed his legal-aid counsel and had been given time to appoint one of his choice. The Court of appeal concluded that the proceedings had been conducted with the requisite speed and without undue delay. Back to Mail Online home. Back into the page you came from. train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 35109/06 and 38112/06) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged in particular that the quashing of their convictions by the Independent Administrative Panel upon an official complaint by the relevant Federal Minister violated Article 6 and Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. They also complained under Articles 6 and 13 about the length of the proceedings and lack of an effective remedy in that respect. The President of the First Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) On 8 April 2002 the Braunau District Administrative Authority found the applicant guilty of the offence of drunk driving. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,162 on him with seventeen days’ imprisonment in the event of default. The applicant appealed, repeating his argument as regards the alleged imprecision of the breathalyser test. The Independent Administrative Panel (Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat) allowed the applicant’s appeal in part. In its decision of 17 June 2002 it found that an alcohol level of 0.59 mg/l could be considered to have been confirmed, since allowance had to be made for a possible inaccuracy. On 18 September 2002 the Federal Minister for Traffic, Innovation and Technology lodged an official complaint (Amtsbeschwerde) against that decision. On 18 February 2005 the Administrative Court, following the official complaint, quashed the Independent Administrative Panel’s decision of 17 June 2002 and referred the case back to it. It found that the decision had applied the law incorrectly, since there was no ground to make allowance for inaccuracy in the breathalyser test. Consequently, his conviction under section 99(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act was upheld. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court, claiming several violations of Article 6 of the Convention. Mr Ortmair (application no. 38112/06) was stopped by a traffic patrol and asked to undergo a breathalyser test. The test showed an alcohol level of 0.60 mg/l in his breath. The applicant was found guilty of drunk driving under sections 5(1) and 99(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act. He was sentenced to a fine of EUR 872.07 with 13 days’ imprisonment in the event of default. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint as being unfounded on 23 May 2006. This decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 21 June 2006. The applicant appealed on 24 January 2002. The Independent Administrative Panel allowed the applicant’s appeal in part. The Federal Minister for Traffic, Innovation and Technology lodged an official complaint under Article 131(1) subparagraph (2) of the Federal Constitution. The Administrative Court quashed the decision of 19 March 2002 and referred the case back to it. The case was dismissed in January 2005 after the applicant submitted observations to the Administrative Court. The application was dismissed as there was not enough evidence to prove the applicant had a net income of EUR 1,100 per month and no maintenance obligations. The fine was reduced to EUR 700, with nine days' imprisonment in the event of default. The Independent Administrative Panel dismissed an appeal by the applicant against the penal order of 17 January 2002. Applying the Administrative Court’s legal view, it held that an alcohol level of 0.60 mg/l had been established by the breathalyser test. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court on 19 May 2005. He raised complaints identical to the ones raised by the first applicant (see paragraphs 19‑21 above). The applicant made submissions on 5 September 2005 to supplement his complaint. The Administrative Court, referring to its previous decision, dismissed the applicant's complaint as unfounded. The judgment was served on the applicant’S counsel on 14 August 2006.

The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged in particular that the quashing of their convictions by the Independent Administrative Panel violated Article 6 and Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. They also complained under Articles 6 and 13 about the length of the proceedings and lack of an effective remedy in that respect. The application was brought by two Austrian nationals, Mr Jochen Penias and Mr Walter Ortmair. The Government was represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. The applicant was found guilty of the offence of drunk driving under sections 5(1) and 99(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act. The fine was reduced to EUR 1,000 with fourteen days’ imprisonment in the event of default. The applicant appealed, repeating his argument as regards the alleged imprecision of the breathalyser test. In its decision of 17 June 2002 it found that an alcohol level in the applicant’s breath of 0.59 mg/l could be considered to have been confirmed, since allowance had to be made for a possible inaccuracy. There was documentary evidence, and also evidence from an expert on weights and measurements, that for this particular type of breath analyser 5% inaccuracy could not be ruled out. The Federal Minister for Traffic, Innovation and Technology lodged an official complaint (Amtsbeschwerde) under Article 131 (1) subparagraph (2) of the Federal Constitution. The Administrative Court, following the official complaint, quashed the Independent Administrative Panel’s decision of 17 June 2002 and referred the case back to it. It found that the decision had applied the law incorrectly, since there was no ground to make allowance for inaccuracy in the breathalyser test. The applicant then lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court, claiming several violations of Article 6 of the Convention. He submitted that the proceedings had been unreasonably lengthy and that he had no remedy in this respect. The applicant was convicted of drunk driving after a breathalyser test showed an alcohol level of 0.60 mg/l in his breath. He claimed that his conviction had been based on a mere presumption. He also claimed that the proceedings had been reopened following the Federal Minister’s official complaint. The Administrative Court dismissed his complaint as being unfounded on 23 May 2006. This decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 21 June 2006. He was sentenced to a fine of EUR 872.07 with 13 days’ imprisonment in the event of default. The case was dismissed for lack of prospects of success on 13 June 2005. Upper Austria Independent Administrative Panel held a hearing on 12 March 2002. It questioned the applicant and an expert on weights and measurements. The offence therefore fell under section 99(1)(b) of the Road Traffic Act. The fine was to be reduced to EUR 700, with nine days’ imprisonment in the event of default. The applicant did not lodge a complaint with the Administrative Court or the Constitutional Court within the statutory six-week time- limit. The Administrative Court, following the official complaint, quashed the Independent Administrative panel’s decision of 19 March 2002 and referred the case back to it. The case was settled out of court in 2005. The applicant was found guilty of driving with an alcohol level of 0.60 mg/l in his breath. The judge found that the breathalyser test did not provide for a conclusion to be drawn from the result of the test. He was sentenced to 13 days in prison but the sentence was reduced to 10 days because of the lengthy duration of the proceedings. The case was then referred to the Administrative Court. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint as unfounded on 14 July 2006. The judgment was served on the applicant’s counsel on 14 August 2006. An appeal by the applicant against the penal order of 17 January 2002 was dismissed in March 2005.

train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 26761/95) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The judge said that there were no compassionate circumstances to allow the applicant to attend his mother's funeral. On 6 August 1994 the applicant made a second application for compassionate leave. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 10424/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been detained for a period of ninety-one days in an overcrowded room at the Foreigners' Department of the Istanbul Security Headquarters. On 29 September 2009 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant has been living in Istanbul on renewable temporary residence permits since September 2004. The Government stated that the applicant had been held in the men's section of the Foreigners' Department of the Istanbul Security Headquarters, which measured 220 square metres. There were three toilets, two showers, twenty bunk beds, a television, two telephones, two air conditioners and a cafeteria. Breakfast, lunch and dinner were served every day. Asylum seekers could be visited by their relatives in the visitors' room. Those who needed medical help were taken to the local State hospital and their medical expenses were born by the State. According to the Government all the rooms were sufficiently lit and ventilated. They were cleaned twice a day.

The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of having stabbed a certain A.T. during a quarrel and being under the influence of alcohol. The trial court justified its decisions by reference to the high probability that the applicant had committed the offence and the gravity of the charges, which might attract a heavy sentence. At the same time, the court rejected the prosecutor’s assertion that there was also a risk of collusion. The applicant’s numerous applications for release and appeals against decisions concerning prolongation of his detention were to no avail. It appears that the applicant did not lodge a cassation appeal and that this judgment became final on 27 January 2005. The letter bears signs of having been opened after being sealed: its left side has been cut open and then resealed with sellotape.

name: Andrzej Wyszczelski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 72161/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Andrzej Wyszczelski. The applicant was born in 1941 and lives in Pruszków, Poland. He claimed PLZ (old zlotys) 100,000,000 from the insurance company “PZU” as compensation for his traffic accident. He also claimed a supplementary disability pension. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The case was opened in 1997, and the case was closed on 18 December 2000. On 15 January 2001 the Warsaw Regional Court gave judgment and ordered the insurance company to pay PLN 25,000 to the applicant. On 25 April 2002 the Warsaw Court of Appeal gave judgment. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy). On 3 March 2005 the applicant filed a complaint with the Warsaw court about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (“2004 Act’) The Court of appeal dismissed the complaint as manifestly ill-founded on 25 April 2005.

The appeal was dismissed again on 3 March 2005 under the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9120/80) against the Republic of Austria, lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 1 September 1980. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. G. Wiarda, the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b). On 27 March 1985, the. President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members, namely Mrs. D. Bindschedler-Robert, J. Pinheiro Farinha, Mr E. García de Enterría and Mrs. J. Ganshof van der Meersch. The Government and the applicant produced documents at the hearings. The Court heard their addresses as well as their replies to its questions. The hearings were held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. There appeared before the Court: H. Türk, Legal Adviser, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, M. Matzka, Federal Chancellery, H. Epp, Federal Ministry of Justice, Advisers;. Gaukur Jörundsson, Delegate, Commission. Mr F. Krall, Rechtsanwalt, Counsel. R. Macdonald, substitute judges (Rule 24 § 1). The applicant's wife and step-daughter attacked him at about midday during a quarrel. He claimed that his wife had inflicted several head wounds with a paper-knife and gashed his forehead close to his eyebrow. He admitted that he had pushed his wife at the time and had tried unsuccessfully to slap his step- daughter in the face. Miss Tappeiner admitted having called her step-father a “convict’ (Zuchthäusler) that morning, and said he had responded by slapping her. She said neither she nor her mother had deliberately caused him any wounds to the head or face. She added that a doctor she had consulted had issued a certificate in respect of her own injury. Wörgl police sent the Kufstein District Court (Bezirksgericht) a report (Strafanzeige) “concerning Alois Unterpertinger and Rosi Unter pertinger, suspected of causing actual bodily harm (Körperverletzung)’ The police went on to say that they had already had to intervene in several quarrels in the household. They added that the three protagonists had given conflicting accounts of the incident on 14 August. Miss Tappeiner who had been questioned as an informant (Auskunftsperson) had clearly taken her mother’s side. Alois Unterpertinger was accused of kicking his wife in the arm on 9 September 1979. He denied injuring his wife, saying that her hand had already been bandaged when he had come home. She had actually attempted to hit him on the head with a hairbrush, but had missed and collided with the stair-rail instead. As the wife of the accused (Beschuldigter), she was entitled to refuse to give evidence. The Kufstein District Court decided on 9 November 1979 to open an investigation against the applicant in respect of the two incidents. After separating the proceedings against Mrs. Unter pertinger inrespect of the first incident, the District Court acquitted her on 28 January 1980. The case was heard on 10 March 1980 by a judge of the Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht), sitting alone. The applicant pleaded not guilty. He admitted that he had hit his step-daughter on the head, but not that she had injured her. He said he had not seen his wife come into contact with the stair-rail and added that he was not sufficiently agile to have been able to kick her thumb. At the request of the Public Prosecutor’s Department, the documents it had mentioned in its application for leave to prosecute (Strafantrag), including the police reports, the accused's criminal record and two files relating to previous convictions of his, were read out. Mr. Unterpertinger was sentenced to six months' imprisonment in 1979. He had struck his step-daughter in the face, bruising her between the eye and nose and scratching her close to her right eye. On 9 September, he had broken his wife's right thumb by kicking her. The court found no mitigating circumstances; on the contrary, it saw the applicant’s criminal record as an aggravating circumstance. In this instance too, the applicant had acted deliberately. The appeal proceedings began on 9 April 1980. He argued that the judgment of 10 March was null and void (Article 281(1)(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure) In spite of Article 152, his former wife and step- daughter had not been informed at the time of his conviction. Innsbruck Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) asked to quash conviction of 10 March and acquit him. Failing this, he asked it to review his sentence in the light of the degree of his guilt. Court decided to re-examine the evidence submitted to the court of first instance and to supplement it (Wiederholung und Ergänzung) by having the file on the divorce proceedings read out and hearing testimony from the wife of Mr. Unterpertinger’s brother. She was unable to say whether the applicant’�s former wife had had a bandage on her. Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal immediately after the hearing on 4 June 1980. Court of Appeal was of the opinion that the evidence it had heard confirmed the findings of the Regional Court. The victims’ statements to the police were plausible and credible; their account of the incident was logically coherent. He had not been acting in self-defence on 14 August 1979. The sentence imposed was consistent with the degree of his guilt (schuld). Except for his sister-in-law, it was unnecessary to hear the witnesses the applicant had sought to have called, since he had referred to them in connection with matters that were either of no importance or else extremely vague. The applicant served his sentence from 22 September 1980 to 22 March 1981. The Commission declared the application admissible on 8 July 1983. In its report of 11 October 1984 the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been no breach of paragraph 3 (d) of Article 6 (art. 6-3-d) The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment. The Court was requested by the Government, “to find that the Republic of Austria violated several provisions of the Convention in these criminal proceedings“ and to require the Republic. of Austria to pay appropriate compensation“.

The applicant, Mr. Unterpertinger, complained of criminal proceedings brought against him. He is an Austrian national born in 1938, lives in Wörgl and is married with three children. He admitted that he had pushed his wife at the time and had tried unsuccessfully to slap his step- daughter in the face. The report was accompanied by several documents, including the statements made by the applicant, his wife and his step-daughter and the certificate issued by the doctor who had examined Miss Tappeiner. The applicant had appeared in person at the police station ten minutes later holding a paper-knife; he had explained that his wife had struck him on the head with it several times. The second incident, which took place on 9 September 1979, was reported to the Wörgl police. Alois Unterpertinger and his wife had a quarrel on 9 September. He kicked his wife's right arm, causing it to be broken. She accused him of injuring her with a hairbrush, but he said she had hit him with a stair-rail instead. The Wörgl police sent a report to the Kufstein District Court on 20 October 1979. On 3 December 1979, she appeared before a judge, who told her that, as the wife of the accused (Beschuldigter), she was entitled to refuse to give evidence. She replied that she nonetheless wished to do so, and gave an account of the facts in dispute. The District Court acquitted her on 28 January 1980. The case was heard on 10 March 1980 by a judge of the Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht), sitting alone. The applicant pleaded not guilty. According to the record of the hearing, the applicant admitted that he had hit his step-daughter on the head. He admitted slapping his wife in the face on 14 August. He added that he was not sufficiently agile to have been able to kick her thumb. In Austrian judicial practice these had to be regarded as documents for the purposes of Article 252(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. At the request of the Public Prosecutor’s Department, the documents it had mentioned in its application for leave to prosecute (Strafantrag), including the police reports, the accused's criminal record and two files relating to previous convictions, were read out. Mr. Unterpertinger was found guilty of causing actual bodily harm and causing grievous bodily harm to his wife and step-daughter. He was sentenced to six months' imprisonment. He appealed and the appeal proceedings took place in the spring of 1980. The court found no mitigating circumstances; on the contrary, it saw the applicant’s criminal record as an aggravating circumstance. The appeal proceedings were finally settled in September 1980. Mr. Unbertertinger and his ex-wife were divorced at the time of the appeal. The case was settled in the Supreme Court of Germany in October of that year, and Mr Unbertinger won his appeal. The Court of Appeal sat on 4 June 1980. Counsel for the applicant submitted the grounds of appeal and requested, inter alia, that additional witnesses be called by the court. The court decided to re-examine the evidence submitted to the court of first instance and to supplement it (Wiederholung und Ergänzung) by having the file on the divorce proceedings read out and hearing testimony from the wife of Mr. Unterpertinger’s brother. She was unable to say whether the applicant’'s former wife had had a bandage on her. Failing this, he asked it to review his sentence in the light of the degree of his guilt. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal immediately after the hearing on 4 June 1980. The victims’ statements to the police were plausible and credible; their account of the incident was logically coherent. Consequently, Mr. Unterpertinger's conviction on the two counts against him was justified; he had not been acting in self-defence. The Commission expressed the opinion that there had been no breach of paragraph 3 (d) of Article 6 (art. 6-3-d) The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Turkish national, Mr Selim Ünay (“the applicant’), on 17 June 2005. He was arrested in Istanbul during a bank robbery in July 1996. On 24 July 1996 he was brought before the investigating judge at the Istanbul State Security Court, who remanded him in custody. In October 2001 the Association, together with several local non-governmental organisations (NGOs), took part in a civil society movement. name: Tomasz Hołowczak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25413/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of murder, involvement in drug trafficking and illegal possession of a firearm. The court held eight hearings during which it heard evidence from sixty-six witnesses, as the applicant and the co-accused asked for all the witnesses to be heard during the hearing and for their testimony not merely to be read from the investigation file. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was heard from the beginning because of the inability of the lay judge to continue to sit in the case. On 13 January 2000 the court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment and forfeiture of his civic rights. On 28 March 2001 the Gdańsk Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and remitted the case to the Kołobrzeg District Procurator (Prokurator Rejonowy) for further investigation. The applicant’s detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. On 1 July 2005 the Szczecin Court of appeal upheld the conviction and sentence. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Szczecin Court of Appeal under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The applicant sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the Koszalin Regional Court had been excessive and an award of compensation in the amount of 10,000 Polish zlotys. On 6 November 2006 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. The court observed that even though the case had been pending for seven years, its length could not be considered unreasonable. It examined the course of the impugned proceedings and held that there were no delays for which the Regional Court could be held responsible.

The case originated in an application (no. 25413/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.
