The case was reopened on 10 December 2002. The applicant’s detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. On 31 May 2004 the Regional Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 1 July 2005 the Szczecin Court of Appeal upheld the conviction. The court repeated the grounds given in the previous decisions. In a number of hearings witnesses failed to appear and the court imposed fines on them. It appears that in the course of the proceedings the applicant made unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against refusals to release him and against decisions extending his detention. The case was settled on a verdict of not guilty. The applicant sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the Koszalin Regional Court had been excessive and an award of compensation in the amount of 10,000 Polish zlotys. The court observed that even though the case had been pending for seven years, its length could not be considered unreasonable. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 6 November 2006. The proceedings concerning a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time were described as 'extremely complex' in the judgment. The hearing was held on a regular basis and evidence from over 100 witnesses and several experts was obtained.

name: Robert Edward Miller
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 55853/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was represented before the Court by Mr Ulf Jacobson, a juris candidate practising in Stockholm. The Swedish Government (“the Government”) were represented by Mrs E. Jagander of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs as their Agent. The case was decided in favour of the applicant, who claimed he was unable to walk because of his Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Patient had incurred extra costs for medical treatment, foot rails, soft shoes, home assistance, and to some extent his food budget because of a limited ability to prepare meals. He also had to pay for the transportation service for disabled persons, and extra travel by personal car, because of his considerably reduced ability to walk. Social Insurance Office rejected the application, finding that the applicant's disability had not reached the level required under Chapter 9, section 2 before he turned 65 years of age. County Administrative Court refused the request with reference to section 9 of the Administrative Court Procedure Act (Förvaltningsprocesslagen 1971:291 - hereinafter “the 1971 Act”). The County Administrative Court rejected the applicant's appeal on the grounds that the medical and other evidence in the case showed that, even before he had reached the age of 65, he had for a considerable time been functionally impaired. The court noted that the applicant had “commented” (yttrat sig) on its rejection of his request for an oral hearing, but did not respond to his renewed request or his reasons invoked therein. The applicant appealed against the lower court's judgment to the Stockholm Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) requesting it to quash the judgment and refer the case back for fresh examination. The applicant was entitled to disability benefits at a level corresponding to 36 % of the basic amount as of July 1994. He further requested that the court hold an oral hearing, on the same grounds as those he had presented to the lower court. The Supreme Administrative Court refused him leave to appeal on 29 February 2000. In this connection the applicant was given a copy of an analysis presented by its legal secretary, which included an opinion to the effect that the County Administrative Court's refusal to hold a hearing was not deemed incompatible with the Convention. The application was rejected on the grounds that it breached Article 6 of the Convention by refusing to hold the hearing.

The case originated in an application (no. 55853/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Swedish Government were represented by Mrs E. Jagander of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs as their Agent. The applicant was represented before the Court by Mr Ulf Jacobson, a juris candidate practising in Stockholm. The application was lodged on 9 April 1999. On 9 December 2003 the Court decided. to communicate to the Government the complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the. Convention concerning the refusal to hold an oral hearing. The patient had incurred extra costs for medical treatment, foot rails, soft shoes, home assistance, and to some extent his food budget because of a limited ability to prepare meals. He also had to pay for the transportation service for disabled persons, and extra travel by personal car, because of his considerably reduced ability to walk. On 16 July 1997 the Social Insurance Office (försäkringskassan -hereinafter ‘the Office’) of the County of Stockholm rejected the application, finding that the applicant's disability had not reached the level required under Chapter 9, section 2 before he turned 65 years of age. On 15 January 1998 the County Administrative Court refused the request with reference to section 9 of the Administrative Court Procedure Act (Förvaltningsprocesslagen 1971:291) The applicant appealed against the lower court's judgment to the Stockholm Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) requesting it to quash the judgment and refer the case back for fresh examination. By a judgment of 13 February 1998 the County Administrative Court rejected the applicant's appeal on the grounds that the medical and other evidence in the case showed that, even before he had reached the age of 65, he had for a considerable time been functionally impaired, but not to such a degree that, on an assessment of the overall need of assistance, he was entitled to disability benefit. The court noted that the applicant had “commented” (yttrat sig) on its rejection of his request for an oral hearing, but did not respond to his renewed request. The applicant was entitled to disability benefits at a level corresponding to 36 % of the basic amount as of July 1994. He further requested that the court hold an oral hearing, on the same grounds as those he had presented to the lower court. The Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) rejected the applicant's request for a hearing and gave him three weeks within which to submit additional written observations. On 29 February 2000 it refused him leave to appeal. In this connection the applicant was given a copy of an analysis presented by its legal secretary, which included an opinion to the effect that the County Administrative Court's refusal to hold a hearing was not deemed incompatible with the Convention.

The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case is currently being heard by the Court of Appeal in Copenhagen, Denmark. The applicant is Mr Robert Edward Miller, who was diagnosed with Charcot-Marie-Tooth0 in September 1982. He claimed that, even before his 65th birthday in 1983, he had incurred extra costs due to his illness, which he had suffered since the 1970's and which had been diagnosed in 1982. The patient had incurred extra costs for medical treatment, foot rails, soft shoes, home assistance, and to some extent his food budget because of a limited ability to prepare meals. He also had to pay for the transportation service for disabled persons, and extra travel by personal car, because of his considerably reduced ability to walk. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Stockholm and requested that an oral hearing be held in his case because he wished to call as witnesses his personal doctor, the doctor appointed by the Office and all the members of the Office who had participated in the decision of his case. In reaching this decision the Court took note of a breakdown of additional costs allegedly caused by his disability, totalling SEK 18,100, which the applicant had initially submitted to the Social Insurance Office on 16 September 1996. name: Clayton Wood
train_texts: The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on 6 June 2002. The applicant complains that the covert recording of his conversations by the police infringed Articles 8 and 13 of the convention. The Court declared the application partly admissible, partly inadmissible, and partly in admissible on 20 January 2004. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The tapes formed the basis of the application. The Government was represented by their Agent, Mr John Grainger of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. Tapes were ruled admissible on 13 March 2000. Trial judge held a ‘voir dire’ on the admissibility of the tapes. Counsel for the applicant argued that the methods of obtaining the evidence violated Articles 5, 6 and 8 of the Convention, and that they should therefore be excluded under section 78 or section 76 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE) The trial judge said: “I find that no mala fides exist in this case and that the Chief Constable acted throughout in good faith.” [6G] The tapes were ruled to be admissible by the trial judge. A man in a police cell is entitled to privacy just as much as a man sitting at his fireside in his own home. There is no statute which provides for lawful bugging of police cells nor to prohibit such an action. If bugging is done it should not be done haphazardly and certainly does not bestow on police officers unfettered power.Applicant's counsel suggested five safeguards that should have been afforded to the accused if the bugging was to be lawful. The trial judge said: “I have considered each one of these matters and have rejected them all. If they were to be required in each case, no covert listening would ever be realistic or possible” In the exercise of my discretion under section 78, I will allow the tapes to be used in evidence. The European Court of Human Rights recognises that to insist on the exclusion of evidence could in itself result in a greater injustice to the public than the infringement of Article 8 creates for the appellants. The Court of Appeal rejected the applicant's argument on the basis that the arrests were for a lawful purpose as well as to enable the surveillance to take place. The appeal was dismissed on 13 February 2002. The applicant and his three co-defendants appealed to the Court of appeal, submitting that the tapes should not have been admitted. The argument that the admission of the tapes in evidence prevented the defendants from receiving a fair trial was also rejected. Lord Woolf CJ said: ‘The complaints of the appellants with regard to the decision of the judge are not to the relevance of the contents of the tape. They were clearly highly relevant.’ The argument is that the surveillance took place contrary to the spirit of the relevant Codes of Practice. On the evidence there were proper grounds for the arrests and ignoring the fact that the police were working to an overall plan, there was nothing improper about the purpose for which the arrests took place. The trial judge may have been unduly rigorous in his approach because the object of the exercise was not to obtain evidence against one or other of the suspects. The Court of Appeal certified a question for consideration by the House of Lords concerning use of evidence obtained by an arrest for the purpose of eavesdropping on the defendant. On 30 May 2002, leave to appeal to the House Of Lords was refused. The case was decided in favour of the defendant and the case was heard in the Court of Criminal Appeal. The jury concluded that the use of taped evidence was not in conflict with any provision of PACE or the Codes. The decision was published in the journal of the Supreme Court of England and Wales on 25 May 2002. It was published with the headline: ‘The Court Of Appeal’, and included the words: “We have no doubt that a statutory code should be established for the surveillance of the sort that occurred here’.

The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complains that the covert recording of his conversations by the police infringed Articles 8 and 13. The Court declared the application partly admissible, partly inadmissible, and partly not admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was decided on just satisfaction by the Court on 20 January 2004. The decision was made by the Chief Constable of the West Midlands, who said that the tapes formed the basis of the case. Tapes were ruled admissible on 13 March 2000. The trial judge rejected the defendants' argument that the circumstances of obtaining the evidence were oppressive and the tapes should therefore be excluded under section 76 of PACE. Counsel for the applicant argued that the methods of obtaining evidence violated Articles 5, 6 and 8 of the Convention. In considering section 78 of the Act, the trial judge said: “I find that no mala fides exist in this case and that the Chief Constable acted throughout in good faith.” [6G] He also said that the police clearly hoped that the covert bugging operation would bear fruit and if it did not the defendant would have to be released. Trial judge said a man in a police cell is entitled to privacy just as much as a man sitting at his fireside in his own home. He is after all innocent until proved guilty and he is in a vulnerable situation. Any bugging of his cell to intrude on his private conversation with another person would, prima facie, amount to an invasion of his privacy and as such a breach of Article 8.1. The main point which I have to decide is as to whether or not the intrusion to privacy was 'in accordance with the law' There is no statute which provides for lawful bugged of police cells nor to prohibit such an action. The applicant together with three others was convicted on 20 July 2000 of various robbery and firearms offences. He was sentenced to a total of 8 years' imprisonment. The appeal claimed that the tapes should not have been admitted in evidence. Lord Woolf CJ gave the judgment of the Court of Appeal on 13 February 2002, dismissing the appeal. None of the defendants gave evidence at trial. He said that there had been a violation of Article 8 because the surveillance was not conducted according to law. In the exercise of my discretion under section 78, I will allow the tapes to be used in evidence, he said. The European Court of Human Rights recognises that to insist on the exclusion of evidence could in itself result in a greater injustice to the public. The argument that the admission of the tapes in evidence prevented the defendants from receiving a fair trial was also rejected. Lord Woolf CJ said: “The complaints of the appellants with regard to the decision of the judge are not to the relevance of the contents of the tape. ... Instead it is argued that the way the evidence was obtained was contrary to PACE. ... This was a situation where the police were responding reasonably and proportionately to a very serious threat to the safety of the public and law and order.” The decision was made by the Court of Appeal and the case was adjourned until November 14. The trial judge came to the conclusion that the Guidelines had not been complied with because of the requirement in the Guidelines for normal methods of investigation to have been tried and failed. The Court of Appeal certified a question for consideration by the House of Lords concerning use of evidence obtained by an arrest for the purpose of eavesdropping on the defendant. Lord Woolf CJ went on to adopt the conclusions reached in other cases that there was no unfairness in admitting such taped evidence where there wasno suggestion that the confessions were oppressively obtained or other than wholly reliable. On 30 May 2002, leave to appeal to the House Of Lords was refused. The case was described as ‘the first case of its kind in the UK’ and ‘one of the most significant in the history of the country’. It was the first of a series of cases to be heard before the Court of appeal.’ The jury was told that the recording of the victim’s phone call to his lawyer was ‘not in accordance with the spirit of PACE or the Codes’

The trial judge held a ‘voir dire’ on the admissibility of the tapes. Counsel for the applicant argued that the methods of obtaining the evidence violated Articles 5, 6 and 8 of the Convention. The tapes should therefore be excluded under section 78 or section 76 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE), the trial judge said. The decision of the Chief Constable was not in accordance with a strict interpretation of the guidelines [Home Office Guidelines on the Use of Police Surveillance Equipment], it does not mean that his authority to use a bugging device or devices is no longer of importance. Trial judge: 'A man in a police cell is entitled to privacy just as much as a man sitting at his fireside in his own home' No statute which provides for lawful bugging of police cells nor to prohibit such an action. 'In fairness, if bugging is done it should not be done haphazardly and certainly does not bestow on police officers unfettered power' 'The weight of his loss of privacy is another matter which I may take into account. ... The main point which I have to decide is as to whether or not the intrusion to privacy was 'in accordance with the law' The applicant and his three co-defendants appealed to the Court of Appeal, submitting, inter alia, that the tapes should not have been admitted in evidence. The appeal was dismissed on 13 February 2002. Lord Woolf CJ said: “The fact that the police were operating in accordance with a strategy designed to obtain additional evidence by covert recording does not turn lawful arrests into unlawful arrests” [§ 68] The European Court of Human Rights recognises that to insist on the exclusion of evidence could in itself result in a greater injustice to the public than the infringement of Article 8 creates for the appellants. The remedy can be the finding, which we have now made, that there has been a breach of Article8 or it can be an award of compensation.” The argument that the admission of the tapes in evidence prevented the defendants from receiving a fair trial was also rejected. Lord Woolf CJ said: “The complaints of the appellants with regard to the decision of the judge are not to the relevance of the contents of the tape. ... Instead it is argued that the way the evidence was obtained was contrary to PACE.” The court also rejected the claim that the police had been acting in ‘bad faith’ and that they had violated PACE’s ‘standards of conduct’. The case was adjourned until next month for further proceedings. Lord Woolf CJ said there was no unfairness in admitting such taped evidence. Lord Woolf said the surveillance was not directly in conflict with any provision of PACE or the Codes. The Court of Appeal certified a question for consideration by the House of Lords concerning use of evidence obtained by an arrest for the purpose of eavesdropping on the defendant. On 30 May 2002, leave to appeal to the House. of Lords was refused. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights. The Lords ruled in favour of the prosecution of the accused. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court of England and Wales. The trial judge said that the case was “a matter of public interest”.

The court noted that this requirement was closely linked to the examination of the grounds on which the Supreme. Court could refuse to entertain a cassated appeal.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 19789/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been unlawfully detained in a regular detention centre pending his transfer to a psychiatric hospital. The court found it established that the applicant had committed the offences with which he was charged. But it found he could not have been held criminally responsible as he was suffering from paranoid schizophrenia. It further referred to the experts' opinion and ordered the applicant be placed in a psychiatric Hospital. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time and grant priority to the application. The applicant was detained in the Nowa Sól Detention Centre. The Supreme Court asked the lower court to examine whether the applicant's motion could be regarded as an appeal against the decision of 9 April 2008. The applicant was admitted to the Lubiąż Psychiatric Hospital on 15 September 2008. It appears that he left the hospital on a later unknown date before February 2009. The court held that all the conditions for imposing the preventive measure on the applicant had been met. The case file was transferred to the Zielona Góra Regional Court. On 29 August 2008 the Zielona Góra Regional Court upheld the 7 July 2008 decision.

name: Inga Allard
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35179/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the demolition of a house had violated her rights to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions and to respect for her home. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 22 May 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. On the land managed by the applicant’s mother – which formed part of Marum 1:8 – the mother owned a number of houses. The applicant applied for a building permit to the Österåker Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden) in 1987 to enlarge one of the houses. On 9 September 1987 the committee granted a permit for the building of a new house further away from the shore. The new house was built in 1988. In 1989 practically all the other joint owners of the two estates brought proceedings against the applicant in the District Court (tingsrätten) of Södra Roslag, requesting that she be ordered to remove the new house. The applicant claimed that the joint ownership of the two estates should be dissolved and individual plots be assigned to the family members. In. 1994 the District Court’s removal judgment was upheld on appeal by the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt). The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen). She later requested, inter alia, that no further action be taken on the case pending the outcome of division proceedings which she had begun in October 1990. By a decision of 1 December 1995, the REFA allowed the creation of four individual plots on Marum 1:8. The house was to be demolished by a construction firm on 3 June 1996. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, requesting an immediate stay of the demolition order. She submitted that enforcement of the removal judgment should be stayed until the division proceedings had been concluded or, in the alternative, until the Real Estate Court had decided the question. She also requested a three-week respite in order to substantiate her appeal. The appellate court’s order for the completion of the appeal was allegedly not received by the applicant until the evening of 5 June, as she had been at the site of the house in issue. It appears from the court that the applicant had not been given the opportunity to remove the house herself. The house in issue was therefore demolished by a construction firm. The applicant had claimed that her appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 May 1996 prevented the enforcement of the removal judgment. However, this claim was rejected by the Enforcement Office on 31 May 1996, referring to Chapter 3, section 21, of the Enforcement Code (Utsökningsbalken) The demolition of the house began on 3 June 1996 and was concluded ten days later. On 25 June 1996 the Enforcement. Office declared that the house had been demolished and that accordingly the removal. judgment had been duly enforced. This decision was appealed against by the other joint owners on the ground that the building material had not been removed from the property. The applicant and her sister were removed from Marum 1:6 and 1:8 in 1994. The Court of Appeal ruled that they did not have a legitimate interest in having their cases heard. On 16 January 1998 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. No further appeal was lodged and the appellate court’s judgment consequently acquired legal force. By decisions of 4 February 1997 and 29 February 2000, the Building Committee granted the applicant building permits for the reconstruction of the demolished house and for the construction of two smaller outbuildings. . On 14 April 2000 the Supreme court refused leave. to appeal against the declaratory judgment of 26 November 1996.

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the demolition of a house had violated her rights to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions and to respect for her home. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The case was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) In a decision of 22 May 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The parties each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing was required. On the land managed by the applicant’s mother – which formed part of Marum 1:8 – the mother owned a number of houses. The applicant applied for a building permit to the Österåker Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden) on 9 September 1987. On 21 December 1989 practically all the other joint owners of the two estates brought proceedings against the applicant in the District Court (tingsrätten) of Södra Roslag. The court stated, inter alia, that it was the applicant who owned the house and that she had built it without the necessary consent. The applicant had requested that the joint ownership of the two estates should be dissolved and individual plots be assigned to the family members. The case had to be referred back by the Court of Appeal to the REFA for re-examination as the latter had made procedural errors. Subsequently, by a decision of 1 December 1995, the Real Estate Court allowed the creation of four individual plots on Marum 1:8. The Central Office of the National Land Survey (Lantmäteriverket) gave its opinion in the division proceedings. On 7 March 1996 the Office ordered the applicant to remove the house before 3 April 1996 or risk having it demolished by the Office at her own expense. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, requesting an immediate stay of the demolition order. She claimed that she had not been given the opportunity to remove the house herself in accordance with the District Court’s judgment of 10 May 1990. She stated that she started to dismantle the house but was not able to complete the work before 3 June 1996. Furthermore, the applicant requested a three-week respite in order to substantiate her appeal. The Appeal Court rejected the applicant's request for a stay, and the house was demolished by a construction firm on 3 May 1996. This could preserve the house and reduce the risk of adverse consequences for the applicant. The house in issue was therefore demolished by a construction firm. The applicant had claimed that her appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 May 1996 prevented the enforcement of the removal judgment. However, this claim was rejected by the Enforcement Office on 31 May 1996. The demolition of the house began on 3 June 1996 and was concluded ten days later. In 1994 the applicant and her sister brought removal proceedings against several other joint owners of Marum 1:6 and 1:8. However, the District Court rejected the claims, finding that the buildings had been erected before 1991. The court also decided that further litigation in this respect should not be paid for through public legal aid. With effect from the date of the judgment, the legal aid previously awarded was withdrawn. On 14 April 2000 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The Court of Appeal upheld the legal-aid decision on 3 October 1997. No further appeal was lodged and the appellate court’s judgment consequently acquired legal force.

name: Morten Sørensen
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that the existence of closed-shop agreements in Denmark in their respective areas of employment had violated their right to freedom of association. The applications were allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) by decisions of 20 March 2003, the applications were declared partly admissible. In a decision of 25 November 2004, a Chamber of judges relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, none of the parties having objected. Third-party comments were received from the Danish Confederation of Trade Unions (Landsorganisationen – LO) The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 2005. The Court heard addresses by Mr Lego Andersen and Mr Taksøe-Jensen, as well as their replies to questions from judges. The first applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Århus, Denmark. He applied for a job as a holiday relief worker in a company, FDB Distributionen (‘FDB’). In a letter of 20 May 1996, the applicant was offered the job from 3 June until 10 August 1996 and informed that his terms of employment would be regulated by an agreement concluded between FDB and a trade union called SID. At the time of his appointment he had applied for membership. Denmark's Free Trade Union (Danmarks Frie Fagforening) represented the applicant in the case. The High Court of Western Denmark (Vestre Landsret) found for FDB, stating as follows: “The High Court finds it established that the applicant was aware that membership of SID was a condition for his employment in the company’”. The Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act was passed by Parliament in 1982 as a result, inter alia, of the British Rail judgment (Young, James and Webster v. the United Kingdom, Series A no. 44) delivered by the European Court of Human Rights. The High Court said the domestic courts should disregard section 2(2) of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act. The starting-point must be taken from the Act of 1992 incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights. On appeal, the Supreme Court (Højesteret) upheld the High Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. A decision abolishing or limiting the existing possibility of entering into closed-shop agreements will have far-reaching consequences for the Danish labour market, the court said. The second applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Haderslev, Denmark. He became a gardener by profession. He was a member of SID in the mid-1980s, but resigned his membership after a few years as he felt unable to support its political affiliations. He was offered a job at a nursery (Gartneriet i Regnmark I/S) on condition that he became a member. The applicant commenced the job on 17 May 1999 and rejoined SID, although he still did not agree with its political views. He died of a heart attack on 17 June 2007, aged 74. He left the Christian Trade Union (Kristelig Fagforening) in 2000. He is survived by his wife and two children.

The Supreme Court (Højesteret) upheld the High Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. The second applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Haderslev, Denmark. He is a gardener by profession. name: Patrick Benjamin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28212/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Patrick Benjamin and Hueth Wilson alleged that they had not had available to them a procedure by which they could challenge the lawfulness of their continued detention. The application was declared admissible by the Commission on 23 October 1997 and transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25): this case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59:2 in fine). The second applicant, Mr Hueth Wilson, was sentenced to life imprisonment for buggery of a young girl in 1977. The court had before it psychiatric evidence to the effect that he suffered from mental illness. Expert psychiatric evidence recommended that he should be made subject to a hospital order. Due to an absence of any beds in hospitals providing the level of security that the trial judge considered necessary, the judge felt unable to make the orders and passed, instead, a discretionary life sentence. His tariff period (the minimum period of detention satisfying the requirements of retribution and deterrence) was set at six years and expired in April 1989. In August 1989, he was made the subject of a transfer direction and a restriction order under, respectively, sections 47 and 49 of the Mental Health Act 1983 (the 1983 Act) and transferred to Broadmoor Special Hospital. The applicants were not eligible for review by the discretionary lifer panels empowered by section 34 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 to order their release on licence. Leave to apply for judicial review of the decisions was granted on 17 May 1993. In June 1993, following consultation with the trial judge and the Lord Chief Justice, the Secretary of State decided that the second applicant should be regarded as a “technical lifer”. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court. The court had before it psychiatric evidence to the effect that he suffered from mental illness. Expert psychiatric evidence recommended that he should be made subject to a hospital order. Due to an absence of any beds in hospitals providing the level of security that the trial judge considered necessary, the judge felt unable to make the orders and passed, instead, a discretionary life sentence. His tariff period (the minimum period of detention satisfying the requirements of retribution and deterrence) was set at six years and expired in April 1989. The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The authorities initially sought to return the applicant to Somaloland. As the applicant did not co-operate with the provision of bio-data, the Government decided that it would be preferable to remove him to Somalia. In July 2006 the Government concluded an agreement with African Express Airlines which made enforced removals to Somalia possible. In the course of the hearing, however, the immigration judge was wrongly informed that enforcedRemovals would be possible in the foreseeable future. The application for interim relief in the form of an order that he be released from detention was refused. Both the applicant and the Secretary of State were granted leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal. The applicant was issued with removal directions set for 29 November 2006. He sought leave to apply for judicial Review of the removal directions and the directions were cancelled pending a decision on that application. On 1 February 2007 the Secretary of State issued a decision refusing to revoke the deportation order. The applicant was granted permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal on 18 December 2009. The applicant denied the rape allegations made against him by Ms T. on 5 March 1990 in Puerto de la Cruz, Tenerife, Canary Islands. Guarantees were requested from the United Kingdom authorities to the effect that, should the extradition be granted and the applicant be convicted in England, the final sentence would not exceed thirty years’ imprisonment (the maximum term of imprisonment under Spanish legislation) On 2 January 1991 the British Embassy in Madrid wrote to the Audiencia Nacional that in the applicant’s case the sentence actually served upon conviction for murder was not likely to be more than ten years. On 24 June 1991 the public prosecutor recommended that the applicant be kept in detention pending his trial for rape unless he could be temporarily handed over to the British authorities. The Audiencia Nacional decided to extend his detention under Article 504 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 10 (3) of the Extradition Act. The applicant lodged an appeal (recurso de súplica) against this decision but on 18 June 1992 a full court dismissed the appeal on the ground that he had been detained in the extradition case on 23 March 1990, independently of his earlier detention for a different matter. Another application for release by the applicant on 7 September 1992 was rejected in similar terms. The appeal was rejected after summary proceedings in a decision (auto) of 6 May 1993. The Court’s case file does not contain any reply. The complainant had formally charged the applicant with, inter alia, rape and forgery of documents. The statement - which was taken at a court hearing in Tuusula, Finland, on 14 December 1992 - confirmed Ms T’s original allegations. In a judgment of 21 March 1994 the Audiencia Provincial of Santa Cruz de Tenerife acquitted the applicant on the rape charge. With respect to the forgery offence the applicant was convicted and sentenced as charged. The applicant was handed over to the United Kingdom authorities, pursuant to the international arrest warrant and theAudiencia Nacional's decision of 22 February 1991 allowing extradition. On 9 November 1995, following a trial at Birmingham Crown Court, Mr Scott was convicted of the murder of his father. He was sentenced to life imprisonment. The trial judge recommended a “tariff period’ (see paragraph 43 below) of twelve years. - nine days under the different orders for detention pending trial on the rape charge and exactly four years in connection with the extradition proceedings. -nine days under a different orders of detention pending the extradition hearing on a rape charge. - eight days under an order of detention in relation to the attempted murder of Mr Scott’s mother. -eight days under another order relating to the alleged rape of his mother.

name: Marc Brauer
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24062/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he was not granted a reinstatement of the proceedings after he overstepped the time‑limit to lodge an appeal on points of law. On 26 May 2015 the complaint concerning the refusal to grant a reinstate was communicated to the Government. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The application was brought by a German national, Mr Marc Brauer (“the applicant”), on 23 March 2013. Appeal on points of law may be lodged either with the record of the registry or in writing. Since you are not at liberty, the special provision of Article 299 of the CCP applies to you. On 21 December 2012 the applicant typed and signed an appeal letter to the Rheine District Court and asked the clinic’s staff to post it. On 8 January 2013 the Regional Court informed the applicant that his appeal was belated. It underlined that the applicant had been instructed after returning to the forensic hospital where, when in contact with others, he showed no more signs of agitation. The applicant has been ordered to pay back the money he spent on the appeal. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law on 22 December 2012. The Federal Court of Justice rejected the applicant’s request for reinstatement and dismissed his appeal as inadmissible because it had been lodged out of time. It held that it was not necessary to examine whether, with regard to the Christmas holidays, it was possible to lodge the appeal in writing. The appeal was returned to the court-appointed lawyer on 14 January 2013. The applicant had been confined to a psychiatric clinic at the time of the appeal because of his mental illness. The court ruled that the oral instructions on the right to appeal given after the delivery of the judgment were correct and complete. An accused who misunderstood the oral instruction and therefore lodged an appeal out of time was himself responsible for this. The Federal Court of Justice distinguished the applicant’s case from case‑law which made exceptions for a foreigner who was not defended by counsel. The applicant filed a constitutional complaint to the Federal Constitutional Court. He stated, inter alia, that another lawyer had advised him that his court‑appointed defence counsel had been under an obligation to file the appeal on points of law. On 29 June 2013 the Federalconstitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint for adjudication, without providing reasons (no. 2 BvR 1243/13).

The case originated in an application (no. 24062/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he was not granted a reinstatement of the proceedings after he overstepped the time‑limit to lodge an appeal on points of law. The German Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Ms K. Behr, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. On 21 December 2012 the applicant received a letter from the court‑appointed lawyer, dated 19 December 2012, who advised him to appeal against the court’s decision and to mandate new defence counsel. Appeal on points of law may be lodged either with the record of the registry or in writing. Since you are not at liberty, the special provision of Article 299 of the CCP applies to you. In your own interest you should take care that the appeal is lodged in time. The Rheine District Court would be competent. On 8 January 2013 the Regional Court informed the applicant that his appeal was belated. It underlined that the applicant had been instructed after returning to the forensic hospital where, when in contact with others, he showed no more signs of agitation. The court-appointed lawyer argued that the applicant had misunderstood his counsel’s instruction on how to lodge an appeal. The Federal Court of Justice rejected the applicant‘s request for reinstatement and consequently dismissed his appeal on points of law as inadmissible because it had been lodged out of time. It held that it was not necessary to examine whether, with regard to the Christmas holidays, the applicant could have expected the appeal, posted on 22 December, to reach the Rheine District Court by 27 December 2012. The applicant had believed that he was able to choose whether he wanted to lodge the appeal in writing or have it recorded by the registry. The Federal Court of Justice distinguished the applicant’s case from case‑law which made exceptions for a foreigner who was not defended by counsel. An accused who misunderstood the oral instruction and therefore lodged an appeal out of time was himself responsible for this. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint for adjudication, without providing reasons (no. 2 BvR 1243/13) It found decisive that the applicant had been expressly instructed on the day of the judgment's delivery that an appeal could only be lodged with the Rheine District Court to the record of the registry, but not in writing.

The case stems from an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he was not granted a reinstatement of the proceedings after he overstepped the time‑limit to lodge an appeal on points of law. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms K. Behr, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. The application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice. The applicant returned to the forensic hospital where, when in contact with others, he showed no more signs of agitation. The court‑appointed lawyer advised the applicant to appeal against the court’s decision and also to mandate new defence counsel. On 21 December 2012 the applicant typed and signed an appeal letter to the Rheine District Court and asked the clinic's staff to post it the following day. On 8 January 2013 the Regional Court informed the applicant that his appeal was belated. It underlined that the applicant had been instructed after the hearing that he had been given the option of changing his legal counsel. The applicant decided to keep his current counsel. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law on 22 December 2012. The court-appointed lawyer for the applicant said that the applicant had misunderstood his counsel’s instruction on how to lodge an appeal. The Federal Court of Justice rejected the applicant’S request for reinstatement and consequently dismissed his appeal as inadmissible because it had been lodged out of time. It held that it was not necessary to examine whether, with regard to the Christmas holidays, the appeal could have been recorded by the Rheine District Court or the Münster Regional Court in time for the appeal to be heard. The appeal was dismissed on 24 April 2013. The Federal Court of Justice distinguished the applicant’s case from case‑law which made exceptions for a foreigner who was not defended by counsel. The applicant's defence counsel had given him instructions on the form and time‑limit for an appeal. The content of this letter was not misleading but reflected correctly the applicable law. There was nothing to show that the applicant might not have understood the oral instructions by the presiding judge for mental health reasons. He misunderstood the subsequent written instructions of his defence counsel in the same way. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint for adjudication, without providing reasons (no. 2 BvR 1243/13).

name: Danuta Gryziecka
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 46034/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged on 30 January 1998 with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that their right to a “hearing within a reasonable time’ had not been respected. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 10 January 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was decided by the Court of Justice of the European Court of Human rights. The case involves a dispute over 728,000 old Polish zlotys. The case was brought by the wife and daughter of the late plaintiff. The court ordered the parties to produce the evidence in support of their submissions. In 1996 the court ordered fresh expert evidence be obtained, in order to determine the value of the land on which the hen house had been constructed. On 12 November 1996 the expert report was submitted to the court. On 11 December 1996 the case was settled out of court and the land was sold to the second applicant. The settlement was agreed at a hearing in January 1997 and the property was sold. The new owner was allowed to keep the proceeds of the sale of the property. The plaintiffs’ lawyer requested the court to list a hearing on 14 January 1997. The applicants requested that the court index the repayment of their bank loan and the payment made to the original plaintiff in 1984. The court fixed a one-month time-limit for the parties to produce the evidence. The plaintiffs withdrew their claims against the first applicant on 12 March 1998 and the court gave judgment on 26 March 1998. The case had been assigned to a new judge. None of the parties submitted a notice of appeal. It partly granted the claim of the original. plaintiff’s daughter against the second applicant and dismissed the claim. of the first.

name: John Beck
train_texts: The case stems from three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that an investigation into their sexuality and their discharge from the armed forces on the basis of their homosexuality violated their rights. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26: 1 of the Rules of Court. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 25: 1) on 1 November 2001. The first applicant was granted legal aid on 31 January 2000. The Court declared the applications admissible on 5 September 2000. 4 May 1976 the first applicant joined the Royal Air Force (“RAF”) By 1993 he had reached the rank of sergeant in the Electronic Warfare Operational Support Establishment (‘EWOSE’) The first applicant’s service evaluations covering the period June 1990 to January 1993 all recorded his conduct as exemplary. He was said to be “widely recognised as one of the most experienced [senior non-commissioned officers] in the trade’. On 12 May 1993 security services were advised. On 17 May 1993 he was suspended from his duties from 17 May 93. He has been awarded the Air Officer Commanding Commendation for Meritorious Service. The EWOSE. police investigation commenced on 20 May 1993 which included their completing a Character Defect Enquiry (“CDE”) on the first applicant. The CDE report was dated 8 June 1993 and outlined the detailed observations made by a number of persons to the service police, which are summarised below. The report also recorded the information received from the first. applicant’s immediate superior and his interest in theology and who had proffered the. view that he was not surprised that the firstApplicant had claimed to be homosexual. The second colleague described a striking change in the first applicants character. The first applicant had admitted his homosexuality to him two weeks before he did so to armed forces’ authorities. The first applicant’s ex-wife (also in the armed forces) provided a detailed statement to the service police which was recorded in the CDE report. She described her hesitations in marrying the first applicant, their marital difficulties, their financial difficulties and their separation in 1987 and their divorce in 1988. The report concluded that no signs of homosexual tendencies were identified by the first applicants ex-wives, colleagues or friends, that the only evidence was his own admission and that the enquiry had not revealed anything to rebut his submissions that he had not had a homosexual physical relationship. Various identified matters could imply that the first. applicant had mercenary reasons for wishing to be discharged and it was noted that he. had threatened to go to the press if he was not treated properly. First applicant took exception to the reference to the sexual orientation of his brother which he considered to be of no concern to the RAF and which he found offensive. Unit Commander noted: “With the current official policy on homosexuality, the simple fact is that [the first applicant] cannot be retained. This is a sad case and I am saddened by it’s outcome.” The first applicant said he had been treated “with very considerable kindness by all concerned” and that “it would be quite wrong if I did not mention this fact”. He also commended in particular the EWOSE security officer (to whom he had spoken on 10 May 1993) for his kindness. The RAF Board of the RAF, two of whose members thought it apt to liken the first applicant’s case to “a murder inquiry without a body”, recommended his administrative discharge on grounds of his homosexuality. The second applicant joined the Royal Army Medical Corps on 1 June 1978 and was indexed as a pupil nurse on 12 November 1979. He passed his autumn assessment in 1981. At the time of his discharge on 29 January 1982 he was a Private. Although he knew that revealing his homosexuality would lead to his discharge, he informed his nurse tutor. The latter informed the personnel officer who conducted four interviews with the second applicant. Second applicant was discharged from the army on 29 January 1982 on grounds of his homosexuality. The psychiatrist’s clinical notes dated 25 January 1982 indicated that it was felt that the second applicant was not suffering from any psychiatric disorder. The third applicant joined the RAF on 10 November 1985 and commenced officer training at the RAF college. He was commissioned as Acting Petty Officer on 27 March 1986, achieved the rank of Flight Lieutenant in September 1991 and served as a second navigator at a RAF base in Scotland. Although he was not yet recommended for further promotion, he was progressing satisfactorily in his current post and should be a contender to become a first navigator in due course. In August 1994 the third applicant’s credit card holder, which he had previously lost, was found by an officer of the service police in the latter's internal mail. The contents aroused suspicion that he might be homosexual. The third applicant confirmed that the cards were his and that he was homosexual. He indicated that his wife knew at the time of his statement of his homosexuality and he confirmed the statements made during his interview as to his previous homosexual relationships. He made it clear that he did not wish to provide the names of those persons with whom he had had a homosexual relationship and stated that he had not made the statement to get a discharge from service. A report was prepared recommending that he be ordered to resign his commission on the grounds of unsuitability. Mr Perkins was dismissed from the RAF in 1995 on grounds of his homosexuality. He appealed to the High Court for leave to take judicial review proceedings. The European Court of Justice ruled that transsexuals were protected from discrimination on the grounds of their transsexuality under European Community law. The High Court referred the question of the applicability of the Equal Treatment Directive to differences of treatment based on sexual orientation to the ECJ pursuant to former Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome (R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins, 13 March 1997). The ECJ declined to maintain the Article 177 reference to the Perkins case in 1998. The applicants argued, inter alia, in favour of the applicability of the Equal Treatment Directive to a difference of treatment based on sexual orientation. Following a hearing before the Industrial Tribunal in August 1996, their cases together with a series of similar cases, were stayed pending the outcome of the above-described Perkins case. That stay was renewed in May 1997 and in June 1998. However, further to the High Court decision of 13 July 1998 in the Perkins case, the applicants, following legal advice, withdrew their applications before the industrial Tribunal. The tribunal consequently dismissed their applications on 23 December 1998. The case was settled at the International Court of Justice.

In June 1981 the second applicant commenced a homosexual relationship with a civilian. Six months later he received a posting order to Germany and applied for a home posting as he wished to remain in the United Kingdom with his partner. His application was refused. He submitted that he then realised that he could not lead a double life or face separation from his. partner. Although he knew that revealing his homosexuality would lead to his discharge, he informed his nurse tutor. The latter informed the personnel officer who conducted four interviews with the first applicant. The first applicant was discharged from the RAF on grounds of his homosexuality on 27 November 1993. The second applicant was discharged from the army on 29 January 1982 on grounds of his homosexuality. The psychiatrist’s clinical notes dated 25 January 1982 indicated that it was felt that the second applicant wasn’t suffering from any psychiatric disorder. The third applicant joined the RAF on 10 November 1985 and commenced officer training at the RAF college. He was commissioned as Acting Petty Officer on 27 March 1986, achieved the rank of Flight Lieutenant in September 1991 and served as a second navigator at a RAF base in Scotland. Although he was not yet recommended for further promotion, he was progressing satisfactorily in his current post and should be a contender to become a first navigator in due course. The third applicant’s credit card holder, which he had previously lost, was found by an officer of the service police. The contents aroused suspicion that the third applicant might be homosexual. The third applicant confirmed that the cards were his and that he was homosexual. He indicated that his wife knew at the time of his statement of his homosexuality. He confirmed the statements made during his interview as to his previous homosexual relationships. He made it clear that he did not wish to provide the names of those persons with whom he had had a homosexual relationship and stated that he had not made the statement to get a discharge from service. He was suspended from his normal primary duties with immediate effect. A report was prepared recommending that he be ordered to resign his commission on the grounds of unsuitability. Mr Perkins was discharged from the RAF on grounds of his homosexuality in 1995. In 1996 he applied to the High Court for leave to take judicial review proceedings. On 3 July 1996 he was granted leave. The High Court referred the question of the applicability of the Equal Treatment Directive to differences of treatment based on sexual orientation to the ECJ pursuant to former Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome. The ECJ enquired in March 1998 whether it wished to maintain the Article 177 reference. After a hearing between the parties, the. High Court decided to withdraw the question from the. ECJ (R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins, 13 July 1998). The applicants argued, inter alia, in favour of the applicability of the Equal Treatment Directive to a difference of treatment based on sexual orientation. Following a hearing before the Industrial Tribunal in August 1996, their cases together with a series of similar cases, were stayed pending the outcome of the above-described Perkins case. That stay was renewed in May 1997 and in June 1998. However, further to the High Court decision of 13 July 1998 in the Perkins case, the applicants, following legal advice, withdrew their applications. The applicants’ employer had previously been cautioned, on 25 November 1996, by the Ministry of Labour concerning its practices on working hours. name: Roman Piekara
train_texts: The applicant was born in 1920 and lives in Łódź, Poland. He asked the Veterans and Persecuted Persons’ Office (Urząd do Spraw Kombatantów i Osób Represjonowanych) to grant him “veteran status.” The Office failed to issue a decision and informed the applicant that he should first lodge an application with the World Veteran Association. On 25 February 1994 the applicant lodged a complaint about the inactivity of the Office with the Supreme Administrative Court. On 5 June 2003 the President of the Fourth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. The applicant was refused ‘veteran status’ because he failed to provide evidence of his participation in the Polish Defence War in September 1939. The applicant lodged a complaint against this decision with the Supreme Administrative Court. The court found that the Office had not examined the case properly and, in particular, had not heard the applicant despite his several applications. The application was dismissed in 1998 and the applicant appealed against the decision in 2000. The appeal was dismissed on 4 April 2000 and the case was dismissed again on 24 June 1998. The case was re-opened on 4 March 2000 and it was dismissed once again on 23 June 2000.

name: Latife Ahmadpour
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 12717/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Iranian national, Ms Latife Ahmadpour (Derya Neverdi) (‘the applicant’), on 14 March 2008. According to her submissions, the applicant had escaped from the violence of her ex-husband. The applicant and the Government each submitted written observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The case was given priority by the President of the Chamber to which the case was allocated. The woman was deported from Turkey on 7 November 2007. She was granted a stay of execution by the Ankara Administrative Court. She requested legal aid but was denied. On 13 March 2008 the UNHCR recognised her as a refugee on the grounds of her political opinion, her membership of a particular social group and her religion. The case was adjourned until 2 January 2008 after she could not be found at her new address. The UNHCR found that her children had been sexually and physically abused by their father and that she had fled to Turkey in order to save them. The application was rejected by the court and the woman was returned to Turkey on 26 February 2008. The applicant was placed in the Kumkapı Foreigners' Admission and Accommodation Centre in Istanbul in February 2008. On 29 August 2008 the applicant's representative lodged a request with the Ministry of the Interior for his client and her children to be released and granted residence permits. She received no reply. The applicant and her kids were subsequently released from detention. Their residence permits were valid until 7 April 2010. On 25 May 2010 the applicant applied to the national authorities to renew her residence permits and the examination of this request is pending. According to the information in the case file, the proceedings before the Sixteenth Chamber of the Ankara Administrative Court are still pending.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 15737/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant admitted, inter alia, to taking part in three separate acts of arson together with Mr M.K. and Mr F.D. The applicants were accused of setting fire to a car and two buildings in 1999. They retracted their earlier submissions, claiming that they had been made under duress. The court heard evidence from the accused and three complainants. In 1999 the Constitution was amended and the military judges sitting on the bench of the State Security Courts were replaced by civilian judges. The judge who had been appointed to replace the military judge sat as a member of the trial court for the first time on 19 August 1999. He further complained that there was nothing to indicate that he was part of an illegal organisation and that therefore Article 168 should not have been applied to him. name: Gerhard Lang
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28648/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights under Articles 4 and 9 of the convention on the ground of his religion. He was liable for military or alternative civilian service whereas members of recognised religious societies holding religious functions comparable to his functions were exempted. On 17 November 2005 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) In 2000 the Federal Minister for Defence (Bundesminister für Landesverteidigung) refused the applicant’s appeals on the ground that he did not belong to a recognised religious society. In 2001 the applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof), requesting it to repeal the wording ‘recognised religious societies’ in section 24(3) of the Military Service Act. In 2003 the Administrative Court dismissed the complaint. The applicant asked the Federal Ministry for Defence to take no action until the European Court of Human Rights had decided on his application. He was informed that an instruction had been issued to the Upper Austrian Military Authority not to call him up.

The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights on the ground of his religion. The application claimed that he should be dispensed from military service since he performed a function within the Jehovah’s Witnesses which was equivalent to that of members of a recognised religious society. To restrict such a privilege to members of recognised religious societies was not objectively justified and was therefore in breach of the Federal Constitution, the Court ruled. In 2000 the Federal Minister for Defence (Bundesminister für Landesverteidigung) refused the applicant’s appeals on the ground that he did not belong to a recognised religious society. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the applicant's complaint for lack of prospects of success. The applicant asked the Federal Ministry for Defence to take no action until the European Court of Human Rights decided on his application.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23188/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the period of their detention on remand exceeded a reasonable time requirement, that the criminal proceedings brought against them were not concluded within areasonable time, and that they did not have an effective remedy at their disposal under domestic law in that respect. On 2 June 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application and decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. This case was assigned to newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) The case-file was transferred to the State Security Court in 1997. The Court of Cassation quashed the lower court’s decision on 23 December 1999. The first and second applicants were sentenced to life in prison. The fourth was sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2002. The case- file was transferred back to the Erzincan State Security court. The third and fourth applicants were sent to prison for 15 years and 12 years respectively. The fifth and sixth applicant was sent to jail for six years and four months. The sentence was commuted to 12 years and five months.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13378/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained under Article 14 taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, when the first of them died, the survivor would be required to pay inheritance tax on the dead sister's share of the family home. The survivor of a married couple or a homosexual relationship registered under the Civil Partnership Act 2004, would be exempt from paying inheritance tax in these circumstances. The hearing on admissibility and merits took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 September 2006. The applicants are unmarried sisters, born on 26 May 1918 and 2 December 1925 respectively. They have lived together all their lives in a house built on land inherited from their parents in Wiltshire. The house is owned by the applicants in their joint names. The sisters also jointly own two other properties, worth GBP 325,000 in total. In addition, each sister owns in her sole name shares and other investments worth approximately GBP 150,000. Each has made a will leaving all her property to the other. They submitted that the value of their jointly-owned property had increased to the point that each sister's one-half share was worth more than the current exemption threshold for inheritance tax.

name: Milenko Stojakovic
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30003/02) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, in particular, under Article 6 of the convention about the lack of a public oral hearing before a tribunal. Since 1984 the applicant was the head of the Federal Bacteriological Serological Research Institute (Bundesstaatiche bakteriologisch-serologische Untersuchungsanstalt) in Linz. According to the activity profile submitted by the Government the tasks of the Institute involved carrying out various examinations. The head of the Institute was responsible for all tasks entrusted to it. He was also responsible for certain matters concerning the regulation of its service. The applicant was found guilty of having violated his professional duties under the Non-Discrimination Act (Bundes-Gleichbehandlungsgesetz) and sentenced to a fine of approximately 2,400 euros (EUR) The Federal Minister for Work, Health and Social Affairs recalled the applicant from his post with immediate effect (Abberufung mit sofortiger Wirkung) and transferred him to a post with a lower grade. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint on 4 September 2003. The applicant argued that he had not made sufficient findings as to the background in which his statements had been made and had placed them in the wrong context. The Appeals Commission (Berufungs-kommission) at the Ministry for Public Service and Sport dismissed the applicant's appeal without holding a hearing. The applicant filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) He complained that the fact that the Appeals Commission had taken its decision after a private meeting was in violation of his right to court proceedings under Article 6 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint on 26 November 2001. It found that rights and obligations which resulted from an employment as a civil servant could not be considered as essential. This decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 13 February 2002. There was no indication of arbitrariness in the proceedings at issue. Article 6 of the Convention was not applicable to the applicant’s case. It followed that Article 6 was not compatible with “civil rights” within the meaning of Article 6. “Civil rights’’ was not a term used to refer to “human rights,” but to ‘the right to a fair trial’. ‘The right to freedom of expression’ is not a right to free speech, but to freedom to express one's opinion.’

The applicant, as head of the Institute, was responsible for all tasks entrusted to it. Under section 3 of the Civil Servants Act (Beamten-Dienstrechtsgesetz) he was further responsible for certain matters concerning the regulation of its service. The applicant was found guilty of having violated his professional duties under the Non-Discrimination Act (Bundes-Gleichbehandlungsgesetz). He was sentenced to a fine of approximately 2,400 euros (EUR) The Federal Minister for Work, Health and Social Affairs recalled the applicant from his post with immediate effect (Abberufung mit sofortiger Wirkung) The applicant was transferred from the Institute for Public Service and Sport in 2000. He appealed the decision to transfer him. The Appeals Commission dismissed his appeal without holding a hearing. The applicant filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant's complaint. It noted that the authority deciding on the transfer did not necessarily need to wait for the outcome of pending disciplinary proceedings. It confirmed the Federal Minister's finding that the applicant could no longer be trusted to perform the tasks of a head of the Institute. In particular, the applicant had deepened the already existent conflicts and tensions at work and there was, therefore, an important official interest which made his transfer to another post necessary. It followed that Article 6 was not applicable to the applicant's case. There was no indication of arbitrariness in the proceedings at issue. It followed that there was not a breach of ‘civil rights’ within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. This decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 13 February 2002. It follows that the applicant was not entitled to a hearing in the European Court of Human Rights. The case was heard in the Supreme Court of Justice of the European Union in March 2002. The applicant was denied a hearing and the case was returned to the High Court in Strasbourg in June 2002.
