train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62543/00) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented by lawyers practising in Pamplona and Madrid. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27) would be the Court's Fourth Section. The applicant association complained that they had not had a fair hearing in the judicial proceedings brought by them to halt construction of the Itoiz dam. They complained that the Autonomous Community law in question had been enacted with a view to preventing execution of a Supreme Court judgment which had become final. The case originated in an engineering project of February 1989 for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits. On 1 April 2003 the Chamber decided, having regard to the circumstances of the case, to dismiss a Rule 39 request submitted by the applicants. The case was decided in favour of the applicants on 14 January 2003. The appeal was based on several allegations of unlawfulness which, in their opinion, had tainted the project. The decision was made on a unanimous basis. The court's attention was drawn to the project's impact on the nature reserves and habitat within the relevant area. It also considered the Council of Europe's recommendations on engineering works in the Pyrenees and the European Union's common agricultural policy. The applicant association applied for immediate enforcement of the judgment and, in particular, for suspension of construction work on the dam. By a decision of 24 January 1996, the Audiencia Nacional granted a suspension order but directed that the necessary measures be taken to ensure the completion of work already begun. In June 1996 the parliament of the Autonomous Community of Navarre (parlamento foral de Navarra) passed Aut autonomous Community Law (foral) no. 9/1996 on natural sites in Navarre. In application of the Autonomous Community law of 1996, the Navarre government adopted Decree no. 307/1996 of 2 September 1996. According to the applicants, this Law enabled construction work on the dam to continue, with the consequent deterioration of the protected natural site. In a judgment of 14 July 1997, the Supreme Court definitively cancelled the dam project in so far as it concerned the 500-metre protection zones around nature reserves. The size of the planned dam, and thus of the area to be flooded, was reduced, so that the village of Itoiz, where the applicants' immovable property was located, was saved from flooding. The applicant association contested the authorities' argument, claiming that the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was inapplicable in the instant case. In the alternative, the applicant association requested that certain provisions in the law be referred to the Constitutional Court for a preliminary ruling on their constitutionality. The Constitutional Court declared the issues raised in the preliminary question admissible in a decision of 21 July 1998. It gave notice of the questions to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate, the government and parliament of Navarre and the Spanish government, and invited them to file their observations within fifteen days. The Speaker of the House of Assembly indicated that the Chamber would take up the matter. The Constitutional Court held that the impugned provisions of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 were compatible with the Constitution. It observed at the outset that enforcement of the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 had become impossible since the entry into force of the new law. The Constitutional Court also ruled that, given the significance of the question raised by the Itoiz dam's construction, which could not simply be ignored, it was justifiable that the law specifically mentioned the aim and means of environmental protection in the peripheral protection zones around the three above-mentioned nature reserves. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. Constitutional Court examined whether the impossibility of executing the Supreme Court's judgment as a consequence of the enactment of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was justified in view of the values and assets protected by the Constitution. It found that the balance of general interests had been respected and that there was no clear lack of proportion between the conflicting interests. The Constitutional Court further noted that the system of peripheral protection zones introduced by this new law had not in itself been considered arbitrary in the Audiencia Nacional's decision. It added that the new law did not amount to ad causam legislation, being general in form and in substance, and pointed out that the impugned provisions could not be held to be contrary to Article 24 of the constitution. The judgment was published in the Official Gazette on 14 April 2000. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. The case originated in an engineering project of February 1989 for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. The first, second, fourth and fifth applicants are members of this association. According to the Government, the total number of landowners affected by the dam's construction is 159. The court accepted the request for precise designation of the protection zones around the nature reserves affected by the dam. In a decision of 6 March 1996, the court prohibited the filling of the reservoir and displacement of the population concerned. In June 1996 the parliament of the Autonomous Community of Navarre (parlamento foral de Navarra) passed Autonomous Law (foral) no. 9/1996 on natural sites in Navarre. This law amended Autonomous community Law no. 6/1987 of 10 April 1987, particularly with regard to the possibility of reclassifying the Protection zones or carrying out. In application of the Autonomous Community law of 1996, Navarre's government adopted Decree no. 307/1996 of 2 September 1996. This identified the peripheral protection zones for certain nature reserves and strict nature reserves in Navarre. According to the applicants, this Law enabled construction work on the dam to continue, with the consequent deterioration of the protected natural site. In a judgment of 14 July 1997, the Supreme Court definitively cancelled the dam project in so far as it concerned the 500-metre protection zones around nature reserves RN 9, 10 and 11. As a result of the judgment, the size of the planned dam, and thus of the area to be flooded, was reduced, so that the village of Itoiz was saved from flooding. The applicant association contested the authorities' argument, claiming that the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was inapplicable in the instant case. In the alternative, the applicant association requested that certain provisions in the Aut autonomous Community law be referred to the Constitutional Court for a preliminary ruling on their constitutionality. The Constitutional Court declared the issues raised in the preliminary question admissible by a decision of 21 July 1998. It gave notice of the questions to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate, the government and parliament of Navarre and the Spanish government, and invited them to file their observations within fifteen days. The Government and Parliament of Navarro submitted their observations on 11 and 15 September 1998 respectively. The Attorney General's observations were submitted on 29 September 1998. In a judgment of 14 March 2000, the Constitutional Court, sitting as a full court, held that the impugned provisions of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 were compatible with the Constitution. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. The Constitutional Court held, firstly, that this was not to be seen as a legislative solution for the particular problem of the three peripheral zones around the three nature reserves affected by construction of the Itoiz dam. Consequently, the impugned provisions could not be held to be contrary to Article 24 § 1 of the Constitution. It added that the new law did not amount to ad causam legislation, being general in form and in substance. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. name: Per Krohn Rasmussen
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8777/79) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Commission on 21 May 1979. The Commission's request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Denmark recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision. as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by. the respondent State of its obligations under Article 14 of the Convention taken in conjunction with Articles. 6 and 8. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. J. Gersing, the elected judge of Danish nationality. The Government's and the applicant's memorials were received at the registry on 19 March. The hearings were held in public on 26 June at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Lehmann and Mr. Melchior for the Government, by. Mr. Opsahl for the Commission and by Mrs. Lindgård for the applicant, as well as replies to its. questions. The applicant, Mr. Per Krohn Rasmussen, is a Danish citizen, born in 1945. He currently works as a clerk and resides in Nyborg. The Commission and the Government were asked to produce certain documents on 7, 12 and 15 June. The applicant had grounds, even before the latter's birth, for assuming that another man might be the father of Pernille. In order to save the marriage, he took no steps to have paternity determined. The applicant and his wife applied for a divorce (skilmisse ved bevilling) on 16 July 1975. On this occasion, he reaffirmed before the authorities that the mother should have sole custody of the children and was once more ordered to pay maintenance for them. The Court of Appeal refused the application on 12 April 1976, for the reason that the statutory conditions for granting leave at that time were not satisfied (see paragraph 19 below) Rasmussen petitioned the Ministry of Justice for leave to appeal out of time to the Supreme Court (Højesteret), but this was refused. His former wife opposed the application, on the ground that such proceedings would have a detrimental effect on the child. Mr. Rasmussen applied again to the Court of Appeal for leave. to institute paternity proceedings. By a decision of 11 December 1978, the Court. of Appeal refused the application for the reason that the applicant had not brought. the action contesting paternity within the time-limits provided for in. section 5(2) of the 1960 Act on the Legal Status of Children (“the 1960 Act’ - Lov nr. 200 af 18.5.1960 om børns retsstilling; see paragraph 19 below)

name: Colin Laskey
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 11 December 1995. It originated in three applications (nos. 21627/93, 21826/93 and 21974/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 14 December 1992. The late Mr Laskey’s father and the two other applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent them. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. Rights International, a New York-based non-governmental human rights organisation, submitted written comments on specified aspects of the case. The comments were received on 16 August 1996. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 October 1996. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr I. Christie, Assistant Legal Adviser, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr D. Pannick QC, Mr M. Shaw, Counsel, Mr S. Bramley, Ms B. Moxon, Advisers. For the applicants Lord Lester of Herne Hill QC, Ms A. Worrall QC, Counsel,. Mr D D. Jonas, Mr A. Hamilton, Mr I I. Geffen, Solicitors, Mr J. Wadham, Adviser. The defendants pleaded guilty to assault charges after the trial judge ruled that they could not rely on the consent of the “victims’ as an answer to the prosecution case. The activities took place at a number of locations, including rooms equipped as torture chambers. Video cameras were used to record events and the tapes copied and distributed amongst members of the group. The prosecution was largely based on the contents of those videotapes. Mr Laskey was sentenced to imprisonment for four years and six months. Mr Jaggard received two years’ imprisonment for aiding and abetting unlawful wounding - contrary to section 20 of the 1861 Act. The applicants appealed against conviction and sentence. The Court of Appeal, Criminal Division, dismissed the appeals against conviction. Since the applicants did not appreciate that their actions in inflicting injuries were criminal, reduced sentences were imposed. On 11 March 1993, the appeal, known as the case of R. v. Brown, was dismissed by a majority of the House of Lords, two of the five law lords dissenting. Lord Templeman, in the majority, held after reviewing the case-law that: “... the authorities dealing with the intentional infliction of bodily harm do not establish that consent is a defence to a charge under the Act of 1861” Lord Jauncey of Tullichettle found that: ‘In my view the line falls properly to be drawn between assault at common law and the offence of assault occasioning actual bodily harm created by section 47 of the 1861 Act’ ‘I am not prepared to invent a defence of consent for sado-masochistic encounters which breed and glorify cruelty ... Society is entitled and bound to protect itself against a cult of violence. Pleasure derived from the infliction of pain is an evil thing. Cruelty is uncivilised.’‘There was, it was said, no question of proselytising by the appellants. No suggestion that appellants are only practitioners of homosexual sado-masochism in England and Wales. Wounds can easily become septic if not properly treated, the free flow of blood from a person who is HIV-positive or who has AIDS can infect another. An inflicter who is carried away by sexual excitement or by drink or drugs could very easily inflict pain and injury beyond the level to which the receiver had consented. The possibility of proselytisation and corruption of young men is a real danger even in the case of these appellants. The taking of video recordings of such activities suggests that secrecy may not be as strict as the appellants claimed. Lord Slynn of Hadley found that as the law stood adults were able to consent to acts done in private which did not result in serious bodily harm. He agreed that it was in the end a matter of policy in an area where social and moral factors were extremely important and where attitudes could change. It was however for the legislature to decide whether such conduct should be brought within the criminal law and not for the courts. All the applicants lost their jobs and Mr Jaggard required extensive psychiatric treatment. The proceedings were given widespread press coverage and were given extensive coverage by the BBC and ITV. The case was described as a ‘trial by ordeal’ by Lord Slynn.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 11 December 1995. It originated in three applications (nos. 21627/93, 21826/93 and 21974/93) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 14 December 1992. The late Mr Laskey’s father and the two other applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent them (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. In 1987, in the course of routine investigations into other matters, the police came into possession of a number of video films which were made during sado-masochistic encounters involving the applicants and as many as forty-four other homosexual men. As a result the applicants, with several other men, were charged with a series of offences, including assault and wounding. The acts consisted in the main of maltreatment of the genitalia (with, for example, hot wax, sandpaper, fish hooks and needles) and ritualistic beatings. One of the charges involved a defendant who was not yet 21 years old - the age of consent to male homosexual practices at the time. The applicants pleaded guilty to the assault charges after the trial judge ruled that they could not rely on the consent of the “victims’ as an answer to the prosecution case. The activities took place at a number of locations, including rooms equipped as torture chambers. Video cameras were used to record events and the tapes copied and distributed amongst members of the group. The prosecution was largely based on the contents of those videotapes. On 19 December 1990, the defendants were convicted and sentenced to terms of imprisonment. The trial judge commented that the unlawful conduct now before the court would be dealt with equally in the prosecution of heterosexuals or bisexuals if carried out by them. The applicants appealed against conviction and sentence. Since the applicants did not appreciate that their actions in inflicting injuries were criminal, reduced sentences were imposed. The appeal, known as the case of R. v. Brown ([1993] 2 All England Law Reports 75), was dismissed by a majority of the House of Lords, two of the five law lords dissenting. Lord Templeman, in the majority, held after reviewing the case-law that: “... the authorities dealing with the intentional infliction of bodily harm do not establish that consent is a defence to a charge under the Act of 1861’”. The question is whether the defence should be extended to the infliction’s of harm in the course of sado-masochistic encounters. Lord Jauncey of Tullichettle found that: ‘In my view the line falls properly to be drawn between assault at common law and the offence of assault occasioning actual bodily harm created by section 47 of the 1861 Act’ ‘ Society is entitled and bound to protect itself against a cult of violence. Pleasure derived from the infliction of pain is an evil thing. Cruelty is uncivilised.‘ ‘I think it right to say something about the submissions that consent to the activity of the appellants would not be injurious to the public interest.’‘I am not prepared to invent a defence of consent for sado-masochistic encounters which breed and glorify cruelty’ There is no suggestion that they and their associates are the only practitioners of homosexual sado-masochism in England and Wales. Wounds can easily become septic if not properly treated, the free flow of blood from a person who is HIV-positive or who has AIDS can infect another and an inflicter who is carried away by sexual excitement or by drink or drugs could very easily inflict pain and injury beyond the level to which the receiver had consented. The possibility of proselytisation and corruption of young men is a real danger. The taking of video recordings of such activities suggests that secrecy may not be as strict as the appellants claimed to your Lordships. House of Lords had to decide whether public interest required penalising the infliction of this degree of harm in private on a consenting recipient, where the purpose was not profit but gratification of sexual desire. Lord Slynn of Hadley found that as the law stood adults were able to consent to acts done in private which did not result in serious bodily harm. He agreed that it was in the end a matter of policy in an area where social and moral factors were extremely important. All the applicants lost their jobs and Mr Jaggard required extensive psychiatric treatment. It was however for the legislature to decide. whether such conduct should be brought within the criminal law.

name: Fikret Çetin
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been fair. On 15 April 1999 he was acquitted of the charges. When acquitting him, the trial court considered that there was insufficient evidence to prove that the applicant was a member of the illegal organisation. It found, however, that he had aided and abetted the organisation. On 6 March 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was found guilty of offences of membership of an illegal organisation and planting explosives. He was sentenced to seventeen years, four months and ten days' imprisonment. In convicting the applicant the trial court relied on the statements taken from him in police custody. The applicant appealed against his conviction and was found not guilty on 13 November 2001. The trial court stated in its judgment that the previous trial had not concerned the bombing incidents in which the applicant was alleged to have been involved. The application was brought before the Diyarbakır State Security Court on 1 August 2000. The prosecutor filed an indictment accusing the applicant of activities carried out for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. The Court of Cassation rejected the appeal and upheld the applicant's conviction. The prosecutor's observations were not communicated to the applicant. The decision was deposited with the registry of the trial court on 16 December 2002. The applicant argued he had been subjected to ill-treatment in police custody and had been forced to sign a number of documents. In his written observations submitted to the Court, the prosecutor referred to the allegations of ill- treatment and drew the court's attention to a video recording which had apparently been made at the time when the police officers took the applicant to the café. Neither the applicant nor his lawyer attended the hearing.

name: Edward Szuluk
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36936/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Edward Szuluk alleged that the monitoring of his medical correspondence while he was in prison breached his right to respect for his correspondence and private life. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr J. Scott, a lawyer practising at Langleys Solicitors in York. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms H. Moynihan of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. The applicant was concerned that his attempts to confirm that he was receiving adequate treatment in hospital might be regarded by the prison medical officer as criticism. He expressed his concerns about his medical correspondence with his external medical specialist being read and applied to the prison governor for a direction that such correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. The prison governor subsequently reconsidered his decision after seeking advice from HM Prison Service Headquarters. On 20 February 2004 the presiding High Court judge, Mr Justice Collins, allowed the applicant’s claim for judicial review. The judge concluded that there were exceptional circumstances in the applicant's case. The applicant, understandably, wanted to ensure that his treatment in prison did not affect him adversely. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal by the Secretary of State and the prison governor. Lord Justice Sedley gave the judgment of the court. It considered that although it was of course possible to verify the existence, address and qualifications of the applicant’s external medical specialist (whose bona fides was not in question), there was no way of ensuring that the latter would not be intimidated or tricked into transmitting illicit messages. While the same was true of, for example, the secretarial staff of members of the House of Commons, it was not possible to ensure that they would not do the same. It was concluded that although the procedure set out in the prison governors letter of 28 November 2002 amounted to an interference with the applicant's right to respect for his correspondence, the interference was justified and proportionate under Article 8 § 2 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal concluded that the monitoring of the applicant’s medical correspondence was a proportionate interference with his Article 8 rights. It did not exclude the possibility that in another case it might be disproportionate to refuse confidentiality to medical correspondence in the prison context. It was recognised that there was an inescapable risk of abuse. But the risk, having been minimised by virtue of confining surveillance to the prison medical officer, was outweighed by the above-mentioned factors. The process by which the measure had been decided upon was not found to be arbitrary. In particular, it had not been the result of the rigid application of a policy. The withdrawal of monitoring had not only been considered but had been implemented until, upon reconsideration, monitoring had been resumed. The applicant’s current conditions of imprisonment are outlined below. Petition for leave to appeal was refused by the House of Lords on the ground that the petition did not raise an arguable point of law of general public importance. The applicant has been located in a Category B prison in Staffordshire since 22 May 2007. name: Maciej Lisiak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37443/97) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his right to have a hearing within a ‘reasonable time’ had not been respected. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The Court declared the application admissible on 23 October 2001. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. The applicant was indicted on the charges of homicide and uttering threats. The trial began on 16 June 1992. On 25 May 1994 the court acquitted the applicant on all charges. On 12 October 1994 the Bielsko-Biała Regional Prosecutor appealed against the acquittal. The appeal was heard before the Katowice Court of Appeal on 9 March 1995. The court quashed the contested judgment and remitted the case. The prosecutor asked the Institute of Forensic Experts to prepare a comprehensive report on S.U.’s psychological profile. The experts set the dates of the examination for 19 December 1995 and for 12 February 1996 respectively. Eventually, S.u. did not keep his appointment for the examination on either of these dates. The trial court remitted the case to the Bielsko-Biała Regional Prosecutor, holding that the prosecution had not complied with the orders given by the Katowice Court of Appeal on 9 March 1995. The trial was to be resumed on 26 March 1999 but it was again postponed. At the hearing held on 9 April 2002 the court, at the Regional Prosecutor’s request, ordered that evidence from a DNA identification test of several hairs found on the victim be obtained to determine whether they belonged to the applicant. However, on 13 May 2002, experts from the Forensic Laboratory of the Silesian Regional Police Headquarters informed the court that the applicant had not been found. The Regional Court had tried to establish the whereabouts of S.U., who was a homeless person. It appears that those efforts have so far been unsuccessful. The proceedings are pending. The court asked the Cracow Institute of Forensic Experts or the Bydgoszcz Forensic Institute to carry out a chondrosome test. On 20 May 2002 the court asked them to make the relevant test and adjourned the trial sine die. In the meantime, the Regional Court has been unable to find S.u., who is believed to be in his 50s or 60s and to have been homeless for some time.

name: Michael Becker
train_texts: The case originated in an application against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, in particular, that in the proceedings for the withdrawing of his driving licence he did not have a hearing before the Administrative Court. The case was communicated to the Government on 28 September 2009. The application was heard by the European Court of Justice on 25 March 2010. The judge found in favour of the Austrian Government and ordered the application to be dismissed. The decision was made to withdraw the applicant’s driving licence for a period of four months as a preventive measure to secure road safety. The Court also found that the applicant's conduct amounted to a refusal to undergo the breathalyser test. Breathalyser tests had been carried out on 15 May 2000 and on 9 November 2000 and each time the breathalyser had been found fully functioning. The applicant appealed and argued that the DAA should have obtained the report of a technical expert on the functioning of the breathlyser as only such an expert could clarify whether the machine was working properly. On 19 December 2005 the Lower Austria Regional Governor (Landeshauptmann) dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The DAA also ordered that an appeal had no suspensive effect because it was necessary to avoid the risk that a person lacking trustworthiness for road traffic might drive. Also the applicant was ordered to follow driver improvement training before his driving licence would be returned. The DAA issued a penal order (Straferkenntnis) and imposed a fine for refusal to take the breathalyser test. The applicant appealed. On 27 September 2007 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. Since no decision had been taken within the prescribed time limit of 15 months after the lodging of the appeal, the fine imposed by the DAA had expired ipso iure. The Administrative Court found that an oral hearing was not likely to contribute to the clarification of the case. This decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 25 October 2007. technical expert on the functioning of the breath analyser.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 44774/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that a ban on wearing the Islamic headscarf in higher-education institutions violated her rights and freedoms. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 2 July 2002 the Chamber declared the application admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 19 November 2002 (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: – for the Government Mr. Ş. Alpaslan, Agent, Mr S. Güran, Counsel. The woman, who was in her early 20s, was wearing the headscarf during a lecture at the University of Bursa. The University issued a circular banning the wearing of the headdress during lectures. The circular was issued in accordance with the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and the law of Turkey. The woman had been wearing the veil for four years. She was allowed to continue to wear it during the lecture but was not allowed to leave the room until the end of the lecture. After the lecture the woman was asked to remove her head scarf. She refused and the university issued a new circular banning her from attending lectures in the future. The student has not been able to attend any lectures since. The applicant was refused admission to a neurology lecture and on 10 June 1998 to a written examination on public health, again for the same reason. The Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the application, holding that by virtue of section 13(b) of the Higher-Education Act (Law no. 2547 – see paragraph 50 below) a university vice chancellor, as the executive organ of the university, had power to regulate students’ dress in order to maintain order. That regulatory power had to be exercised in accordance with the relevant legislation and the judgments of the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Administrative Court. The Administrative Court held that neither the regulation in issue, nor the individual measures, could be considered illegal. The applicant was suspended from Vienna University for one semester for taking part in an unauthorised assembly. Istanbul University argued that the disciplinary penalty was lawful as the reason for the applicant’s one-semester suspension. On 30 November 1999, the Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's appeal. The applicant was granted an amnesty releasing her from all the disciplinary penalties and their effects. On 28 September 2000, the Supreme Administrative Court held that the aforementioned legislation made it unnecessary to examine the merits of the applicants appeal on points of law against the judgment of 30 November. 1999. In the meantime, the applicant had enrolled at Vienna University and pursued her university education.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 13 April 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12875/87) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by an Austrian, Mrs Ingrid Hoffmann, on 20 February 1987. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 9 and 14. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 January 1993. There appeared before the Court: the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the applicant’s representative on the organisation of the proceedings. The Court heard their addresses as well as replies to the questions of some of its members. The application was brought by Mrs Ingrid Hoffmann, a housewife from Austria, who had two children with her husband. She had left the Roman Catholic Church to become a Jehovah's Witness. The applicant applied to the Innsbruck District Court (Bezirksgericht) to be granted parental rights (Elternrechte) Ingrid S. claimed to be better placed to take care of the children than the father. Mr S. submitted that if the children were left in the applicant’s care, there was a risk that they would be brought up in a way that would do them harm. The children had stronger emotional ties with the applicant, having lived with her for a year and a half already, and separating them from her might cause them psychological harm. It followed that it was preferable to leave the children with the mother. By decision of 8 January 1986, the District Court granted parental rights to the applicant. According to its reasoning, only the children's well-being fell to be considered. In no case are parents’ religious convictions as such a relevant criterion in deciding on parental rights and duties pursuant to Article 177 para. 2 of the Civil Code. These rights cannot be refused to a parent or withheld from him for the sole reason that he or she belongs to a religious minority. However, in the concrete case it needs to be examined whether the mother’s religious convictions have a negative influence on her upbringing of the children. It appears in particular that Ingrid S. would not allow blood transfusions to be given to her children. For herself she rejects communal celebration of such customary holidays as Christmas or Easter. Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht) rejected the appeal by decision of 14 March 1986. Mother’s religious convictions thus do not deprive Martin and Sandra of the possibility of celebrating these holidays in the usual way, so that no detriment to the children can be found in this regard either. It appears to be more in the interest of the children's welfare to grant parental rights to the mother than to transfer them to the father. The Jehovah's Witnesses, formerly known as Serious Bible Students, are not outlawed in Austria; it may therefore be assumed that their objectives neither infringe the law nor offend morality (see Article 16 of the Basic Law in conjunction with Article 9) The first-instance court has already dealt at length with part of the appellant’s arguments that relate thereto. The new points raised on appeal - relating to a lack of understanding of democracy and a lack. of subordination to the State - cannot cast doubt on the first- instance decision. ’s welfare ... Admittedly, the mother's religion will in all probability affect the children’S care and upbringing, and they may come to experience a certain tension in relation to an environment which does not correspond to their faith. But the way in which they reached the place where they are currently being taken care of is not necessarily decisive. Even illegal conduct would be of relevance only to the extent that it might, in an individual case, be possible to infer therefrom a lack to suitability. The Supreme Court overturned the judgment of the Innsbruck Regional Court, granting parental rights to Mr S. instead of the applicant. It gave the following reasons: “The appellant has not hitherto claimed that the children belonged to the Roman Catholic faith; however, he has stated, and it has in fact been established, that the mother is bringing them up according to the principles of the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ teaching.” The court added that it was ‘uncontested’ the children do not belong to this confession. According to Article 1 of the 1921 Act the religious education of a child shall be decided upon by an agreement freely entered into by the parents, in so far as the responsibility for his or her care and upbringing is vested in them. The children do not belong to the faith of the Jehovah’s Witnesses. Education according to the principles of this sect (which is not, as the appellant rightly points out, a recognised religious community) contravenes Article 2, paragraph 2, of the 1921 Act. The stress caused to the children by being transferred to the care of the other parent, which in any case is usually transitory, has to be accepted in their own best interests. Although it is preferable for young children to be taken care of by their mother ..., this applies only provided that all other things are equal ... . There is no maternal privilege as regards the attribution of parental right. The Jehovah’s Witnesses form a particular religious movement. It originated in America in the 1870s. A central feature of doctrine is the belief that the Holy Scriptures in the original Hebrew and Greek are the revealed word of Jehovah God and must be taken as literal truth. The refusal to accept blood transfusions is based on several scriptural references, most notably Acts 15: 28-29, which reads: “For you carefully keep yourselves from these things, you will prosper ...“ If you keep abstaining from things sacrificed to idols and from blood and from things strangled and from fornication. is assured.“

Even illegal conduct would be of relevance only to the extent it might, in an individual case, be possible to infer therefrom a lack of suitability for care or upbringing. Mr S. lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) The Supreme Court overturned the judgment of the Innsbruck Regional Court, granting parental rights to Mr S. instead of the applicant. It gave the following reasons: “The appellant has not hitherto claimed that the children belonged to the Roman Catholic faith; however, he has stated, and it has in fact been established, that the mother is bringing them up according to the principles of the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ teaching.” The court added that neither child has suffered any harm in his or her physical or - particularly - psychological development. The children do not belong to the faith of the Jehovah’s Witnesses. Their education according to the principles of this sect (which is not a recognised religious community) contravenes Article 2, paragraph 2, of the 1921 Act. The lower courts also failed in their decisions to give due consideration to the children's welfare. It has been established that if the children are educated according to a religious teaching, they will become social outcasts. Although it is preferable for young children to be taken care of by their mother, this applies only provided that all other things are equal. There is no maternal privilege as regards the attribution of parental right. The stress caused by being transferred to the care of the other parent has to be accepted in their own best interests. Jehovah’s Witnesses form a particular religious movement. They originated in America in the 1870s. They believe that the Holy Scriptures in the original Hebrew and Greek are the revealed word of Jehovah God and must therefore be taken as literal truth. The refusal to accept blood transfusions is based on several scriptural references, most notably Acts 15: 28-29, which reads: “For the holy spirit and we ourselves have favored adding no further burden to you, except these necessary things, to keep abstaining from things sacrificed to idols and from blood and from things strangled and from fornication.“
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 13 April 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12875/87) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by an Austrian, Mrs Ingrid Hoffmann, on 20 February 1987. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 9 and 14. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 January 1993. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court, replaced Mr Ryssdal, who was unable to attend (Rule 21 para. 5, second sub-paragraph) There appeared before the Court: for the Government Mr W. Okresek, Federal Chancellery, Agent, Mr F. Haug, Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Adviser; for the Commission Mrs J. Liddy, Delegate; and for the applicant Mrs Ingrid Hoffmann. Mr S. submitted that if the children were left in the applicant’s care, there was a risk that they would be brought up in a way that would do them harm. He claimed that the educational principles of the religious denomination to which the applicant belonged were hostile to society. The applicant claimed that she was better placed to take care of the children, being in a position to devote herself to them completely, and as a mother better able to provide them with the necessary family environment. She acknowledged, however, that she intended to bring the children up in her own faith. The children had stronger emotional ties with the applicant, having lived with her for a year and a half already, and separating them from her might cause them psychological harm. In no case are parents’ religious convictions as such a relevant criterion in deciding on parental rights and duties pursuant to Article 177 para. 2 of the Civil Code. These rights cannot be refused to a parent or withheld from him for the sole reason that he or she belongs to a religious minority. However, in the concrete case it needs to be examined whether the mother’s religious convictions have a negative influence on her upbringing of the children. It appears in particular that Ingrid S. would not allow blood transfusions to be given to her children; that for herself she rejects communal celebration of such customary holidays as Christmas or Easter. The court cannot consider this so detrimental to the children’s welfare that they should for that reason not be entrusted to their mother, with whom they have such a close psychological relationship and to whose care they are accustomed. “The mother's religious convictions thus do not deprive Martin and Sandra of the possibility of celebrating these holidays in the usual way, so that no detriment to the kids can be found in this regard either.” The Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht) rejected the appeal by decision of 14 March 1986. ‘It appears to be more in the interest of the children's welfare to grant parental rights to the mother than to transfer them to the father' Father's objections against assigning parental rights and duties to the mother cannot in the final instance be decisive. New points raised on appeal cannot cast doubt on the first-instance decision as regards the children’s welfare. Even illegal conduct would be of relevance only to the extent that it might, in an individual case, be possible to infer therefrom a lack of suitability for care or upbringing. No expert medical opinion was sought regarding the question, which was raised anew on appeal, of blood transfusions, which are rejected by the Jehovah's Witnesses. In the event that a judicial remedy arrives too late, it will be up to the physician treating the patient, when confronted with the problem, to reach a decision. The Supreme Court overturned the judgment of the Innsbruck Regional Court, granting parental rights to Mr S. instead of the applicant. “The appellant has not hitherto claimed that the children belonged to the Roman Catholic faith,” the court said. ‘The mother is bringing them up according to the principles of the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ teaching. It is also uncontested that the kids do not belong to this confession.’ ‘Neither child has suffered any harm in his or her physical or - particularly - psychological development,’ the court added. � ‘In fact the appellant could not seriously claim that they had actually suffered in the latter respect’ The Regional Court’s failure to apply this provision is obviously in breach of the law. It has also been established that if the children are educated according to the religious teaching of the Jehovah's Witnesses, they will become social outcasts. The stress caused to the children by being transferred to the care of the other parent, which in any case is usually transitory, has to be accepted in their own best interests. The file contains no documentary basis for the assumption that a change to another carer ‘would with a high degree of probability cause the children serious psychological harm’ The children have a good relationship with their father and with their grandmother, who would take charge of their care and upbringing during the father's absence at work. Jehovah’s Witnesses form a particular religious movement. It originated in America in the 1870s. A central feature of doctrine is the belief that the Holy Scriptures in the original Hebrew and Greek are the revealed word of Jehovah God and must be taken as literal truth. The refusal to accept blood transfusions is based on several scriptural references, most notably Acts 15: 28-29, which reads: “For you carefully keep yourselves from these things, you will prosper ...’” The Jehovah's Witnesses believe that only transfer of parental rights and duties to the father is in the children's best interest.

name: Derya Gazioğlu
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29835/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the intervention of a number of police officers and the force used by those police officers against them in a demonstration in which they were taking part had been in violation of their rights under Articles 3 and 11. On 17 October 2003 the applicants took part in an anti-war demonstration in Istanbul and were arrested and taken into police custody where they remained until their release the following day. On 6 April 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The applicants told the prosecutor that by attending the demonstration they had been exercising their democratic rights. They also alleged that the police had arrested them without any previous warnings. With the exception of the third applicant, Mr Hacı Badem, the applicants complained of ill-treatment. Between 10 December 2003 and 13 April 2004 the Bakırköy prosecutor questioned eleven police officers. Ten of the police officers denied having been at the demonstration or having seen any of the demonstrators. The remaining officer, police chief M.T., said he had not taken part in the dispersal of the demonstration but had questioned the applicants in police station. The Bakırköy prosecutor decided to close the investigation into the applicants’ allegations of ill-treatment. He denied having ill-treated any of the arrestees or having sworn at them. The applicants' objection against the prosecutor’s decision was rejected by the Eyüp Assize Court on 8 December 2004. On 28 January 2008 the Bak Istanbul Criminal Court of First Instance acquitted the applicants, holding that they had exercised their democratic rights and not committed any offences. The decision stated that it was to be served on the applicants. According to a hand-written note on this decision, it was communicated to the applicants on 9 February 2005. On 21 October 2003 criminal proceedings were instigated against the applicants for having taken part in an unlawful demonstration.

name: Bernard Fox
train_texts: The case was brought before the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 13 July 1989. It originated in three applications (nos. 12244/86, 12245/86 and 12383/86) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention. The object of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 5 and 13 ( art. 5, art. 13) The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Buildings, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Kerr for the Government, by Mr Rozakis for the Commission and by Mr Weir for the applicants, as well as their replies to its questions. The first and second applicants, Mr Bernard Fox and Ms Maire Campbell, are husband and wife but separated. Both reside in Belfast, Northern Ireland. On 5 February 1986 they were stopped by the police in Belfast and brought to Woodbourne Royal Ulster Constabulary (“RUC”) station, where a full search of the vehicle in which they were travelling was carried out. Twenty-five minutes after their arrival at the police station, at 3.40 p.m., they were formally arrested. The applicants were detained under section 11 (1) of the 1978. (Emergency Provisions) Act 1978 (“the 1978 Act’; see paragraph 16 below) They were informed that they were being arrested under this section and that this was because the arresting officer suspected them of being terrorists. They were also told that they could be detained for up to 72 hours. No charges were brought against either applicant. The first applicant was released at 11.40 a.m. on 7 February 1986 and the second applicant five minutes later. On 6 February they both initiated proceedings for habeas corpus but were released before the applications came on for hearing before a judge. The third applicant, Mr Samuel Hartley, resides in Waterfoot, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, was arrested at his home, in his parents’ presence, on 18 August 1986. He was informed at the time of his arrest that he was being arrested as he was suspected of being a terrorist. Mr Hartley was suspected of involvement in a kidnapping incident in Ballymena. A young man and woman were forcibly taken away by masked armed men. Those involved in the kidnapping were thought to have connections with the Provisional IRA. The motive behind the kidnapping was believed to have been an attempt to force the young woman to retract an allegation of rape made the previous year as a result of which a person had been convicted and sentenced to 3 years’ imprisonment. No charges were brought against him. He was released on 19 August 1986 at 2.10 p.m. after 30 hours and 15 minutes in detention. He brought no proceedings in connection with his arrest or detention.

name: Johann Aigner
train_texts: The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings against him had been unfair because the Austrian courts refused to grant his request for the further hearing of witnesses. The applicant and his lawyer were given the opportunity to put questions to Mrs K and the hearing was recorded on video. In the course of the struggle she had injured her hand on the knife. Mrs K also stated that she had worked as a prostitute between 1990 and 1996/97, but said that the applicant had been unaware of this. Neither the applicant nor the Government filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court declared the application admissible on 15 February 2007. The application was lodged under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The Graz Regional Court convicted the applicant of attempted rape with violence. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) which upheld his plea of nullity and quashed the conviction. The Supreme Court found that the proceedings before the Regional Court were defective under Article 258 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozeßrechtsordnung) The Regional Court had based its findings on Mrs K’s statements to the police, which had not been read out at the trial. At the trial Mrs K refused to give evidence. At hearings on 1 July, 26 August, 15 October and 19 November 2002, it heard evidence from the applicant and further witnesses. Mrs K refused to give evidence and requested that the statements she had made to the police and the investigating judge be read out instead. The Court also granted the applicant’s request for the video recording of her deposition before the investigatingJudge to be shown. When played, the video Recording turned out to be a blank tape. The court dismissed the applicant's requests for the further taking of evidence. It did not consider it useful to visit the scene as the room in question was no longer in the state it had been in at the material time. It dismissed the request for Mrs K to be called again to give further evidence as she had refused to giving evidence at the trial and there was no indication she would change her mind. Court relied partly on Mrs K’s statements to the police and the investigating judge. It noted that Mrs K had been under the influence of alcohol to a considerable degree at the time of the events. The court did not believe the applicant's account that he had invited Mrs K for drinks all afternoon and then to his room out of sympathy for her. It sentenced the applicant to three years’ imprisonment. Referring to a psychiatric expert opinion, it further ordered that he be detained in an institution for mentally ill offenders. The applicant filed a plea of nullity with the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) in which he complained about the dismissal of his requests for further evidence. On 20 February 2003 the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s plea of nullity. The applicant had not submitted any reasons why Mrs K would be prepared to give evidence after refusing to do so at the trial on 1 July 2002. The Supreme Court also found that the request to hear further evidence from Mr H had not been sufficiently substantiated as it was conditional. On 9 April 2003 the Graz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) dismissed the applicant's appeal, but granted the Public Prosecutor's cross-appeal and increased the sentence to four years’ imprisonment. That decision was served on the applicant and his counsel on 9 May 2003. Victims of sexual offences by the accused are exempted from giving evidence at the trial if there has been an adversarial hearing of the victim in the preliminary proceedings. This provision was introduced as part of the 1998 reform of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Prior to this reform, only minors aged under fourteen at the time of an alleged sexual offence were exempted fromGiving evidence at trial. The argument in favour of increasing procedural safeguards for the alleged victims of sexual offence is the danger of the court proceedings causing damage and traumatisation to the victim. However, it would also appear to be in the interest of victims aged over fourteen for them to be questioned only once, as making a statement places a heavy mental burden on them. Article 250 of the 1975 Code of Criminal Procedure provides that the presiding judge at the trial may exceptionally order an accused to be held in an adjacent room while a witness gives evidence. The accused must be informed of all statements made in his absence. Article 3 of Council Framework Decision no. 2001/220/JHA requires each Member State inter alia to supply evidence and to take appropriate measures to ensure that its authorities question victims only in so far as necessary for the purpose of criminal proceedings. The European Court of Justice stated that the objectives of these provisions consist, in particular, in ensuring that particularly vulnerable victims receive “specific treatment best suited to their circumstances”

The public prosecutor, the defendant and the defendant’s lawyer should be given an opportunity to attend the hearing and question the witness. name: Resul Sadak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 74318/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were members of the Peoples’ Democracy Party (Halkın Demokrasi Partisi, hereinafter ‘HADEP’) in Şırnak, which was a province in the State of Emergency region. On 3 November 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the applicants’ right to be brought promptly before a judge. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. Erdal Güler was taken into custody on 27 September 2000. He was kept in custody until 11 a.m. on 1 October 2000. The applicants were then taken to the Şırnak provincial gendarmerie command. Criminal proceedings were brought against the applicants on charges of aiding and abetting the PKK contrary to Article 169 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of Law no. 3713. In 2002 and 2003 the applicants were acquitted of the charges against them. In December 2000 the Diyarbakır State Security Court ordered the applicants’ release pending trial, and they were released in December 2000.

name: H. Rydz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13167/02) lodged on 1 March 2002 with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the length of his detention was excessive and that the criminal proceedings in his case exceeded a “reasonable time’ The applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed multiple gang rape (including statutory rape), of inducing the victims to take intoxicants and of persuading the victims not to inform the police about those crimes. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. In October 1999 the public prosecutor ordered expert opinions on the kind of injuries the victims had suffered. The opinions were submitted on 6 and 15 October 1999. In 2000 the first-instance court held 11 hearings during which the evidence of the witnesses and defendants was heard. The applicant was charged with seven offences: participation in an organised criminal gang, gang rape (including statutory rape) committed with extreme cruelty and in conjunction with deprivation of liberty, and with threatening the victims and persuading them not to inform the police about the crimes. The court found that the grounds for detention on remand were still valid and owing to the fact that the crimes had been committed in co-operation with other persons. The case involved thirteen defendants and sixty-six witnesses. In 2001 nineteen hearings were held and three had to be adjourned or cancelled because of the illness of a judge, the absence of a witness or the fact that the case file was with the Court of Appeal. Fines were imposed on eleven absent witnesses. Several witnesses had changed their testimonies and the reading out of their earlier statements had been justified. The court remanded in custody one of the defendants who had failed to appear at a hearing and lifted the detention of another. The hearing scheduled for 30 January 2001 was adjourned in order to have one. of the victims heard with the assistance of a psychologist. The applicant served a one-year prison sentence imposed in separate proceedings. The Wrocław Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 15 February 2002. The court noted that, since June 2000, the first-instance court had held seven hearings and examined ten witnesses. The absence of other witnesses was the major reason for the prolongation of the proceedings. The defendants (among them the applicant) made almost twenty applications for the examination and cross-examination of witnesses, the ordering of expert opinions and inspections of the crime scene. and to cross-examine them. From 10 April 2002 until 9 December 2002 the applicant was serving a prison sentence imposed on him in separate proceedings. Opole Regional Court found the applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to nine years' imprisonment and a four-year period of deprivation of his civic rights. The court dismissed the defendant's request to summon other absent witnesses, having found that their examination would not add anything to the case. The police were ordered to determine the whereabouts of two defendants. All the accused appealed. On 2 June 2003 the Wrocław Court of Appeal upheld the judgment with respect to the applicant. The case originated in an application (no. 13167/02) lodged on 1 March 2002 with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The judge ruled that the application was not in breach of any of the constitutional provisions. The case was settled at the Supreme Court of Poland in November 2006. The ruling was made by the majority of the court, with the decision by the minority, the minority and the majority being upheld. The applicant was charged with seven offences: participation in an organised criminal gang, gang rape (including statutory rape) committed with extreme cruelty and in conjunction with deprivation of liberty. The court requested the police to determine the whereabouts of nine witnesses. Fines were imposed on eleven absent witnesses. Several witnesses had changed their testimonies and the reading out of their earlier statements had been justified. Almost thirty witnesses remained to be heard at that stage of the proceedings and there was a need to summon further witnesses. The applicant served a one-year prison sentence imposed in separate proceedings from 11 April 2001 until 10 April 2002. train_texts: The San Marinese government issued an expropriation order in respect of certain plots of land belonging to the applicant church. The latter was awarded 114,790,590 Italian lire (about 59,284 euros) in compensation. The applicant church applied to the government seeking to recover possession of the unused land. On 20 October 1987 the government refused the application on the ground that the land in question could still be used in the interests of the community. The court dismissed the applications on the grounds that, firstly, the expropriated order was an administrative act and thus fell outside the civil court’s jurisdiction. The first hearing was held on 9 April 1992. The applicant church alleged that the authorities’ conduct had breached Article 1 of Protocol No. 18/1980. The parties lodged their final submissions on 10 February and 24 March 1994. Preparation of the case was concluded on 27 April 1994. In December 1994 the appeal Judge C.P. died. No other judge could replace him, as the organisational structure of the court of civil appeals provided for only one judge. On 25 April 1995 the General Grand Council appointed Judge P.G.P to replace the deceased judge. However, P. G.P asked the Council of the XII for leave to withdraw from the proceedings in question on the ground that he had been involved as the first-instance civil judge. Church had asked the government on 3 March 1992 to return its assets. A new land-use plan had taken effect, changing the designated use of the land in question from industrial to agricultural. On 20 April 1993 it applied to the first-instance administrative court. A hearing took place on 3 August 1993. The court declared the expropriation order of 7 March 1985 void in so far as it had lapsed in respect of that particular property, but pointed out that declaring it void did not create a right to reconveyance. The government then lodged an appeal, disputing the existence of an implied refusal which would legitimise an application. He concluded that the applicant church’s request of 20 April 1993 was inadmissible. The Council of the XII upheld the appeal court's judgment on 27 September 1994. It ruled that the public-interest declaration in connection with the urban development work had transformed Beneficio Cappella Paolini's right of property into a mere legitimate interest. On 7 March 1985 the San Marinese government issued an expropriation order in respect of certain plots of land belonging to the applicant church. The applicant church applied to the government seeking to recover possession of the unused land. On 20 October 1987 the government refused the application on the ground that the land in question could still be used in the interests of the community. In December 1994 the appeal Judge C.P. died. No other judge could replace him, as the organisational structure of the court of civil appeals provided for only one judge. On 25 April 1995 the General Grand Council appointed Judge P.G.P to replace the deceased judge. However, P. G.P asked the Council of the XII for leave to withdraw from the proceedings in question on the ground that he had been involved as the first-instance civil judge. Under section 17 of Law no. 2/1995, the Council was responsible for ruling on requests to withdraw or applications challenging a judge. Church had asked government to return its assets. But it pointed out that declaring it void did not create a right to reconveyance. The judge found that the State had acquired ownership of the plots of land in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law. He concluded that the applicant church’s request of 20 April 1993 was inadmissible, since the government's behaviour could not be described as an implied refusal. Finally, he stated that, in declaring the expropriation order partially void – an order which, moreover, had never been contested – the first-instance administrative court had exceeded its jurisdiction. On 27 September 1994 the Council of the XII upheld the appeal court's judgment. It concluded that, while the public-interest declaration in connection with the urban development work had transformed Beneficio Cappella Paolini's right of property into a mere legitimate interest, section 14(3) of Law no. 15/1980 conferred not only a legitimate interest in the lawfulness of the authorities’ actions.

The San Marinese government issued an expropriation order in respect of certain plots of land belonging to the applicant church. The latter was awarded 114,790,590 Italian lire (about 59,284 euros) in compensation. The land, which was earmarked for urban development projects that were scheduled for completion by 31 December 1987, was only partially used. The applicant church applied to the government seeking to recover possession of the unused land. On 20 October 1987 the government refused the application on the ground that the land in question could still be used in the interests of the community. The parties submitted their written pleadings on 23 May 1991. Preparation of the case was concluded on 14 November 1991. The first hearing was held on 9 April 1992. The applicant church alleged that the authorities’ conduct had breached Article 1 of Protocol No. 18/1980. The parties lodged their final submissions on 10 February and 24 March 1994. Preparation of the case was concluded on 27 April 1994. In December 1994 the appeal Judge C.P. died. No other judge could replace him, as the organisational structure of the court of civil appeals provided for only one judge. On 25 April 1995 the General Grand Council appointed Judge P.G.P to replace the deceased judge. In September 1995 the Council of the XII granted the request and sent the case in question to an appeal judge in question. The applicant church had asked the government on 3 March 1992 to return its assets. It sent the government a formal notice asking it to adopt the necessary measures for restitution. On 20 April 1993 it applied to the first-instance administrative court. A hearing took place on 3 August 1993. The court declared the expropriation order of 7 March 1985 void in so far as it had lapsed in respect of that particular property, but pointed out that declaring it void did not create a right to reconveyance. The government then lodged an appeal, disputing the existence of an implied refusal which would legitimise an application. By a judgment of 17 August 1993, deposited at the registry on the same date, the court stated that it did not have jurisdiction to “recognise the possible right to restitution of unused land’ The judge found that the State had acquired ownership of the plots of land in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law. He concluded that the applicant church’s request of 20 April 1993 was inadmissible. The Council of the XII upheld the appeal court's judgment, thus endorsing the expert's conclusion that the public-interest declaration in connection with the urban development work had transformed Beneficio Cappella Paolini's right of property into a mere legitimate interest. The case file was sent to the council on an unspecified date, and on 27 September 1994 the council ruled that the expropriation order had lapsed because the deadline for completion of the work had expired.

name: Uğur Eşim
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 59601/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Uğur Eşim (‘the applicant’), was born in 1969 and lives in İstanbul. In 1990 the applicant was severely wounded by gunshots during a clash between the security forces and a group of terrorists. On 2 April 1992 he was declared to be suffering from a permanent disability and discharged from the army. He was also awarded a sixth-degree disability pension. On 19 September 2007 the applicant applied to the Ministry of Defence for compensation in respect of his injury. He alleged that, on account of medical negligence, the bullet in his head had remained unnoticed and he had sustained further pecuniary damage. On 21 January and 18 February 2009 respectively the Supreme Military Administrative Court, by a majority, rejected both actions as being out of time. In both decisions the court held that notwithstanding the fact that the applicant had not been aware of the bullet in his head until 2007, pursuant to section 43(1), his compensation claims should have been lodged within five years of the incident. Its decision was served on the applicant on 6 May 2009. On 22 April 2009 the Supreme military administrative court rejected a rectification request lodged by the applicant. On 6 June 2009 the applicant was awarded a compensation payout of £1,000. name: Mustafa Tamamboğa
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1636/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants were arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the PKK. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mr M.A. Altunkalem, a lawyer practising in Diyarbakır. At each hearing, the court considered releasing the applicants pending trial both ex officio as well as upon their requests. By a letter dated 28 August 2006 the Court was informed that the second applicant was purging his sentence in Bolu prison. The applicants were held in custody for more than a decade. They were convicted as charged and sentenced to life imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment in respect of 14 of the accused, including the applicants. The case was sent back to the Diyarbakır State Security Court where the proceedings against the applicants commenced on 29 July 1997. The applicants failed to attend some of the hearings. At each hearing the court, relying on the nature of the offence, the state of the evidence and the content of the case-file, decided to prolong their remand in custody. The court also considered releasing the applicants pending trial both ex officio as well as upon their own requests. The case was brought before the Diyarbakır State Security Court on 15 May 2001. The judge who had been appointed to replace the military judge, sat as a member of the trial court for the first time. On the same day the court convicted the applicants as charged and sentenced them to life imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment in respect of the first applicant on 7 November 2001 and upheld the second applicant's conviction on 17 March 2003. The first applicant's sentence was reduced to six years and three months' imprisonment on 22 June 2005. The applicant was given time to prepare his observations on the merits of the case.

On 15 May 2001 the Diyarbakır State Security Court decided to disjoin the case of the two co‑accused who could not be found.
