name: Gerhard W. Luedicke
train_texts: The case originated in three applications against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission by Mr. Gerhard W. Luedicke, Mr. Mohammed Belkacem and Mr. Arif Koç in 1973, 1974 and 1975 respectively. The application was lodged on 1 October 1977, the request on 10 October. Their purpose is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 para. 3 (e) and 14 (art. 6-3-e, art. 14) of the Convention. The President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges called upon to sit as members of the Chamber. The five judges thus designated were Mr. J. Cremona, Mrs. H. Pedersen, Mr D. Evrigenis, Mr P.-H. Teitgen and Mr G. Lagergren. The Government filed their memorial on 30 January 1978. The Secretary to the Commission advised the Deputy Registrar on 17 April that the Delegates had decided not to file a memorial in reply. Mr Balladore Pallieri, acting in pursuance of Rule 24 para. 4, granted himself exemption from sitting on the case. On 21 November, Mr. Wiarda, the Vice-President of the Court, became a full member of the Chamber. The oral hearings took place in public at the Human Rights Building, Stras. The hearing was adjourned until 25 May, with the Government undertaking responsibility for the interpretation into French or English of their oral arguments. Three applicants were charged before the German courts with the commission of various criminal offences. Since they were not sufficiently familiar with the language of the country, they were assisted by an interpreter in accordance with German law. After conviction they were ordered, amongst other things, to pay the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. They consider that the inclusion of this latter item is contrary to, inter alia, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. The Commission produced to the Court certain documents referred to by the Principal Delegate at the hearings. These documents were the subject of a letter, received on 16 August, from the Agent of the Government. Interpretation costs are part of the costs of the proceedings, according to Article 464 (a) para. 1, first sentence, of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozeßordnung) In the event of acquittal or of proceedings being discontinued, the Treasury in principle bears the costs. If the individual concerned is convicted, he has to pay the costs, but only such proportion thereof as relates to the criminal charges upheld by the court. The obligation to employ an interpreter is, however, subject to one exception, namely when all the participants are familiar with the foreign language (section 185 para. 2 of the Constitution of the Courts Act). Gerhard W. Luedicke was convicted of a road traffic offence in 1972. He was fined DM 900 and ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings. He appealed against the decision, claiming that it breached Article 6 para. 3 (e) of the Convention. The matter was referred to the Bielefeld Regional Court, which upheld the decision. Mr. Luingicke is a citizen of the United Kingdom and was, at the time of his application to the Commission, a member of the British Forces stationed in the Federal Republic of Germany. He is the only person to have been found guilty of the offence. Mohammed Belkacem is an Algerian citizen, born in 1954. After completing his apprenticeship as a locksmith in Algeria, he rejoined his father in the Federal Republic of Germany where he followed various occupations. In December 1973, he was involved in a dispute in a Berlin night-club during which another client lost his coat. He was sentenced to six months in prison, suspended for three years and fined €1,000. The sentence was suspended for two years and the fine was reduced to €600. Mr. Belkafem was also ordered to pay the costs of interpreters for the duration of the trial. Berlin-Tiergarten Juvenile Court convicted Mr. Belkacem of assault occasioning bodily harm. He was sentenced to four weeks’ imprisonment (Dauerarrest) and to a fine of DM 500. On 11 April 1975, the Berlin- tiergarten District Court served him with a notice to pay costs amounting to DM 665.63, including DM 321.95 for interpretation costs. The applicant unsuccessfully challenged the inclusion of interpretation costs in this assessment of the costs. On 29 May 1975, his appeal was dismissed by the District Court which held, inter alia, that Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention granted him exemption. Arif Koç was convicted of causing grievous bodily harm in 1973. He was sentenced to a year’s imprisonment, but the balance of his sentence remaining after allowance had been made for his detention on remand was commuted. Mr. Koç notified the relevant authorities in Alsdorf, near Aachen, his last place of residence in Germany, of his intention to return to Turkey. On 5 May 1977, following a request by Mr. Belkacem, the Berlin Justizkasse allowed him to defer payment “until the decision of the Commission of Human Rights be known’ From that time, he has not been required to pay the costs in question. Assize Court held that the “free’ assistance of an interpreter is to be understood as being free once and for all time. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28388/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The case was subsequently remitted to the Ankara Commercial Court. The applicant and Global A.Ş. appealed the judgment of 7 November 2001. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment on 10 October 2002. The applicant requested rectification of the decision on 13 January 2003. On 11 April 2003 the Court ofCassation dismissed the applicant’s request. The appeal was dismissed again on 17 April 2003. The judge ordered the defendants to pay the applicant TRL 1,512,000,000 with simple interest. The decision was upheld on 9 November 2003 and the applicant appealed again. The case was dismissed on 17 November 2003. It was dismissed by the Court on 11 April 2004 and the appeal was settled.

name: Radosław Antonicelli

Mr Radosław Antonicelli, (“the applicant”), complained that he had been deprived of access to the Supreme Court. The Polish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was represented by Mr T. Sak, a lawyer practising in Głubczyce. He was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. The lawyer requested the court to be exempted from the obligation to represent the applicant. In his view, there were no grounds on which to accept that any grounds for a cassation appeal obtained in the case. This was so because in the appeal against the first-instance judgment he had relied only on the disproportionate nature of the sentence, which could not be argued before the Supreme Court. The Wrocław Court of Appeal informed the applicant of this refusal by a letter dated 22 March 2005. It was further stated that in these circumstances the only course of action left to the applicant was to request the Ombudsman to lodge a cassity appeal on his behalf.

train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The court took some procedural decisions and heard several of the co-accused, including the second applicant who maintained that he had nothing to say. The civilian judge who had been appointed to replace the military judge sat as a member of the trial court for the first time. This decision was pronounced, in the absence of the applicants’ representative, on 14 June 2000, in Erzurum. The court examined and dismissed the requests of the Applicants to be released from jail. The Court ofCassation dismissed the applicants' appeal and upheld the judgment of the first‑instance court. The Applicants were sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment. The applicants alleged that they were denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal. The applications were allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. By a decision of 8 March 2005 the Court declared the applications admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings. Both applicants repudiated the statements they had given to the police, claiming that they had been made under duress. The applicants maintained that, in view of the judgment of the European Court on Human Rights concerning State Security Courts, they were boycotting the court and were not going to give any statements. The first applicant requested the rectification of some of his words contained in the previous minutes of the hearings. The civilian judge who had been appointed to replace the military judge sat as a member of the trial court for the first time on 13 July 1999. On 5 October 1999 before the court two persons filed petitions to intervene as third-parties in the proceedings. The applicants were convicted and sentenced to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. They appealed to the Court of Cassation against the judgment of the State Security Court. The applicants were released from prison on an unspecified date in 2000. The appeal was dismissed in the absence of the applicants’ representative on 5 June 2000. This decision was pronounced, in the presence of the applicant’s representative, on 14 June 2000, by the first-instance court. The appeals were dismissed at a second hearing on 5 July 2000 by the court of cassation. The case was decided by the third-party intervention of two persons. The applications were heard on 26 October 1999 by a court in Erzurum.

The case originated in an application (no. 37555/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged principally that he had not been arrested on a reasonable suspicion. He also alleged that he did not have an enforceable right to compensation in respect of these matters. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 June 2001. The Court heard addresses by Mr MacDonald, Mr Freeland and Mr Paulin. The Chamber declared the application partly admissible on 14 March 2000. The decision is obtainable from the Registry. This case concerns his arrest in 1985 in relation to the murder of Mr Kurt Konig. In or about January 1994 he was awarded damages of 2,500 pounds sterling (GBP) for an incident in Guildhall Square on 16 March 1993. The judge found that he had been wrongfully arrested by police officers who had purported to arrest the applicant for obstruction in failing to give his name. The Government submitted that Special Branch received intelligence that the applicant and three other persons were involved in the murder. The intelligence derived from four informants who had proved reliable in the past and had provided information leading to seizures of explosives or firearms. None of the informants had a criminal record. He was interviewed on thirty-four occasions. He did not respond to any questions. The applicant was released without charge on 3 January 1986 at 9 p.m. after six days and thirteen hours in custody. He instituted a civil action for damages before the High Court in Northern Ireland in respect of, inter alia, assault, seizure of documents, false imprisonment and unlawful arrest. It was common ground that the murder was a terrorist offence. The superior officer was not called as a witness in the proceedings. He had been told by his superior officer, Inspector B., that the applicant was involved in the murder and stated that these were the reasonable grounds for suspecting the applicant. Judge McCollum found that there had been an unlawful taking of the applicant’s notes by a police officer and awarded Mr O’Hara GBP 100 in damages. He rejected the applicant's claims of assault and ill-treatment, finding that he had not satisfied him on the balance of probabilities that his version of events was right and that of the police officers wrong. The judge found on the evidence that the detective constable had a suspicion that the [applicant] was involved in the murder of Kurt Konig and that this suspicion was reasonably based on information given to him by a superior officers at the briefing that morning. The applicant gave notice of appeal to the Court of Appeal in Northern Ireland concerning the claim of unlawful arrest and false imprisonment. On 6 May 1994 the appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the decision of the High Court that reasonable suspicion could be derived from information provided by a superior officer. “Notwithstanding his concern that more detail of the briefing had not been given, the learned trial judge was able to conclude: ‘(1) that the arresting officer ... did have a suspicion that the [applicant] was involved in a terrorist murder and it was implicit that that suspicion was genuinely held by him.’ These were factual findings and clearly contained in our view all the essential proofs ...” An appeal to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal was dismissed on 12 December 1996. In his judgment, with which the other judges agreed, Lord Hope of Craighead held that it was not necessary for an arresting officer to possess all the information which had led to the decision to arrest. Lord Steyn stated, inter alia, concerning the general principles: “Certain general propositions about the powers of constables under a section such as section 12(1) can now be summarised. (1) In order to have a reasonable suspicion the constable need not have evidence amounting to a prima facie case. (2) Hearsay information may therefore afford a constable reasonable grounds to arrested. Such information may come from other officers ... (3) The information which causes the constorable to be suspicious of the individual must be in existence to the knowledge of the police officer at the time he makes the arrest. (4) The executive ‘discretion’ to arrest or not ... vests in theconstable ... and not in his superior officers. "A mere request to arrest without any further information by an equal ranking officer, or a junior officer, is incapable of amounting to reasonable grounds for the necessary suspicion," the court said. "How can the badge of superior officers and the fact that he gave an order make a difference? ... In practice it follows that a constable must be given some basis for a request to arrested someone under a provision such as section 12(1), e.g. a report from an informer’s report," it said. The court ruled that the ruling was incorrect and that the judge should have been able to make his own decision.

name: Antonius Adrianus van der Tang
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 18 July 1994 by the Government of the Kingdom of Spain. It originated in an application (no. 19382/92) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Netherlands national, Mr Antonius Adrianus van der Tang, on 2 December 1991. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The President gave the lawyer leave to use the Dutch language (Rule 27 para. 3). The Netherlands Government, who had been notified by the Registrar of their right to intervene, indicated that they did not intend to do so. On 26 August 1994, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members of the Court. Antonius Adrianus van der Tang was born in 1959 and lives in Haarlem in the Netherlands. He was found driving a lorry which contained 1,300 kg of hashish. The lorry belonged to the applicant. The applicant was also found in possession of a pistol with its serial number chiselled off and of a radio pre-tuned to a station which coincided with that of another set found. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg on 20 February 1995. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr J. Borrego Borreago, Head of the Legal Department for Human Rights, Ministry of Justice and of the Interior. The applicant was arrested on 25 May 1989 in Vigo, Spain. The drugs were in the possession of Luciano Núñez, who was also arrested. At least eight more people were subsequently detained for allegedly being involved in a three-stage operation to deliver about 7,000 kg of hashish. The judge held that there was sufficient reason to believe that the applicant was criminally responsible for the commission of a public-health offence. The applicant's detention was confirmed. An appeal by the applicant against this order appears to have been dismissed. On 25 September 1989 Mr van der Tang was charged with an offence against public health (sections 344 and 344 bis (a) of the Criminal Code) and unlawful possession of a firearm. Mr van der Tang lodged his first applications for provisional release in October 1989. These applications were rejected on 9 October and 25 November 1989. On 26 September 1990 the Audiencia Provincial refused the applications for release, briefly stating: “The original circumstances on which the detention pending trial was decided remain unchanged’ (see paragraph 45 below) In the applicant's submission, only the fact of his being a foreigner seemed to account for his long period of detention. In the course of 1989 the Spanish public prosecutor stated that he would not oppose the applicant’s release provided that he paid security of 500,000 pesetas, handed in his passport and reported daily to police. Authorities had launched a nationwide operation to combat a large-scale drug-trafficking organisation which operated mainly in Galicia. The applicant's case was considered to be closely linked with other files relating to Nécora and was therefore transferred to Madrid on 29 October 1990. He was now charged not only with an offence against public health and unlawful possession of a firearm of foreign origin but also with smuggling and criminal association. An appeal by the applicant against these orders which included a request for release was eventually rejected on 8 July 1991 by the Third Criminal Division of the Audiencia Nacional. The grounds for the decision not to release the applicant were the seriousness of the alleged offences, considerations of public order and the high risk of absconding on account of the applicant's foreign nationality. Van der Tang was arrested in January 1991 on suspicion of smuggling illegal drugs. He was detained for two years before his case was referred to the Audiencia Nacional for trial. On 29 April 1992 the applicant lodged a new application for release, subject to the following conditions: (a) the applicant was to pay in cash a security of 8 million pesetas; (b) he was to give an address and inform the court of any subsequent change; (c) he had to report daily to the police in Vigo; and (d) he wasn't to leave Spanish territory. The application was granted on 11 June 1992. Mr van der Tang has been in detention for over three years. The period of time that has elapsed clearly - why not be frank about it? - owes much to ill fortune and the vicissitudes of the proceedings. He could have been tried in Galicia several months ago, when the Pontevedra public prosecutor did not oppose his provisional release. The same lapse of time argues in favour of varying the order placing him in detention pending trial, relaxing the conditions of detention by making it possible to avoid it altogether. The court did not consider that the accused's foreign nationality constituted an insurmountable obstacle to reaching this conclusion, because other foreign defendants in the case are in fact not being held in detention. Van der Tang travelled to the Netherlands in order to spend Christmas with his family. The prosecutor demanded a total prison sentence of fourteen years and a fine of 60 million pesetas in respect of an offence against public health. On 9 July 1993 the police informed the court that the applicant's whereabouts were unknown. Thereupon the applicant and his surety - his wife - were ordered to appear before it on 23 July 1993 at a hearing concerning the forfeiture of the bail. Neither the applicant nor his representatives appear to have contacted the Audiencia Nacional at this stage, nor do they seem to have informed that court of his new address. The Spanish authorities have not requested Mr van der Tang's extradition. Luciano Núñez (see paragraph 8 above) was held to have played a leading role in importing very large quantities of hashish. He was accordingly sentenced to a total of thirteen years' imprisonment and a fine of 100 million pesetas. It does not appear from the facts set out in this judgment that the applicant was involved in drug-trafficking activities beyond the transporting of 1,300 kg ofHashish for which he was arrested. The Spanish authorities haven't requested Mr Van der Tang’s extradition. They have not asked for his extradition.

The second offence in itself attracting a prison sentence of “prisión menor en su grado medio’ (that is, from two years, four months and one day to four years and two months) The applicant's case was transferred to Madrid on 29 October 1990. An appeal by the applicant against these orders which included a request for release was eventually rejected on 8 July 1991 by the Third Criminal Division of the Audiencia Nacional. However, the summons could not be served on him, as he no longer lived at the address he had originally given the Spanish authorities. On 9 July 1993 the police informed the court that the applicant's whereabouts were unknown. Thereupon the applicant and his surety - his wife - were ordered to. appear before it on 23 July 1993 at a hearing concerning the forfeiture of the bail. The Spanish authorities have not requested Mr van der Tang's extradition. Luciano Núñez (see paragraph 8 above) was held to have played a leading role in importing very large quantities of hashish. train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 29 May 1995, and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation (“the Government’s) on 26 June 1995. It originated in an application (no. 23218/94) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Turkish national, Mr Riza Gül, on 31 December 1993. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8 ( art. 8) of the Convention. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 October 1995. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr O. Jacot-Guillarmod, Assistant Director, Head of the International Affairs Division, Federal Office of Justice, Agent, Mr F. Schürmann and Mrs S. Marconato. For the applicant Mr R. Plender QC, Mr J. Walker, Fürsprech, Counsel. Mr Gül is a Turkish national, who was born in 1947 and now lives with his wife at Pratteln in the canton of Basle Rural, Switzerland. In 1987 the applicant’s wife, who had remained in Turkey with their two sons, seriously burned herself during a fit brought on by her epilepsy, from which she had suffered since 1982. In December 1987 she joined her husband in Switzerland, where she was taken into hospital as an emergency case. Two of the fingers of her left hand were amputated. On 19 September 1988 in Switzerland Mrs Gül gave birth to her third child, Nursal, a daughter. As she still suffered from epilepsy, she could not take care of the baby, who was placed in a home in Switzerland. He worked in a restaurant there until 1990, when he fell ill. Since then he has been in receipt of a partial-invalidity pension. Mr Gül asked the Basle Rural Cantonal Aliens Police for permission to bring to Switzerland his two sons, Tuncay and Ersin, who had remained in Turkey. The conditions for the issue of such a permit laid down in Article 13 (f) of the Federal Council’s Order Limiting the Number of Aliens (‘the OLNA’ - see paragraph 21 below) had been satisfied. In a decision of 19 September 1990 the Aliens Police rejected his request, on the ground that the conditions for family reunion had not been satisfied (Article 39 of the OLNA - see paragraphs 21 and 22 below) The Swiss government has ruled that there is no right to a child to live in the country without a permit. The decision was based on the fact that the father of the child does not have a permit to reside in Switzerland. The father does, however, have the right to stay in Switzerland if he has a residence permit from the Swiss government. The court ruled in favour of the father's right to remain in Switzerland as his son has a right to be part of the family and to live with him in the same house as his parents. The case was decided by the Court of Appeal and the decision was made on the basis of the merits of the case, not the content of the facts. The Liestal Cantonal Hospital sent the case to the cantonal government in October 1990. Mr Gül's net monthly income is CHF 2,060, which falls CHF 650 short of the amount required for the minimum standard of living as calculated by the social security services. The cost of keeping the youngest child, Nursal, in a children’s home has not been taken into account, as it is not known who pays for this. The calculation of income is based on pay-slips from 1989, the latest available. The case was referred to the Swiss Court of Human Rights, which ruled that the case should be dismissed. Basle Rural Aliens Police a medical certificate stating that Mr Gül was 100% unfit for work and would remain so for a period that it was not possible to determine. The social security services cannot be expected to provide for children arriving from abroad when it is known in advance that they will have to support them. For that reason alone the application for family reunion must be refused. It is not at all certain that firm arrangements could be made for the care of the family's eight-year-old son Ersin. He too would presumably have to be brought up in a children’s home, which is not the aim of family reunion. Ersin Gül has lived with Tuncay since birth. He has been separated from his father and mother for eight years and three and a half years respectively. Ersin and Tuncays would be separated. The question arises, at the very least, whether it is reasonable to separate him from his brother and the environment he is used to in order to bring him to live with his mother, who is seriously ill and unable to keep him with her or look after him. In any case, there is no important reason within the meaning of Article 36 of the OLNA which requires him to be admitted to Switzerland. Mr Gül argued that the same considerations which had prevailed in the decision to grant that residence permit should prevent any withdrawal thereof. The Federal Court declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible. The court gave this ruling in the following terms: “Article 8 (art. 8) of the European Convention on Human Rights guarantees the right to respect for family life. In certain circumstances the. right to be issued with a residence permit can be deduced from this (see ATF [Judgments of the Swiss Federal Court] 118 Ib 152 at 4, 157 at c; 116 Ib 355 at 1b; 109 Ib 185 at 2)” According to the Federal Court’s established case-law, however, a breach can occur only where the family members living in Switzerland themselves possess a well-established right of abode (Anwesenheitsrecht) For that purpose, it is in principle necessary to have Swiss nationality or possess a settlement permit. A mere residence permit is at any rate not sufficient unless it is based on a firmly established right (see ATF 111 Ib 163/4 at 1a) ... That is, moreover, consistent with the new provisions on the legal status of aliens having family members in Switzerland (sections 7 and 17 (2) of the RSAA, as amended on 23 March 1990) The only effect of a finding that a case is an extremely serious one within the meaning of Article 13 (f) of the Federal Council’s Order Limiting the Number of Aliens of 6 October 1986 (hereinafter the OLNA - SR 823.21) is to exclude the alien concerned from the quotas laid down in that Order; it does not imply the existence of a right to a residence permit. The Aliens Police prefer to remain free to decide when such a permit should be issued (see ATF 119 Ib 35 at 1a). In the instant case the possibility cannot be entirely ruled out that in the future the medical or other reasons which led the authorities to grant the residence permit will lose their significance. Ersin Gül lived with Kurdish families who used to live in the village where he was born, including the family of his elder brother. The applicant maintained that Ersin frequently moved from one home to another and spent two or three days staying with various Kurdish families. Owing to his grandfather’s limited financial resources and the distance between the homes of some of these families and the school it was not possible for the boy to attend school on a regular basis. As is evidenced by an article which appeared in the Turkish newspaper Sabah on 25 July 1995, Mr and Mrs Guel visited their son in Turkey in July and August 1995.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 29 May 1995, and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation (“the Government’s) on 26 June 1995. It originated in an application (no. 23218/94) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Turkish national, Mr Riza Gül, on 31 December 1993. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8 ( art. 8) of the Convention. Mr Gül is a Turkish national, who was born in 1947 and now lives with his wife at Pratteln in the canton of Basle Rural, Switzerland. On 25 April 1983 he travelled to Switzerland, where he applied for political asylum as a Kurd and former member of the Turkish Social Democratic Party (“the CHP’) The Court heard addresses by Mr Danelius, Mr Plender and Mr Jacot-Guillarmod, and the latter’s reply to the question asked by one member. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 October 1995. In 1987 the applicant’s wife, who had remained in Turkey with their two sons, seriously burned herself during a fit brought on by her epilepsy. In December 1987, having found that it was impossible for her to obtain proper treatment in the area where she was then living, she joined her husband in Switzerland. Two of the fingers of her left hand were amputated. On 19 September 1988 in Switzerland Mrs Gül gave birth to her third child, Nursal, a daughter. As she still suffered from epilepsy, she could not take care of the baby, who was placed in a home in Switzerland, where she has remained ever since. In a written declaration dated 31 March 1989, a Pratteln specialist in internal medicine stated that a return to Turkey would be impossible. Mr Gül applied for political asylum on humanitarian grounds in respect of himself, his wife and his daughter Nursal. The authorities took formal note of this on 8 November 1989. The final decision to grant a residence permit was given by the Federal Aliens Office on 15 February 1990. The conditions for the issue of such a permit laid down in Article 13 (f) of the Federal Council’s Order Limiting the Number of Aliens (‘the OLNA’ - see paragraph 21 below) had been satisfied. In a decision of 19 September 1990 the Aliens Police rejected the application. On 1 October 1990 the applicant appealed against this decision to the Basle Rural cantonal government (Regierungsrat) The cantonal government ruled that the children could not have a right to stay in Switzerland unless they had a residence permit. The decision was made on the basis that the father had the right to make such a decision. The court ruled that it was the responsibility of the father to make a decision that was in the best interests of the children. The children can now move back and forth between Switzerland and Germany without fear of reprisals from the Swiss authorities. The case is still pending before the European Court of Human Rights, which will decide whether the children can return to Switzerland or not. For more information on the case, go to: http://www.charter.org/news/features/article/1989/09/07/08/3899/charter-of-human-rights.html#storylink=cpy Cantonal government: Mr Gül has not satisfied the condition laid down in Article 39 para. 1 (c) of the OLNA. He does not have sufficient means to support his family during their residence in Switzerland. He should have a monthly net income of at least 2,710 Swiss francs (CHF) if he is not to fall below the minimum standard of living. The cost of keeping the youngest child, Nursal, in a children’s home has not been taken into account, as it is not known who pays for this. The calculation of income is based on pay-slips from 1989, the latest available. On 23 October 1990 the Liestal Cantonal Hospital sent the case to the Aliens Police. Basle Rural Aliens Police a medical certificate stating that Mr Gül was 100% unfit for work and would remain so for a period that it was not possible to determine. The social security services cannot be expected to provide for children arriving from abroad when it is known in advance that they will have to support them. For that reason alone the application for family reunion must be refused. For the first three months of this year alone the social security. services have paid the GüL family CHF 8,731.75, and the family will remain. dependent on social security payments. At present the social. security services are paying the family the amount needed by a three-person family, but no more. Ersin Gül has lived with Tuncay since birth but has been separated from his father and mother for eight years and three and a half years respectively. Ersin's mother is seriously ill and unable to keep him with her or look after him, and his father, who went away to Switzerland three month’s after his birth, which means that he hardly knows him. The question arises, at the very least, whether it is reasonable to separate him from his brother and the environment he is used to in order to bring him to live with his mother. In view of all the circumstances, and having regard to the child’S welfare, the cantonal government considers that Ers in should not be authorised to join his parents in Switzerland. The applicant lodged an administrative-law appeal with the Swiss Federal Court. He argued that, because of the “special circumstances’, Article 8 (art. 8) of the Convention gave his sons the right to obtain permission to reside in Switzerland. The earlier issue of a residence permit on humanitarian grounds to himself, his wife and his daughter had been based on the finding that a return to Turkey was impossible. Mr Gül argued that the same considerations which had prevailed in the decision to grant that residence permit should prevent any withdrawal thereof. In a judgment of 2 July 1993 the Federal Court declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible. According to the Federal Court’s established case-law, however, a breach can occur only where the family members living in Switzerland themselves possess a well-established right of abode (Anwesenheitsrecht) For that purpose, it is in principle necessary to have Swiss nationality or possess a settlement permit. A mere residence permit is at any rate not sufficient unless it is based on a firmly established right (see ATF 111 Ib 163/4 at 1a) ... That is, moreover, consistent with the new provisions on the legal status of aliens having family members in Switzerland (sections 7 and 17 (2) of the RSAA, as amended on 23 March 1990, which came into force on 1 January 1992) The only effect of a finding that a case is an extremely serious one within the meaning of Article 13 (f) of the Federal Council’s Order Limiting the Number of Aliens of 6 October 1986 (hereinafter the OLNA - SR 823.21) is to exclude the alien concerned from the quotas laid down in that Order; it does not imply the existence of a right to a residence permit. The Aliens Police prefer to remain free to decide when such a permit should be issued (see ATF 119 Ib 35 at 1a). In the instant case the possibility cannot be entirely ruled out that in the future the medical or other reasons which led the authorities to grant the residence permit will lose their significance, or that new grounds justifying a refusal to renew the permit will become apparent. Ersin Gül was born in the village where he was born. He lived in Istanbul with his mother until 1987, and then with the family of his elder brother Tuncay until 1993. The applicant maintained that Ersin frequently moved from one home to another and spent two or three days staying with various Kurdish families. Owing to his grandfather’s limited financial resources and the distance between the homes of some of these families and the school it was not possible for the boy to attend school on a regular basis. Mr and Mrs Gür visited their son in Turkey in July and August 1995. The application was rejected.

name: Hacı Zeki Uzun
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11564/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, a gynaecologist, was arrested and taken into police custody at his medical practice on 19 October 1999. He alleges that, while he was in police custody, he was ill‑treated. In particular, he complains of having received electric shocks, of having been suffocated, and of being beaten and threatened. He also alleges that during the first three days of his detention, he had been deprived of food and medication. The applicant was heard first by the public prosecutor and later by a judge at the İzmir State Security Court. The latter ordered his release from custody. The applicant did not object to this decision. The criminal proceedings brought against the applicant for aiding and abetting an illegal armed organisation ended on 23 May 2000 with his acquittal. The prosecution noted that none of the persons put forward as witnesses by the applicant were able to confirm the applicant’s version of events, that the applicant was unable to identify the alleged perpetrators and thatNone of the medical reports, dated 19 October 1999, 23 October 1999 and 25 October 1999 save for one dated 11 November 1999, i.e. fifteen days after the events, noted any physical findings of ill-treatment.

The applicant was arrested and placed in the anti‑terrorist branch of the Istanbul police headquarters after, during a road check, police officers saw a photograph of Abdullah Öcalan and the slogans “Biji Serok Apo” and “Long live Kurdistan” on his mobile phone. The first hearing in the case was held on 25 October 2002. On 5 September 2003 the Istanbul State Security Court ordered the release of the applicant. The trial was adjourned until April 4, 2006. The case is expected to be settled by the end of the month or early March. The prosecution is seeking to have the case thrown out of court. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 58757/00) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 27 June 2000. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr B. Mégevand, a lawyer practising in Geneva. The Swiss Government were represented by their Agent, Mr P. Boillat, former Deputy Director of the Federal Office of Justice in charge of the Human rights and Council of Europe Section. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. In 1976, shortly after his death, a blood-type analysis did not rule out his being the latter’s father. In 1997 the applicant contacted the Geneva University Institute of Forensic Medicine to have a private paternity test carried out, but his request was refused. In 1999 the applicant applied to the Canton of Geneva Court of First Instance for revision of the judgment of 30 January 1948. In the course of the proceedings he also requested a DNA test on the mortal remains of A.H. The Court of Justice argued that the applicant was not entitled to such an amendment of the register as a result of the 1976 revise of the Civil Code. The applicant, who is 60 years old, has been able to develop his personality and pursue a large portion of his existence without suffering any medically attested damage to his physical or mental health. The Court of Justice was entitled to restrict the applicant’s personal freedom by taking into consideration that of the respondents, in view of the lack of public interest in having this parental tie established and the disproportionate nature of the steps required to establish it. The Federal Court observed that there were no consequences of a civil-law nature that could justify implementing the measure sought. On 18 May 2000, the Court rejected the application for an expert examination.

name: Richard Cross
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62776/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the United Kingdom authorities' refusal to grant him Widowed Bereavement Allowance or equivalent constituted discrimination on grounds of sex. The Court declared this application admissible in so far as the complaint concerned Widow's Bereavement Tax Allowance and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The application was joined to other applications (nos. 60525/00, 60933/00 and 60937/00). The applicant was unrepresented before this Court.

name: Samuel Betteridge
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 23 December 2009. The applicant alleged that he did not have a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention, in violation of Article 5 § 4 of the convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 14 December 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant was convicted of rape in 2005 and was originally sentenced to life imprisonment with a tariff of five years. Upon appeal, this was reduced to a sentence of imprisonment for public protection. The applicant’s tariff expired on 18 December 2008, by which time no Parole Board review had taken place. The applicant challenged, by way of judicial review proceedings, the delay in fixing a hearing in his case. The hearing was eventually rescheduled for September 2009. The panel noted from your answers that you appear to have no more than a superficial understanding of the reasons why you committed the index offences. They feared that there had been an underestimate of risk and an insufficient attention to the sadistic elements of the offences in other assessments. They would therefore counsel against the formulaic approach in this case, which appears at least partly to be responsible for the conclusion that once RSOTP [a sexual offenders treatment programme] has been completed no further work is required. The High Court handed down its judgment in the judicial review proceedings on 23 June 2009. The judge outlined the background to the applicant’s claim, as follows: “4. a breach, having regard in particular to the fact that the pre-tariff advisory opinion of the Parole Board had effectively made it clear there was no chance of release upon expiry of the tariff (see paragraph 7 above)” “The Secretary of State routinely does refer post-Tariff lifers to the Paroles Board. The reason behind that is that it is common ground that Article 5(4) of the European Convention on Human Rights requires there to be a speedy hearing”  Article 5(4) requires a speedy hearing to determine the lawfulness of the detention. Lack of man power in the Parole Board has meant that it has been unable to provide the necessary panel. He concluded that the September 2008 advisory opinion in the applicant’s case could not address the question whether the post-tariff detention was lawful. However, it did mean that any breach would not require payment of damages, because it was plain that in any case the parole board would not have ordered the applicant's release. The judge observed that the delay problem was being addressed in that steps were being taken to seek further manpower to enable the Par parole board to meet its obligations under Article 5. The applicant had originally sought a mandatory order requiring that his case be heard in September, but that remedy was no longer pursued. The judge agreed with the decision not to pursue the claim for such an order, observing that it would be inappropriate for an individual, seeking judicial review, to ‘jump the queue’ at the expense of those who did not seek judicial review. He decided: “In all the circumstances I do not think that it is necessary for me to make any formal declaration in the circumstances of this case. I have already recorded that there was a breach, but it is a breach that will not provide, for this particular claimant, any great advantage” The judge noted that the measures put in place to alleviate the problem will not have immediate effect. The delays continue and the backlog has not improved, he said. It is not now appropriate for any prisoner to take proceedings against the Parole Board alleging breaches of Article 5(4) Unless there are very special circumstances, something has gone badly wrong despite the new arrangements in that prisoner’s particular case. It will not be helpful, either to the prisoner or to the court, if claims are brought which in reality, because of the existing situation, are not likely to achieve any sensible redress and merely add to costs. We cannot make orders which are only going to create difficulties for others. The applicant was advised by his counsel that no appeal would be successful as the Court of Appeal would be bound to conclude that it could not prioritise any individual case. The Parole Board recommended that the applicant be moved to open conditions. The Secretary of State accepted the recommendation and the case was dismissed. The court welcomes the steps that are clearly being taken now to ensure that that situation does not continue. The application has brought home to the court, and enabled the court to make the point, that the situation that existed was unsatisfactory, potentially contrary to law, and the court welcome the steps being taken to ensure it does not happen again.

name: Dariusz Karwowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the imposition of the “dangerous detainee” regime on him amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms J. Chrzanowska of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The complaint was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The application was filed by a Polish national, Mr Dariusz Karwowski, on 19 March 2013. The applicant was kept in a cell which was constantly monitored via closed‑circuit television. He was subjected to a body search every time he left or entered the cell. He had to strip naked in front of prison officers. The Warsaw Regional Court dismissed the appeal. name: Cécile Lecomte
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 80442/12) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a French national, Ms Cécile Lecomte. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the conditions of her detention for preventive purposes in two police stations had violated Article 3 of the convention. On 12 May 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. The Government of the French Republic indicated that they did not wish to exercise their right to intervene in the proceedings. The District Court found that the applicant, who had been represented by counsel throughout the proceedings before the domestic courts, and three further persons had let themselves down on a rope on a railway bridge. They had unrolled banners protesting against the castor transport. A commuter train had to be stopped because its passage would have put the protesters at risk. The detention was to last until the arrival of the ‘castor’0 containers in Dannenberg train station and until 10 November 2008, 0.00 p.m. at the most. The Lüneburg District Court quashed the order of 6 November 2008 for the applicant’s detention for preventive purposes and ordered the applicant's immediate release. The applicant suffered from serious rheumatism and was in a poor mental condition. Her detention in Braunschweig Police Station, with little possibility to move, had already led to her joints having stiffened. She was detained in a cell in the Lüneburg Police Station from 7 p.m. onwards until 7 November 2008 at approximately 1.40 p.M. The applicant’s small cell, equipped with a mattress and a chair, was lighted at least via a ventilation slot and by electric light. She went outside for a walk on the banks of the Ilmenau river with the police officers three times during that period. The applicant was taken out for a walk on the premises of the Braunschweig Police Station, which did not dispose of a closed courtyard, on 8 November 2008. The applicant had climbed on the cupboard in her cell and passed the night thereon, failing to comply with the police’s order to descend. On 9 November 2008 the applicant was allowed to stay outside on those premises from 12.22 p.m. until 12.35 p.M. without being shackled. She was also allowed to telephone her lawyer and her partner several times. The proceedings before the Lüneburg District Court were dismissed on 15 July 2009. District Court in Lower Saxony made a finding that both the order for her detention and the conditions of its execution had been unlawful. The photographs of shackled persons exposed in the detention wing of the Braunschweig Police Station may have been tasteless, but did not render the applicant’s detention unlawful as a result of intimidation. The recommendations of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) were irrelevant here. The District Court considered that the manner in which the detention had been enforced had been lawful and had complied, in particular, with the provisions of the Police Custody Regulations. The Lüneburg Regional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 July 2009. The Regional Court found that the conditions of the applicant’‘onerous’ detention, albeit onerous for the applicant, had complied with the applicable legal provisions and had not been so unacceptable as to render the execution of her detention unlawful. In that police station there were no detention cells suitable for a deprivation. The doctor who had visited the applicant in detention and had persuaded the then competent District Court judge to order her release had probably been a sympathiser. The court noted that on 8 November 2008 the applicant had been outside on the premises of the Braunschweig Police Station. The applicant had complained to the police about the noise at night emanating from a ventilator. The Lüneburg police had taken care of the applicant’s well-being after her hearing before the Regional Court. The court considered that it had been lawful for the police to leave the light switched on during the night. Shackling the applicant to a female police officer on 8 November 2008 had been necessary in order to prevent the applicant from being shackled. The Regional Court found that the right provided by no. 10 of the Police Custody Regulations to be allowed to stay outside for 45 minutes per day in so far as the staffing and infrastructural situation permitted had not been breached. The applicant had not been shackled during her time outside and had been allowed to climb on a tree. She had also been able to move within her cell in order to alleviate ailments resulting from her rheumatism. The Regional Court noted that the Braunschweig Police had received some 200 telephone calls of sympathisers of the applicant, some of whom had insulted the police. The applicant argued, in particular, that her right to liberty, the principle of proportionality and her right of assembly and of expression had been violated by her long illegal detention in unreasonable conditions. Her complaint was registered under file no. 2 BvR 2794/09. The decision of the Federal Constitutional Court to not consider the case was made on 28 October 2009. The decision was confirmed on 21 September 2010. The case is still pending. The court has not given a reason for not considering the case. The hearing is expected to take place in February or March 2012. The ruling will be made on whether the case should go before the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France. It will then be decided if the case can go to the Supreme Court of Justice in Luxembourg or to the Court of Appeal in Luxembourg, where it would be heard in Brussels. The German court of human rights is in the process of deciding the case's future.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) by a French national, Ms Cécile Lecomte (‘the applicant’), on 9 December 2012. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the conditions of her detention for preventive purposes in two police stations had violated Article 3 of the convention. The Government of the French Republic, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, indicated that they did not wish to exercise that right. The application was communicated to the Government on 12 May 2014. The District Court found that the applicant, who had been represented by counsel throughout the proceedings before the domestic courts, and three further persons had let themselves down on a rope on a railway bridge. They had unrolled banners protesting against the castor transport. A commuter train had to be stopped because its passage would have put the protesters at risk. The applicant’s detention was indispensable in order to prevent the imminent commission of a regulatory offence of considerable importance to the general public, as required by section 18 § 1 no. 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act. On 9 November 2008 at 5.25 p.m. the Lüneburg District Court quashed the order of 6 November 2008. The applicant suffered from serious rheumatism which necessitated her to move continuously and was in a poor mental condition. Her detention in Braunschweig Police Station, with little possibility to move, had already led to her joints having stiffened. The applicant’s small cell, equipped with a mattress and a chair, was lighted at least via a ventilation slot and by electric light. She went outside for a walk on the banks of the Ilmenau river with the police officers three times during that period. She was released on the same day at 6.32 p.m. after a hearing at the Lüneburg Regional Court. The applicant was detained in the Braunschweig Police Station from 8 November 2008. Her cell was equipped with a bed, an empty desk, a chair and an open cupboard and had a barred window with frosted glass. In the corridor of the detention wing, which she had to pass to go to the toilet, photographs of shackled persons were exposed. The applicant had climbed on the cupboard in her cell and passed the night thereon, failing to comply with the police’s order to descend. She was also allowed to telephone her lawyer and her partner several times. The proceedings before the Lüneburg District Court were dismissed on 15 July 2009. The District Court in Lüneburg ruled that the order for the applicant's detention and the conditions of its execution had been unlawful. The District Court considered that the manner in which the detention had been enforced had been lawful and had complied, in particular, with the provisions of the Police Custody Regulations. The recommendations of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) were irrelevant here. The photographs of shackled persons exposed in the detention wing of the Braunschweig Police Station may have been tasteless, but did not render the applicant’s detention unlawful as a result of intimidation. The Lüneburg Regional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against the District Court's decision of 15 July 2009. The Regional Court confirmed that the applicant’s detention as such had complied with section 18 § 1 no. 2 of the Lower Saxony Public Security and Order Act. On 9 November 2008 the applicant had been outside and had not been shackled and had been allowed to climb on a tree. In that police station there were no detention cells suitable for a deprivation. The cell had been uncomfortable, but complied with no. 15.1 of the Police Custody Regulations in the version then in force (see paragraph 49 below) The Regional Court noted that the applicant arrived at that station on 8 November 2008 at 2.10 a.m. after the crew of the ambulance called by the police and a police doctor had confirmed her fitness for detention. The court considered that it had been lawful for the police to leave the light switched on during the night. Shackling the applicant to a female police officer had been necessary in order to prevent the applicant from being shackled. The Regional Court found that the right provided by no. 10 of the Police Custody Regulations (see paragraph 46 below) to be allowed to stay outside for 45 minutes per day in so far as the staffing and infrastructural situation permitted had not been breached. The Regional Court noted that the Braunschweig Police had received some 200 telephone calls of sympathisers of the applicant, some of whom had insulted the police. It had not been unlawful in these circumstances for the police not to permit visits by persons who had presented themselves at the police station without having lodged a request for a visit. The applicant had been visited by three persons while in detention, in addition to two visits by her doctor, C., who had prescribed her necessary medication and had brought a couple of magazines. The Regional Court’s decision was served on the applicant’S counsel on 6 November 2009. Her complaint was registered under file no. 2 BvR 2794/09. The Federal Constitutional Court has refused to consider the complaint. The case was brought by a group of former employees of the Ministry of Justice. The court ruled in favor of the employees, saying they were entitled to a hearing. The decision was made on 28 October 2009, but no date was given for the hearing to take place. The complaint was filed on 21 September 2010, but the court did not give a reason why the decision was not made sooner. The hearing was held on 18 June 2012, and the case was adjourned until September. The judge ruled in favour of the workers, but didn’t say why this was the case, so the matter was referred to again.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the United Kingdom authorities’ refusal to grant him widows’ social security and tax benefits or equivalent constituted discrimination on grounds of sex contrary to Article 14 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court decided to communicate the complaint in connection with his claim for widows' benefits, relating to discrimination suffered by him during the period after the date on which he lodged his ‘second’ claim. It declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. It subsequently decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under United Kingdom law. The case was settled out of court and the applicant was awarded £300,000 in damages.

name: Collette Hemsworth
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 58559/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants mainly complained under Article 2 that there had been an unlawful use of lethal force against the deceased, Mr John Hemsworth. The application was communicated to the Government on 18 October 2011. The applicants were born in 1961 and 1933, respectively and live in Belfast. John Hemsworth died of a cerebral infarction on 1 January 1998. The RUC began an investigation supervised by the Independent Commission for Police Complaints (‘ICPC’) An expert in forensic medicine instructed by the first applicant found that it was ‘highly likely’ that the assault was the sole underlying cause of death. The Attorney General ordered the Coroner to hold an inquest. The Coroner opened a pre-inquest hearing, in 16 cases including into John Hemsworth’s death, to hear submissions on the implications of the judgments of this Court of 4 May 2001 in certain cases concerning deaths in Northern Ireland. The first applicant applied for legal aid for the inquest under the Lord Chancellor’s Extra-Statutory Scheme. The first applicant was legally represented, as she was for all domestic proceedings. The applicants claimed that, during that hearing, the Coroner advised that there was no evidence that the deceased had been struck by RUC officers. The High Court found against her on 7 January 2003 and the Court of Appeal on 9 March 2005. On 26 April 2004 the High court found in her favour. The case was heard at the Grand Chamber of this Court. The hearing was adjourned given the possibility of the referral of those cases to the Grand chamber of this court. The first applicant applied to the Coroner to recuse himself. The Coroner refused but indicated that he would receive further representations as to why RUC witnesses were required. The first applicant began a judicial review action. On 9 March 2009 the High Court found in her favour. The inquest began on 21 September 2009. It did not sit each day and certain witnesses were unavailable through ill-health. On 8 October 2009 the jury discharged the jury due to evidence which had emerged. It emerged therefrom that Officer M had interviewed a soldier (Private G) in 2000. Private G had told Officer M that, on the day of the alleged assault, he had been assaulted by a RUC officer. Officer M was also the Deputy Investigation Officer and was due to be called as a witness. Private G had seen an officer in the RUC Blues OSU assaulting a civilian with a baton in an area close to the location of Mr Hemsworth’s alleged assault. Private G had also told Officer M that a senior military officer, as well as a senior RUC officer, had told him that he should not report this incident to his superiors. Given the time it would take to recall witnesses and to call Private G, the Coroner considered it preferable to discharge the jury and conduct the inquest afresh. The Coroner ordered the PSNI to prepare a paginated and indexed bundle of all material held by them in relation to the death of John Hemsworth. John Hemsworth was killed in a road accident on 7 July 1997. Inquest jury accepted that his injuries included fractures to both the right and left hand sides of his jaw bone, tramline bruising to the left jaw, neck and lower left side of his back. Coroner announced he would refer the matter to the Director of Public Prosecutions (‘DPP’) and ensured the production, from public funds, of a transcript of the inquest proceedings. On 3 February 2012 the DPP’s office acknowledged the referral. Further to the applicants’ queries, on 23 April 2012 the Coroner confirmed the referral and on 14 May 2012 the case was closed. The Government submitted that the matter was the subject of ‘active consideration’ by the DPP. The Police Ombudsman reviewed the police file. In his report of 1 May 2007 he considered that the medical experts did not agree on the extension of a causal link between the July 1997 injuries and the subsequent death. There was no evidence that any RUC officer was responsible for John Hemsworth’s death and he could identify nothing further that he could do to take the matter forward. The RUC began an investigation supervised by the Independent Commission for Police Complaints (“ICPC”). Jury accepted that his injuries included fractures to both the right and left hand sides of his jaw bone, tramline bruising to the left jaw, neck and lower left side of his back. The applicant was convicted of rape and abduction and of one count of attempted rape and deprivation of liberty committed in 1984. He served his full prison sentence in Freiburg Prison. He was then placed in preventive detention, executed in that same prison, for the first time on 27 June 1989. On 11 December 2001, in judicial review proceedings under Article 67e of the Criminal Code, the Regional Court refused to suspend the applicant's preventive detention and grant probation. The first set of proceedings (application no. 27360/04) took place in the Stuttgart Regional Court on 18 June 1999. The applicant was sentenced to five years' imprisonment and placed into preventive detention pursuant to Article 66 of the criminal code. The applicant had. accepted social-therapeutic treatment from August 1985 until June 1988. However, he had then terminated that treatment. In 1992 the detention authorities had proposed certain relaxations in the conditions of the applicant's detention, but the applicant had refused to cooperate. In his report of 12 April 1999 the neurologic expert had found that the applicant still suffered from the said personality disorder. The Karlsruhe Court of Appeal, fully endorsing the reasons given by the Regional Court, dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The decision of the Federal Constitutional Court upheld the decision of both the Regional and Federal Courts. The application had been dismissed on the grounds that Article 67d of the Criminal Code of January 1998 (see paragraph 40 below) was constitutional. The applicant's constitutional complaint (file no. 2 BvR 664/02) was ill-founded. The Freiburg Regional Court, having consulted a psychiatric expert, W., again refused to suspend the applicant's preventive detention and grant probation. The applicant's appeal was dismissed by the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal in 2006. The second set of proceedings (application no. 42225/07) took place in 2007 and 2008. The application was based on the principle of proportionality (see paragraph 32 below) and the right to liberty under Article 2 § 2, second sentence, of the Basic Law. The court decided that the applicant still suffered from a personality disorder which had, in the past, manifested itself by violent sexualised behaviour. Subsequent developments in the case have led to the case being re-heard by the German Supreme Court in May 2013. The case is still pending and a decision is expected later in the year. The court responsible for the execution of sentences must review, before completion of the prison term, whether the person's preventive detention is still necessary in view of its objective. If that is not the case, it suspends on probation the executions of the detention order. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. The application of the Court's findings in the M. v. Germany case by the domestic courts has been deemed to be in violation of Article 7 of the Convention. Therefore, court decisions concerning orders of. preventive detention had to be based on the law in force at the time of the offence. The maximum period of ten years laid down in Article 67d § 1 of the Criminal Code in its version in force before 31 January 1998 could not be effected retrospectively and therefore. still applied to preventive detention ordered in relation to offences committed prior to that date. As a consequence, these courts declared. terminated the preventive detention of the detainees concerned whose first period was executed beyond that maximum period and ordered their release. Several Courts of Appeal considered that the Court's findings in the case of M. v. Germany could not be applied at present by the domestic courts responsible for the execution of sentences. This was because the Criminal Code as it stood did not permit its interpretation in compliance with Articles 5 and 7 of the Convention. Section 1a § 3 of the Introductory Act to the Criminalcode had expressly stipulated that the abolition of the maximum duration of ten years for a first period of preventive detention also applied to persons who had committed the offences in question prior to the entry into force of that abolition. It was therefore for the legislator to execute the Court’s judgment in the M. case.

name: Ingo Hub
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1182/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The application was lodged by a German national, Mr Ingo Hub, on 4 January 2005. S. declared that he wished to see his father only occasionally under the supervision of a third person. The parties agreed on supervised contact for the applicant on 23 August 1999. On 22 February 2000 the applicant applied for the appointment of a guardian ad litem and a contact supervisor (Umgangsbegleitperson) arguing that the mediation proceedings had failed. S. firmly declared that his father no longer existed for him on 22 November 2001. The District Court commissioned a psychological expert report on the question of contact. The report found that S. had refused to see the contact supervisor and that the contact centre had replaced him with another person. The mother’s representative challenged the expert for bias on 26 March 2002. On 10 April 2002 the District Court ordered the expert to stop his examinations. The mother withdrew her challenge of bias on 6 June 2002. The applicant appealed to the Berlin Court of Appeal, and on 18 January 2004 he submitted his statement of grounds of appeal, which the court received on 2 February 2004. The court upheld the decision of the D.C. District Court, arguing that S. had suffered from the persistent conflict between his. father and the expert. The judge also ruled that the applicant should not be able to see his son for a period of two years. The boy refused to expose himself to this conflict, by refusing to see his father. On 30 June 2004 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. On 19 July 2004 the decision was served on the applicant. The case has been pending now for more than five years and had led to lasting psychological damage to the child. The child has been allowed to contact his father again. The boy was allowed to visit his father for the first time on 14 July 2004. The court refused to admit the application and the boy has been able to see him again on 18 July 2004 after a two-month delay. The application has been dismissed and the case dismissed.

name: Anna Białas
train_texts: The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The parties were invited to settle the case, between 15 November 1990 and 6 May 1991 the proceedings were stayed at their request in order to negotiate a settlement. The Supreme Court rejected the applicant's cassation appeal as inadmissible on 26 October 1998. The applicant repeatedly sought exemption from payment of the expert’s fee. She was ordered to pay the fee, failing which the evidence provided by the expert opinion would be excluded. The applicant failed to comply with the order. On 31 May 2000 the Tarnobrzeg District Court decided to omit the evidence. It examined as evidence the case files of three other sets of related proceedings and on that basis delivered a judgment dismissing the action. The court agreed with the first-instance court that the defendant had the right of co-ownership to the plot on the date on which the proceedings were instituted and that the applicant's claim was accordingly inadmissible.

name: Anders Fredin
train_texts: Case was referred to the Court on 13 April 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 24 May 1993 by Sweden. The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs E. Palm, the elected judge of Swedish nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 September 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Ehrenkrona, Mr Trechsel and Mr Axelsson, as well as replies to a question put by it. The applicant applied to the County Administrative Board for a special extraction permit, so that he could continue his activities on the land. The revocation of the permit, and the lack of a court remedy against this and a related measure, gave rise to an earlier case before the Court, which held in a judgment of 18 February 1991 that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. The application was dismissed by the Board on 14 March 1989 and an appeal by the applicant against this decision was rejected by the Government (the Ministry of Environment and Energy) on 21 June 1989. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the latter request by three votes to two, finding that there were no grounds under section 9 of the Administrative Procedure Act 1971 for holding a hearing. As to the merits, on the basis of written observations submitted by the. applicant and the County Administrative Board, it concluded unanimously that the Government’s decision was not unlawful and confirmed. it. The decision was also incompatible with the aim of nature conservation laid down in section 1(3) of the Act. It was not possible under Swedish law for the applicant to appeal from the Supreme Administrative Court’s decision of 13 December 1990. There was disagreement between him and the County Administrative Board as to whether the above-mentioned restoration plan required the further extraction of gravel from the pit or simply the moving of gravel within it. The same two judges considered that the Government should have submitted written observations on the case. and also also with the Strasbourg Court's case-law in this area (see paragraph 11 below). They noted that certain essential points of Mr Fredin's case remained unclear, since there was disagreement over whether the restoration plan needed further gravel extraction.

The revocation of the permit, and the lack of a court remedy against this and a related measure, gave rise to an earlier case. The application was dismissed by the Board on 14 March 1989. An appeal by the applicant against this decision was rejected by the Government (the Ministry of Environment and Energy) on 21 June 1989. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the latter request by three votes to two, finding that there were no grounds under section 9 of the Administrative Procedure Act 1971 for holding a hearing. As to the merits, the court concluded unanimously that the Government’s decision was not unlawful and confirmed it. The decision was also incompatible with the aim of nature conservation laid down in section 1(3) of the Act. The applicant asked the Supreme Administrative court to hold an oral hearing in his case. Mr Fredin’s case remained unclear, since there was disagreement between him and the County Administrative Board as to whether the above-mentioned restoration plan required the further extraction of gravel from the pit or simply the moving of gravel within it. It was not possible under Swedish law for the applicant to appeal from the Supreme Administrative Court's decision of 13 December 1990. The same two judges considered that the Government should have submitted written observations on the case. They drew attention to the lack of clarity in Mr Fredin's plea against the Government. and also with the Strasbourg Court's case-law in this area (see paragraph 11 below)

They also drew attention to the lack of clarity in Mr Fredin's plea against the Government. and also also with the Strasbourg Court's case-law in this area (see paragraph 11 below).
