name: Andrzej Rybacki
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 52479/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 9 October 2007 the Court declared admissible the applicant’s complaints relating to the excessive length of his detention and the lack of unsupervised contacts with his lawyer at the investigation stage of the proceedings. The applicant's detention was prolonged twice, on 1 August, until 31 October 1996. The courts relied on a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had actually committed the offence with which he was charged. On 23 December 1996 the prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and his co-accused with the Wrocław Regional Court. The first hearing in the case was held on 21 March 1997. The court held subsequent hearings on 11 and 12 September and 18 November 1997, and 10 February and 3 March 1998. On 16 April 1998 the court heard evidence from two anonymous witnesses who answered questions which had previously been formulated in writing by the applicant’s lawyers. In 1998 Wrocław Regional Court requested the Supreme Court to prolong the applicant’s detention, which was about to exceed two years. The court found that apart from the reasonable suspicion that he and the two co-accused persons had committed the offence at issue, there existed an actual risk that they would obstruct the proceedings if released. The Supreme Court also recommended that the trial court should “schedule the hearings in a more rational way so as to avoid further intervals of several months in the instant case’. The application was rejected by the court on 1 October 1998. The applicant was arrested and jailed again on 3 November 1998. The applicant and his co-accused were found guilty of robbery committed by an organised criminal gang. The applicant was sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment and a fine. The Wrocław Regional Court closed the trial and rendered its judgment on 28 June 1999. On 4 January 2000 the applicant’s lawyer lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court. On 16 November 2001 that court dismissed the appeal as manifestly unsubstantiated. The case is now before the Court of Appeal for the Republic of Poland, which has the right to hear appeals against sentences of imprisonment and fines of up to 10 years. The hearing for the appeal is expected to take place in December. The Wrocław Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 15 July 1996. The court noted that the applicant could at that time see his lawyer whenever he requested. The restrictions imposed on his contacts with his lawyer did not impair his defence rights. The only restriction imposed on the applicant concerned the possibility of having unsupervised contact with his lawyers. a defence strategy. The fact that a prosecutor was to be present during these visits did not affect the applicant’s defence rights at that stage, the more so as the restriction was to apply only during the investigations. the court further stated that the defence strategy could also be discussed in accordance with the law in the presence of a person appointed by the prosecutor.

name: Yavuz Aksaç
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that he had been denied a fair hearing on account of the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Ankara State Security Court which tried and convicted him. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) In a decision of 15 January 2004 the Court declared the application partly admissible. It retained the applicant’s complaints concerning his right to a fair hear by an independent and impartial tribunal and his right. to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence. The applicant was born in 1971 and lives in Ankara. He was accused of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, the DHKP-C (Revolutionary People’s Liberation Party-Front). He was sentenced to three years and nine months’ imprisonment and debarred from public service for three years. The applicant appealed. On 11 June 1997 the chief public prosecutor at the Court of Cassation submitted his written opinion (tebliğname) on the merits of the appeal. The written opinion of the Chief public prosecutor was read out during the hearing. The Court ofCassation dismissed the applicant's appeal upholding the Ankara State Security Court's judgment.

name: Szymon Węgrzynowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33846/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their rights to respect for their private life and reputation had been breached. The court observed that the journalists had failed to contact the applicants and that their allegations were, to a large extent, based on gossip and hearsay. The allegations had not been shown to have had a plausible factual basis. The application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. Journalists had smeared the applicants’ good name and reputation. The court ordered the journalists and the editor‑in‑chief to pay, jointly, PLN 30,000 to a charity and to publish an apology in the newspaper. The defendants appealed. On 24 April 2003 the Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed their appeal, endorsing the findings of fact and the reasoning of the first‑instance court. The obligations imposed by the courts were subsequently complied with by the defendant newspaper. On 7 July 2004 the applicants sued again the newspaper under the same provisions of the Civil Code (see paragraph 6 above). They alleged that they had recently found out that the article remained accessible on the newspaper’s Internet website. The Warsaw Regional Court, by a judgment of 28 September 2005, dismissed the applicants’ claim. The court was of the opinion that the discovery of a new source of publication, namely the newspaper’s website, of the defamatory article had given rise to a new claim on the Applicants’ part. It said removing the article from the website would have been devoid of any practical purpose and would amount to censorship and to rewriting history. It noted that the journalists’ right and obligation to inform the general public of matters of public interest was incompatible with the Constitution. The applicants have already received a public apology. Allowing the claim to have a new apology published would not offer adequate protection. The court noted that the applicants had already received compensation in the first set of the proceedings. Traditional principles governing the archiving of various printed materials and documents in traditional archives were not the same as those applicable to the operation of a website. The term “archive” was to be understood as a set of documents which had lost their currency. The Internet was not an instrument for archiving materials, but had to be regarded as a means of communication of information on current topics. The court had unequivocally acknowledged that the impugned article had violated their rights. It had, however, limited itself to dismissing the claim and failed to consider other remedial measures, including those it had expressly referred to in its judgment. The applicants had appealed against an article published on the newspaper’s website in December 2000. The court noted that the applicants had submitted that they had only learned of its online publication a year after the judgment given in April 2003 had become final. The applicants submitted an appeal on points of law, invoking their right to the effective legal protection of their personal rights, including their reputation. On 17 November 2006 the Warsaw Court of Appeal rejected the appeal in so far as it related to the first applicant, having regard to the fact that the relevant court fee had not been paid. No appeal was lodged against this decision. By a decision of 7 February 2007 the Supreme Court, sitting in camera, refused to entertain the first applicants’ cassation appeal (odmówił przyjęcia kasacji do rozpoznania).

The applicants submitted an appeal on points of law, invoking their right to the effective legal protection of their personal rights, including their reputation. It was the journalists’ right and obligation to inform the general public of matters of public interest. The applicants have already received a public apology. The applicants appealed. They argued that the case was important in that it raised new issues which had hitherto not been addressed by judicial practice. They submitted that each new reading of the article on the newspaper’s website, which was open to the general public, amounted to a new publication of that article. The court had unequivocally acknowledged that the impugned article had violated their rights. It had, however, limited itself to dismissing the claim. It failed to consider, contrary to its duty, other remedial measures, including those it had expressly referred to in its judgment. It was of the view that it was of cardinal importance for the assessment of the case that the article was removed. The original article was published on the newspaper’s website in December 2000. The court noted that the applicants had submitted that they had only learned of its online publication a year after the judgment given in April 2003 had become final. The applicants submitted an appeal on points of law, invoking their right to the effective legal protection of their personal rights, including their reputation. The Warsaw Court of Appeal rejected the appeal in so far as it related to the first applicant, having regard to the fact that the relevant court fee had not been paid. No appeal was lodged against this decision. By a decision of 7 February 2007 the Supreme Court, sitting in camera, refused to entertain the first applicants’ cassation appeal.

name: Hilmi İzmirli
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30316/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of a violation of his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The application was brought by a Turkish national, Mr Hilmi İzmirli, on 11 June 2002. The applicant was released from prison on 14 November 1988. He appealed to the Military Court of Cassation. While the appeal was pending, martial law was terminated. Following the promulgation of the Law of 27 December 1993 abolishing the jurisdiction of the martial law courts, the Court of. Cassation acquired jurisdiction over the case. It quashed the applicant's conviction on 27 December 1995. It re-qualified the offence under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code, which entailed a more severe sentence. It transmitted the case to the Ankara Assize Court, which held its first hearing on 6 May 1996. On 16 July 2002 the Assize. Court handed down its verdict on the applicant and numerous other accused.

name: Werner Gabriel

name: David Adetoro
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46834/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a fair trial as a result of the trial judge's misdirection to the jury on the drawing of adverse inferences as regards his refusal to answer questions during police interviews. The evidence against the applicant was almost entirely circumstantial and the case relied heavily on evidence from a police surveillance exercise carried out over a period of about one year. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms J. Gladstone, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to rob and other offences arising out of the conspiracy. During interviews, he was asked to give an explanation for his movements as recorded by the police in their surveillance exercise, his association with a variety of individuals and his whereabouts at the time of the robberies. On each occasion, he replied “no comment”. At trial before the Crown Court, the applicant gave evidence in his own defence. He claimed that he was not even aware of the robbery conspiracy or his associates' involvement. However, he admitted being involved in the buying and selling of stolen cars and argued that the police observations showed his involvement in that business. The judge noted that the applicant had not answered questions put to him during the police interviews, replying “no comment” to each of the questions posed. The judge concluded with the following direction: “I have to tell you as a matter of law, that the fact that a defendant tells a lie, is not of itself, evidence of guilt.” He added: ‘If you think that the defendant has lied in evidence, but you think there is or might be some innocent explanation for any lie, then ignore it, take no notice of it at all’ The judge also said that any such lie can be evidence going to support the prosecution’s case. On 18 June 1998 the jury found the applicant guilty of the offences charged. He was sentenced to 26 years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing, inter alia, that the summing up contained a Lucas direction (a direction to the jury in relation to lies – see paragraph 33) The judge was not prepared to place reliance on anything he said and made no finding in respect of Mr Shearer and Mr Stephenson's presence or absence in the circumstances of the sixth robbery. The judge noted that he was satisfied that Mr Adetoro was involved in the sixth robbers and ignored his assertion that he had been with them at the time. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed. However, his sentence was reduced to 22 years' imprisonment. The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the applicant's conviction to the Court of Appeal on the basis of the trial judge's direction to the jury. The main ground of appeal was that the direction on adverse inferences was defective in that the jury were not directed that an adverse inference could only be drawn where it was satisfied that the real reason for the applicant’s silence was that he had no answer to the questions asked, or no answer that would hold up to scrutiny. The Court of appeal disagreed and found that, despite the misdirection by the trialJudge, the conviction was safe. The court also noted that the judge had given the jury an unnecessary Lucas direction. The jury were told that if they thought there was an innocent explanation for any such lie told by the appellant they should not hold it against him. So, as the jury must have concluded that the appellant's explanation for his silence ('I wanted to protect others') was a lie, following the judge's direction they would have had to consider whether there was a innocent explanation. It concluded that: ‘The direction the judge gave could only have related to lies told byThe court referred to the accused's defence itself. It found that the jury had rejected the applicant's defence and, in doing so, must also have rejected the applicants explanation of why he failed to answer questions. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed on 7 June 2006. The appeal judge ruled that the evidence against the applicant was 'overwhelming' and that the 'correct direction would have tipped the balance' The appeal was rejected on 9 June 2006 and the appeal judge dismissed the appeal. The judge said that the case was 'not therefore a case in which one could say that the correct direction would've tipped the. balance' in favour of the applicant. The case was described as 'a case of a miscarriage of justice' by the judge in the case. It was the first of three appeals to be heard by the Court of Appeal in the UK.

David Adetoro, born in 1972, is currently detained in HMP Whitemoor, Cambridgeshire. He denies any involvement in the conspiracy to rob and was interviewed under caution in March and June 1997. The evidence against the applicant was almost entirely circumstantial and the case relied heavily on evidence from a police surveillance exercise carried out over a period of about one year. The applicant alleged that he did not have a fair trial as a result of the trial judge's misdirection to the jury on the drawing of adverse inferences as regards his refusal to answer questions during police interviews. The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to rob and other offences arising out of the conspiracy. At trial before the Crown Court, the applicant gave evidence in his own defence. He admitted being involved in the buying and selling of stolen cars and argued that the police observations showed his involvement in that business, rather than in any conspiracy. He provided answers to all the questions which he had declined to answer during the police interviews in March and June 1997. He accounted for his association with various individuals, provided explanations for why he had moved certain vehicles on certain dates, gave detailed accounts of his movements on relevant dates and gave explanations for conversations recorded by covert surveillance. He responded that he had not wanted to incriminate people in relation to the stolen vehicles. The judge told the jury that a defendant may lie for many reasons. He said that the applicant had not answered questions put to him during the police interviews, replying ‘no comment’ to each of the questions posed. The judge also reminded the jury of some of the specific questions asked of the applicant during police interviews and of the subsequent answers relied upon by the applicant in his evidence at trial. He concluded with the following direction: “The applicant admits that he failed to mention any of the facts to which I have just referred, when he was interviewed and he says his reason for that, was that although well knowing that others had been arrested for the much more serious offence of armed robbery, as he had been, he didn't want to incriminate them” The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing that the summing up contained a Lucas direction (a direction to the jury in relation to lies – see paragraph 33) The judge noted that he was satisfied that Mr Adetoro was involved in the sixth robbery. He was a 'rather clever and determined liar' and his alibi 'fell apart' The judge was not prepared to place reliance on anything he said and made no finding in respect of Mr Shearer and Mr Stephenson's presence or absence in the circumstances of the sixth Robbery. The applicant was found guilty of the offences charged and was sentenced to 26 years' imprisonment. The judge said that the jury may hold such failures against the defendant when deciding whether he is guilty, that is to say, you may take them into account. The Court of Appeal disagreed and found that, despite the misdirection by the trial judge, the conviction was safe. The main ground of appeal was that the direction on adverse inferences was defective. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed. However, his sentence was reduced to 22 years' imprisonment. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (“CCRC”) referred the applicant's conviction to the Court of appeal on the basis of the judge's direction to the jury in relation to the applicant’s silence at the police interviews. The court concluded, having regard to the transcript of the trial Judge's summing up, that the judge had given such a direction to. the jury. The CCRC report noted that legal advice dated 9 July 1998 made reference to the omission in the jury direction. The court also noted that the judge had given the jury an unnecessary Lucas direction which, in the event, provided assistance to the jury in how to approach the question of adverse inferences. The jury were told that if they thought there was an innocent explanation for any such lie told by the appellant they should not hold it against him. So, as the jury must have concluded that the appellant's explanation for his silence ('I wanted to protect others') was a lie, following the judge's direction they would have had to consider whether there was a innocent explanation before they could have used it as supportive of the Crown's case. It concluded that: “The direction the judge gave could only have related to lies told in court.” The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed on 7 June 2006. the earlier judgment of the Court of Appeal, which found the evidence against the applicant to be overwhelming, and concluded: “This was not therefore a case in which one could say that the correct direction would have tipped the balance”. The applicant was convicted of two counts of perverting the course of justice. The conviction was quashed on appeal on 14 February 2006. The appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 6 June 2006, and the case was settled out of court for £1.5 million. The judge ruled that the jury should have been allowed to consider the evidence before giving their verdict.

The case originated in an application (no. 46834/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a fair trial as a result of the trial judge's misdirection to the jury on the drawing of adverse inferences as regards his refusal to answer questions during police interviews. The evidence against the applicant was almost entirely circumstantial and the case relied heavily on evidence from a police surveillance exercise carried out over a period of about one year. The application was given notice to the Government on 25 May 2009. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to rob and other offences arising out of the conspiracy. During the interviews, he was asked to give an explanation for his movements as recorded by the police in their surveillance exercise, his association with a variety of individuals and his whereabouts at the time of the robberies. On each occasion, he replied “no comment’. The judge instructed the jury as to the burden of proof and the standard of proof in the case: “...The burden [of proof] lies upon the prosecution throughout the case, to prove their case against the defendant. The defendant does not have to prove anything at all, there is no burden upon him to prove something. ... The next matter of law, ... which I should mention, concerns the telling of lies or being untruthful” The judge noted that the applicant had not answered questions put to him during the police interviews, replying ‘no comment’ to each of the questions posed. The judge also reminded the jury of some of the specific questions asked of the applicant during police interviews and of the subsequent answers relied upon by the applicant at trial. The applicant admitted that he failed to mention any of the facts to which I have just referred, when he was interviewed and he says his reason for that was that although well knowing that others had been arrested for the much more serious offence of armed robbery, as he had been, he didn't want to incriminate them in the stealing of cars. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing that the summing up contained a Lucas direction (a direction to the jury in relation to lies – see paragraph 33) Mr Adetoro did not take part in the first four robberies because he was in prison in respect of a previous matter connected with armed robbery. He was released in September and by October was associating with his co-accused ... Thereafter he joined the conspiracy. Once he had joined the tactics and execution of the various robberies increased in gravity. The judge noted that he was satisfied that Mr Adeteoro was involved in the sixth robbery and ignored his assertion he was with Mr Shearer and Mr Stephenson at the material time. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed. However, his sentence was reduced to 22 years' imprisonment. The main ground of appeal was that the direction on adverse inferences was defective. The Court of Appeal disagreed and found that, despite the misdirection by the trial judge, the conviction was safe. It distinguished between cases where an accused exercised his right to silence pursuant to legal advice or because he was tired or ill and those where, as in the present case, the reason for not answering questions was linked to the case. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (“CCRC”) referred the applicant's conviction to the Court of appeal on the basis of the judge's direction. The court found that the jury had rejected the applicant's defence and, in doing so, must also have rejected his explanation of why he failed to answer questions in the police interview. The court also noted that the judge had given the jury an unnecessary Lucas direction which, in the event, provided assistance to the jury in how to approach the question of adverse inferences. It concluded that: “The direction the judge gave could only have related to lies told by the appellant in court.” The jury were told that if they thought there was an innocent explanation for any such lie told by him they should not hold it against him. So, as the jury must have concluded that the appellant's explanation for his silence ('I wanted to protect others') was a lie, following the judge's direction they would have had to consider whether there wasan innocent explanation. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed on 7 June 2006. The Court of Appeal found the evidence against the applicant to be overwhelming, and concluded: “This was not therefore a case in which one could say that the correct direction would have tipped the balance”. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 11 June 2006, and the conviction was quashed on 13 June 2006 by the Supreme Court of England and Wales. The decision was made on the basis of the evidence presented by the applicant, which had been overwhelming at the time of the appeal. The application was dismissed because of the 'overwhelming' evidence against it.

name: Folke Schmidt
train_texts: The Schmidt and Dahlström case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights. The case originated in an application against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission by two Swedish subjects in June 1972. The President of the Court deemed it conducive to the proper administration of justice to constitute a single Chamber to consider both the present case and that of the Swedish Engine Drivers’ Union (Rule 21 para. 6) The five judges so selected were Mr H. Mosler, Mr E. Rodenbourg, Mr. A. Favre, Mr G. Wiarda and Mr. P. O’Donoghue. The Government of Sweden was required to file a memorial within a time-limit expiring on 14 February 1975. The delegates of the Commission were also required to submit a memorial in reply within two months. The Government’s memorial was received at the registry on 17 February and that of the delegates on 26 March 1975. On 22 September 1975, the Court held a preparatory meeting to consider the oral stage of the procedure. The oral hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building in Strasbourg on 25 September 1975. There appeared before the Court: Mr. H. DANELIUS, Head of the Legal Department at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Agent; Mr. B. HÅRDEFELT, Chief Legal Adviser at. the Ministry of Finance, Mr. G. NORMARK, Chief legal Adviser at the National Collective Bargaining Office, Advisers. The applicants are members of trade unions affiliated to two of the main federations representing Swedish State employees. In 1971, after expiry of one collective agreement and during negotiations for a new agreement, the applicants’ unions called selective strikes not affecting the applicants, who thus did not come out on strike. Mr. Schmidt and Mr. Dahlström complain that they, as members of the “belligerent“ unions, were denied certain retroactive benefits paid to members of other trade unions and to non-union employees who had not participated in the strikes. The case was heard by the Labour Court, which was competent to hear cases of alleged violation of the 1936 Act on the Right to Organise and Negotiate. The Act of 1936 guarantees two distinct rights to the parties on the labour market. The right to organise is defined in Section 3 of the Act as being the right of employers and employees to belong to an employers’ organisation or a trade union. As from 1 January 1966, the 1965 State Officials Act (statstjänstemannalag) has virtually assimilated State employees to employees in the private sector. The only way in which such associations enjoy the protection of the 1936 Act is that they may be awarded damages if the other party violates the right to organising of an individual member. This provision is applicable to all trade unions. It imposes on the otherParty an obligation to enter into negotiations and, where necessary, to make proposals for the settlement of the issues involved. The Act made the 1928 Collective Agreement Act, the 1928 Labour Court Act and the 1936 Act on the Right to Organise and Negotiate applicable in the public sector. The Act provided for collective agreements to be concluded, subject to certain exceptions, between the National Collective Bargaining Office (Statens Avtalsverk) and the organisations of State employees. About forty trade unions are affiliated to these organisations. The few independent trade unions represent only about 2,000 State employees in all. Insofar as they are union members at all, university teachers and army officers generally belong to SACO and SR respectively. These two organisations, which are respectively open to staff possessing a university degree or the school leaving certificate, recently merged. Negotiations in the public sector of the labour market are centralised in that they are conducted by the federations on behalf of their member unions. Collective agreements in Sweden are normally concluded for a period of two or three years. For various reasons, however, the new collective agreement is often concluded some time after the previous agreement has expired. In such cases the new agreement has often specifically provided that its terms shall apply retroactively as from the date of expiry of previous agreement. In the case of a strike during the bargaining period, employers have customarily refused to grant retroactive benefits in order to deter unions from taking industrial action in the future. In 1969 a global agreement for the years 1969 and 1970 was concluded by the Office and the four federations. When this period expired on 31 December 1970, the parties were still engaged in negotiations regarding the new global agreement. No agreement was reached and a Commission of Conciliation was appointed, but negotiations before it broke down as well. Consequently, SACO and SR proclaimed selective strikes which became effective on 5 February 1971 and involved about 4,000 members. This resort to strike action, which was quite lawful, did not apply to university teachers or the Army so that neither Mr. Schmidt nor Mr. Dahlström took any part in the strikes. The previous collective agreement was reinstated on 13 March 1971 for a period of six weeks. All strikes and lock-outs terminated forthwith. In June 1971 in a new global agreement for the years 1971 to 1973. According to this agreement, certain posts were upgraded and the salary scales were generally increased retroactively as from 1 January 1971. Clause 18, however, provided for an exception in this respect: “Officials who were members between 1 January and 12 March 1971 (or any part of this period) of organisations that organised industrial action ... shall not be entitled to the increased wage benefits applicable under the agreement, unless the Collective Bargaining Office decides otherwise” Mr. Dahlström, who was upgraded under the new agreement, was affected for the whole period up to 12 March 1971. During these periods the applicants performed work for a lower salary than that paid to other employees who were in the same salary brackets but not members of SACO or SR. Their financial losses amounted to Kr. 300 and Kr. 1,000 respectively. Mr. Schmidt, following the conclusion of the collective agreement, gave notice to the Office that, through his special treatment in regard to wages, his right to organise had been violated. When the Office nevertheless refused him the benefit of retroactivity, SACo and SR brought an action against the State before the Labour Court. The Court found that no such purpose on the part of the State could be established. The adoption of such a position, and its enforcement after a conflict, were not to be regarded in themselves as an attack on the right to organise. The employer’s duty to respect this right did not include any obligation in principle to pay equal wages to union and non-union employees or to members of different organisations. Any favouring either of members of the organisation which reached agreement or of non- union employees, with the aim of exercising against the members of other organisation, would constitute a violation of Section 3 of the 1936 Act. The Court did not consider the granting of retroactive benefits to non-Union employees who had not organised industrial action. In their application, lodged with the Commission on 9 June 1972, the applicants complained that in the particular circumstances the Government’s policy regarding payment of retroactive benefits had amounted to preferential treatment. The Commission declared the application admissible by a decision of 18 October 1972. In its report of 17 July 1974, the Commission: (i) confirmed its opinion, previously expressed in the report in the Swedish Engine Drivers’ Union case, that Article 11 para. 1 (art. 11-1) may legitimately extend to cover State responsibility in the field of labour-management relations and thus to provide some protection for unions against interference by employers. (ii) expressed the opinion. that the policy of denying retroactive. benefits to non-striking members of belligerent unions did not in the circumstances infringe the applicants’ right. to form and join the trade unions. The report contains a separate concurring opinion. The report concludes that the differential treatment complained of was in the circumstances justified as an industrial relations policy. There had been no violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 11 para. 1 (art. 14+11-1). The report contains an opinion that the complaint had been made in good faith and that the treatment had been justified. The opinion was published in the report's third edition, which includes an extract from the report that was published on June 8. It is available to read at www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-285563/Report-claims- differential-treatment-was-in-the circumstances justified.

The case originated in an application against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission by two Swedish subjects in 1972. The President of the Court deemed it conducive to the proper administration of justice to constitute a single Chamber to consider both the present case and that of the Swedish Engine Drivers’ Union (Rule 21 para. 6) Five of the seven judges required to sit as members of the Chamber were selected by lot on 15 October 1974. The five judges so selected were Mr H. Mosler, Mr E. Rodenbourg, Mr. A. Favre, Mr G. Wiarda and Mr P. O’Donoghue. The oral hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building in Strasbourg on 25 September 1975. There appeared before the Court: Mr. H. Danelius, Head of the Legal Department at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Agent; Mr. B. HÅRDEFELT, Chief Legal Adviser at the ministry of Finance, Advisers; and Mr. O. BERGQVIST, Legal Adviser to the Ministry of Labour. The Commission produced the document recently called for by the Court. The Court heard the addresses of Mr. Fawcett and. Mr. Schmidt for the Commission and for the Government, as well as their replies to questions put by the. Court. The applicants are members of trade unions affiliated to two of the main federations representing Swedish State employees. In 1971, after expiry of one collective agreement and during negotiations for a new agreement, the applicants’ unions called selective strikes not affecting the sectors in which worked the applicants. The applicants complain that on conclusion of the new agreement they were denied certain retroactive benefits paid to members of other trade unions and to non-union employees who had not participated in the strikes. The case was heard by the Labour Court, which had jurisdiction in disputes relating to the interpretation or application of collective agreements, but proceedings could also be heard by other courts. The Act of 1936 guarantees two distinct rights to the parties on the labour market. The right to organise is defined in Section 3 of the Act as being the right of employers and employees to belong to an employers’ organisation or a trade union. It imposes on the other party an obligation to enter into negotiations, to attend meetings for negotiations and, where necessary, to make proposals for the settlement of the issues involved. The 1965 State Officials Act (statstjänstemannalag) has virtually assimilated State employees to employees in the private sector. This provision is applicable to all trade unions. The only way in which such associations enjoy the protection of the. Act is that they may be awarded damages if the otherParty violates the right to. organise of an individual member in such a way that the violation is. to be regarded as intervention in the affairs of the association. The Act made the 1928 Collective Agreement Act, the 1928 Labour Court Act and the 1936 Act on the Right to Organise and Negotiate applicable in the public sector. The Act provided for collective agreements to be concluded, subject to certain exceptions, between the National Collective Bargaining Office (Statens Avtalsverk) and the organisations of State employees. The Ministry of Finance has a nominee on the governing board of the Office. About forty trade unions are affiliated to these organisations. The few independent trade unions represent only about 2,000 State employees in all. Insofar as they are union members at all, university teachers and army officers generally belong to SACO and SR respectively. The Royal Order of 30 June 1965 relating to Certain Public Collective Agreements (KK om vissa statliga kollektivavtal m.m.) includes the following provisions: Article 3 “Collective agreements as to such conditions of employment or service as are determined by the King-in-Council or by Parliament.“ Article 4 “An Authority which is bound by a collective agreement shall apply the provisions of the agreement to any employee within the occupational group and region to which the agreement refers“ Collective agreements in Sweden are normally concluded for a period of two or three years. For various reasons, however, the new collective agreement is often concluded some time after the previous agreement has expired. In such cases the new agreement has often specifically provided that its terms shall apply retroactively. Negotiations between the Office and the federations result in one single agreement which regulates the increase in salaries, the grading of different categories of employees, working hours, various salary allowances, etc. The agreement is normally signed by all the Federations. and other collective action may not be taken by the different trade unions independently but rather on the basis of a decision by, or after receiving the approval of, the federation concerned, which chooses and designates in accordance with its pre-arranged policy or tactics those of its members who are to take part in the action. The question whether an individual employee has any means of challenging his union’s decision to go on strike is a matter exclusively governed by the internal rules of the union concerned. By virtue of this Act the previous collective agreement was reinstated on 13 March 1971 for a period of six weeks and all strikes and lock-outs terminated forthwith.Subsequent negotiations before the Commission of Conciliation resulted in June 1971 in a new global agreement for the years 1971 to 1973. According to this agreement, certain posts were upgraded and the salary scales were generally increased retroactively as from 1 January 1971. Clause 18, however, provided for an exception in this respect: “Officials who were members between 1 January and 12 March 1971 (or any part of this period) shall not be entitled to the increased wage benefits’ Mr. Dahlström, who was upgraded under the new agreement, was affected for the whole period up to 12 March 1971. During these periods the applicants performed work for a lower salary than that paid to other employees who were in the same salary brackets but not members of SACO or SR. Their financial losses amounted to Kr. 300 and Kr. 1,000 respectively. Mr. Schmidt, following the conclusion of the collective agreement, gave notice to the Office that, through his special treatment in regard to wages, his right to organise had been violated. When the Office nevertheless refused him the benefit of retroactivity, SACo and SR brought an action against the State before the Labour Court. The Court found that no such purpose on the part of the State could be established. No support had appeared for the idea that the State intended to induce members of SACO and SR to switch over to TCO-S and SF. The employer’s duty to respect this right did not include any obligation in principle to pay equal wages to union and non-union employees or to members of different organisations. In the case before it, the Court did not consider the granting of retroactive benefits to non- union employees who had not taken industrial action. The reason why they were granted a special benefit had nothing to do with their position as being non-Union. The Court indicated that the plaintiffs’ view concerning the State’s purpose in its treatment of non-union officials might have appeared more reasonable if it had been possible to show that the large majority were active within the main field of activity of SACO and SR. The uncertainty in regard to these circumstances argued in favour of the States declaration that its purpose did not extend beyond upholding the principle that a strike destroys retroactivity. The Commission declared the application admissible by a decision of 18 October 1972. The applicants relied on Article 11 (art. 11) and also Article 14, read in conjunction with Article 14+11. The report concludes that the differential treatment complained of was justified as an industrial relations policy and that there had been no violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 11 para. 1 (art. 14+11-1). The report contains a separate concurring opinion. The report also says that there was no breach of any of the Article 14/11 para. entions, that the treatment was in the circumstances justified and that no violation had been committed. The opinion is published in full in today's edition of this newspaper, and is available at www.dailymailonline.co.uk/news/article-294936.html.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 10434/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were born in 1941, 1946 and 1948 respectively and live in Bursa. In 2004 the General Directorate of Highways seized a plot of land belonging to the applicants without any formal expropriation, for the construction of a highway. They requested 6,500 Turkish liras (TRY) as compensation from the court and reserved their right to increase this claim in due course. On 16 November 2006 the Karacabey Civil Court awarded the applicants TRY 6,000 as compensation. The Karacabey Civil Court upheld the judgment of the Court of Cassation on 16 October 2007. On 20 March 2009 the administration paid TRY 10,297.75. According to the information provided by the applicants, there has been no outstanding debt in the execution files. The case is still pending and the judgment is likely to be heard in September or October. The judgment is currently being appealed by the court of cassation in Istanbul. The appeal is expected to be decided in November or December 2007. The decision will be made on a case-by-case basis and the appeal will be heard by the appeals court in October or November 2008.

Three Turkish nationals filed an application against the Republic of Turkey under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants were represented by Mr A.F. Demirkan, a lawyer practising in Bursa. In 2004 the General Directorate of Highways seized a plot of land belonging to the applicants for the construction of a highway. The applicants brought an action before the Karacabey Civil Court to obtain compensation for the de facto expropriation of their property. They requested 6,500 Turkish liras as compensation from the court and reserved their right to increase this claim in due course. On 16 October 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Karacabey Civil Court. According to the information provided by the applicants, there has been no outstanding debt in the execution files. On 20 March 2009 the administration paid TRY 10,297.75 to the applicants. The cost of the appeal was estimated to be around TRY 8,000,000. The appeal was dismissed on 15 October 2008. The case was adjourned until 10 March 2009. The judge ruled that the appeal should be dismissed on 9 March 2009, and the case was dismissed. The judgment was dismissed again on 16 October 2009, the cost was approximately TRY 2,400,000 and the damages were estimated at TRY 1,700.

name: Sonja Mendel
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that her right to access to a court had been violated since she had not been able to appeal against a decision to withdraw permission for her to participate in a programme. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The case was settled in the Court of Appeal on 6 November 2008. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant and the decision was quashed. The case is now being appealed to the Supreme Court of Sweden. Employment Service (Länsarbetsnämnden) decided to withdraw its approval for the applicant to take part in the programme in which she was participating. According to the Employment Service, the applicant had not been acting in a proper manner in relation to the demands laid upon her. The decision was taken on the basis of a report drawn up by the Employment service. The applicant appealed against the decision to the National Labour Market Board (Arbetsmark-nadsstyrelsen –hereafter ‘the Board’). She claimed that there were several statements in the report which were not true. On 29 March 2006 the Board decided to reject the appeal. In the Board’s decision, it was expressly stated that there was no possibility in accordance with Section 39 of the 2000 Ordinance to appeal against the decision. Therefore, the Board concluded that there were grounds to withdraw her entitlement to participate in the programme. On 11 September 2006 the applicant submitted a complaint to the Chancellor of Justice (Justitiekanslern) where she complained, inter alia, about the decisions and their handling of her case. She requested damages, but did not claim that there had been a breach of her rights under Article 6 of the Convention. This complaint seems still to be pending before the chancellor of Justice.

name: Srdan Pesukic
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25088/07) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his criminal conviction was based to a decisive extent on testimony given by an anonymous witness. The Government of Montenegro did not express an intention to take part in the proceedings. The application was communicated to the Government on 26 November 2009. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The hearing was adjourned until 1 January 2013. The witness interrogations did not allow for an adequate exercise of the rights of the defence. According to X’s submissions, he was the only person who had observed the crime and who dared to testify. It thus appeared comprehensible that X feared reprisals. It was further obvious that the applicant had a motive to take revenge on the witness who had contributed to his conviction and to prevent him from making further testimonies. The applicant was convicted of manslaughter (vorsätzliche Tötung) and of several counts of drug-trafficking and sentenced to fourteen years and nine months’ detention. The court considered that the testimony given by X was credible and pertinent. The court considered that the measures taken were both necessary and sufficient to prevent identification of the witness X. The court had taken a number of measures to compensate the restrictions imposed on the rights of the defence. The witness had not been examined by the regional prosecutor (Bezirksanwalt), but by the president of the court. It had thus been known that X had no criminal record and that there was no indication that he had any contact with the drug trafficking scene. It was further known that he spoke the Serbo-Croatian language. The jury court considered, however, that this information was of minor importance for the assessment of credibility. A criminal conviction must not be exclusively based on testimony given by an anonymous witness. The jury court resumed its examination by laying out general principles for the assessment of the credibility of evidence by witnesses. Relying on all available evidence, the jury court concluded that there was no doubt that N. B. had been shot by the applicant. The applicant lodged a nullity appeal (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) with the Court of Cassation (Kassationsgericht) of the canton of Zurich. By decision of 19 December 2005 the Court decided that the applicant was not guilty of murder and that he should not be sentenced to prison time. The jury court further considered that there had been other evidence linking the applicant to the crime. There was, in particular, witness and circumstantial evidence allowing the conclusion that he had known the victim. Court noted that the anonymous witness had been heard in camera and that the applicant’s counsel did not have the possibility directly to question the witness. Adequate compensation could only be conceivable if at least the defence had the right directly to take part in the interrogation of the witness and was given the opportunity to assess the witness’ credibility. As this had not been the case, the court considered that the criminal court could not rely on the testimony given by the Anonymous Witness. The court did not call into question that the legal conditions for granting anonymity were fulfilled in the instant case and confirmed the first instance court's finding that it had been necessary to protect X against possible reprisals. The court examined whether the testimony given by the anonymous witness had to be regarded as being “decisive’ for the applicant’s conviction. The Federal Tribunal quashed the decision of 19 December 2005 and remitted the case to the Court of Cassation. The senior public prosecutor (Oberstaatsanwalt) of the canton of Zurich lodged a nullity appeal against the decision. The tribunal confirmed that it had been necessary to protect the witness by shielding his appearance both from the applicant and from the applicants’ counsel. It considered that the counsel was not under any legal obligation to transmit information on the witness’ identity to the applicant. The tribunal concluded that the anonymous testimony only served as one piece of a mosaic which enforced the conclusion drawn from the remaining evidence. of guilt. It followed that the criminal courts were not prevented from taking this evidence into account. The jury court had considered that the testimony given by the witness X had been credible and that it was, furthermore, in line with the scientific conclusion that the victim had been killed by gunshot in the back of his neck on 15 October 2001. The Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s nullity appeal on 12 February 2007. On 19 April 2007 the Federal Tribunal rejected the appeal. of the applicant's appeal.

name: Manuel Tejedor García
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 28 October 1996. It originated in an application (no. 25420/94) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by a Spanish national, Mr Manuel Tejedor García, on 4 August 1994. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr J.M. Morenilla, the elected judge of Spanish nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President. Manuel Tejedor García, who was born in 1948, now lives in Saragossa. He was an officer in the national police force and lived at Mataró (Barcelona) On 21 May 1989, while off duty, he was in Gallur (Saragossa) where he joined members of his family and friends to celebrate his niece’s first communion. At about 8.30 p.m., after a banquet which followed the ceremony and at which he drank, in addition to the wine that accompanied the meal, three glasses of champagne, a cognac and two half-measures of. the wine, he had a drink of cognac. The facts underlying the procedure in issue were described in the judgment of the SaragOSSa Audiencia Provincial of 6 November 1991. Manuel Tejedor García shot a shot into the ceiling of the 'Diodon' café in Gallur. He then kicked a man in the testicles after throwing his identity card to the floor. After forcing the two Africans to leave the café with their hands above their heads, he took them to the guardia civil barracks, where he handed them over to the officers on duty. The court heard that García had been drinking cognac at the time of the incident and his alcohol level was high. The case was referred to the High Court of Justice in Madrid, which took up the case in August 2013. A preliminary inquiry was opened in respect of the applicant for wrongful arrest, assault and disobeying orders. On 18 September 1989 the ANPU (Asociación Nacional de la Policía Uniformada) brought a private prosecution against the guardia civil officers of Gallur. It requested the court to declare that the applicant was innocent, and to investigate the responsibility of the two officers who had arrested him. On 10 September 1990 the investigating judge, having regard to the contradictory evidence as to the assault and the offer of drugs to the applicant, considered that no offence had been made out and decided, in accordance with Article 789 of the CCP. In a decision of 4 December 1990 the investigating judge rejected Mr Gallego’s observations. The investigating judge held that the public prosecutor had made an application for an order setting aside the decision that no further action be taken in the correct form. The judge said that it would be better to test the evidence at an adversarial hearing. In a decision (auto) of 4 September 1990 the judge rejected the ANPU's application on the grounds that it had been lodged out of time (see paragraph 16 below) and confirmed the decision of 10 September 1990. In an order (providencia) of 8 November 1990, the judge ruled that the application had been made within the statutory three-day time-limit. The case was brought against two guardia civil officers accused by the ANPU. The investigating judge made a final discontinuance order and committed the applicant for trial. On 6 November 1991 the Audiencia Provincial dismissed the preliminary objection that the public prosecutor’s application had been made out of time and found the applicant guilty of the alleged offences. It sentenced him to six months and fifteen days’ imprisonment, and a fine of 200,000 pesetas, and ordered him to pay compensation to the victims. He was also suspended from duty for six months. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 28 May 1993. It found that there was nothing in the case file to show when it had been sent to the publicProsecutor or when the prosecutor had been served with the decision. The Constitutional Court ruled that the application had no constitutional basis. The court said the interpretation of the application was not in line with the law. It said the application should have been allowed to stand on its own merit. The decision means the application could have been rejected on the grounds that it did not meet the legal requirements to be heard by the court. The appeal was rejected on two grounds: 1) The application was in breach of the law; and 2) The law does not allow the court to dismiss an appeal based on a lack of evidence; and 3) The court found that the appeal was based on an incorrect interpretation of a law that should not have been applied to the case.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 28 October 1996. It originated in an application (no. 25420/94) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by a Spanish national, Mr Manuel Tejedor García, on 4 August 1994. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr J.M. Morenilla, the elected judge of Spanish nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 September 1997. The accused, Mr Manuel Tejedor García, was an officer in the national police force and lived at Mataró (Barcelona) The facts underlying the procedure in issue were described in the judgment of the Saragossa Audiencia Provincial of 6 November 1991. Mr Thór Vilhjálmsson replaced, as President of the Chamber, Mr Ryssdal who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case, and Mr I. Foighel, substitute judge, became a member of the chamber. Manuel Tejedor García shot a shot into the ceiling of a Gallur café. He then kicked a man in the testicles. The victim lost two teeth. He forced two Africans to leave the café with their hands above their heads and took them to the guardia civil barracks, where, finally, he handed them over to the officers on duty. The people present gathered round the police officer and his prisoners after following them from the café. They ultimately formed a group in front of the entrance to theGuardia Civil barracks, protesting against the events they had just witnessed and noting that the accused came out of the building in an aggressive manner on several occasions. A preliminary inquiry was opened in respect of the applicant for wrongful arrest, assault and disobeying orders. He was cautioned and, the following morning, at about 3 a.m. he was taken to Saragossa and brought before the duty investigating judge, who, after questioning him in the presence of the police lawyer, Mr Luis Saldaña Estevan, ordered his release. On 18 September 1989 the ANPU (Asociación Nacional de la Policía Uniformada) brought a private prosecution (acusación particular) against the guardia civil officers of Gallur. It requested the court to declare that the applicant was innocent, and to investigate the responsibility of the two officers who had arrested him. In an annotation of 7 November 1990 the registrar attested that the public prosecutor had returned the case file and lodged an application for the decision to be set aside. On the following day, the decision was served on Mr Gallego. In a decision (auto) of 4 December 1990 the investigating judge rejected MrGallego’s observations. He held that the application had been made in time, on the ground that in the absence of any indication as to when the. public prosecutor received the decision of 10 September 1990 and the case. file, it had to be deemed to have been made within the statutory three-day time-limit. The application was brought by two guardia civil officers accused by the ANPU. The judge ordered an oral hearing and committed the applicant for trial in the Audiencia Provincial. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on the grounds that there was nothing in the case file to show when the public prosecutor had been served with the decision. The applicant was sentenced to six months and fifteen days’ imprisonment, and a fine of 200,000 pesetas, and ordered him to pay compensation to the victims. He was also suspended from duty for six months. The application was referred to as the ‘Antonio Tejedor García case’. The case was to be decided on the basis of a broad interpretation of the law. The court ruled that the interpretation was not susceptible of constitutional relief. The appeal was dismissed because it was not consistent with the law as it stood. The case was settled by a majority of two-to-one in favour of the appeal. The decision was made on the grounds that the application had not been allowed to be heard in its entirety by the Court of Appeal. The result was a ruling that the appeal was not justified by the law and was therefore not valid. It was decided that the decision was not in the public interest and that it should be dismissed as a result.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 28 October 1996. It originated in an application (no. 25420/94) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 on 4 August 1994. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr J.M. Morenilla, the elected judge of Spanish nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 September 1997. Mr Tejedor García, who was born in 1948, now lives in Saragossa. At the material time, he was an officer in the national police force and lived at Mataró (Barcelona) He drank, in addition to the wine that accompanied the meal, three glasses of champagne, a cognac and two half-measures of his niece’s first communion. At about 8.30 p.m., after a banquet which followed the ceremony and at which he drank, Mr Ryssdal who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case, Mr I. Foighel became a member of the Chamber. Manuel Tejedor García shot two Africans in the ceiling of a Gallur café. He kicked one of the men in the testicles and cut his lips with his revolver. He forced them to leave the café with their hands above their heads and took them to the guardia civil barracks, where he handed them over to the officers on duty. The court ruled that the men were lawfully resident in Spain and had the right to show their identity papers. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Spain, which decided to throw out the guilty verdicts. The sentence was handed down by the court of appeals in Granada. A preliminary inquiry was opened in respect of the applicant for wrongful arrest, assault and disobeying orders. On 18 September 1989 the ANPU (Asociación Nacional de la Policía Uniformada) brought a private prosecution against the guardia civil officers of Gallur. It requested the court to declare that the applicant was innocent, and to investigate the responsibility of the two officers who had arrested him. On 10 September 1990 the investigating judge, having regard to the contradictory evidence as to the assault and the offer of drugs to the applicant, considered that no offence had been made out and decided, in accordance with Article 789 of the CCP. In an annotation of 7 November 1990 the registrar attested that the public prosecutor had returned the case file and lodged an application for the decision to be set aside (recurso de reforma) or, in the alternative, an appeal (see paragraph 16 below), dated 13 September 1990. On the following day, the decision was served on Mr Gallego. In a decision (auto) of 4 December 1990 the investigating judge rejected MrGallego’s observations and held that the application had been made in time. As to the merits he stated that it would be better to test the evidence at an adversarial. The judge ordered an oral hearing and committed the applicant for trial in the Audiencia Provincial. The judge noted that both the ANPU and the applicant were represented by Mr Gallego and requested him to clarify the situation. On 6 November 1991 the judge dismissed the preliminary objection that the public prosecutor’s application had been made out of time and found the applicant guilty of the alleged offences. It sentenced him to six months and fifteen days’ imprisonment, and a fine of 200,000 pesetas, and ordered him to pay compensation to the victims. He was also suspended from duty for six months. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 28 May 1993. It found that there was nothing in the case file to show when it had been sent to the publicProsecutor. The Constitutional Court ruled that the application had no constitutional basis. The court found that the interpretation of the law was not susceptible of constitutional relief. The case was settled by the High Court on 21 February 1994. The appeal was dismissed on 24 July 1994. It was ruled that there was no basis for the application to be heard by the court in the first place and that the appeal could not be heard in its current form. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 24 August 1994 and the case was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 24 September 1994. After the appeal was rejected, the court ruled that it had no grounds to hear the case again.

name: Mehmet Tanay
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that a factual error made by the Court of Cassation had infringed his right of access to court. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 20 November 2007. It also decided to examine the merits of the case at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention). The applicant was represented by Mrs Fatma Kalsen Demirdaş, a lawyer practising in Tunceli. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The Tunceli Court accepted the medical report and began examining the merits of the case. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision, quoting the applicant’s name, instead of that of his representative, as the person who had been ill. In an application for rectification Mrs Demirdaş argued that it was she who was ill, not her client, and that the Court had made a factual error which should be rectified. On 12 May 2003, the Court of. Cassation held that “amending the factual error would not affect the outcome’, and dismissed the rectification request.

The case originated in an application (no. 18753/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that a factual error made by the Court of Cassation had infringed his right of access to court. On 20 November 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the applicant's application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention) The application was brought by Mr Mehmet Tanay (“the applicant”), and the Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. Medical reports confirmed that Mrs Demirtaş had been ill between 23 August 2000 and 17 September 2000 and had thus been unable to lodge the case within the statutory time-limit. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision, quoting the applicant’s name, instead of that of his representative, as the person who was ill. In an application for rectification Mrs Demirdaş argued that it was she who had was ill, not her client. On 4 July 2003 the Tunceli Court concurred and dismissed the case. On 13 November 2003 the Court ofCassation upheld the final ruling and awarded the applicant additional compensation.

name: Gösta Håkansson
train_texts: The case was brought before the Court on 14 December 1988 by the European Commission of Human Rights and on 27 January 1989 by the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden. The case originated in an application (no. 11855/85) against Sweden lodged with the Commission in 1984 by Mr Gösta Håkansson and Mr Sune Sturesson, both Swedish citizens. The purpose of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (P1-1) The oral proceedings opened on 25 September 1989 in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. The Government's memorials were received on 31 July and 4 August 1989. The applicants’ replies were received at the registry on 20 October 1989 and the Government’s comments thereon on 20 November 1989. On 4 December 1989 the President rejected an application from the Government to file additional evidence and on 23 January 1990 the Chamber rejected a similar application. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government, by Mr Rozakis for the Commission and by Mr Ravnsborg for the applicants, as well as the Government's replies to its questions. The property had been seized in July 1979 in order to secure the payment of the previous owners’ debts to three banks. The applicants maintained that a representative of the County Administrative Board had stated, at the public viewing of the property on 27 November 1979, that, in this case, the requisite permit would certainly be granted speedily. In support of these allegations, the applicants submitted three affidavits, each of which was signed in 1989 by a person who had been present either at the auction or at a public viewing. The applications for a permit to retain the estate Risböke 1:3 were granted by the County Agricultural Board on 7 January 1980. The application for a permit to retain Risböke 1:3 was rejected by the County Agricultural Board on 25 January 1982. The Board stated that the estate was considered to be a unit suitable for rationalisation purposes, which ought to be used to consolidate properties within the area that were capable of further development. It added that, as neighbours were interested in acquiring the property, the request might be refused under section 4 para. 1, sub-section 3, of the 1979 Act (see paragraph 30 below). The applicants appealed to the National Board of Agriculture (lantbruksstyrelsen), which rejected the appeal on 5 September 1980. The Risböke 1:3 was to be redeemed for 240,000 SEK. The applicants brought proceedings before the Real Estate Court of Växjö. The Court rejected the claim, stating that in view of the clear wording of section 14 this provision could not be applied by analogy to the applicants’ situation. In April 1984 the Senior Land Surveyor (överlantmätaren) of the County of Kronoberg made a new valuation of the property. The County Administrative Board ordered, on 10 November 1983, the compulsory resale by auction of the estate. The Enforcement Office (kronofogdemyndigheten) in VäXjö was responsible for arranging the auction. The Government decided not to take any further action in respect of the request. The applicants appealed against this decision to the Supreme Court, which on 23 August 1984 refused leave to appeal. On 26 June 1984, at the applicants’ request, the County Administrative Board appointed two special valuers. In their report of October 1984, the valuers concluded that the property had an estimated market value of 172,000 SEK. After the costs of the valuation and the auction had been deducted the applicants received 155,486.50 SEK (“the 1985 auction”) The Enforcement Office decided that the lowest bid which could be accepted would be 172,00 SEK and it was accepted. At the auction, there was, in fact, only one bid. The Court of Appeal in Denmark refused to grant the application on the basis that it was not in line with the law. The appeal was made on the grounds that the application was in contravention of the law and that the decision to grant it was based on the fact that they did not know the full extent of the problem. The case was decided by the Court of Appeals on 17 August 1985. The decision was made to deny the application as the application did not meet the legal requirements. The court ruled that the request was not valid and the appeal was dismissed. The application had been denied because the decision was not made in the public interest.

The case was brought before the Court on 14 December 1988 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 27 January 1989 by the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden. The case originated in an application (no. 11855/85) against Sweden lodged with the Commission in 1984 by Mr Gösta Håkansson and Mr Sune Sturesson, both Swedish citizens. The purpose of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13 and 14. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. There appeared before the Court: H. Corell for the Government, by Mr Rozakis for the Commission and by Mr Ravnsborg for the applicants. The applicants’ replies were received at the registry on 20 October 1989 and the Government’s comments thereon on 20 November 1989. On 4 December 1989 the President rejected an application from the Government to file additional evidence and on 23 January 1990 the Chamber rejected a similar application. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell. for the government, by. Rozakis, for the commission and by. Ravns Borg for the applicant, as well as the Government's replies to its. questions. Risböke 1:3 in the municipality of Markaryd was bought for 240,000 Swedish crowns (SEK) at a compulsory sale by auction. The property had been seized in July 1979 in order to secure the payment of the previous owners’ debts to three banks. According to a valuation made public before the auction, the market value (saluvärde) of the property was estimated at 140,000 SEK. The applicants submitted three affidavits, each of which was signed in 1989 by a person who had been present either at the auction or at the public viewing. The applications for a permit to retain the estate were approved on 5 February 1980. The applicants had intended to build up units which would create opportunities for employment and, in the long run, become financially sound properties to be exploited by their children. On 15 February 1980 the County Agricultural Board rejected the applicants’ request on the ground that the estate was a “rationalisation unit’ (rationaliseringsfastighet) which ought to be used for the purpose of consolidating other properties in the area. The applicants appealed to the National Board of Agriculture (lantbruksstyrelsen), which rejected the appeal on 5 September 1980. A new request, dated 4 January 1982, for a permit to retain Risböke 1:3 was rejected by the County agricultural Board on 25 January 1982. The applicants brought proceedings before the Real Estate Court of Växjö requesting that the State redeem the Risböke 1:3 in accordance with section 14 of the 1979 Act. In a judgment of 11 December 1981 the court rejected the claim, stating that in view of the clear wording of section 14 this provision could not be applied by analogy to the applicants’ situation. The applicants appealed to the Göta Court of Appeal (Göta hovrätt), which on 1 July 1982 confirmed the judgment. The Supreme Court (högsta domstolen) refused leave to appeal on 14 July 1983. The County Administrative Board ordered, on 10 November 1983, the compulsory resale by auction of the property. The Enforcement Office (kronofogdemyndigheten) was responsible for arranging the auction. In April 1984 the Enforcement Office determined that the estate had a value of 125,000 SEK. The applicants challenged this before the Göta Court of Appeal but the court dismissed the action on 4 June 1984. On 26 June 1984, at the applicants’ request, the County Administrative Board appointed two special valuers (see paragraph 37 below) In their report of October 1984, the valuers concluded that the property had an estimated market value of 172,000SEK. After the costs of the valuation and the auction had been deducted the applicants received 155,486.50 SEK (‘the 1985 auction’) The Court of Appeal refused to grant permission for the sale of the property in 1985. The sale was approved on 17 January 1986. The deal was for the property to be sold off at a cost of £2,000,000. It was never sold and the sale was never consummated. The land was sold to a private company for £1.5 million. The property was sold off to raise funds for a new development. The new project was to be named after the former owner, who was named after his great-great-grandfather. The name of the new company was chosen as a tribute to the memory of his father.
