name: Phyllis Bowman
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. It originated in an application (no. 24839/94) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by Mrs Phyllis Bowman, a British citizen, on 11 March 1994. The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention), and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 27 August 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides, Mr Pannick and Mr Robertson. Mrs Bowman was born in 1926 and lives in London. She is the executive director of the Society for the Protection of the Unborn Child (‘SPUC’) The case was heard by the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights. The Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of a Grand Chamber (Rule 51). The Grand Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr Ryssdal, the President of the Court, and Mr Bernhardt, the Vice-President. The SPUC is an organisation of approximately 50,000 members which is opposed to abortion and human embryo experimentation. It seeks changes to the present United Kingdom law which permits abortion up to twenty-two weeks and embryo experimentation up to fourteen days. The major political parties have no policies with regard to abortion or embryo experimentation: these are regarded as moral issues and members of Parliament are allowed to vote on proposed legislation according to their consciences. name: Józef Majcher
train_texts: The case originated in an application (nos. 12193/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Józef Majcher (‘the applicant’), on 15 October 2001. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The application was brought by Mr Majcher on behalf of his wife, who had filed a petition for divorce in 1987. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Łańcut District Court against the actions taken by the bailiff (skarga na czynności komornika). He submitted that those actions had been incorrect, because the money obtained from the debtor had been distributed wrongly. He also complained about the ineffectiveness of the enforcement. The court held that no valuable objects had been found in the debtor’s house which could be sold and used to satisfy the debt. On an unspecified date the applicant appealed. On 21 July 1999 the Rzeszów Regional Court dismissed his appeal. It held that the order of distribution had been in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39958/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant filed a claim for payment against his former employer with the Łódź Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) on 22 May 1991. On 2 December 1991 the court gave judgment. Upon the applicant's appeal the Court of Appeal remitted the case. On 9 June 1998 the applicant lodged a cassation appeal. The applicant appealed to the Olsztyn District Court against a decision to dismiss him from work. The applicant lodged a claim for damages under section 16 of the 2004 Act read in conjunction with Article 417 of the Civil Code. He sought compensation for the alleged mistakes in the examination of his claims and for the protracted length of the proceedings. His appeal against the judgment was dismissed by the Łódź Court of Appeal on 18 May 2006. The Government maintained that such an appeal was pending before the Supreme Court. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the applicant had not lodged a cassation appeal. The appeal was dismissed as it was inadmissible in law.

name: Johannes Werner
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 28 October 1996 and by the Government of the Republic of Austria on 25 November 1996. It originated in an application (no. 21835/93) against Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by an Austrian national, Mr Johannes Werner, on 16 March 1993. On 29 October 1996 the President decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the case of Szücs v Austria should be heard by the same Chamber. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31 of Rules of Court B). The lawyer was given leave by the President to use the German language. The hearing in this case and in the Szücs case took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 June 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Weitzel, Mr Bürstmayr, Mr Schreiner, Mr Cede and Mrs Gartner. Commission had produced various documents relating to the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. The circumstances of the case were as follows: A. Mr Johannes Werner, an Austrian national born in 1963, lives in Vienna. B. Mr Szüc, a Turkish national, was arrested in Austria in 1991 for allegedly forging the signature on a stolen credit card. The applicant and Mr and Mrs Hauser sought compensation from the State for the pecuniary damage sustained on account of their detention. A Vienna Regional Court refused their compensation claims on the ground that, contrary to the requirements of section 2 (1) (b) of the 1969 Act, the suspicion concerning them had not been dispelled. They appealed against that decision to the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) in 1992. The appeal was dismissed on 29 October 1992, and the case is now in the hands of the Supreme Court of Austria. The application was brought by Mr Werner and Mr Hauser against the Austrian Government for compensation for their detention under the Compensation (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1969. The trial of Johannes Werner, who was detained after his arrest in 1991, ended in a mistrial. The case was adjourned until March this year. No representative of the principal public prosecutor’s office attended the deliberations. No compensation was awarded to the appellants. The conditions which must be met under section 2 (1) (b) of the Compensation (Criminal Proceedings) Act in order to be able to claim compensation have accordingly not been satisfied and the appellant's claims must therefore fail, says the Court of Appeal. The court ruled that the prosecution was abandoned because the witnesses’ memories had begun to falter and could not be considered adequate to establish guilt.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 28 October 1996 and by the Government of the Republic of Austria (“the Government”) on 25 November 1996. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31 of Rules of Court B). The lawyer was given leave by the President to use the German language (Rule 28 § 3). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality. Hearing in this case and in the Szücs case took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 June 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Weitzel, Mr Bürstmayr, Mr Schreiner, Mr Cede and Mrs Gartner. Commission had produced various documents relating to the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. Court heard evidence from Mr Werner, Mr Szüc and Mr G. BürSTmayr. The hearing was adjourned until 19 July 1997, when Mr Werner was released. The application was returned to the Vienna Regional Court (Landesgericht) in February 1992. The applicant and Mr and Mrs Hauser sought compensation from the State for the pecuniary damage sustained on account of their detention. The claim for compensation for detention was rejected by the Vienna Regional Court on the ground that the suspicion concerning them had not been dispelled. They appealed against that decision to the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) The appeal was dismissed on 29 October 1992 and the case was thrown out. The case was heard by the German Federal Court of Justice (Bundesverfassungsgericht), which was the first German court of appeal to hear the case. The court ruled that suspicion must be dispelled sufficiently to establish that the detained person is not punishable, and cannot be prosecuted. There is no justification for giving the appellants, as they demanded, the opportunity to prove their innocence by taking further evidence. The evidence they propose to adduce cannot be considered likely to lead to such a result. The main reason why the prosecution was abandoned was that with the passing of time those witnesses’ memories had begun to falter. If their memories were so defective that they could no longer be considered adequate to establish guilt, neither can they in the present proceedings form an adequate basis for awarding compensation. The conditions which must be met under section 2 (1) (b) of the Compensation (Criminal Proceedings) Act in order to be able to claim compensation have accordingly not been satisfied.”

If their memories were so defective that they could no longer be considered adequate to establish guilt, neither can they in the present proceedings form an adequate basis for awarding compensation. The appeal was scheduled to be heard by the High Court of Justiciary (sitting as an appeal court in Edinburgh) on 15 February 2005. On the morning of that day, the High court made a section 4(2) order prohibiting the publication of a report of any part of the appeal hearing. The order was posted on the Scottish Courts Service website and circulated to the Scottish media. BBC Scotland were then contacted and advised that a hearing would be fixed but not before 18 Feb 2005. The Government, in their observations to this Court, maintain that BBC Scotland did not challenge that decision. BBC Scotland's application for the recall of the section 4(2) order was made on 15 February 2005. The Government maintain that BBC Scotland did not contest the decision not to hold a hearing before 18 February 2005 and, because no application had been made to recall or vary the interim order before 17 February 2005, the order became final on 17 February2005. The Appeal Court recalled the order of the trial judge and substituted an order for desertion pro loco et tempore, which allowed for the re-indictment of one of the original accused.

name: Bettina Malek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 16174/02) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) by an Austrian national, Mrs Bettina Malek (‘the applicant’), on 3 April 2002. The applicant was represented by her husband, Mr H. Malek, a lawyer practising in Krems. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint as being unfounded. This decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 20 February 2002. The decision was made in relation to a case brought against the Government of Zimbabwe by a former prime minister. The case was settled in the High Court and the appeal was dismissed in November 2001. The appeal was upheld by the Court of Appeal in March 2002 and the case was heard again in November 2002. In November 2002, the Appeal Court found the case not to have been heard. The Appeal Court ruled that the applicant had not brought a case against the government, and dismissed the appeal. The High Court heard that the case had been settled on the basis of an agreement between the applicant and the government.

name: Hasan Sepil
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant claimed he had been convicted on the basis of unlawful evidence provided by undercover police officers. He further argued that the domestic court had failed to evaluate substantive evidence, namely, records of the telephone conversations he had had prior to his arrest. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 March 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The case was heard by a jury of three women and two men. The applicant was charged with possession of and trafficking illegal drugs under Article 188 (3) of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) He claimed he was merely an addict and that the police records falsely stated that he had accepted money in exchange for drugs. The investigating judge held that he should be placed in detention pending the outcome of the proceedings. The applicant's lawyer argued that police evidence was unlawful in that the officers had conducted the operation without any judicial supervision and that their acts amounted to inciting the commission of an offence. The Istanbul Criminal Police Laboratory established that the light brown substance, which had a net weight of 2.1 grams, was indeed heroin. The Bakırköy Assize Court found the applicant guilty of trafficking drugs and sentenced him to six years and three months’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. On 21 April 2010 the applicant was granted conditional release. The court took into account the statements of the police officers, the testimony of M.T. and the evidence resulting from the police operation. the court rejected the request of the applicant’s lawyer to determine to whom those numbers belonged, noting that it would have no effect on the judgment. The judge ruled that the evidence relied on by the public prosecutor was obtained unlawfully.

name: Fatma Ormancı
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43647/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The defendants appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court against the court's decision. The case was settled in 1996 after the applicants paid an advance on the court fees. The decision of the court to award them compensation for pec uniary damage in respect of their husband's death was published in the book "A.O.'s Case", published by Oxford University Press, in which the author also published the first draft of the judgment. The applicants submitted their observations to the Supreme Administrative Court. The case was allocated to the 10th Division. of the Gaziantep Administrative Court in 1997. The applicants were paid the amount awarded to them on 5 November 1997 and 30 April 1998. The court upheld the decision of the first-instance court on 10 March 1998 and awarded the amount to the applicants on 5 and 30 November 1997. In 1998 the applicants were also paid the money on 5 April 1997 and 5 November 1998. At the time of the award, the case was being heard by the 11th Division of the Court of Appeal for the Appeals Court of the Supreme Court of Justice of Turkey.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37715/97) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that her son Patrick Shanaghan was killed by an unknown gunman in circumstances disclosing collusion by members of the security forces. She invoked Articles 2, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building on 4 April 2000. The Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of Hugh Jordan v. the United. Kingdom, no. 24746/94, McKerr v the United UK,No. 28883/95 and Kelly and Others v the U.K. no. 30054/96 (see judgments of the same date) Patrick Shanaghan was a thirty-year-old Catholic and active member of Sinn Fein when he was killed. Between 15 April 1985 and 19 May 1991 he was arrested and detained pursuant to investigations into acts of terrorism in Northern Ireland. Six of the ten arrests resulted in detention for four or more days. Patrick Shanaghan gave several written statements to his solicitors alleging physical assaults by RUC officers while in custody, including being punched in the back, punched under the chin with a clenched fist, stabbed in the throat with extended fingers, slapped in the face, and being hit and kicked in the testicles. The applicant alleged that on several occasions RUC detectives threatened to kill her son during interrogations. Patrick Shanaghan instituted proceedings against the Chief Constable of the RUC for alleged assault, battery, trespass to the person, unlawful arrest and unlawful imprisonment in respect of his detention from 9 to 15 April 1986. The applicant also claimed that there was an attempt on Patrick Shanaghan's life, on 17 February 1989, but that he managed to escape. On 10 December 1990, a RUC detective informed him that security force documentation containing information about him, including a photographic montage, had accidentally fallen out of the back of an army vehicle. He was advised to take measures for his personal safety as there was a risk that the material had come into the hands of loyalist paramilitaries. The Government gave further details about the loss of the photographs. Patrick Shanaghan was stopped and questioned by RUC and UDR officers on a daily basis. The Shanaghan family home, which the applicant shared with her son, was searched sixteen times between 1985 and 1991. The applicant alleged that the behaviour of the police at the scene was not consonant with any concern for her son's life or proper police procedures. She claimed that no ambulance was called to the scene and that the police prevented a priest approaching to give the last rites. The UFF (Ulster Freedom Fighters – a loyalist organisation) later claimed responsibility for the murder in the local press. The RUC informed Patrick Shanaghan promptly of the loss of the photographs. There was no evidence who, if anyone, recovered the photographs or that they played any later role in events. Patrick Shanaghan was shot dead in the chest in November 1994. The inquest into the killing was opened on 26 March 1996, over four and a half years after the murder. Several suspects had been arrested and interviewed but no evidence of admission had been obtained from them. The RUC discovered a car which they believed had been used by the people involved in the shooting. However, a forensic and fingerprint examination disclosed no evidence to connect it with any person suspected of murder. Enquiries showed that the car had been recently bought for cash by unknown persons from a private vendor. An inquest was heard over six days, between 26 March and 20 June 1996. It was presided over by the Coroner. Patrick Shanaghan's family claimed the RUC had prior knowledge that he was to be murdered and that the police investigation had been inadequate. The Coroner accepted that the evidence should be admitted. The RUC Chief Constable applied for judicial review of those decisions. On 18 June 1996, the High Court quashed the Coroner's decision, holding that it is now well-settled in the jurisprudence on this topic that a Coroner is not to conduct a wide-ranging inquiry into the broad circumstances in which a deceased has met his death. It is now clearly established by the decisions to which I have referred that the word “how” should receive the connotation “by what means” The Coroner refused to admit in evidence statements made by Patrick Shanaghan to his solicitors. The applicant made a complaint about the conduct of the RUC at the scene of the shooting in denying Dr Stewart access to the body and in failing to call an ambulance. This complaint was investigated by an assistant chief constable, under the supervision of the Independent Commission for Police Complaints. The Inspector concerned was given advice which was recorded in the Divisional Discipline Book. The RUC conducted further enquiries and reported to the Director of Public Prosecutions (the DPP). The applicant's daughter sent a copy of the unofficial inquiry report to the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland (see below) A community inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the murder was organised by family and friends after the conclusion of the inquest. The inquiry, conducted by the Castlederg-Aghyaran Justice Group and chaired by a retired United States Judge, heard thirteen witnesses over the period from 17 to 19 September 1996. The Judge concluded that the applicant had been murdered by the British Government and, more specifically, with the collusion of the RUC. Two witnesses claimed that they had seen Patrick Shanaghan still moving after the shooting had occurred. The applicant claimed damages for loss and damage sustained by her and the estate of her son by reason of negligence, breach of confidence and misfeasance in public office.

name: Mehmet Pehlivan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4233/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to be released pending trial, to a fair hearing within a reasonable time and to be informed promptly of the nature and cause of the accusations against him. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Pehlivan, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant was charged under Article 125 of the former Criminal Code, and with killing B.C. in 1992. The applicant made statements before the first‑instance court, denying the charges against him. The First Division of the Diyarbakır State Security Court ordered the applicant’s continued detention on remand in view of the nature of the offence, the state of evidence and the content of the case file. The court subsequently postponed the hearings until 24 December 1998 on account of the failure of the gendarmerie command to submit the relevant information. On 22 November 1999 the First Division held a hearing and found the applicant guilty of carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. The Diyarbakır State Security Court held forty-five hearings. At the end of every hearing the first-instance court considered the applicant’s detention during judicial proceedings. The court found no convincing evidence that the offence committed by the applicant was linked to terrorist activities. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 26 March 2002 because the applicant had been unable to examine three witnesses against him during the trial. The applicant was convicted of homicide and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. On 8 April 2004 the Court ofCassation upheld this judgment. The case was subsequently remitted to the First Division.

train_texts: The applicants were detained in Niğde Prison for being members of the IBDA-C (Great East Islamic Raiders-Front) The prison officers together with soldiers intervened in the uprising in order to bring it to an end. During the incident the applicants and the security forces both sustained injuries which were recorded in medical reports. The applicants were represented by Mr H. Tuna, Mr S. Kar, and Mr M.E. Kaya, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The application was lodged under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were sent to jail for four years for insulting a police officer. The court took the applicants' statements and ordered them to appear before the court again. The applicants appealed the decision and were sentenced to another four years in prison. The case was settled in the High Court of Justice of the Republic of Turkey. The judges ruled in favour of the applicants on all counts. They were also ordered to pay a fine of more than $1,000 to the police officer who was involved in the incident. The judge also ordered the applicants to pay an additional fine of $2,000. The hearing was held in front of a jury of seven members. The jury decided on the sentence. The defendants claim that they were not asked to submit their final statements and the judgment was pronounced in their absence. On 1 June 2005 the new Criminal Code came into force. The Nigde Assize Court has scheduled a hearing for 20 March 2007 with a view to adjusting the applicants' sentences, pursuant to the provisions of thenew Criminal Code. The defendants say that they had requested legal representation, which had not been forthcoming. On 25 June 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Niğde Criminal Court. The case was heard in Turkey's highest court, the Supreme Court of Justice, which heard it in the absence of the defendants.

During the incident the applicants and the security forces both sustained injuries which were recorded in medical reports. The court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case is one of the most high-profile in the history of the Turkish legal system. The application was made under Article 226 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicants were sentenced to four years in prison in 2000. They appealed, but the appeal was rejected by the Court of Cassation in 2001. The case was re-opened in 2002, and the applicants were sent back to court. The appeal was dismissed, and in 2001 the applicants returned to the court to make their case. They were sentenced again to four and a half years in jail, this time without the possibility of parole. The court of cassation ruled in favour of the applicants, and sentenced the defendants to a further two years. The applicants had requested legal representation, which had not been forthcoming. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26390/95) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that certain criminal proceedings against him in relation to fraud charges had exceeded a reasonable time. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine), decided the case on the basis of the case-file as it stood. The decision was made on 16 November 1999, when the Court declared the application admissible. Geneve and Cosmesin were accused of defrauding several thousand persons. The companies went into bankruptcy in February 1987. No goods containing the cultivated substances were ever marketed or produced. One of the two leading figures in the criminal activity concerned, Mr D.R., disappeared. In November 1987 a search for him with an arrest warrant was made via Interpol. On 7 November 1990 he was arrested by the Spanish police. The Norwegian authorities requested his extradition on 23 November 1990. In October 1991 and April 1992 the police interviewed 12 cultivators. In April 1989 the police held meetings with Swedish and English police authorities. On 29 February 1988 the Probate Court (skifteretten) received the final report from the administrators of the estates. The case was submitted to the Oslo City Court on 4 September 1991. The applicant was convicted of all but the VAT charges, and sentenced to 2 years’ imprisonment. The City Court found the defendants’ conduct particularly reprehensible and emphasised that the suffering which they had caused to innocent cultivators must be viewed as an aggravating factor in sentencing. “With the exception of D.R., the accused were of a young age at the time of the commission of the proscribed conduct. ... There were thus important years for settling down which elapsed between the criminal acts and judgment in the case. ... In the court’s view, had greater caution been used, the case would have been heard sooner.” The prosecution transmitted the case to the Oslo City Court in December 1991. Two other co-defendants, including Mr D.R., who were considered to have played a more prominent role in the proscribed activity, were sentenced to 3 years’ imprisonment. The applicant sought to appeal to the Supreme Court, alleging a procedural error in the first instance proceedings and requesting a new trial. After taking evidence on 14 December 1993 and holding a hearing on 6 September 1994, the Supreme court rejected the appeal on 13 September 1994. The Supreme Court held that, although more time had elapsed since the City Court’s judgment, it saw no reason for reducing the sentence.

name: Ian Le Petit
train_texts: The case was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, Ian Le Petit, complained that his naval court-martial did not constitute a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By decision dated 5 December 2000, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Government filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant was charged with obtaining property and a service by deception. He made certain admissions at his first interview and gave the investigators access to his bank accounts. The court-martial took place on 8-10 July 1996. He pleaded guilty as charged. On 10 July 1996 he was sentenced to three months’ imprisonment. The Admiralty Board rejected his petition against conviction and sentence. It was considered that his admissions in interview were not the result of oppression and that, given the seriousness of the offences, his sentence was neither manifestly excessive nor wrong in principle. In the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the jury could not reach a verdict.

It was considered that his admissions in interview were not the result of oppression and that, given the seriousness of the offences, his sentence was neither manifestly excessive nor wrong in principle.

name: Süleyman Erkan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26803/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant alleged that, contrary to what was indicated in the arrest protocol, he had been arrested on 5 September 1999. He was allegedly punched, kicked, beaten on the head and the back with a truncheon and threatened with death. He also alleged that his testicles were squeezed. On 19 September 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The applicant was kept in police custody for about one week in 1999. He maintained that he had been subjected to ill-treatment while in custody and that, therefore, he had started a hunger strike. The judge ordered the applicant's release as there was no strong evidence demonstrating he had committed the offences of which he was accused. The applicant filed a complaint with the Büyükçekmece public prosecutor's office against the police officers from the anti-terror branch of the Security Directorate, who had allegedly ill-treated him. He finally maintained that on 12 September 1999 the doctor had drawn up the medical report without examining him. In his petition, the applicant maintained he had was arbitrarily deprived of his liberty between 5 and 8 September 1999. On 15 September 1999 the applicant was examined by two medical experts from the Human Rights Foundation who noted the following marks and considered that the applicant's account of events was consistent with the marks observed on his body. The Büyükçekmece public prosecutor issued a decision of lack of territorial jurisdiction and sent the investigation file to the Fatih public prosecutor's office. Two police officers who were on duty at the anti-terror branch of the Istanbul Security Directorate at the time of the applicant’s detention in police custody denied the allegations against him. The first officer contended that the minor marks mentioned in the medical report of 14 September 1999 did not result from torture. He alleged that they might have been the marks resulting from handcuffing. The Fatih public prosecutor issued a decision not to prosecute in respect of the police officers. He found that there was no evidence other than the applicant's allegations on which to initiate criminal proceedings. The applicant filed an objection against the decision of 20 February 2001. On 29 August 2001 the Beyoğlu Assize Court dismissed the applicant’s objection. This decision was served on the applicant and his lawyer on 9 October 2001. The court ruled that the applicant had been arrested on 5 September 1999, although the date on the arrest protocol was 8 September 1999. The case was settled out of court in August 2001. In October 2001, the judge ruled in favour of the applicant.

name: Michael P. Hapeshis
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35214/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Two Cypriot nationals alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived them of their home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 8 February 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). In addition, third-party comments were received from the Government of Cyprus, which had exercised its right to intervene. The applicants left their house on 13 August 1974, as the Turkish troops were advancing. On 17 August 1974 their father tried to visit his property but was arrested by Turkish soldiers. He was released on the same day, since he was a British citizen. On 19 May 1991 the applicants' father died. According to his will, dated 18 May 1988, the house and land in question was to be equally shared by the two applicants. On 10 July 1995 the applicants registered, in equal shares, their titles with the Department of Lands and Surveys of the Republic of Cyprus. The first applicant got the west residence, while the second applicantgot the east one.

The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The Government of Cyprus exercised its right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b)). The applicants left their house on 13 August 1974, as the Turkish troops were advancing. On 17 August 1974 their father tried to visit his property but was arrested by Turkish soldiers. He was released on the same day, since he was a British citizen. On 19 May 1991 the applicants' father died. According to his will, dated 18 May 1988, the house and land in question was to be equally shared by the two applicants. The first applicant got the west residence, while the second applicantgot the east one.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 6684/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his trial for terrorism related offences was unfair because of the way the courts in Northern Ireland had approached the question of non-disclosure of prosecution papers to the defence on grounds of public interest immunity. He is currently detained at HMP Maghaberry, Northern Ireland. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant's case was that he had simply given M. a lift and that he knew nothing about the articles that he brought into the car. The applicant was arraigned on 8 June 2001 and pleaded not guilty to one count of possession of firearms and ammunition with intent. A defence statement was served on his behalf on 12 June 2001. It contained the following: “The defendant believes that he may have been entrapped by a person known to him working with the police either for the purpose of incriminating this defendant or his co-defendant” The application for an order preventing disclosure was made to a judge other than the trial judge. That judge is designated by the Lord Chief Justice of Northern Ireland and is referred to as the ‘disclosure judge’ (see domestic law and practice below) On 18 February 2002, the disclosure judge allowed the prosecution's application for non-disclosure. He outlined this Court's judgments in Rowe and Davis v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, §§6 60-62, ECHR 2000‑II. The majority took the view that it was important for the trial judge to see the material personally. That is certainly true if the material is not prejudicial to the accused and where the trial is before a judge and jury. However, in the case [of] a non-jury trial it is obviously undesirable that prejudicial material which is not going to be part of the evidence should be seen by the judge who will be tribunal of fact, especially if it is not disclosed to the defence. The judge ruled that none of the material could be expected to undermine the case for the prosecution or to assist the accused’s defence. The judge then said that one way of proceeding would be to appoint special counsel who would be shown the material and remain throughout the trial. A hearing took place on 1 August 2002 to allow the parties and counsel appearing for the Attorney-General to make submissions as to whether it was appropriate either for special counsel to be appointed or for the trial judge himself to consider the undisclosed material. The hearing was adjourned until the next hearing, which was to be held on 17 and 19 June 2002. The trial judge said that he did not anticipate any circumstances which would result in the material becoming of value to the defence. The trial judge said that he considered that it was in the interests of justice that he should see the statement of reasons. He stressed that he had not himself seen the material seen by the disclosure judge. Counsel for the applicant's co-accused also suggested that the trial judge recuse himself since he had seen the statement. The trial judge ruled that it wasn't appropriate for him to recused himself. He also found that the disclosure. judge was best equipped to know what procedural safeguards could be put in place as to the. non-disclosed material, including whether it was appropriate to appoint special. counsel, since he knew the nature of that material. The judge says he cannot foresee any circumstance in which the undisclosed material, that is the material undisclosed to the trial judge, would be of assistance to the defence. But it may be that the defence may advance a proposition or raise an issue that might by remote possibility make that so. I would not regard the case as requiring the appointment of special counsel. The trial judge said there were two types of material involved. The first could not assist the applicant because it was adverse to him. The second related to police procedures, was general in nature and content, and did not relate directly to the applicant. The case made on behalf of the applicant at trial was that the reason that the controller did not pass to those on the ground the registration number of the Renault and information as to the place where it was last seen, was that this was an operation. The trial judge rejected both applications. the defence of entrapment, further disclosure was required. The trial judge found that taking the circumstantial evidence and the inferences to be drawn from it, he was satisfied of the applicant's guilt of the two offences beyond reasonable doubt. On 12 November 2002 the applicant was convicted by the trial judge, without a jury, of two offences: possession of firearms and ammunition with intent, contrary to Article 17 of the Firearms (NI) Order 1981; and possession of articles for a purpose connected with terrorism. The applicant was sentenced to concurrent terms of imprisonment of twelve years and two years respectively. The applicant appealed against his conviction on both charges. The non-disclosed material was not considered by the Court of Appeal before it gave judgment. It considered the House of Lords ruling in R. v. H and C [2004] A.C. 134 (see paragraph 32 below) and reviewed this Court's judgments in Rowe and Davis and Jasper, both cited above; Fitt v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 29777/96, ECHR 2000‑II; Edwards and Lewis v the United UK, nos. 39647/98 and 40461/98, 22 July 2003. The judge dealing with an application for non-Disclosure must have a full understanding and appreciation of all the issues in the trial and in particular the nature of the defence. The Court of Appeal rejected the applicant's argument that the trial judge had given insufficient weight to the entrapment theory. No new line of defence ever emerged that might have prompted a reconsideration of the disclosure judge's decision that the material did not assist the applicant. The trial judge's consideration of this material has not brought about any unfairness to the appellant and we do not consider that this rendered his conviction in any way unsafe”. The appeal was dismissed on 19 November 2004, by the Court of appeal. The case was heard by the Lord Chief Justice, the Lord Chancellor and the Chief Justice of the High Court. The Appeal Court dismissed the appeal on November 19, 2004, and ruled that the appeal had been dismissed. The appeals court also dismissed the case on November 21, 2004.

No procedure exists to ensure that an assessment of the possible value to the defense of such material other than by the prosecutor or at his. The trial judge said that none of the material was likely to undermine the case for the prosecution or to assist the accused's defence. The judge then suggested that one way of proceeding would be to appoint special counsel who would be shown the material and remain throughout the trial. The trial judge ordered that it is not in the public interest to disclose the material, and that the reasons for his decision shall remain confidential to the prosecutor and the trial judge. A hearing took place on 1 August 2002 to allow the parties and counsel appearing for the Attorney-General to make submissions as to whether it was appropriate either for special counsel to be appointed or for the judge himself to consider the undisclosed material. Trial judge said that he considered that it was in the interests of justice that he should see the statement of reasons. He stressed that he had not himself seen the material seen by the disclosure judge. He also found that the disclosureJudge was best equipped to know what procedural safeguards could be put in place as to the non-disclosed material. In an ex tempore judgment he ruled: “There is no further safeguard that I am aware of that would be of any assistance” The disclosure judge said there were two types of material involved. The first could not assist the applicant because it was adverse to him. The second related to police procedures, was general in nature and content, and did not relate directly to the applicant. I would not regard the case as requiring the appointment of special counsel... The present reality is that I cannot foresee any circumstance in which the undisclosed material would be of assistance to the defence. But it may be that the defence may advance a proposition or raise an issue that might by remote possibility make that so, and I think if the Crown concedes that that is the position then the Crown should make the matter known to the trial judge. The trial judge rejected the defence of entrapment. The trial judge found that taking the circumstantial evidence and the inferences to be drawn from it, he was satisfied of the applicant's guilt of the two offences beyond reasonable doubt. On 12 November 2002 the applicant was convicted by the trial judge, without a jury, of two offences: possession of firearms and ammunition with intent, contrary to Article 17 of the Firearms (NI) Order 1981; and possession of articles for a purpose connected with terrorism. The applicant was sentenced to concurrent terms of imprisonment of twelve years and two years respectively. His co-accused, his co-defendant and his friend were acquitted. The applicant appealed against his conviction on both charges. On 28 October 2004, the Court of Appeal in Northern Ireland unanimously dismissed the appeal. The non-disclosed material was not considered by the Court before it gave judgment. Instead, it considered the House of Lords ruling in R. v. H and C [2004] A.C. 134 (see paragraph 32 below) and reviewed this Court's judgments in Rowe and Davis and Jasper, both cited above; Fitt v the United Kingdom [GC], no. 29777/96, ECHR 2000‑II; Edwards and Lewis v the UK, no. 39647/98 and 40461/98, 22 July 2003. Court of Appeal found that the applicant's defence of entrapment was well known to the trial judge, the prosecution, and the disclosure judge and no other issue had been identified that might sound on the question of disclosure. The disclosure judge had been unable to envisage any circumstances in which the non-disclosed material could assist the defence either by enhancing the case that was being made for the applicant or by undermining or weakening the prosecution case. The Court of Appeal noted that it had been the central plank of the applicant’s defence and had been thoroughly explored not only in cross-examination of the witnesses but in extensive canvassing of the various “coincidences” relied on by the applicant. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 19 November 2004. It refused to certify a point of law of general importance. It also refused to grant leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 17 December 2004. The decision was quashed by the High Court the next day. The application was dismissed on 18 November 2004, after the appeal was rejected by the Court of appeal. The former judge, Lord Tebbit, was jailed for three years in July 2004 for his part in the case. He was released on licence in April 2005. The case was settled in September 2005, and the judge was sentenced to two years' imprisonment.

name: Erich Kiefer
train_texts: The case concerns the duration of the proceedings instituted by the applicant and whether they were terminated within a ‘reasonable time’ The case was referred to the Court by an Austrian national, Erich Kiefer (“the applicant”) on 30 December 1998 pursuant to former Article 48 § 1 (e) of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The applicant is represented by Mr B. Gachnang, a lawyer practising in Lucerne in Switzerland. The Swiss Government are represented by their Agent, Mr Ph. Boillat. The Court ruled in favour of the applicant. In 1983 the applicant suffered an injury and became partly disabled. On 7 November 1985 he requested pension benefits from the Swiss Invalidity Insurance. The Compensation Office dismissed the applicant's request on 23 December 1987, as he was only partly hindered in exercising his profession as a lorry driver. In 1989, various reports were filed by Austrian experts. Based on these various reports, Dr. M.-L., a Swiss, applied to the Austrian authorities to undertake a most thorough examination of his case by means of a further medical expert. In February 1990 the Austrian orthopaedist Dr. L.-K. submitted another report. The case was then referred back to the Compensation Office for renewed examination. The Invalidity Insurance Commission considered in its proposal of 19 July 1990 that the applicant had not sufficiently demonstrated his invalidity. The applicant was granted a time-limit of 30 days to reply. In 1992 the Compensation Office dismissed the applicant's request for pension benefits as he had not been insured at the time concerned. On 10 May 1993 he filed an appeal against this decision which was dismissed by the Federal Appeals Commission for Old Age, Survivors and Invalidity insurance on 21 February 1993. The case has been referred to as the "Austrian Lorry Driver Case" and the "Lorry Driver Pension Case" by the Insurance Commission of Austria. The applicant filed an administrative law appeal in 1994. The Commission declared the application admissible on 16 April 1998. In its report of 21 October 1998 (former Article 31), it expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1. The appeal was dismissed on 18 November 1994 by the Federal Insurance Court (Eidgenössisches Versicherungsgericht), the decision being served on 25 November 1994. In 1998, the applicant applied to the Commission on 13 April 1995, complaining under Article 6§ 1 about the length of social security proceedings. The application was declared admissible in 1998.

name: Maria Buckland
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40060/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Court of Appeal’s decision to dismiss her appeal and uphold the judgment making a possession order constituted an unjustified breach of her right to respect for her home and her family life. The application was communicated to the Government on 3 May 2011. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Cardiff. The Gypsy Council issued a notice of termination of licence to the applicant which expired on 6 February 2005. The Gypsy Council issued a claim for possession against the applicant and five members of her extended family, including her parents, in Neath Port Talbot County Court. In a witness statement lodged prior to the hearing, the applicant indicated that she intended to leave the site when her parents left. Judge Bidder QC gave a judgment on the preliminary issue of whether the applicant could challenge the making of a possession order in her case. He concluded: “58. ... I do not consider it to be arguable that the decision of the claimants to seek possession against her was unreasonable or that their decision to invoke their domestic law rights could be castigated as unreasonable ...” Judge made an order for possession against the applicant. He invited submissions from the applicant as to the possible temporary suspension of any possession order. The judge was satisfied that her son, who resided part of the time with her, had been involved in an incident on site in which he threatened someone with a gun. He was, however, not satisfied that Maria Buckland has herself been guilty of any offensive behaviour on site, or of any breach of licence, apart from the relatively minor failure to pay the water charges. He also said that he was clear that the behaviour of [her son] on this site and his attitude towards the Farrows [the family of the site manager] is such that I have to impose conditions. The applicant, who was still resident at the site, was granted permission to appeal the possession order to the Court of Appeal. A stay of execution of the order of 28 July 2006 was also ordered. The real difference between the present case and Connors is not that the appellant had been in occupation for a shorter period than was the family in Connors. In Connors, once the licence had been terminated, the authority was entitled to evict the occupier. In this case, the claimant submits to the jurisdiction of the court, which has power to investigate all the circumstances of the case. On 12 December 2007 the applicant’s appeal was dismissed. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35605/97) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the proceedings before the Gaming Board Panel were in violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 14 September 1999, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. London Clubs would apply for new licences for the casinos, via re-constituted operating companies, to which the Gaming Board would not object. If the applications were successful and new licences were granted, LCL would undertake to surrender its existing licences, thereby avoiding the necessity for the applications for cancellation or renewal to be heard. The Gaming Board issued LCL with certificates of consent, which LCL were statutorily obliged to obtain before making an application to the Licensing Magistrates. Objections to the issuing ofnew licences were made by a rival casino owner. However these objections were rejected and new licenses were granted in October 1992, after a three day hearing. Lady Littler made a speech to the British Casino Association at their annual luncheon. The Gaming Board alleged that the ‘persons’ referred to were minority shareholders and no reference to the applicant was intended. The applicant did not accept this explanation, however defamation proceedings were not commenced. In 1993, the Gaming Board informed the applicant formally that it was “minded to revoke’ the applicant’s Section 19 certificates and that the applicant would be given the opportunity to state his case against revocation either in writing or orally at an interview. The hearing had, in fact, never taken place. The Complaints, numbered B1 to B9, claimed, inter alia, that there had been breaches of Section 16 of the Gaming Act 1968. The Gaming Board rejected the request for an independent tribunal and a Section 19 hearing commenced on 11 April 1994 before a panel of three, all members of the Gaming Board (“the Panel”). The hearing was conducted in private and lasted for seven and a half days. The Gaming Board’s solicitors, a senior Gaming Board official and a representative of thegaming board’S accountants also attended the hearing. The application was challenged on the grounds that the Panel was biased, or had the appearance of bias, and that its findings were vitiated by errors of law and were irrational. The effect of the revocation of the Section 19 certificates was that the applicant was unable to obtain employment in any sector of the gaming industry in the United Kingdom. The application for judicial review was dismissed on 11 January 1996 by Mr Justice Jowitt after a hearing lasting over 16 days. He delivered three separate judgments in respect of the applicant’s appeal. The first judgment dealt with the scope of the phrase “a fit and proper person” in Schedule 5 of the Gaming Act 1968. The second judgment considered the applicant's claim that he had a “legitimate expectation” that the Gaming Board would be precluded from taking account of breaches of its guidelines. The third judgment which dealt with “Wednesbury challenges and allegations of bias runs to 165 pages.57 pages of the third judgment were devoted to the issue of bias. Jowitt J. described the test of bias under English law in the following terms (pp. 93-96 of the judgment): “[Counsel for the applicant] submits that the decision to revoke the applicant’s Section 19 certificates of approval should be quashed because the Panel was biased’ It is a two stage test. The applicant has first to show from the evidence that there is an appearance of bias. Having done so, he has to go on to show that on a proper examination by the court of the evidence before it there is demonstrated a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias" Jowitt J. concluded that there was no unconscious bias on the part of any of the Panel members. He said: ‘It is not necessary for the applicant to demonstrate a real possibility that the ... decision would have been different but for the bias. What must be established is the real danger of bias having affected the decision in the sense of having caused the decision-maker, albeit unconsciously, to weigh the competing contentions, and so decide the merits, unfairly’ Jowitt said that if, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias, the “doctrine of necessity” fell to be considered. Jowitt J. ruled that there was a real risk that the decision of the Tribunal had been actuated by bias even though they were not in fact biased against him. The Court of Appeal, after an oral hearing on 4 July 1996, refused an application for leave to appeal. Morritt L.J. (with whom Hobhouse L.T. agreed) held, on the “doctrine of necessity,” as follows: “I am prepared to assume in favour of [the applicant] that he would have an arguable case sufficient to justify leave to appealed.” The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court. "The decision for the Board was, at the end of the day, whether or not Mr Kingsley was a fit and proper person. That could not be delegated to an independent panel and if they were actuated by bias, apparent or real, then the decision would still have to be made by them," he said. "The question of bias, therefore, depends on the very limited point on whether it is arguable that Jowitt J was wrong in that respect. I am bound to say that, on that limited point, I think he was manifestly right. impermissible delegation. It seems to me that there is no arguable point, susceptible on this part of the case, which would justify giving leave to appeal," he added.

It is a two stage test. The applicant has first to show from the evidence that there is an appearance of bias. Having done so, he has to go on to show that on a proper examination by the court of the evidence before it there is demonstrated a real danger of injustice having occurred. Jowitt J. concluded that there was no unconscious bias on the part of any of the Panel members. He said: ‘It is not necessary for the applicant to demonstrate a real possibility that the ... decision would have been different but for the bias. What must be established is the real danger of bias having affected the decision in the sense of having caused the decision-maker, albeit unconsciously, to weigh the competing contentions, and so decide the merits, unfairly’ Jowitt said that the ‘doctrine of necessity’ fell to be considered if some of those charged with the power or duty to decide are potentially affected by bias. Jowitt J. indicated that if, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias on the part of the Panel, the doctrine of necessity would apply, and the Panel would stand. The Court of Appeal, after an oral hearing on 4 July 1996, refused an application for leave to appeal. Morritt L.J. held, on the “doctrine of necessity,” as follows: “I am prepared to assume in favour of [the applicant] that he would have an arguable case sufficient to justify leave to Appeal” Hobhouse L. J. (with whom Hobhouse H.J.) agreed. “The decision for the Board was, at the end of the day, whether or not Mr Kingsley was a fit and proper person. That could not be delegated to an independent panel and if they were actuated by bias, apparent or real, then the decision would still have to be made by them.” “There is no arguable point, susceptible on this part of the case, which would justify giving leave to appeal,” he said. “I am bound to say that, on that limited point, I think he was manifestly right. impermissible delegation,’ he added.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24265/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant began work in the Culloden Hotel, Belfast, as a silver service waiter. Of all the full-time and permanent staff in the restaurant the applicant believes that he was the only Catholic. The applicant's lawyer filed a complaint with the Diyarbakır Public Prosecutor's Office, requesting the public prosecutor to bring criminal proceedings against the police officers who had been on duty when the applicant was in their custody. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that criminal proceedings against him had not been determined within a reasonable time. By a decision of 8 July 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. Customs wrote to the solicitors who had acted for the applicant at trial and asked how and when he intended to pay the sum ordered. On 25 June 1996 a warrant was issued for the. applicant's arrest to bring him to court for a means inquiry to take place in. respect of the sum of GBP 17,670 outstanding. The inquiry took place on 10 July 1996. The High Court refused the applicant's application for a Certificate of Inadequacy on 18 November 1997. On 10 December 1997 the Magistrates' Court ordered that proceedings to enforce the confiscation order should take place. The proceedings were subsequently adjourned several more times. On 13 May 1998 the case was listed for 3 June 1998, and on the latter date the applicant was committed to prison for 15 months for non-payment of the sum outstanding. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25801/94) against Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged principally that her home and property had been destroyed during an operation by gendarmes carried out in her village in south-east Turkey. The application was declared admissible by the Commission on 23 May 1996. In its report of 6 September 1999, the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been a violation of Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The case was referred to the Court on 23 October 1999. Mr Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case. The facts of the case, particularly concerning events on or about 8 November 1993 when the gendarmes carried out an operation at Çitlibahçe, were disputed by the parties. The Commission, pursuant to former Article 28 § 1 (a) of the Convention, conducted an investigation with the assistance of the parties and heard witnesses in Ankara on 7 February 1997. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The Commission’s findings of fact are set out in its report of 6 September 1999 and summarised below (Section A). The applicant accepts the Commission's findings of Fact. On 8 November 1993, PKK terrorists went to the village of Dadaş in the Hazro district and took away five teachers. The Commission’s Delegates found Lieutenant Altınoluk to be an evasive witness, with a volubly unhelpful response to questioning. On the other hand, the villagers, Remziye Çakıcı, Fevzi Okatan and Mehmet Bitgin, were on the whole consistent and credible. Their evidence was found to support the testimony of the witnesses heard in this case. While there were some inconsistencies in her accounts, the Commission considered that they could be attributed to the applicant's advanced years and the passage of time since the events in question. The Commission found in conclusion that the applicant’s property, furniture and possessions were deliberately burnt and destroyed during an operation by security forces in the village of Çitlibahçe on 8 November 1993. The Commission did not find the matters referred to by the Government as being indicative of bad faith or as materially undermining the credibility and reliability of the applicant and her witnesses. The applicant had gone into her house when she saw all the soldiers but had been forced to leave by the soldiers. The possessions burned included a fridge, television, kitchen utensils, household goods, and produce (including tobacco, wheat, barley, lentils, and winter provisions) The Government’s submissions on the facts emphasised the terrorism which was prevalent in this region from the early 1990s. The operation in this case concerned an investigation into the kidnapping and killing of teachers and an imam. The applicant had made no complaint to the public prosecutor about the alleged burning of her house and property by the gendarmes during the operation on 8 February 1993. She only made a statement when he summoned her after the case was communicated to the Government by the Commission. He issued a decision of non-jurisdiction, transferring the file to the Hazro governor. The Hazro Administrative Council began an investigation and found that her claims were unsubstantiated. After the village burned down, she went to Diyarbakır. She said that she thought her application was going to Ankara to claim her rights. She was illiterate and ignorant and did not know anything about European human rights. The application which had been read out was accurate though and she had no complaints to make about the person who wrote it down. She did not want to start a case in Europe in the way that he [the public prosecutor] had explained. It was for the State to look after her rights, she said. She made her statement to them as she thought this would get something done about the damage which she had suffered.

The family stored provisions, crops and wheat inside and these, along with the furniture and other household goods, were destroyed. About fifty houses in the village were burned down. This led to the evacuation of the village. The Commission found in conclusion that the applicant’s property, furniture and possessions were deliberately burnt and destroyed. The Government submitted that the applicant’s various accounts, oral and written, were inconsistent and implausible. She only made a statement to the public prosecutor when he summoned her after the case was communicated to the Government by the Commission. He issued a decision of non-jurisdiction, transferring the file to the Hazro governor. The Hazro Administrative Council began an investigation and found that her claims were unsubstantiated. The Government submitted a copy of the statement taken by the Diyarbakır public prosecutor from the applicant via an interpreter on 10 October 1995. She acknowledged that the thumbprint on the document was hers and that she did not remember who took the statement. The statement recorded that she was shown the application and letter of authority and asked about them. She said that she thought her application was going to Ankara to claim her rights. The application which had been read out was accurate though and she had no complaints to make about the person who wrote it down. She had not started any court case in Hazro or Diyarbakır as she was poor and ignorant and did not know what to do. She did not want to start a case in Europe in the way that he [the public prosecutor] had explained. It was for the State to look after her rights, she said.

The applicant alleged principally that her home and property had been destroyed during an operation by gendarmes carried out in her village in south-east Turkey. The application was declared admissible by the Commission on 23 May 1996. In its report of 6 September 1999, the Commission expressed the opinion unanimously that there had been a violation of Articles 8 and 13. The case was referred to the Court on 23 October 1999. Mr Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr F. Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge. The facts of the case, particularly concerning events on or about 8 November 1993 when the gendarmes carried out an operation at Çitlibahçe, were disputed by the parties. The Commission, pursuant to former Article 28 § 1 (a) of the Convention, conducted an investigation with the assistance of the parties and heard witnesses in Ankara on 7 February 1997. The Government’s submissions concerning the facts are summarised below (Section B). The applicant accepts the Commission's findings of fact. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). PKK terrorists went to the village of Dadaş in the Hazro district and took away five teachers. All, save one of the teachers, were shot. The imam’s brother, though wounded, survived. The gendarme commander who gave evidence before the Delegates denied that this occurred but recalled that he had destroyed hemp crops. The Commission did not make any finding in regard to this aspect as it was not the subject-matter of any specific complaint. In this regard, the applicant was found to be a convincing witness, an elderly, simple and unsophisticated lady who was on the whole credible. Her oral testimony was largely consistent with the statement given by her to the Human Rights Association shortly after the incident. The Commission found in conclusion that the applicant’s property, furniture and possessions were deliberately burnt and destroyed during an operation by security forces in the village of Çitlibahçe on 8 November 1993. The Commission did not find the matters referred to by the Government as being indicative of bad faith or as materially undermining the credibility and reliability of the applicant and her witnesses. The Hazro Administrative Council began an investigation and found that her claims were unsubstantiated. As regarded the events, she could not remember the exact date but about two years before 20 or more army vehicles had arrived. After the village burned down, she went to Diyarbakır. She was illiterate and ignorant and did not know anything about European human rights. The application which had been read out was accurate though and she had no complaints to make about the person who wrote it down. She did not want to start a case in Europe in the way that he [the public prosecutor] had explained. It was for the State to look after her rights. She made her statement to them as she thought this would get something done about the damage which she had suffered. She had not started any court case as she was poor and ignorant.

name: Ulf Arne Hammern
train_texts: The application was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Norwegian national, Mr Ulf Arne Hammern. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 of the convention on account of the reasoning relied on by the Norwegian courts in refusing his compensation claim with respect to damage sustained in criminal proceedings in which he had been acquitted. The application was allocated to the former Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 September 2002. The Court heard addresses by Mr Krokeide (counsel for Mr O, who pleaded the common issues relevant to both his case and that of Mr Hammern), Mr Wiig and Mr Elgesem. The applicant spent three periods in pre-trial detention – respectively 7, 7 and 32 days – a total of 46 days. He denied the accusations and was suspended from his post at Botngård kindergarten in Bjugn. His wife, two employees at the kindergarten and the local sheriff were also indicted for sexual offences in relation to the same matter. He was found guilty and sentenced to 10 years in prison. The applicant's trial took place before the Frostating High Court (lagmannsrett), sitting with three judges and a jury, over a period of 43 days, between 15 November 1993 and 31 January 1994. After the jury had answered all of the 25 questions relating to the indictment in the negative, the applicant was acquitted. They later claimed compensation under Articles 444 to 446 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (straffeprosessloven) The High Court ordered the State to award him the entirety of his claim of NOK 45,000 in compensation for pecuniary damage under Article 445. The applicant appealed against the High Court's decision of 28 February 1995 to the Appeals Selection Committee of the Supreme Court (Høyesteretts kjæremålsutvalg) The Appeals Selection Committee rejected the appeal against the High Court's application of Article 444 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 's decision contained assumptions of criminal liability and that, consequently, it violated Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The compensation case must be determined on an independent basis and the rules on evidence applying in such compensation cases do not differ from those which apply to ordinary compensation claims. The legislator has as a starting point opted for a solution whereby the financial burden caused by the institution of criminal proceedings, which are discontinued or which end with an acquittal, must be borne by the accused unless he is able to show that it is probable he did not commit the act. The Appeals Selection Committee must determine whether the reasoning of the High Court conflicted with the requirements of Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The Committee affirms that it would base itself on this view in its assessment of the present case. The High Court clearly specifies that Mr Hammern is not liable under the criminal law. The question is whether he, in view of the rules of evidence under the law of compensation, is able to show that he did not carry out the acts which were referred to in the indictment,' the Committee points out. The Supreme Court had expressed the following view on the Sekanina judgment: “[In this case] decisive importance was attached to the reasoning in the particular case for rejecting the compensation claim” Mr Hammern's lawyer argues that the High Court's reasoning contains assumptions about criminal liability. He points to certain intermediate passages in which the Court states: 'Medical experts have in the light of their investigations reached conclusions which in practice imply a very high degree of probability that the 10 children referred to in the indictment have been exposed to sexual abuse' The children themselves gave statements to their parents, during the judicial examinations and to a psychologist, about abuse by Mr Hammern. The children markedly changed their behaviour, inter alia, in the form of bedwetting, refusing or expressing fear about going to the kindergarten, several children had a sore crotch, sore abdomen and, on one or several occasions, blood on their underwear. The High Court does not find any reason to go further into the discussion about the possibility of paedophilia. The Appeals Selection Committee said the High Court' s reasoning does not go further than is necessary to carry out a careful examination of the compensation claim. The Committee once more emphasises that a refusal to award compensation under Article 444 does not imply that the previous acquittal is being undermined.” In the light of the foregoing, the appeal must be rejected.“The Committee once again emphasised that a refused compensation award does not mean the acquittal of the defendant is undermined’, the committee said. The appeal was rejected by the Court of Appeal at the end of last year, and the case was described as an ‘internal dispute’ by the Supreme Court.
