The case was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Norwegian national, Mr Ulf Arne Hammern. The application was allocated to the former Third Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 September 2002 (Rule 59): for the Government Mr H. Harborg, Attorney-General's Office, (Civil matters) Agent, Mr F. Elgesem, Advokat, Counsel/Adviser Mr K. The Court heard addresses by Mr Krokeide (counsel for Mr O), Mr Wiig and Mr Elgesem. The applicant was born in 1949 and lives in Bjugn. On 13 March 1992 the applicant was interrogated. He denied the accusations. On the same date he was suspended from his post as an assistant at Botngård kindergarten. On 22 September 1993 the. applicant was formally indicted under Articles 195, 198 and 213 of the Penal Code for. having allegedly committed various offences of sexual abuse against 10 kindergarten children. The. applicant spent three periods in pre-trial detention – respectively 7, 7 and 32 days – a total of 46 days. The applicant's trial took place before the Frostating High Court (lagmannsrett), sitting with three judges and a jury, over a period of 43 days, between 15 November 1993 and 31 January 1994. After the jury had answered all of the 25 questions relating to the indictment in the negative, the applicant was acquitted. They later claimed compensation under Articles 444 to 446 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (straffeprosessloven) The High Court, sitting with two of the judges who had taken part in the trial and a new judge (replacing the judge who had presided at the trial, disqualified from sitting in the compensation case), held an oral hearing between 13 and 15 February 1995. The Appeals Selection Committee rejected the appeal. 's decision contained assumptions of criminal liability and that, consequently, it violated Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The compensation case must be determined on an independent basis and the rules on evidence applying in such compensation cases do not differ from those which apply to ordinary compensation claims. The legislator has as a starting point opted for a solution whereby the financial burden caused by the institution of criminal proceedings, which are discontinued or which end with an acquittal, must be borne by the accused unless he is able to show that it is probable that he did not commit the act. The Supreme Court concluded that the rules in Article 444 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not, as such, contrary to Article 6§2 of the convention. The Appeals Selection. Committee further recalled that in the above case the Supreme Court considered the relationship between the conditions for compensation under Article 444. and the case-law of the European Court of Human Rights. The Appeals Selection Committee said the reasoning of the High Court conflicted with the requirements of Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The High Court had to justify why it considered that the conditions for making an award for compensation under Article 444 of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been fulfilled. The Committee said it would base itself on this view in its assessment of the present case. It said that the Supreme Court had expressed the following view on the Sekanina judgment: “[In this case] decisive importance was attached to the reasoning in the particular case for rejecting the compensation claim.” The Committee pointed to the fact that here the. High Court clearly specifies that Mr Hammern is not liable under the criminal law. Mr Hammern was accused of sexually abusing 10 children at a kindergarten in Germany. The children themselves gave statements to their parents, during the judicial examinations and to a psychologist about abuse by Mr Hammern. The High Court does not find any reason to go further into the discussion about the possibility of paedophilia. It is not only the so-called real paedophiles who commit abuse against children. Nor can a diagnosis which excludes paedophili be deemed accurate, or notional paedophila be defined precisely. The Court finds it established that at the kindergarten it was possible to perpetrate such abuse without it being revealed either from a technical or practical point of view. The Appeals Selection Committee finds that the High Court' s reasoning does not go further than is necessary to carry out a careful examination of the compensation claim. The Committee once more emphasises that a refusal to award compensation under Article 444 does not imply that the previous acquittal is being undermined.” In the light of the foregoing, the appeal must be rejected, the Committee says. It adds that the ruling does not entail any infringement of the presumption of innocence laid down in the Convention. The appeal is therefore rejected, and the appeal against the decision is dismissed, the committee says. The case is appealed at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.

name: Henryk Urban
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23614/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their case had not been heard by an “independent tribunal” The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mr Z. Cichoń, a lawyer practising in Cracow. The Polish Government (“the Government’s” Agent) was represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court gave notice of the application to the Government on 30 June 2009. The applicants were found guilty of failing to disclose their identity to the police and sentenced to a fine of PLN 100. The first applicant was acquitted of the other charge. The applicants appealed, alleging that their case had been decided by an assessor who was not a judge. They referred to the Constitutional Court's judgment of 24 October 2007 and submitted that the assessor could not exercise judicial powers because she did not offer sufficient guarantees of independence. On 10 December 2007 the Krosno Regional Court upheld the District Court's decision. No further appeal lay against the Regional Court's ruling. The case continues at the European Court of Human Rights.

name: Brian Curley
train_texts: Brian Curley was convicted of murder in 1979 and sentenced to be detained during Her Majesty’s pleasure. His case was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Government of the United Kingdom were represented by their Agent, Mr Ian Christie of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The application was declared admissible and decided that it was not necessary to hold a hearing. The case was decided not to go to court as the application was not a breach of Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant was jailed in 1987. Following the expiry of his tariff, the applicant’s case was the subject of review by the Parole Board on a number of occasions. The applicant absconded from prison in 1991. name: John Boyle
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand pending his trial by court martial was in breach of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. The Court declared the application admissible and the parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), the parties each filed further written observations. It was decided that no further hearing was required. The application was dismissed and the case was dismissed. The applicant was transferred to the Military Correctional Training Centre (“the MCTC”) in the United Kingdom on 16 November 1999. A certificate dated 6 November 1999 and signed by the applicant confirms that the applicant received the pamphlet “The Rights of a Soldier Charged with an Offence under the Army Act 1955” The final report dated 7 February 2000 recorded for the first time an additional charge against the applicant pursuant to section 70 of the 1955 Act: rape contrary to section 1(1) of the Sexual Offences Act 1956. The applicant was given a four-page document immediately before that hearing, which document was taken back from him immediately thereafter. No reasons were noted as to why the applicant had been detained except in the last form (dated 7 February 2000) which recorded the same reasons as in the above-noted 8-day reports. The applicant's representative applied for a writ of habeas corpus to the High Court. The application was served on the CO of the MCTC on 19 February 2000. On 22 February 2000 the applicant was released from close arrest and he was posted to the 47th Regiment Royal Artillery. His solicitor sought a review of the applicant's detention by the general officer commanding 4th Division. He was initially orally informed that the review would take place on 15 February 2000 but was then informed on 16 February 2000 that thereview had not taken place. The latter alleged that the accused advisor had taken no part in the review procedures. The applicant and his two co-defendants were tried by Army General Court Martial on a joint charge of rape between 14 May and 25 May 2001. All three defendants were acquitted. I decided that the Applicant should be posted with immediate effect to a different unit in a different country namely the UK. I issued with specific orders preventing him from being able to influence the witnesses. The applicant was released into open arrest even though the allegation against him was that he had committed rape and indecent assault...and despite the fact that there was evidence that he, with others, concocted a story and interfered with a witness. The Applicant was released from open arrest and placed under house arrest.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34611/97) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that after having been arrested he had not been brought before a “judge” or “officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power’ The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 21 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The court deemed the complaint to be an appeal against the detention order of 4 January 1996. The court considered that the applicant should be detained because there was a reasonable risk that he might obstruct the proper conduct of the proceedings. The applicant complained to the Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor and the Ombudsman that, after having been arrested, he had not been brought before a judge but before the prosecutor. The prosecutor replied that, under the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as they stood at the material time, the prosecutor had a power to detain him on remand. Under the amendments to Polish criminal legislation, which were to enter into force on 4 August 1996, only the courts of law could impose detention.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4789/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that there had been a violation of Article 8 of the. Convention, on account of the refusal by the national authorities to. indicate her forename in the civil register of births as that of the mother of her adopted child. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) on 25 September 2013. The jury heard evidence from both sides and the case was returned to the ECJ on 26 September 2014. The court dismissed the application on the ground that it had no legal basis. On 14 April 2008 the applicant appealed on points of law. On 15 March 2009 a new regulation entered into force entitled “Regulation on the implementation of mediation services for the adoption of minors’ (“the Regulation”) enabling a single adoptive parent to have his or her forename registered in the place of that of the biological parent. On 5 November 2009 the Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the court below in a judgment which made no mention of the legislative change. On 9 November 2010 she applied to the registry office for the registration of her fore Name as that of E., relying on the new Regulation. That request was granted on the same day and the record entries concerning the child were consequently amended with immediate effect.

She argued that in relation to single-parent adoptions there was a lacuna in the Civil Code which required the court to make provision for such a situation. On 15 March 2009 a new regulation entered into force entitled “Regulation on the implementation of mediation services for the adoption of minors’ (“the Regulation”) enabling a single adoptive parent to have his or her forename registered in the place of that of the biological parent. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the court below in a judgment which made no mention of the legislative changes. The applicant was notified of that judgment on 14 December 2009. On 9 November 2010 she applied to the registry office for the registration of her fore name.

name: Snjezana Vostic
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38549/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the court decisions in compensation proceedings for detention on remand violated the presumption of innocence. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 19 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 25 § 1) The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). Immediately after the pronouncement of the acquittal, the applicant requested compensation for her detention on remand. The Wels Regional Court, with the same composition as above, dismissed the applicant’s claim. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Linz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) She argued that section 2 (1)(b) of the 1969 Act was incompatible with Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The decision was served on the applicant after her acquittal had become final on 17 December 1996. On 20 June 1997, the LinZ Court of appeal dismissed her appeal. The appeal was dismissed by the Constitutional Court on 29 September 1994. The trial court held that the testimony given by the parents of the appellant, whose alibi related to the night of 31 March to 1 April 1996, was not credible. Snjezana Vostic’s own testimony to the effect that she had last seen Sejdo Nadarevic in mid-February 1996 was in the end disproved by the witnesses who gave evidence at the trial. The trial court thus rightly held that  ‘suspicion has not been dispelled’ depends not on proven guilt but on the possibility that the person concerned may have committed the offence and therefore on a (persisting) suspicion.

The case originated in an application (no. 38549/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the court decisions in compensation proceedings for detention on remand violated the presumption of innocence. By a decision of 19 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 59 § 1) on 1 November 2001. The applicant requested compensation for her detention on remand. The Wels Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s claim. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Linz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht). She argued that section 2 (1)(b) of the 1969 Act was incompatible with Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The decision was served on the applicant after her acquittal had become final on 17 December 1996. The appeal was dismissed on 20 June 1997 and the applicant was released from prison. ‘Nor does the principle of the presumption of innocence prevent the prosecuting authorities from suspecting someone of having committed an offence’ The trial court held that the testimony given by the parents of the appellant, whose alibi related to the night of 31 March to 1 April 1996, was not credible. Snjezana Vostic’s own testimony to the effect that she had last seen Sejdo Nadarevic in mid-February 1996 was in the end disproved by the witnesses who gave evidence at the trial. The trial court thus rightly held that  the testimony given by the parents was not credible; and Snjzana Vostics’ own testimony was disproved. The court also held that it was still possible that SnjZeana's gun had been the murder weapon; and inconsistencies remain unresolved.

Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The decision of the First Section was made on 1 November 2001. Vostic that had not been wholly dispelled,” the court said.

name: Eie Enhorn
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56529/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5 of the convention. The application was initially allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section on 1 November 2004. The applicant kept three appointments with the county medical officer in September 1994 and one in November 1994. He failed to appear as summoned five times during October and November 1994 and was ordered to be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months. The applicant is prohibited from giving blood and donating organs or sperm. He is to visit his consulting physician again and to keep appointments fixed by the countyMedicalOfficer. It appears to be in dispute whether the instructions were included in the applicant's medical record. It is not in dispute, however, that the applicant was informed of the instructions, which were issued to him on 1 September 1994, both orally and in writing. The applicant's lack of social contact and his feeling of being an outsider, in combination with possible alcohol abuse, could increase the risk of destructive sexual relations. While being isolated the applicant had the opportunity to go outdoors every day together with members of the hospital staff, but not on his own. The applicant absconded from the hospital several times, first on 25 April 1995. The police, whom he had contacted voluntarily, returned him to the hospital on 11 June 1995. On 27 September 1995 he ran away again and was at large until the police found him on 28 May 1996. He ran away for a fourth time on 26 February 1997 and was not returned until 26 February 1999. During the period from 26 February until 2 March 1999 the applicant was detained in his room. While he was on the run, the applicant had had no sexual relations. He had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant has a healthy liver. It was noted that subsequent to his return the applicant continued to have sexual relations with a woman. with psychiatric problems, with whom he had had a longer sexual relationship, was likewise the initiator. A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. He claimed that on the latest occasion, in March 1999, the applicant made a lunge at him. The county medical officer, who gave evidence before the court, is recorded, inter alia, as follows: “During the last two years when he was on the run, [the applicant] sought medical treatment twice and it has been established that both times he said that he had the HIV virus” HIV-positive man has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995. Court finds against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been living a very secluded life, obviously owing to the risk of being discovered. A life at liberty makes great demands upon the person carrying the infection. During the time preceding his compulsory isolation, [the applicant] was not able to follow the practical instructions issued. Subsequently, he has consistently declined the help offered by the consulting physician and the psychiatrist and has instead responded with aversion and mistrust – and by escaping.” The applicant had appealed against the above judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal. He relied on an opinion of 14 May 1999 by the aforementioned chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., which stated that he was a man with a paranoid personality disorder, who misused alcohol. The Court has not been convinced that [the applicant] is not misusing alcohol and finds that, especially in connection with alcohol consumption, he is likely to be unable to control his sexual behaviour. It is not correct to talk in terms of lack of awareness of a disease, since it is not considered that a disease is involved but rather a variation in personality. The judge found that the applicant fulfilled the criteria for a paranoid personality disorder. The Supreme Administrative Court of Appeal found against the applicant. The applicant could be described in everyday terms as an odd person, but not as mentally ill. The judge concluded that neither he nor anyone else could do anything but guess as to whether the applicant might pass on the HIV infection to other persons. Leave to appeal against the judgment was refused by the Supreme Administrative. Court (Reger), and the decision was upheld by the High Court of Justice in 1999. The verdict was made on 18 June 1999, and the applicant was sentenced to six months in prison. The sentence was suspended for five years, and he was released on 14 July 2001. Several applications for an extension of the applicant's compulsory isolation were submitted by the county medical officer after June 1999 and granted. On 12 December 2001 an application was turned down by the County Administrative Court, which referred to the fact that the applicant’s whereabouts were unknown and that therefore no information was available regarding his behaviour, state of health and so on. It appears that since 2002 the. applicant's whereabouts have been known, but that the competent county medical. officer has made the assessment that there are no grounds for the applicant.'s further involuntary placement in isolation. The application was made by the family of the man who had been diagnosed with a rare form of cancer known as acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) in October 1999.

The case originated in an application (no. 56529/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5 of the treaty. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Court’s decision on whether the application was admissible was made in November 2004. The Chamber's decision was, however, not made until January 2005. The applicant kept three appointments with the county medical officer in September 1994 and one in November 1994. He failed to appear as summoned five times during October and November 1994 and was ordered to be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months. The applicant was prohibited from giving blood and donating organs or sperm. He was also ordered to visit his consulting physician again and to keep appointments fixed by the countyMedical officer. It appears to be in dispute whether the instructions were included in the applicant's medical record as prescribed by section 16 of the 1988 Act. It is not in dispute that the applicant was informed of the instructions, which were issued to him on 1 September 1994. HIV-infected man was confined to hospital for three months in 1995. He absconded from the hospital several times, first on 25 April 1995. The applicant's compulsory confinement was repeatedly prolonged by periods of six months at a time. During the period from 26 February until 2 March 1999 the applicant was detained in his room. He told a court that he had had ten to twelve sexual relations per year. The boy, who was 15 years old when they met, took the initiative both emotionally and sexually. Today [the applicant] realises that he infected the boy, which he finds very regrettable. A relative of the applicant's also told the court that the applicant had sexually abused him in the past. While he was on the run from [26 February] 1997 until [26 Feb] 1999, he had had no sexual relations. He had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant had a healthy liver. It was noted that subsequent to his return the applicant continued to drink beer. The applicant had taken precautions against spreading the disease and, having had to visit physicians twice during his period at large, had informed them about his HIV infection. A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N.,connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. He claimed that on the latest occasion, in March 1999, the applicant made a lunge at him. After the applicant's involuntary return he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. The chances of eliminating or limiting the continuous risk of the infection being spread by means of a prolonged placement in isolation in accordance with the Act are deemed – all facts considered – to have not yet completely vanished. The applicant has accepted that he infected the young man with whom he had a long-lasting relationship from the beginning of the 1990s, thus admitting that it was not the other way around. On 23 April 1999 the County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years” “During these two years he did not have any contact with the county medical officer or the consulting physician. Periodically he has used a false name and has been living a very secluded life. A life at liberty makes great demands upon the person carrying the infection.” The Court finds that there is good reason to suppose that, if he remains free, [the applicant] will not comply with the practical instructions issued. This entails a risk of the infection spreading. On 12 June 1999 the applicant again absconded, leaving his whereabouts unknown. In the meantime, he had appealed against the above judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal. He relied on an opinion of 14 May 1999 by the aforementioned chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., which stated: “The opinions [by other psychiatrists and one psychologist] resulting from previous examinations were fairly unanimous in their conclusion that [ the applicant] was a man with a paranoid personality disorder, who misused alcohol.” In a judgment of 18 June 1999, the Administrative Court of Appeal found against the applicant. Leave to appeal against the judgment was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court (Reger). In conclusion, C.G., found that the applicant fulfilled the criteria for a paranoid personality disorder, and that, judging from previous information, the applicant suffered from misuse of alcohol but not from alcohol dependency. The applicant could be described in everyday terms as an odd person, but not as mentally ill. He was fully aware that he was carrying the HIV virus and had no longer any particular sexual desires or fantasies. His attitude towards medication against the HIV infection was negative. The reasons for this were that such medication could have side effects. Several applications for an extension of the applicant's compulsory isolation were submitted by the county medical officer after June 1999 and granted. On 12 December 2001 an application was turned down by the County Administrative Court, which referred to the fact that the applicant’s whereabouts were unknown and that therefore no information was available regarding his behaviour, state of health and so on. It appears that since 2002 the. applicant's whereabouts have been known, but that the competent county medical. officer has made the assessment that there are no grounds for the. further involuntary placement in isolation. The application was made by the family of a man who had been admitted to a hospital in the town of Dusseldorf. The man was admitted to hospital on 5 October 1999 and placed in isolation on 12 December 1999.

The case originated in an application (no. 56529/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Eie Enhorn alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5 of the convention. The applicant was born in 1947 and is homosexual. In 1994 it was discovered that he was infected with the HIV virus and had transmitted the virus to a 19-year-old man with whom he had first had sexual contact in 1990. The application was initially allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The applicant kept three appointments with the county medical officer in September 1994 and one in November 1994. He failed to appear as summoned five times during October and November 1994 and was ordered to be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months. It appears to be in dispute whether the instructions were included in the applicant's medical record as prescribed by section 16 of the 1988 Act. It is not in dispute, however, that the applicant was informed of the instructions, which were issued to him on 1 September 1994, both orally and in writing. The court's record reads, inter alia, as follows: “After learning about his HIV infection he had hardly had any sexual relationships. Henceforward he would only have sexual relations with other HIV infected persons” HIV-infected man kept in compulsory isolation for up to three months. He absconded from the hospital several times, first on 25 April 1995. He ran away for a third time on 6 November 1996 but returned of his own accord on 16 November 1996. During the period from 26 February until 2 March 1999 the applicant was detained in his room. The applicant's compulsory confinement was repeatedly prolonged by periods of six months at a time. Before 1994 the applicant had ten to twelve sexual relations per year. His partners were partly old acquaintances, partly new ones, whom he met in parks and so on. The boy, who was 15 years old when they met, took the initiative both emotionally and sexually. Today the applicant realises that he infected the boy, which he finds very regrettable. While on the run from 26 February 1997 until 26 February 1999, he had had no sexual relations. He had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He spent his time shopping, cooking, watching TV, spending money on lottery games and drinking beer. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant had a healthy liver. It was noted that subsequent to his return the applicant continued to drink alcohol. A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. He claimed that on the latest occasion, in March 1999, the applicant made a lunge at him. The chances of eliminating or limiting the continuous risk of the infection being spread by means of a prolonged placement in isolation in accordance with the Act are deemed – all facts considered – to have not yet completely vanished. The applicant has finally accepted that he infected the young man with whom he had a long-lasting relationship from the beginning of the 1990s. The County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years. During these two years he did not have any contact with the county medical officer or the consulting physician. During [the applicant's] contact with [the doctors in question, they did not discuss the risk of spreading the disease at all. A treatment plan was not formally signed [by the applicant]. In conclusion, [if released the applicant] will not voluntarily comply with the instructions given or limit the spreading of the disease” The applicant was diagnosed with paranoid personality disorder and misused alcohol. He was also unable to control his sexual behaviour. The Court has not been convinced that [the applicant] is not misusing alcohol and finds that, especially in connection with alcohol consumption, he is likely to abscond. It is not correct to talk in terms of lack of awareness of a disease, since it is not considered that a disease is involved but rather a variation in personality, although the latter may well cause complications in relations with other individuals and society. When such complications occur, an individual with a personality disorder may display different symptoms such as depression, anxiety, etc. The applicant showed empathy as far as other people from those years were concerned. He was partly able to shoulder responsibility for his own mistakes, without blaming others. From 1996, he had not experienced feelings of persecution, inter alia since he had secured his own liberty. He preferred sexual contact with boys around the age of 17. He had been celibate since 1996 and had no longer any particular sexual desires or fantasies. The applicant could be described in everyday terms as an odd person, but not as mentally ill. With regard to the risk that the applicant might pass on the HIV infection to other persons, C.G. believed that neither he nor anyone else could do anything but guess. Several applications for an extension of the applicant's compulsory isolation were submitted by the county medical officer after June 1999. On 12 December 2001 an application was turned down by the County Administrative Court, which referred to the fact that theApplicant's whereabouts were unknown and that therefore no information was available regarding his behaviour, state of health and so on. It appears that since 2002 the applicant’s whereabouts have been known, but that the competent countyMedical officer has made the assessment that there are no grounds for his further involuntary placement in isolation. The application was made by the local branch of the Red Cross, the Rotherham branch of which was responsible for the case, on 5 October 1999.

name: Qadam Shah Mohammadi
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 71932/12) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his forced transfer to Hungary under the Dublin II Regulation would subject him to inhuman and degrading treatment. The Court decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings not to expel the applicant to Hungary until further notice. It further requested the Hungarian Government to provide information regarding the status of the applicant’s asylum proceedings, as well as the reception conditions for unaccompanied minor asylum-seekers. The applicant left Afghanistan to seek asylum in Hungary. He claimed he was forced to lodge an asylum request and placed in an open camp. In December 2011 the Traiskirchen Federal Asylum Office (Bundes­asylamt) rejected the applicant’s asylum request. On 11 January 2012 the Asylum Court quashed that decision pursuant to Article 66 of the Code of General Administrative Procedure (Allgemeines Verwaltungsverfahrensgesetz) The decision had not established the legal framework under the Dublin II Regulation, the asylum court ruled. The asylum applicant is now living in Vienna with his family. On 28 February 2012 the Asylum Office again rejected the applicant’s asylum request and ordered his expulsion to Hungary under the Dublin II Regulation. Hungary expelled asylum-seekers to Serbia, if their first asylum proceedings were terminated and there was no obstacle under the non-refoulement rule. A person lodging a subsequent asylum request was not allowed to remain in Hungary. The Hungarian authorities stated that they did not have a list of safe third countries and evaluated each case individually. However, in most cases Serbia was considered to be a safe third country. It was further established that appeals against asylum decisions at first instance and during the first proceedings had automatic suspensive effect. The asylum proceedings in Hungary had been discontinued on 24 October 2011. The first asylum proceedings would not be reopened upon his return to Hungary. The asylum request would be considered a subsequent request if there were no new circumstances supporting his application but there was a safe third country which he could be returned to. Hungarian authorities stated that unaccompanied minor asylum-seekers were usually immediately assigned a guardian, except when the applicant would reach the age of majority before the decision on the merits was made. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21906/09) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention from a period of ten years, which had been the maximum for such detention under the legal provisions applicable at the time of his offence, violated Article 5. The case was adjourned until the judgment in the case of M. v. Germany, no. 19359/04, had become final. The President decided on 20 May 2010 that the proceedings in the application at issue be resumed and granted priority to the application (Rule 41 of the Rules of Court). Regensburg Regional Court convicted the applicant of rape. It sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment and ordered his placement in preventive detention pursuant to Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code. The court found that in July 1989, some four months after his release from prison, the applicant had raped a woman whom he had come across in Regensburg at night. A psychiatric expert, N., considered that the applicant suffered from a dissocial personality disorder since his youth and that it was very likely that he would reoffend if released. His disorder could only possibly be treated in a psychiatric hospital. The applicant was accordingly transferred to Straubing Psychiatric Hospital on 15 December 2005. On 25 October 2007 the Regensberg Regional Court prolonged the execution of the applicant’s preventive detention. Regensburg Regional Court considered that the applicant, if released, would commit further serious offences resulting in considerable physical or psychological harm to the victims. Psychiatrists had diagnosed the applicant with a serious dissocial personality disorder which was notably reflected in a number of sexual offences he had committed. Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed decision to execute the applicant’s preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital and decided to retransfer the applicant to prison in accordance with Article 67a § 3 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 37 below) The applicant was accordingly transferred from Straubing Psychiatric Hospital toStraubing Prison on 19 June 2008. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal as ill‑founded. The reasons why the applicant’s therapy in Straubing Psychiatric Hospital had not been successful were irrelevant for the question whether there was still a risk that the applicant, if released, might commit further sexual offences. The psychiatric expert report drawn up by expert K. was clear and conclusive and complied with the minimum standards required for such reports. The court further referred to the leading judgment dated 5 February 2004 of the Federal Constitutional Court, in which the latter had considered the retroactive extension of a convicted person's preventive detention beyond a period of ten years to be constitutional. The applicant was considered by the Straubing Prison authorities to be a self-confident, demanding and mistrustful person. Since July 2009 he has been working in the prison’s furniture factory. He consistently refused the treatment offered, questioning the therapists’ expertise. He was not granted any relaxations in the execution of the preventive detention order against him for fear of abuse. The Federal Court of Justice decided to adjourn the case pending a decision of its grand senate on the legal question at issue. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 66689/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant declared that she aided and abetted the members of the TIKB and that she provided information to the TikB members who were held in prison. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1) The judge ordered the applicant’s detention pending trial. The applicant was convicted under Article 169 of the Criminal Code and sentenced to three years and nine months’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed against this decision to the Court of Cassation. The court upheld the decision of State Security Court on 20 September 1999. The application was deposited with the registry of İzmir State security Court on 14 October 2000. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant and the case was quashed on 30 June 2001. The appeal is still pending at the Supreme Court of Justice of Turkey, which will make a decision on the case in March 2014. The case has been adjourned until the end of the year.

The case originated in an application (no. 66689/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Revolutionary Communists’ Union of Turkey (“the TIKB”, Türkiye İhtilalci Komünistler Birliği) and placed in custody. She denied all the charges against her. She declared that her statement in police custody was taken under duress and that she had been given electric shocks. The judge ordered the applicant’s detention pending trial. The applicant was convicted under Article 169 of the Criminal Code and sentenced to three years and nine months' imprisonment. She appealed against this decision to the Court of Cassation who upheld the decision of State Security Court. She was convicted of providing information to members of the organisation who were imprisoned and participating in the demonstrations organised by the organisation. The applicant was sentenced to 3 years and 9 months’ imprisonment. On 14 October 2000, the decision was deposited with the registry of   İzmir State Security court. She has appealed against the decision and is still serving her sentence. The case has not yet been heard in the Supreme Court of Justice.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13471/06) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 24 March 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr J. Postlmayr, a lawyer practising in Mattighofen. The Austrian Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador F. Trauttmansdorff, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. On 13 June 2008 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The applicant was convicted of failing to check the fire extinguisher in a heavy goods vehicle. He appealed the conviction on the grounds that it infringed the principle of ne bis in idem and that the fine imposed on him was excessive. The case was dismissed by the IAP on 18 September 2000. The IAP remitted the case to the Administrative Court at the applicant's request. The Administrative Court quashed the decision on 18 October 2005. The applicant filed a request with the Melk DAA for the proceedings to be discontinued on 14 November 2006. On 27 September 2002 the Constitutional Court gave its ruling following its review of the Dangerous Goods Transportation Act. It rejected a request to strike down provisions concerning the minimum fine. The proceedings were discontinued on 24 November 2006. The court's last hearing was held on November 24, 2006. It was the last in a series of hearings to be held before the Supreme Court before the court was dissolved. The case was the first to be decided by a jury, and the last to be heard by a single judge. The trial was held in the jury's home town of Cambridge, Massachusetts. The jury was presided by Judge David Rhodes, who ruled that the case was a miscarriage of justice. The verdicts of the jury were: "no", "not guilty," and "not eligible for appeal"

The judge was sentenced to a total of four years in prison. The sentence was suspended on 18 November 2006 and he was released on 18 December 2006. The court was then dissolved on November 24, 2006, after the judge's acquittal.

name: Yüksel Yiğitdoğan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 72174/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Yüksel Yiğitdoğan (“the applicant”) is currently serving a prison sentence in Kocaeli. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of being a member of an illegal organisation on 25 July 1999. He was put in police custody at the Anti-Terrorist Branch of the Istanbul Security Headquarters. According to his submissions, he was subjected to ill-treatment during his time there. The application was communicated to the Government on 14 January 2013. In 1999 the applicant made statements to the police, in the absence of a lawyer. He was not legally represented when he made his statements. In 2000 the applicant informed the Istanbul State Security Court that he would not attend the hearing that was to be held that day, as he had had no opportunity to have prior consultation. In this respect, the public prosecutor noted that the applicant had taken part in several armed acts of the illegal organisation, including murder. The applicant maintained that he did not object to the content of the medical report drawn up earlier that day. According to the applicant’s submissions, on 2 August 1999 he was examined by a doctor at Haydarpaşa Numune Hospital. The Government stated that there had been no such examination. The court asked the public prosecutor to ensure the applicant’s attendance at the subsequent hearing. The court noted that the applicant had been transferred to another prison and that the order for him to attend the hearing had not been sent there. On 24 October 2002 the applicant was brought before the court. He submitted his defence, indicating that he had been severely beaten during his arrest in Izmir and had been subjected to electric shocks, hung by the arms, hosed with cold water and sexually assaulted during his seven-day police custody at the Istanbul Security Headquarters. He claimed that although his right arm had been broken and he had developed facial paralysis, he had not be taken to the Forensic Medicine Institute. In 2004 State Security Courts were abolished. The court found that the police had not done their job properly. The judge said that the report was based on false information. The court ordered a retrial in the case. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty. The conviction was quashed and the case was dismissed. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court of Turkey. The appeal was rejected. The verdict was overturned on appeal. The trial has been adjourned until December 31, 2013. The prosecution had asked the court to re-examine the evidence. The decision was made to dismiss the case, and the appeal was thrown out of court. The victim was sentenced to two years in prison. The father of the victim was killed.

Platou Amble, Attorney-general's Office. The application was communicated to the Government on 7 June 2010. The case was decided by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) on 16 November 2012. The ECJ ruled in favour of the applicants. NIPO had asked the Military Supreme Command whether the application should be kept secret on national security grounds, which the latter answered in the negative in March 1993. The first applicant was informed in June 1993. NIPO reiterated its request of 21 March 1991 that the first applicant provide evidence from tests showing the technical effect and concrete features of the invention. The required tests were therefore superfluous, in his view. On the ground of the applicant’s failure to comply with the time-limit of 5 November 1999, NIPo decided to discontinue (henlegge) its examination of his application under section 15(2) of the Patents Act. The first applicant applied for a patent on 5 May 1999. NIPO refused the application on the ground that the applicant had not made it probable that the subject-matter of the application had the alleged technical effect. The first applicant appealed to the Board of Appeals (Patentstyrets annen avdeling) on 27 November 2001. The Board concluded that the invention in application no. 19905214 had a technical effect, but the Board did not consider whether other patent requirements had been fulfilled. Thereafter, mostly both applicants, occasionally only the first applicant, acted as claimants in the relevant proceedings (to simplify “applicants” is used in the following). NIPO's decision was set aside and the application was referred back to NIPO for further consideration. The Board did not find any grounds to continue processing of the application. The applicants appealed to the Board of Appeals on 20 August 2007. On 29 November 2007, they were informed that the Board, after having examined the case, had found it clear that the conditions for granting a patent had not been fulfilled in so far as concerned aircrafts. However, the application might succeed in respect of a more limited field of sea vessels. It was proposed that the patent requirements be formulated in a similar manner as proposed in the Board. of Appeals’ letter of 29 September 2004. NIPO and the Board of Appeals found that the application did not involve any novelty in respect of aviation, though the reasoning differed. The applicants had been advised that in order to succeed, the patent requirements would have to be defined so as to exclude aviation, but had not been willing to do so. The application as presented did therefore not fulfil the conditions for grant of patent. The patent applications they had filed in 2003, made in light of the patent application of 30 November 1990 (no. 19905214), had been granted in the United States of America, Russia, China and Singapore and “through the EPO [European Patent Office] as well”. The EPO patent claims were based on additional features that had made the invention patentable. from no. 19905214. The invention was based on the addition of features that made it patentable, according to the EPO. The EPO granted the patent on the device in 2007. The patent was granted in 2010, and the company was awarded the patent in 2011. The device was the first of its kind to be patented in the U.S. in the 1990s, but it was not patented until 2010. The current patent claims are based on features that have now been added to the device, including the use of sensors and other technology that allow it to track movements.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr H. Meyer-Mews, a lawyer practising in Bremen. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs K. Behr, Regierungsdirektorin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The Court advised the parties on 14 January 2014 that it would continue processing the application under the name Schatschaschwili v. Germany, which was the applicant’s name as referred to in the domestic proceedings at issue. The crimes were committed in Kassel on 14 October 2006 and in Göttingen on 3 February 2007 respectively. The applicant, acting jointly with an unidentified accomplice and according to a previously agreed plan, entered by force into an apartment. The men were aware that the apartment was used for prostitution and expected its two female occupants to keep valuables and cash in there. The court imposed an accumulated prison sentence (Gesamtfreiheitsstrafe) of nine years and six months. The Regional Court found it established that in the evening of 14 October 2007 the applicant robbed another apartment in the city of Götteden. The victim of the crime committed in Kassel on 14 October 2006 was one of the victims of the crimes in Göttingen. O. and P. were friends of L., who was the victim of a similar crime in October 2006. One of the applicants and one of his co-accused gained access to the women’s apartment pretending to be potential clients. The two men reported to the residual members of the criminal gang that they had spotted a safe in the kitchen of the apartment. In the meantime inside the apartment, B. threatened to kill O. with his knife should she not disclose where the women kept their money or should she refuse to open the safe for him. The Regional Court based its finding of facts regarding the first crime committed in Kassel on the statements made by the victims L. and I. on the occasion of their police interrogations as well as in the course of the subsequent trial. Both witnesses had identified the applicant without any hesitation as the perpetrator who had carried the gun when presented with his photo and later when confronted with him personally at trial. The Regional Court found L and I’s testimonies to be consistent and credible and noted that they were supported by the statements of the police officers who had attended the crime scene and had interviewed L. The said article provides for such possibility in the event insurmountable. Witnesses O. and P. had been summoned to appear before the Regional Court on 24 August 2007, the third day of the trial. Both had refused to attend the hearing relying on medical certificates dated 9 August 2007 that indicated their unstable post‑traumatic emotional and psychological condition. The court suggested to the competent Latvian judge to have the witnesses examined by a public medical officer (Amtsarzt) and, alternatively, to coerce them to appear at the hearing. However, a witness hearing scheduled by the competentLatvian court for 13 February 2008 was cancelled shortly before by the presiding judge on the ground that the witnesses were still suffering from post-traumatic disorders as a consequence of the crime. The Regional Court held that the trial as a whole had been fair and had complied with the requirements of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention. The applicant had not been informed about the preliminary criminal proceedings initiated against him with a view to not putting the investigations at risk. The investigating judge had excluded the applicant from the hearing since he had been concerned that the witnesses would be afraid of telling the truth in the presence of the accused. The court was thus not prevented from admitting O. and P.’s pre-trial statements as evidence in the proceedings. It concluded that it was impossible to have the witnesses examined in the foreseeable future. The Regional Court observed that O. and P. had given detailed and coherent descriptions of the circumstances of the crime. Minor contradictions in their statements could be explained by their concern not to disclose their illegal residence status and activities to the authorities. The court observed that the witnesses’ attention during the incident had been focussed on the further perpetrator carrying the knife and that the applicant himself had only stayed a short period of time in the apartment. Their inability to identify the applicant also showed that they had not testified with a view to incriminating him. The fact that the detailed description of the events in the pre-trial statements were consistent with the account they had given the morning after the crime to their neighbour E., was a further strong indication for their credibility and the veracity of their statements. The Regional Court noted that neither the defence nor the court itself had had an opportunity to observe the main witnesses’ demeanour at trial or by means of an audio-visual examination. The court further emphasised that when taking into account the testimonies given by the witnesses' neighbour E. and their friend L. it had paid special attention to the fact that their statements constituted hearsay evidence and had to be assessed particularly carefully. The link between the evidence obtained in the course of such separate investigations and the crime at issue could only be made after O. and P. had reported the incident of 3 February 2007 to the police. It followed from the recordings of two mobile phone conversations between one of the co-accused and the applicant. The applicant and the co-accused had denied any participation in the robbery as such or any premeditated criminal activity in this respect. Their own statements at trial had at least confirmed that one of them had visited the apartment at Göttingen on the evening before the crime. The applicant had testified that he and B. had come to the apartment with a view to making use of the women’s services as prostitutes. He further had conceded that he had followed P. when she escaped over the balcony in order to prevent her from calling the neighbours or the police since he had been afraid of getting problems in view of his criminal record. The Prosecutor General argued that while it was true that the proceedings had been characterised by a “complete loss’ of the applicant’s right to examine O. and P. (“Totalausfall des Fragerechts”), they had as a whole been fair and there had been no reason to exclude the witness statements as evidence. In view of the various layers of corroborating evidence the applicant had had ample opportunities to put into question the credibility of the two main witnesses and to effectively defend himself. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint against the decisions of the Federal Court of Justice dated 30 October and 9 December 2008 for examination without providing reasons. Behr, Regierungsdirektorin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The judge imposed an accumulated prison sentence (Gesamtfreiheitsstrafe) of nine years and six months. The court sentenced the applicant to 9 years and 6 months in prison and imposed a fine of 9.5 million euros (EUR) The applicant and a further accomplice, B., gained access to O. and P.’s apartment pretending to be potential clients while one of the co-accused was waiting in a car. Once inside the apartment B. produced a knife that he had carried along in his jacket. Fearing for her life O. opened the safe from which B. removed EUR 300 and also handed over the contents of her wallet in the amount of EUR 250. B. left the apartment at around 8.30 p.m. taking the money. The applicant jumped after her but abandoned the chase after some minutes when passers-by appeared nearby. The Regional Court based its finding of facts regarding the first crime committed in Kassel on the statements made by the victims L. and I. on the occasion of their police interrogations as well as in the course of the subsequent trial. Both witnesses had identified the applicant without any hesitation as the perpetrator who had carried the gun when presented with his photo. The Regional Court found the victims’ testimonies to be consistent and credible and noted that they were supported by the statements of the police officers who had attended the crime scene. The records of O. and P.’s interrogations by the police and the investigating judge will be read out at the trial and be admitted as evidence in the proceedings. Witnesses O. and P. had been summoned to appear before the Regional Court on 24 August 2007, the third day of the trial. They both had refused to attend the hearing relying on medical certificates dated 9 August 2007 that indicated their unstable post‑traumatic emotional and psychological condition. The Regional Court asked for the witnesses to be heard by a court in Latvia and the hearing to be transmitted by voice and image (audiovisuelle Vernehmung) However, a witness hearing scheduled by the competent Latvian court for 13 February 2008 was cancelled shortly before by the presiding judge on the ground that the witnesses had demonstrated that they were still suffering from post-traumatic disorders. Regional Court considered that it did not dispose of any further legal means to enforce a hearing of O. and P. The Regional Court held that notwithstanding the resulting restrictions for the defence, the trial as a whole had been fair and had complied with the requirements of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention. The court was thus not prevented from admitting the witnesses’ pre-trial statements as evidence in the proceedings. It concluded that it was impossible to have the witnesses examined in the foreseeable future. The judge said he had been concerned that the witnesses would be afraid of telling the truth in the presence of the accused. The applicant had not been informed about the preliminary criminal proceedings initiated against him with a view to not putting the investigations at risk. No warrant for his arrest had yet been issued. The Regional Court had made considerable efforts to enable a direct examination of O. and P. by the accused and counsel for the defence at trial. Minor contradictions in their statements could be explained by their concern not to disclose their illegal residence status and activities to the authorities. The court observed that the witnesses’ attention during the incident had been focussed on the further perpetrator carrying the knife and that the applicant himself had only stayed a short period of time in the apartment. Their inability to identify the applicant also showed that they had not testified with a view to incriminating him. The fact that the detailed description of the events in the pre-trial statements were consistent with the account they had given the morning after the crime to their neighbour E. was a further strong indication for their credibility and the veracity of their statements. The Regional Court noted that since neither the defence nor the court itself had had an opportunity to observe the main witnesses’ demeanour at trial or by means of an audio-visual examination, it had to exercise particular diligence in assessing the evaluation of the witnesses' credibility. The court paid special attention to the fact that their statements constituted hearsay evidence and had to be assessed particularly carefully. The link between the evidence obtained in the course of such separate investigations and the crime at issue could only be made after O. and P. had reported the incident of 3 February 2007 to the police. It followed from the recordings of two mobile phone conversations between one of the co-accused and the applicant in the evening of 3 Feb 2007 at 8.29 p.m. and 8.31 p.M. The applicant and the co-accused had denied any participation in the robbery as such or any premeditated criminal activity in this respect. Their own statements at trial had at least confirmed that one of them had visited the apartment the evening before the crime. The applicant had testified that he and B. had come to the apartment with a view to making use of the women’s services as prostitutes. He further had conceded that he had followed P. when she escaped over the balcony. He had done so in order to prevent her from calling the neighbours or the police since he had been afraid of getting problems in view of his criminal record. The applicant was convicted of murder in 2008. The trial had been characterised by a “complete loss’ of the applicant’s right to examine O. and P. (“Totalausfall des Fragerechts”). The Prosecutor General argued that the proceedings had as a whole been fair and there had been no reason to exclude the witness statements as evidence. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the appeal on points of law as manifestly ill-founded. The applicant complained of a violation of his right to be heard (Anhörungsrüge) on the ground that no hearing had been held in the appeal proceedings. name: Krzysztof Nurzyński
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46859/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right to respect for his family life had been infringed. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (former Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, now Article 29§ 1). The applicant and his wife were granted a divorce on 27 June 2007. The applicant's pre-trial detention was lifted on 8 October 2008. After that date he was visited by his mother on 11 occasions. On 29 July 2008 the Łódź District Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to two years' imprisonment. The. applicant's mother was granted permission to visit the applicant in prison. He was sentenced to 2 years in prison and a fine of £3,000. He has since been released from prison and is serving a suspended sentence. He is now living with his wife in the city of Szeged, Poland.

The trial judge’s summing up to the jury contained the following direction: “We all know this is a horrific, a disgusting episode. We all know that, and we all know – there has not been any argument about this, has there? – where moral responsibility lies. ... We are not here to dish out admonitions for immoral conduct, disgusting behaviour. We are here to judge whether a crime has been committed, whether the criminal law of the land has been broken. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32580/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. It retained the applicant's complaints concerning his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The case was heard by the Court's Second Section (Rule 52 § 1) on 23 September 2003. The case was referred to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay) following the promulgation of Law no. 3953 of 27 December 1993, which abolished the jurisdiction of the martial law courts. The applicant was sentenced to five years' imprisonment and debarred from public service for three years. On 23 May 1996 the applicant was dismissed from his post at the Ankara Municipality on account of his conviction. He was permitted to return to his previous post and to work as the head of the research and planning department of the municipality. The case was settled in a settlement between the applicant and the Turkish government.

name: Stephen Jordan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30280/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 by the applicant Mr Stephen Jordan. The applicant made numerous complaints under Articles 5, 6 and 13 of the Convention in relation to his pre-trial detention and the early stages of the court-martial proceedings against him. On 14 January 1998 the Commission declared the application partly inadmissible. After the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 on 1 November 1998, and in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 2 thereof, the case fell to be examined by the Court. The Court declared the applicant’s complaints under Article 5 §§ 3 and 5 admissible. The applicant was due for release on 27 May 1995 but his detention continued on the basis of the suspected offences that were being investigated by the SIB. On 29 August 1995 a further charge sheet was read to the applicant which included eight additional and similar charges (obtaining property by deception) and the applicant was remanded for trial by court-martial. On 11 December 1995 the army authorities undertook to the Court to release the applicant from close to open arrest and he was so released on the same day. The applicant alleged unlawful detention, breach of a duty of care, false imprisonment and trespass to the person. The army authorities admitted that due to an “administrative oversight” the applicant had not been charged until 16 June 1995. He was released from open arrest in mid-1996 and was sent on leave. The authorities accepted that the applicant’s detention between 27 May and 16 June 1995 was unlawful. The matter was settled on 21 October 1996, the applicant being paid a substantial sum of money and his costs. In March 1997 the applicant was charged with further but similar offences and, on 27 November 1997, the army authorities directed that he be tried by court-martial on the 27 outstanding charges against him. He pleaded guilty to offences of obtaining property by deception to the value of £15,000 and was sentenced to 14 months’ imprisonment of which he was to serve 7 months. The reviewing authority later reduced this sentence to 3 months' imprisonment and the appeal to the Courts-Martial Appeal Court is pending.

train_texts: The Tyrer case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights. The case originated in an application against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission on 21 September 1972. The purpose of the Commission’s request is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 3 (art. 3) of the Convention. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Sir Gerald Fitzmaurice, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr. G. Balladore Pallieri, the President of the Court. The Government of the Isle of Man requested that the Chamber carry out an investigation on the spot in the Island pursuant to Rule 38 para. 2 of the Rules of Court. At a meeting held in private in Strasbourg on 13 December 1977, the Chamber resolved to defer its decision on this request until after the oral hearings. The oral hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 January 1978. There appeared before the Court: Mr. D.H. Anderson, Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr. L.J. Blom-Cooper and Mr. J.W. Corrin for the Government. Anthony M. Tyrer, a citizen of the United Kingdom born on 21 September 1956, is resident in Castletown, Isle of Man. On 7 March 1972, being then aged 15, he pleaded guilty before the local juvenile court to unlawful assault occasioning actual bodily harm to a senior pupil at his school. The applicant was sentenced on the same day to three strokes of the birch in accordance with the relevant legislation (see paragraph 11 below). He appealed against sentence to the Staff of Government Division of the High Court of Justice of the Isle of man. The appeal was heard and dismissed on the afternoon of 28 April 1972; the court considered that an unprovoked assault was always very serious and that there were no reasons for interfering with the sentence. The applicant was sentenced pursuant to section 56 (1) of the Petty Sessions and Summary Jurisdiction Act 1927. He was sentenced to a fine not exceeding thirty pounds or to be imprisoned for a term not exceeding six months. The sentence was governed by the following provisions: “(a) the instrument used shall, in the case of a child, be a cane, and in any other case shall be a birch rod; (b) the court in its sentence shall specify the number of strokes to be inflicted, being not more than six strokes; (c) the whipping shall be inflicted privately as soon as practicable after sentence; and (d) it shall not take place after the expiration of six months from the passing of the sentence. The Isle of Man is not a part of the United Kingdom but a dependency of the Crown with its own government, legislature and courts. The Island’s parliament, the Court of Tynwald, is one of the oldest in Europe. It consists of a Lieutenant-Governor appointed by and representing the Crown, an Upper House (the Legislative Council) and a Lower House. The punishment is to be administered over ordinary cloth trousers in all cases irrespective of the offender's age. A medical practitioner shall be present during a birching and may at his discretion order the stopping of the punishment at any time. A report of the facts shall be forwarded immediately to His Excellency. Judicial corporal punishment of adults and juveniles was abolished in England, Wales and Scotland in 1948. The punishment remained in existence in the Isle of Man. In May 1977, by thirty-one votes for and only one against, Tynwald passed a resolution, inter alia, “that the retention of the use of judicial Corporal punishment for crimes of violence to the person is a desirable safeguard in the control of law and order in this Island’”. A privately organised petition in favour of the retention. of judicial corporal punished had obtained 31,000 signatures from amongst the approximate total of 45,000. persons entitled to vote on the Island. The average number of crimes of violence to the person per annum was: between 1966 and 1968 - 35; between 1969 and 1971 - 52; between 1972 and 1974 - 59; and between 1975 and 1977 - 56. In the three years 1975 to 1977, only one young male was convicted of a crime of violence. At the 1976 census, the Island’s population stood at 60,496. The name and address of a juvenile sentenced in the Isle of Man, whether to corporal punishment or otherwise, are not published. The offence with which the applicant was charged had been omitted from the specified list of offences. The applicant also claimed damages as well as repeal of the legislation concerned. The Commission decided not to proceed further with an examination of the original complaint under Article 14 (art. 14) which the applicant had subsequently withdrawn. The Commission decided that it could not accede to this request “since the case raised questions of a general character affecting the observance of the Convention’. The applicant took no further part in the proceedings. In its report of 14 December 1976, the Commission expressed the opinion that the judicial corporal punishment inflicted on the applicant was degrading and was in breach of Article 3 (Art. 3) of the convention. The report contains one separate opinion on the issue of age contrary to Article 14.
