train_texts: The case originated in six applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr L. García Quinteiro, a lawyer practising in Barcelona. The Spanish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr F. Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 11 December 2008 the President of the Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applied at the same time, as allowed by former Article 29 § 3. The applicants sought to secure recognition by their employer of their special ‘salaried worker’ status. The applicants and the Government filed memorials before the Grand Chamber. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 December 2010. The Court heard addresses by the applicants and addresses by them. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and the Court of Justice (ECJ) (Rule 59 § 3). TheECHR ruled that there had been no violation of Article 10 of the Convention and that no separate question arose under Article 11. The ECHR concluded that the applicants' claim for recognition of their salaried status had been denied. The applicants joined the union’s executive committee. No changes concerning the appointment of the union members or their duties have taken place since the union was formed. The union published a monthly newsletter. On the cover of the newsletter, a cartoon with speech bubbles showed a caricature of the human resources manager, G., sitting behind a desk under which a person on all fours could be seen. The applicants were dismissed on grounds of serious misconduct, namely for impugning the reputations of G., A. and B., under Article 54 §§ 1 and 2 (c) of the Labour Regulations. The tribunal dismissed their claims and found that the dismissals were justified. The cartoon and article were published on a noticeboard inside the company. The noticeboard contained caricatures of A. and B., showing them gagged by a handkerchief tied behind their heads. The text underneath read as follows: “We knew who they were and how they behaved, but we didn’t know how far they were prepared to go in order to hold onto their seats and cushy jobs without doing anything’. The tribunal noted that the text was a response to what had happened during proceedings brought by the applicants before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 13. The article entitled “When you’ve rented out your arse you can’d shit when you please” read as following: ‘If you belong to a works council and you have to sign agreements with your employers that will never be honoured, just to keep you quiet, and agree to changes that only benefit their cronies, and to pay cuts and other sell-outs, then you have swapped your dignity for an armchair’ You’re fed up with your work, pissed off, anxious, stressed and in despair, because of the longer working hours and the responsibilities, products, promotions and pressures. You could break everything up, tear it to pieces, crush and demolish it all ... but your hands are tied by credits, IOUs and debts. You are crushed by your new SUV, your children’s after-school activities, and the twenty-five year mortgage on your semi-detached house. And you let yourself be humiliated, you swallow your pride, you shut up and you accept, because when you’ve rented out your arse, you can’t shit when you please. The tribunal took the view that the cartoon and speech bubbles on the cover, together with the articles inside, were offensive and exceeded the limits of freedom of expression and information. The High Court of Justice of Catalonia upheld the judgment under appeal in so far as it concerned the applicants. The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, seeking harmonisation of the relevant case-law. In a decision of 11 March 2004, the Supreme Court of Spain ruled in favour of the applicants in their case against the company P. P. The court referred, among other things, to the limits imposed by the principle of good faith between parties to a contract of employment and to the necessary balance that judicial decisions had to strike between a worker’s obligations under the contract and his free speech. The applicants lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. In a decision of 11 January 2006 the Court found the appeal inadmissible for lack of constitutional content. The decision reads as follows: “... there is not enough evidence to show that the [appellants’] dismissal was an act of reprisal on the part of the respondent company’s ...” The Court held recently that although the Constitution does not prohibit the use of hurtful, embarrassing or vituperative expressions in every circumstance, the Constitution doesn’t prohibit them in all circumstances. The appeal was dismissed on the ground that the decision produced for purposes of comparison, namely a judgment of the High Court of Justice of Madrid of 31 July 1992 was not pertinent.  constitutional protection afforded by Article 20 § 1 (a) of the Constitution does not, however, extend to absolutely vexatious expressions. The Court concludes that the appellants’ right to freedom of expression has not been infringed. ‘They used that right in an excessive manner by means of value judgments expressed through cartoons and comments that were offensive and humiliating for the persons concerned and impugned their honour and reputation,’ says the court in its ruling in the case of the South African National Union (South Africa) (emphasis in the original). ‘It is not necessary for others to form an opinion about the facts of which they wished to complain, and therefore gratuitous.’ ‘The Court’s decision does not extend to expressions which, taking into account the actual circumstances of the case and regardless of their veracity or lack of veracity, are offensive or defamatory.”

Six Spanish nationals, Mr Juan Manuel Palomo Sánchez, Mr. Francisco Antonio Fernández Olmo, Mr Agustín Alvarez Lecegui, Mr Francisco José María Blanco Balbas, Mr José Antonio Aguilera Jiménez and Mr Francisco Beltrán Lafulla lodged the applications on 13 July 2006. Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel. The applications relied on Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention. The applicants sought to secure recognition by their employer of their special ‘salaried worker’ status. They were employed as delivery men by the company P. The applicants set up the trade union Nueva Alternativa Asamblearia (NAA) to defend their interests and those of the other delivery staff who were under pressure from the company to renounce their claim to salaried status. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 December 2010 (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel, Agent; (b), for the applicants Mr L. García Quinteiro, lawyer, Counsel. The applicants joined the union’s executive committee. No changes concerning the appointment of the union members or their duties have taken place since the union was formed. The applicants were dismissed on grounds of serious misconduct, namely for impugning the reputations of G., A. and B., under Article 54 §§ 1 and 2 (c) of the Labour Regulations. The tribunal took the view that the company's decision to dismiss the applicants had been based on a genuine and serious cause, and dismissed their claims. A judgment of 8 November 2002, dismissed the claims and found that the dismissals were justified, in accordance with Article 54. Tribunal ruled that a cartoon and two articles were offensive and impugned dignity. The cartoon showed caricatures of A. and B., with them gagged by a handkerchief tied behind their heads. The article entitled “When you’ve rented out your arse you can’t shit when you please” read as follows: “If you belong to a works council and you have to sign agreements with your employers that will never be honoured, just to keep you quiet, then you have the dubious merit of achieving the same level of infamy as politicians and policemen” The tribunal noted that the text was a response to what had happened during proceedings brought by the applicants before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 13. name: Ernst Lughofer
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by. Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants’ application to the. Court referred to Article 48 as amended by Protocol No. 90, which Austria had ratified. The object of the application was to obtain a decision. as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach. by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The case relates to the transfer of land from the Gmunden District, Germany. The owners of the land complained that they had not received adequate land in exchange for their land. The appeal was dismissed in 1990. The case was reopened in 2010 and the case is still pending. The application was brought by the descendants of those who lived in the district at the time of the original land transfer. The decision was made to dismiss the appeal on 5 July 2010. The complaint was brought again on 15 December 2010, this time the decision was again dismissed. The current case is being heard by the Administrative Court of the Republic of Germany (ACR)

It originated in an application (no. 22811/93) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25. The Chamber ultimately constituted within the Section included Mr J.-P. Costa, Mr P. Kūris, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mr W. Fuhrmann, Mr H.S. Greve and Mr K. Traja. On 17 May 1999 the Government conceded that there had been a violation of Article 6 of the Convention in the circumstances of the case. The land was to be transferred to the rightful owners. But the owners appealed, claiming that they had not received adequate land. The appeal was dismissed, and the land was returned to the owners. The land was then transferred to a new owner. The new owners of the land then appealed again, but the decision was also upheld. The final decision was made to transfer the land back to the original owners. That decision was then overturned. The current owners now live on the other side of the road in the village of Bremen.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 19 April 1991. It originated in an application (no. 10533/83) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Istvan Herczegfalvy, a Hungarian national, on 27 November 1978. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 (paras. 1, 3 and 4), 8, 10 and 13. Istvan Herczegfalvy, a Hungarian citizen, has lived in Austria since 1964. He served two prison sentences in succession for assaults on his wife, clients of his television repair business and public officials. He was declared partly incapacitated (beschränkt entmündigt) and appointed an adviser. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 April 1992. The Court heard addresses by them and heard evidence from the Government, Commission and the applicant's lawyer. The case was heard by the International Human Rights Court, which heard evidence in English, French and German. The applicant was held in pre-trial detention (Untersuchungshaft) before the trial. He was suffering from paranoia querulans, which was equivalent to a mental illness and meant that he was not responsible for his acts. According to a ruling of the guardianship court of 19 July 1984, his position was equivalent as from 1 July 1984 to that of a curator (Sachwalter) within the meaning of Article 273 (3), sub-paragraph 3, of the Civil Code. The applicant unsuccessfully appealed to the Review Chamber (Ratskammer) of the Regional Court and to the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), whose rulings were given in May and June 1978. The hearing before the Regional Court took place on 9 and 10 January 1979. Mr Herczegfalvy was detained under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 45 below) The court relied on the opinions of three psychiatrists who had each diagnosed paranoia querulans which from 1975 at least had been equivalent to a mental illness. The applicant brought an application for a declaration of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) to the Supreme Court. The Vienna Court of Appeal, to which the applicant had appealed, held on 29 August 1979 that it had no jurisdiction: as Article 429 (4) was the only provision which could apply, it was for the Review Chamber to hear the appeal. Mr Herczegfalvy's hunger strike started on 2 August 1979. On 10 September 1979 he was admitted to ward 23 of a psychiatric hospital. On 4 December 1979 he requested his release. On 14 December the investigating judge informed him that he continued to be detained in accordance with Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 17 January 1980 the psychiatric hospital submitted a report expressing the opinion that it was not possible to place the applicant in ordinary pre-trial detention. On 30 October 1980 the applicant withdrew his appeal and application for a declaration of nullity in writing. The judgment was on the latter date declared binding by a final order (Endverfügung) On 8 February 1982 the Regional Court, acting under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code, extended Mr Herczegfalvy’s detention, as a psychiatric report produced at the request of that court stated that he was a dangerous person. On 16 February 1984 the latter court ordered a further extension of the detention in issue. On 4 April 1984 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal and confirmed that the requirements for his release under Article 47 (2) were not satisfied. He was conditionally released on 28 November in accordance with the court's decision of 14 November, itself based on a Psychiatric report dated 14 September (see paragraph 34 below) Mr Herczegfalvy had begun a hunger strike on 2 August 1979 as a protest against his detention and the refusal to give him his files. He collapsed on 28 August and was transferred to a clinic where he received intensive medical care. On 10 September 1979 he was transferred back to the Vienna psychiatric hospital, where he remained until his release on 28 November 1984 (see paragraph 23 above). He was force-fed and given sedatives against his will. He was injected by force with 90mg of Taractan on 15 January 1980, in order to bring about a state of somnolence in which it would be possible to treat him by means of perfusions. Mr Herczegfalvy. made a complete recovery when he left, and he still needed treatment with antibiotics and neuroleptics. On his return to the closed unit he was handcuffed and a belt placed around his ankles because of the danger of aggression and the death threats he was making. According to the Government, their position was changed regularly, in order to avoid nervous paralysis, and on 12 February he had agreed to be fed by a woman doctor. The applicant stated, however, that other belts had been put around his thighs and stomach and had been untied for the first time only on 2 February. In order to obtain his files and writing materials with which to write his complaints, he had continued his hunger strike without interruption. Mr Herczegfalvy was released on 28 November 1984, after a further expert report dated 14 September 1984. He was deprived from time to time of writing materials, and his unstamped letters were frequently returned to him, with the exception of those addressed to the public authorities, in particular the courts. He also claimed that he had been deprived of reading matter, radio and television for long periods during his detention. The applicant was given six binders containing the originals of these letters and also about fifty sealed letters. The postal register showed that the latter had never been sent to their addressees, namely the police, the public prosecutor’s office and the Courts. The measures had been justified for therapeutic reasons, and had lasted for a short time only on each occasion. been taken for disciplinary purposes only. According to the Government, these measures were based on section 51 (1) of the Hospitals Law (see paragraph 51 below), and had been used for a brief time only. The Government said the measures were taken for short-term therapeutic purposes only and not for long-term disciplinary purposes. The measures were only used for short periods of time only, and were not intended to be permanent. No disciplinary action was taken against the patient who had taken part in one of the activities in question for more than a few hours.

On 4 April 1984 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal and confirmed that the requirements for his release under Article 47 (2) were not satisfied. He was conditionally released on 28 November in accordance with the court's decision of 14 November, itself based on a Psychiatric report dated 14 September (see paragraph 34 below) Mr Herczegfalvy had begun a hunger strike on 2 August 1979 as a protest against his detention and the refusal to give him his files. He collapsed on 28 August and was transferred to a clinic where he received intensive medical care. On 10 September 1979 he was transferred back to the Vienna psychiatric hospital, where he remained until his release on 28 November 1984. He was also given sedatives against his will (three doses of 30mg each of Taractan IM); on 14 and 15 September he was attached to a security bed, the net and straps of which he succeeded in cutting through. He stopped refusing food on 27 September 1979, after being allocated a single room and being given some of his files, but later denied that his consent was validly given. Mr Herczegfalvy was handcuffed and a belt placed around his ankles because of the danger of aggression and the death threats he was making. The restraints were not removed until 14 February 1980. The applicant continued his hunger strike without interruption, and had been artificially fed throughout this period. On 22 February he was given paper and a ballpoint pen and allowed to write his complaints. He continued to refuse, at least in part, to take nourishment other than through a tube, but on 12 November 1982 he stated that he no longer needed to be fed artificially. In March 1983 an expert considered that conditional release of the applicant would be possible if certain accompanying psychiatric and social measures were taken. An expert noted the progress which the applicant had made and expressed the opinion that troublesome behaviour did not constitute a risk. However, in a letter of 25 January 1984, the director of the hospital advised the court not to terminate Mr Herczegfalvy’s detention. The Regional Court thereupon on 16 February 1984 refused to release the applicant. He eventually recovered his liberty on 28 November 1984, after a further expert report dated 14 September 1984 (see paragraph 23 above).C. The control of correspondence while in detention and the restrictions on access to information during his time in detention.D. The restrictions on information during and after his detention. According to the Government, these measures were based on section 51 (1) of the Hospitals Law. The measures had been justified for therapeutic reasons, and had lasted for a short time only on each occasion. They were taken for disciplinary purposes only and were not part of a larger plan to reform the health service. The Government said the measures were not intended to be seen as a result of the NHS’s failures to meet its obligations under section 51 of the law. The government said they were intended to ‘strengthen’ the NHS and its ability to respond to patients’ needs for treatment. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 19 April 1991. It originated in an application (no. 10533/83) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Istvan Herczegfalvy, a Hungarian national, on 27 November 1978. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. Mr Istvan Herczegfalvy is a Hungarian citizen who has lived in Austria since 1964. He currently resides in Vienna. He served two prison sentences in succession, following convictions pronounced by the Vienna Regional Criminal Court. He was declared partly incapacitated (beschränkt entmündigt) and appointed an adviser. The Court heard addresses by them by them in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 April 1992. The hearing was held in public in the human rights building of the Court of Justice of the European Court of Human Rights. There appeared before the Court: Mr H. Türk, Ambassador, Legal Adviser, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr W. Okresek, Federal Chancellery, Mrs E. Schindler, Federal Ministry of Justice, Advisers. In 1977 a court ordered Mr Herczegfalvy to remain in detention under Article 180 (2), sub-paragraphs 1 and 3, of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The pre-trial detention (Untersuchungshaft) was confirmed by the presiding judge of the Regional Court on 2 November 1977. On 9 August 1983 the District Court appointed a new adviser, who has acted as such since then. According to a ruling of the guardianship court of 19 July 1984, his position was equivalent as from 1 July 1984 to that of a curator (Sachwalter) within the meaning of Article 273 (3) of the Civil Code (see paragraph 54 below). The hearing before the Regional Court took place on 9 and 10 January 1979. The court found that the charges against Mr Herczegfalvy had been proved and ordered him to be detained under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 45 below) The court relied on the opinions of three psychiatrists who had each diagnosed paranoia querulans which from 1975 at least had been equivalent to a mental illness. The applicant brought an application for a declaration of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) to the Supreme Court. The Regional Court decided, however, that pending the decision he should remain provisionally detained in prison. Mr Herczegfalvy's hunger strike started on 2 August 1979. He was admitted to ward 23 of a psychiatric hospital on 10 September 1979. On 4 December 1979 he requested his release. But he continued to be detained in accordance with Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. His aggressive behaviour was still causing danger to those around him. In 1980 the Review Chamber and the Court of Appeal extended the detention in question. The applicant subsequently challenged the validity of his declarations. He said that he had made them only with a view to his repatriation to Hungary, which was discussed on 6 November 1980 but did not take place. On 8 February 1982 the Regional Court, acting under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code, extended Mr Herczegfalvy’s detention, as a psychiatric report produced at the request of that court stated that he was a dangerous person. On 4 April 1984 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal and confirmed that the requirements for his release under Article 47 (2) were not satisfied. He was conditionally released on 28 November in accordance with the court's decision of 14 November, itself based on a psychiatric. report dated 14 September (see paragraph 34 below) The court found that the applicant’'s paranoia had admittedly worsened, but that it was primarily due to his detention (Haftquerulanz) and that the vexatious complaints and petitions did not constitute a danger. Mr Herczegfalvy was returned to prison after his stay in the Vienna psychiatric hospital from 29 June to 23 July 1979. The director of the hospital ordered him to be force fed, pursuant to section 8 (3) of the Hospitals Law. The applicant refused all contact and refused to have any medical examination or treatment. He was also given sedatives against his will (three doses of 30mg each of Taractan IM); on 14 and 15 September 1979 he was attached to a security bed, the net and straps of which he succeeded in cutting through. As he considered that he did not have the necessary money, he refused on several occasions to put stamps on his letters, or sent them to the Ministry of Justice for that purpose. He was deprived from time to time of writing materials, and his unstamped letters were frequently returned to him, with the exception of those addressed to the public authorities, in particular the courts. He eventually recovered his liberty on 28 November 1984, after a further expert report dated 14 September 1984. The measures were based on section 51 (1) of the Hospitals Law. name: Carola van Kück
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35968/97) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Ms Carola van Kück alleged that German court decisions refusing her claims for reimbursement of gender reassignment measures were in breach of her right to a fair trial. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Court declared the application admissible on 18 October 2001. This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. In 1992, the applicant brought an action with the Berlin Regional Court against a German health insurance company. Having been affiliated to this company since 1975, she claimed reimbursement of pharmaceutical expenses for hormone treatment. As an employee of the Berlin Land, she was entitled to allowances covering half of her medical expenses; the private health insurance was to cover the other half. She further requested a declaratory judgment to the effect that the defendant company was liable to reimburse 50% of the expenses for gender reassignment operations and further hormone treatment, which the court ruled in her favour. The psychiatrist Dr H., having examined the applicant in January 1993, delivered his opinion in February 1993. In his conclusions, he confirmed that the applicant was a male-to-female transsexual and that her transsexuality had to be regarded as a disease. The court considered that under the relevant provisions of the General Insurance Conditions the applicant was not entitled to reimbursement of medical treatment regarding her transsexuality. The court was not convinced that, on account of the applicant’s resistance to therapy, the intended operation was the only possible treatment. In its reasoning, the court, having regard to the opinion prepared by Dr H. and to the expert opinions prepared in the proceedings before the Schöneberg District Court, considered that the. applicant was a male-to-female transsexual and that her condition had to be regarded as a disease. The question whether the treatment in question was recognised by medical science was irrelevant. In the court's view, hormone treatment and gender reassignment surgery could not reasonably be considered as necessary medical treatments. The applicant underwent gender reassignment surgery in November 1994. The Court of Appeal valued the claims at stake at 28,455.92 German marks. The applicant had failed to prove that the conditions for reimbursement of medical treatment were met in her case. According to the opinion of the expert Dr H., her transsexuality constituted a disease, a matter not in dispute between the parties to the proceedings. In his view, consensus existed on the improved psycho-social situation following the change of the sexual role, although the effect of the operation as such was often overrated. In the applicant’s case, the advantages of an operation would, in the expert's view, prevail, while psychotherapy could not cure the transsexuality. The Court of Appeal found in particular that the applicant was born as a male child and did not claim that she was a female on account of chromosomal factors. In its view, the applicant’s “fear of bigger boys” at school was not gender-specific. The applicant was not entitled to reimbursement under clause 5.1(b) of the General Insurance Conditions on the ground that she had herself deliberately caused the disease, as argued by the defendant in earlier submissions. According to the applicant, the “turning-point”, as stated by the Court of Appeals, had been the moment when, after an unsuccessful operation in 1986, she had realised she was infertile. The German Transsexuals Act was adopted following the decision of 11 October 1978 of the Federal Constitutional Court according to which the refusal to change the sex of a post-operative transsexual in the register of births was an unjustified interference with human dignity and everyone’s fundamental right to develop his personality freely. The recognition that he was infertile is a decisive factor confirming the subsequent transsexual development. On 25 October 1996 the German Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint. The case was decided in favour of the applicant, who now lives as a woman in Germany. The decision was published in the ‘European Court of Human Rights’. The German health insurance system is governed by the Social Security Act, Book V, Health Insurance (Sozialgesetzbuch, Fünftes Buch, Gesetzliche Kranken-versicherung) The basic rules for private health insurance, as for any other private insurance, are laid down in the Insurance Contract Act. Under the relevant provisions, persons insured under the health system are entitled to medical treatment which is necessary in order to diagnose or to cure a disease. The cost of gender reassignment surgery had to be reimbursed if, in the circumstances of the individual case, the psychophysical state of the transsexual amounted to a disease and ifGender reassignment was the sole means of finding relief, psychiatric and psychotherapeutic treatment having remained unsuccessful. Private health insurance covers expenses for curative treatment which is medically necessary on account of a disease or injuries suffered as a result of an accident or for other medical services for illness. The insurer is exempted from liability if the insured person has deliberately caused his or her own disease or accident (section 178.l). The contractual relations are standardised in general insurance conditions. The European Court of Justice (ECJ) found that discrimination arising from gender reassignment constituted discrimination on grounds of sex and, accordingly, Article 5 of the Council Directive 76/207/EEC of 9 February 1976 precluded dismissal of a transsexual for a reason related to a gender reassignment. Community law as it stands at present does not cover discrimination based on sexual orientation, says ECJ. Treaty of Amsterdam amending the Treaty on European Union, the Treaties establishing the European Communities and certain related acts, signed on 2 October 1997, provides for the insertion in the EC Treaty of an Article 6a. It will allow the Council under certain conditions (a unanimous vote on a proposal from the Commission after consulting the European Parliament) to take appropriate action to eliminate various forms of discrimination, including discrimination on sexual orientations, the European Court of Justice says. The refusal by an employer to allow travel concessions to the person of the same sex with whom a worker has a stable relationship does not constitute discrimination prohibited by Article 119 of the Treaty.

name: Hikmet Yılmaz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11022/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 20 September 2011 the application was declared partly inadmissible and the complaints concerning the lack of legal assistance to the applicant during his police custody and his right to a fair trial were communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights and Human Rights Protection. The applicant was found not guilty of the charges against him. The judge ordered his pre-trial detention. The applicant was accused of being a member of the PKK. He was convicted and sentenced to 12 years and 6 months in prison. The Court of Cassation upheld the first-instance court's decision to convict him. The applicant appealed the conviction and was released on bail in November 2002. He has since resumed the practice of law in Istanbul. A. T. was the applicant's lawyer when he was charged with being a PKK member. He claimed that his police statement was taken under duress and that he had been under the influence of the pressure exerted on him by the public prosecutor and the investigating judge respectively. In his appeal petition, he denied being involved in the PKK and claimed that he was innocent.

name: Patrick Grattan Foley
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 39197/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that civil proceedings brought by him were not determined within a reasonable time. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 11 September 2001 the Court declared the application partially admissible and decided to dispense with a hearing (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. The case is still pending. The defendants applied for security for their costs, and the court granted the application on 26 September 1985. The proceedings were stayed until the security was paid. The appeal was dismissed on 31 January 1986 and the plaintiffs paid the security on 28 February 1986. The plaintiffs’ solicitors filed a Notice of Intention to Proceed on 5 January 1989 as required by the rules of court since no steps had been taken in the prosecution of the claim for more than a year. On 10 February 1989 the plaintiffs served a Summons for Directions, the deadline for which had expired on 2 February 1985. A further hearing was proposed for 1 September 1989 but was also adjourned. The Government state that it was due to the parties not having ensured that sufficient court time would be available. The trial began on schedule, but had to be adjourned on 18 June 1991 as the applicant was ill. It was recommenced on 29 April 1992 and ran until 11 June 1992. On 2 October 1992, judgment was given in the plaintiffs’ favour. However, the damages award was limited to GBP 5 to each plaintiff since they could not establish that the venture would have been a commercial success had it proceeded. The plaintiffs appealed in December 1992. The appeal was stood out of the list by consent until 31 March 1995. On 18 June 1996 the applicant informed the CAO that he would be proceeding in person. The application for security for costs for the appeal was dismissed. The applicant's request for a hearing date was passed to the Court of Appeal’s Registrar on 14 November 1996. The CAO liaised with the defendants to ascertain their status, which was confirmed in a letter from the defendants’ solicitors received on 25 March 1997. In August 1998 the CAO learnt that Ferranti Instrumentation Limited had been struck off the register of companies. Even if the applicant had won he would not have benefited financially given the financial state of the one remaining defendant (Ferranti plc) The plaintiffs’ request for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was dismissed on 19 April 1999. The applicant was offered an ex gratia payment to cover his wasted costs.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 7 June 1991. It originated in an application (no. 13191/87) against the French Republic lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 paras. 1, 2 and 3 (c) (Art 6-1, art. 6-2, 6-3-c). The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). Mr Tuan Tran Pham Hoang, a French national who was born in Saigon in 1963, was unemployed and living at Auln. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Belliard for the Government, Mr Schermers for the Commission and Mr Lestourneaud for the applicant, as well as replies to its question. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 April 1992. There appeared before the Court:. Mrs E. Belliard, Deputy Director of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr B. Gain, Head of the Human rights Section, Department of Legal. Affairs,. Ministry of. Foreign Affairs. Miss M. Picard, magistrat. On 3 January 1984 he was arrested in Paris with four other people from Hong Kong, Cambodia or Vietnam. Two other people, Mr Jip Quang Duong and Mr Hanh Phuoc, were arrested after weapons and 5kg of caffeine were discovered by police while searching a flat visited by the applicant. In an order of 25 March 1984 the investigating judge committed the applicant and the six others mentioned above for trial on the charge that they had “conspired in Paris during 1983-84, in particular up to 3 January, to produce, possess and supply drugs, namely heroin’. He was sentenced to a fine of 2,835,000 (two million eight hundred and thirty-five thousand) francs. The defendants' statements and the police surveillance disclosed the following: Cheng Man Ming and Fu Wing Kin left Bangkok together by air on 26 december 1983 carrying a suitcase with a false bottom containing the heroin subsequently seized. When they arrived in Athens, Cheng continued his journey by air to Paris and instructed Fu to bring the suitcase by rail in order to avoid the thorough checks made at airports in Paris. In France Ngo Pan accompanied Cheng to make a number of purchases: the receptacle which would have served to mix the heroin and the caffeine [and] the secateurs for cutting open the hidden compartment in the suitcase. The heroin was to be transported in Pham’s motor vehicle, and Tran was to drive with it to the home of Jip Quang Duong and Hanh Phuoc, where the 5kg of caffeine were seized. It has therefore been established that the seven defendants constituted a group of individuals (whether or not all of them were in possession of the smuggled goods) formed with a view to importing heroin base, converting it, possessing it, transporting it and mixing it with caffeine.

name: John Hirst
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that as a convicted prisoner he was subject to a blanket ban on voting in elections. He invoked Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 14, as well as Article 10. By a decision of 8 July 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 16 December 2003 (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr J. Grainger, Agent, Ms N. Pittam, Mr M. Rawlings, Ms E. Willmott, Advisers, and for the applicant Ms F. Krause. Convicted prisoners are barred by the Representation of the People Act 1983 from voting in parliamentary or local elections. The applicant’s application was heard before the Divisional Court on 21 and 22 March 2001, together with the application for judicial review of two other prisoners, Mr Pearson and Mr Feal-Martinez, who also sought a declaration of incompatibility. In Europe only eight countries, including the United Kingdom, did not give convicted prisoners a vote, while 20 did not disenfranchise prisoners and eight imposed a more restricted disenfranchisement. Lord Justice Kennedy concluded: “... I return to what was said by the European Court in paragraph 52 of its judgment in Mathieu-Mohin. If an individual is to be disenfranchised that must be in the pursuit of a legitimate aim’ Convicted prisoners have forfeited their right to have a say in the way the country is governed. The European Court also requires that the means employed to restrict the implied Convention rights to vote are not disproportionate. Parliament in this country could have provided differently in order to meet the objectives which it discerned, and like McLachlin J in Canada, I would accept that the tailoring process seldom admits of perfection. The courts must afford some leeway to the legislator. That applies even to the ‘hard cases’ of post-tariff discretionary life sentence prisoners. They have all been convicted and if, for example, Parliament were to have said that all those sentenced to life imprisonment lose the franchise for life the apparent anomaly of their position would disappear. An application for permission to appeal was filed on behalf of Pearson and Feal-Martinez, together with a 43-page skeleton argument. On 15 May 2001, Lord Justice Buxton considered the application on the papers and refused permission on the grounds that the appeal had no real prospect of success. On 7 June 2001, his application was considered by Lord Justice Simon Brown who refused permission for the same reasons. The applicant’s renewed application, along with the renewed applications, were refused on 18 June 2001. After oral argument, the application was rejected. The appeal was dismissed. The case was settled at the Supreme Court of England and Wales.

train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were born in 1977 and 1979 respectively. train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 28 May 1996. It originated in an application (no. 20022/92) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by a Swedish citizen, Mrs Anne-Marie Andersson, on 11 February 1992. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs E. Palm, the elected judge of Swedish nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 March 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Thune, Mrs Westerberg and Ms Jagander. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Ms E. Jagander, Director, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr G. Schäder, Director-General of Legal Affairs. For the applicant Mrs S. Westerberg, Counsel, Mrs C. Bokelund, Lawyer, Mr M. Eliasson, Attorney, Mrs R. Harrold-Claesson, Counsel. Mrs B. Hellwig, Delegate of the Commission, Assistant. Anne-Marie Andersson had a polyclinical contact with a psychiatrist at the clinic since 19 April 1989. The reason has been a pain condition in connection with dental problems and this has caused her being on sick-leave as from May 1988. The patient does not consider herself to be mentally ill but she has accepted the contact with us solely due to her need to be put on the sick-list. The undersigned, as well as others in the medical service with whom the patient has been in contact, have worried about the possible effect of her severe pain condition on the son whom she cares for alone. As I do not find that, from a psychiatric point of view, we can do more for the patient, I now send a written account of the case. The psychiatrist's concern for the applicant's son was shared by the headmaster and a teacher at the school he attended. In October 1991 they had contacted the Social Council and expressed concern about his learning difficulties and his general state of health. Following this, the Council commenced an investigation which, with Mrs Andersson's agreement, led to the placement of her son in a non-residential therapeutic school on 2 March 1992. The psychiatrist contacted the applicant the same day to inform her of the information he had imparted to the Council. The Council subsequently placed the boy in a therapeutic school. The case was heard at the European Court of Human Rights.

The Chamber decided, by six votes to one, that the finding of a violation constituted sufficient just satisfaction for the non-pecuniary damage sustained by the applicant. The Grand Chamber dismissed the remainder of the applicant's claims for just satisfaction. The Court heard addresses by Lord Goldsmith and Mr Greenwood, and also their replies to questions from its individual members. The applicant was the sole managing director of London Clubs Limited (“LCL”), a company which owned and controlled six of the twenty casinos licensed to operate in London between 1984 and 1992. In June 1991 a raid took place at the various premises of LCL. The raid was carried out by the police in the presence of officials of the Gaming Board for Great Britain. London Clubs applied for new licences for the casinos via reconstituted operating companies. If the applications were successful and new licences were granted, LCL would undertake to surrender its existing licences, thereby avoiding the necessity for the applications for cancellation or renewal to be heard. The Gaming Board issued LCL with certificates of consent, which LCL was statutorily obliged to obtain from the Gaming Board as a prerequisite to making an application to the Licensing Magistrates. Objections were made by a rival casino owner. However, these objections were rejected and new licence were granted in October 1992, after a three day hearing before the Licensed Magistrate. The applicant's legal advisers entered into correspondence with the Gaming board's solicitors, on the basis that the speech made by Lady Littler was defamatory. The Gaming Board was considering whether the applicant was a fit and proper person to hold the Board's certificate of approval, as required by section 19 of the Gaming Act 1968. The applicant's legal advisers objected to the Gaming Board presiding the section 19 hearing, suggesting that an independent tribunal be set up as an alternative. The hearing never took place and no reference was intended to be made to the applicant. The Gaming Board informed the applicant formally that it was “minded to revoke’ the applicant's section 19 certificates and that the applicant would be given the opportunity to state his case against revocation either in writing or orally at an interview. The application for judicial review was dismissed on 11 January 1996 by Mr Justice Jowitt after a hearing lasting over sixteen days. The effect of the revocation of the section 19 certificates was that the applicant was unable to obtain employment in any sector of the gaming industry in the United Kingdom or in any jurisdiction which had a relationship with the UK gaming authorities. The decision was challenged on the grounds that the Panel was biased, or had the appearance of bias, and that its findings were vitiated by errors of law and were irrational. The first judgment dealt with the applicant's appeal. The application was dismissed after a court heard the case for three days in January 1996. Mr Justice Jowitt described the test of bias under English law in the following terms (pp. 93-96 of the judgment): “[Counsel for the applicant] submits that the decision to revoke the applicant's section 19 certificates of approval should be quashed because the Panel was biased’’ “The grounds on which leave to move for judicial review were granted asserted firstly that the Board could not and did not approach its decision with objectivity and impartiality. Secondly, it was asserted that whether or not there was actual bias the applicant reasonably believed there was.” “There was no evidence that the Panel had been biased,” the judge added. ‘The Board should have had regard to the appearance of bias which had been created by its actions,' he said. The applicant has first to show from the evidence that there is an appearance of bias (R. v. Inner West London Coroner, ex parte Dallaglio [1994] 4 All England Law Reports 139) He then has to go on to show that on a proper examination by the court of the evidence before it there is demonstrated a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias. By “real” is meant not without substance. A real danger clearly involves more than a minimal risk, less than a probability. One could, I think, as well speak of a real risk or a real possibility. The court is not concerned strictly with the appearance of. bias but rather with establishing the possibility that there was actual although unconscious bias. Mr Justice Jowitt concluded that there was no unconscious bias on the part of any of the Panel members. If, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias, the ‘doctrine of necessity’ fell to be considered. The decision will not be liable to be impugned on account of bias provided that: (i) if only some of those charged with the power or duty to decide are potentially affected by bias such of them as can lawfully withdraw from the decision-making do so; and (ii) those of the. decision-makers who are potentially affect by bias use their best endeavours to avoid the effect of bias. Mr Justice Jowitt rejected the submission, on the grounds that no useful reference could have been made to an independent tribunal which did not involve an impermissible delegation. The applicant failed to establish that the Panel's decision was irrational or unreasonable or to make out any sufficient ground for judicial review. Lord Justice Morritt (with whom Lord Justice Hobhouse agreed) held that there was a real risk that the decision of the tribunal had been actuated by bias. The decision for the Board was, at the end of the day, whether or not Mr Kingsley was a fit and proper person. That could not be delegated to anindependent panel and if they were actuating by bias, apparent or real, then the decision would still have to be made. "There is no arguable point, susceptible on this part of the case, which would justify giving leave to appeal," he says. "The decision would stand because the decision has to be made by the Board and could not be delegated to the independent tribunal," he adds. "There would have been no meaningful independent panel and the decision would still stand," the judge adds. 'I would have thought there would be a lot of interest in the case,' adds the judge. 'It seems to me that there is noarguable point,' he adds, 'which would justify the appeal.' 'There would be no interest in it,' says the judge, who adds that the case was not an issue for an independent panel. train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the use of covert audio and video surveillance within his cell, the prison visiting area and upon a fellow prisoner. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The parties also filed observations on their own merits, which the Court agreed to. The application was declared partly admissible on 28 August 2001. In February 1995 an anonymous informant told the police that the applicant had been involved in the murder of David Beesley. On 20 February 1995 Detective Chief Inspector Dunn requested permission for the cell and the visiting areas used by the applicant and Leroy Grant to be bugged with audio and video technology. On 28 June 1995 the applicant was taken away from the prison to be interviewed by the police concerning the Kwik-Save robbery. The applicant was invited to comment on the recordings made in February and March 1995. He made no comment to any question. According to the applicant, he was interrogated. He availed himself of that right. After 20 April 1995 he associated regularly with the applicant who was remanded at Strangeways Prison. The applicant was interviewed again in the presence of his solicitor on 29 June and 26 July 1995 and remained silent when faced with the allegations against him. The thrust of the applicant's case was that he was discussing robberies and did not accede to H.'s efforts to channel their conversation into a discussion of the murder. No evidence, other than the alleged admissions, connected the applicant with the killing of Mr Beesley. The judge concluded that there was evidence on tapes from which the jury could infer that the applicant was involved in the events of 3 February 1995, and it was not so unreliable that it could not be left to the jury to assess for themselves. The judge's ruling on the admissibility of the evidence was given on 26 January 1998, after a voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of a jury) and consisted of a judgment of eighteen pages. H. was accordingly admitted before the jury. In his summing-up to the jury on 10 and 11 February 1998, the trial judge gave directions on the way in which the jury should assess the reliability of the disputed evidence. He told them that they were to judge whether the police had deliberately wound up the applicant during the interview on 28 June 1995 and how to approach the evidence put forward by H. The applicant was convicted of murder before the Crown Court at Manchester. He was sentenced to life imprisonment. His renewed application was refused by the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on 18 January 1999, after a hearing at which he was represented by leading counsel. In the court's judgment of that date, Lord Justice Rose found that the trial judge gave a very careful and impeccable ruling as regards the admissibility of the tapes and evidence put forward by H. The judge also directed the jury concerning the possible drawing of inferences from the applicant's silence in police interview on 28 and 29 June and 26 July 1995, pursuant to section 34 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994. On 31 July 1998 he was refused leave to appeal against his conviction by a single judge.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the use of covert audio and video surveillance within his cell, the prison visiting area and upon a fellow prisoner. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The parties responded to the Court's observations in writing. The application was declared partly admissible by the Court in August 2001. An anonymous informant told the police that the applicant had been involved in the murder of David Beesley. On 20 February 1995 Detective Chief Inspector Dunn requested permission for the cell and the visiting areas used by the applicant and Leroy Grant to be bugged with audio and video technology. In the interviews with the police which followed, the police told the applicant that he was not obliged to say anything. He availed himself of that right. During this time visits to the applicant by his female friend, J.N.S, were recorded on audio and videotape in the prison visiting area between 12 and 28 March 1995. On 28 June 1995 the applicant was taken away from the prison to be interviewed by the police concerning the Kwik-Save robbery. H. had been fitted with recording devices. He was interviewed by the police in an attempt to ‘rattle’ or unsettle him. The recording thereby obtained was adduced in evidence at the applicant's trial. No evidence, other than the alleged admissions, connected the applicant with the killing of Mr Beesley. The judge concluded that there was evidence on the tapes from which the jury could infer that the applicant was involved in the events of 3 February 1995, and it was not so unreliable that it could not be left to the jury to assess for themselves. He considered that the use of an informant to talk and listen to the accused over a substantial period of time did not result in any unfairness to the applicant. The judge's ruling on the admissibility of the evidence was given on 26 January 1998, after a voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of a jury) and consisted of a judgment of eighteen pages. H. was accordingly admitted before the jury. In his summing-up to the jury on 10 and 11 February 1998, the trial judge gave directions on the way in which the jury should assess the reliability of the disputed evidence. He told them that they were to judge whether the police had deliberately wound up the applicant during the interview on 28 June 1995 and how to approach the evidence put forward by H. On 17 February 1998, after the jury had deliberated for a total of twenty-one and a half hours, the applicant was convicted of murder before the Crown Court at Manchester by a majority of ten to two and sentenced to life imprisonment. On 31 July 1998 he was refused leave to appeal against his conviction by a single judge. His renewed application was refused by the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on 18 January 1999, after a hearing at which he was represented by leading counsel. The applicant complained of the use of covert audio and video surveillance within his cell, the prison visiting area and upon a fellow prisoner. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was decided in favour of the applicant. Informant told police that applicant had been involved in murder of David Beesley. Cell and visiting areas used by the applicant and Leroy Grant were bugged with audio and video technology. Telephone conversations between the police and the informant included comments by the police instructing H. to “push him for what you can” and disclosed evidence of concerted police coaching. The applicant was invited to comment on the recordings made in February and March 1995. He made no comment to any question. According to the applicant, he was interrogated according to the police. He availed himself of that right. After 20 April 1995 he associated regularly with the applicant who was remanded at Strangeways Prison. H. had been fitted with recording devices. The high point of H.'s evidence was the assertion that the applicant had admitted his presence at the murder scene. This asserted admission was not part of the recorded interview and was disputed. The thrust of the applicant's case was that he was discussing robberies and did not accede to H.''s efforts to channel their conversation into a discussion of the murder. No evidence, other than the alleged admissions, connected the applicant with the killing of Mr Beesley. The judge concluded that there was evidence on the tapes from which the jury could infer that the. applicant was involved in the events of 3 February 1995, and it was not so unreliable that it could not be left to the jury to assess for themselves. The judge's ruling on the admissibility of the evidence was given on 26 January 1998, after a voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of a jury) and consisted of a judgment of eighteen pages. H. was accordingly admitted before the jury. In his summing-up to the jury on 10 and 11 February 1998, the trial judge gave directions on the way in which the jury should assess the reliability of the disputed evidence. He told them that they were to judge whether the police had deliberately wound up the applicant during the interview on 28 June 1995 and how to approach the evidence put forward by H. train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were all former members of the Turkish Armed Forces, who had been discharged for disciplinary reasons. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42967/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights under Articles 4 and 9 of the Convention on the ground of his religion. By a decision of 1 February 2005 the Court declared the application partly admissible.Neither the applicant nor the Government filed further written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court ruled that the application was admissible on the grounds of the case's merits. The Court also dismissed the claim that the applicant had been denied equal protection under the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was ordered to undergo another examination as to his ability to perform military service pursuant to section 24(8) of the Military Service Act (Wehrgesetz), as in force at the relevant time. The applicant appealed against that order, claiming in particular that he should be dispensed from military service since he performed a function within the Jehovah’s Witnesses which was equivalent to that of members of a recognised religious society. To restrict such a privilege to members of recognised religious societies was not objectively justified and was therefore in breach of the Federal Constitution. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint on 26 March 1998. On 1 December 1997 the Constitutional Court refused to deal with the applicant’S complaint for lack of prospects of success. The Lower Austrian Military Authority issued another conscription order for an examination of the applicant’s fitness to perform military service. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court against the order. He submitted in particular that by virtue of the 1998 Act, the Jehovah's Witnesses had been granted the status of a “registered religious community’. However, the ten-year period for a successful application for recognition under the Recognition Act (Anerkennungsgesetz) lacked objective justification, he argued. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint for lack of prospects of success. He filed a request for recognition as a conscientious objector (Zivildiensterklärung), which was granted.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56827/00) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court (Second Section) declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the military court. The applicant was represented by Ms A. J. Stock, Mr M. Muller, Mr T. Otty and Ms J. Gordon of the Kurdish Human Rights Project in London. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The case brought before the Ankara Military Court of the Office of the Chief of Staff was concluded on 29 August. The public prosecutor at the Ankara State Security Court took the applicant's statement in which the applicant reiterated the content of his petition. He maintained that, by publishing and distributing the above-mentioned leaflet, he had committed the same offence for which O. M. U. had been convicted. He concluded that his aim was to obtain the abolition of compulsory military service in Turkey. He claimed that the leaflet was not intended to dissuade people from doing military service or to incite them to desert. He further stated that in the Netherlands conscientious objectors did not do their military service, but were given other jobs. He commented that maybe in the future the same would be true for Turkey. O. M. U. was sentenced to two months' imprisonment and a fine of 1,520,000 Turkish Liras (TL) (approximately 3.5 Euros (EUR) at the time of the events) The court held that it had competence to deal with the case pursuant to the Constitution and domestic law. The court, relying on Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution, affirmed that freedom of expression and the free dissemination of ideas was not an absolute right. In its decision the court, referring to domestic law and the jurisprudence of the Court, concluded that the judgment given by the General Staff Court was in accordance with the law.

It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 §§ 3). The applicants were born in 1951, 1950, 1964 and 1962 respectively. The first three applicants live in Turkey and the fourth applicant lives in France. The applicants brought an action before the Kahta Civil Court of First Instance for prohibition of the third party's unlawful occupation of their land. The third party brought a counter action against the applicants. The case was heard at the Kahta Cadastral Court. The applicants and the Directorate appealed. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment on 29 January 2001. On 13 July 2004 it dismissed the third party's rectification request. The appeal was dismissed on 19 July 2004. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court of Justice of the Republic of Slovenia. The court has the power to order the registration of the land in the name of the applicants. The application was heard in front of a panel of seven judges, three of whom were women. The hearing was held at the  Kahta Cadastral Court on 17 April 2003.

name: Metin Gültekin
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their close relative, Toğay Gültekin, had died while doing his compulsory military service owing to the authorities’ failure to ensure prompt access to medical treatment for his serious health problems. The application was communicated to the Government on 2 April 2014. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The first two applicants are the parents, the third applicant is the brother and the fourth applicant is his fiancée. The incident took place on 22 March 2004 in Kırklareli. At 5.15 p.m. on 27 March 2004 he died at the GATA Hospital. No autopsy was performed. Toğay Gültekin had spoken to his commanding officer on 16 February 2004 and told him that a friend of his had hepatitis and that he had suspected that he might also have contracted the same disease. His superior had then transferred him to the regiment’s infirmary where tests had been conducted, establishing that he did not have hepatitis. The military officers who carried out the investigation concluded, on the basis of the statements referred to above, that the military authorities had acted in accordance with their duties. Toğay Gültekin had been performing his military service and had thus not had the opportunity to leave his military unit and seek medical assistance of his own volition. A blood test had been conducted, but the results had not revealed any abnormalities. The applicants argued that it had been these inordinate delays that had caused Toğay Gül Tekin’s death. The Ministry of Defence maintained that the military authorities had not acted in a negligent fashion when dealing with Toğays' medical problems. The case is still pending at the Military Administrative Court of Turkey, where the judge will rule on whether or not to order a retrial of the case. Military Administrative Court appointed three medical experts to clarify whether the military authorities had acted negligently. Medical experts reached the following conclusion in their report of 20 September 2005. Toğay Gültekin started his military service on 22 August 2003. On 2 January 2004 he was treated for a retractile testicle at Çorlu Military Hospital. He was prescribed medication at the regiment’s infirmary for an upper respiratory tract infection on 5 January 2004. On 17 March 2004 the regimentalinfirmary doctor decided to refer him to an infectious diseases clinic, but that was not done. On 20 March 2004 he. was diagnosed with and treated for an infection of the upper respiratory. tract. On 22 March 2004, he was referred to the University Hospital with suspected hepatitis and. he was sent there. On 23 March2004 he was diagnosed. with fulminant hepatitis. He died on 27 March 2004. Gültekin was contaminated with both hepatitis A and hepatitis B viruses within a short period of time and his liver was infected with both viruses at the same time. This is a condition which worsens the damage to the liver and increases the risk of fulminant hepatitis (fast-deteriorating acute liver failure) The applicants lodged an objection to this report. They maintained that the authorities had acted negligently as they had delayed Toğay Güllekin’s transfer to hospital. On 26 October 2005 the Military Administrative Court dismissed the applicants’ claim. In its decision the court relied on the medical expert report summarised above (see paragraph 18) and concluded that no fault could be attributed to the authorities for Toğy Gülekin's death. Military Administrative Court refused to entertain the rectification request lodged by the applicants. in failing to refer Toğay Gültekin to hospital between 17 and 23 March 2004. On 28 December 2005 the Military Administrative court refused to entertained the rectified request lodged. At 5.15 p.m. on 27 March 2004 he died at the GATA Hospital. No autopsy was performed. An investigation was carried out at the military unit where Toğay Gültekin had been doing his military service. The military officers who carried out the investigation concluded that the military authorities had acted in accordance with their duties and that there had been no fault attributable to them in his death. The applicants initiated compensation proceedings against the Ministry of Defence before the Supreme Military Administrative Court. They argued that he had not received prompt or adequate medical care in his regiment. When his condition had deteriorated he had been examined by a doctor attached to his regiment and that the doctor had recommended his transfer to a hospital. Toğay Gültekin had been performing his military service and had thus not had the opportunity to leave his military unit and seek medical assistance of his own volition. He had been under an obligation to protect his well-being and to ensure timely medical treatment for him. The Ministry of Defence maintained that the military authorities had not acted in a negligent fashion when dealing with his medical problems. It argued that the soldiers from the same regiment had told his superior that his friend had contracted hepatitis and that he suspected that he himself might have been infected as well. The applicants submitted that there was no evidence to show that a blood test had been carried out on 16 February 2004. Medical experts reached the following conclusion in their report of 20 September 2005: “... Toğay Gültekin was contaminated with both hepatitis A and hepatitis B viruses within a short period of time. His liver was infected with both viruses at the same time. This is a condition which worsens the damage to the liver and increases the risk of fulminant hepatitis (fast-deteriorating acute liver failure) The Military Administrative Court dismissed the applicants’ claim. In its decision the court relied on the medical expert report summarised above (see paragraph 18) and concluded that no fault could be attributed to the authorities for Toğay Güllekin’s death. Gültekin was accused of failing to refer him to hospital between 17 and 23 March 2004. Military Administrative Court refused to entertain the rectification request lodged by the applicants in December 2005. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court of Justice of the Republic of Turkey, which is in the process of deciding whether or not it should be reheard. The appeal was denied by the court on December 29, 2005, and the case was dismissed on December 30, 2005. name: Sahro Osman
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38058/09) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8 of the convention. On 1 February 2011 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed First Section. The case was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant's father returned to Denmark in 2003. He was summoned for an interview with the Immigration Service on 10 November 2003. The Immigration Service found that the applicant’s residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. They also considered that she was not entitled to a new residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii) since the applicant was 17 years old. Finally, it found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permitunder section 9 c, section 9(1), section 9 (2) and 9 (3) of the Alien Act. Immigration Service received a questionnaire from the applicant dated 12 July 2007 used for requests for exemption from the authorities revoking a residence permit. It was partly filled out and stated, inter alia, that it had been the applicant’s parents’ decision that she should leave Denmark at the relevant time. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg, Denmark. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. On 1 October 2007 the Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs upheld the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. The Ministry emphasises that there is no information available of any circumstances that would lead to [the applicant's] residence permit being deemed not to have lapsed. The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret) The applicant’s representative in his written submissions stated that the applicant remained in Kenya. On 25 April 2008 it found against the applicant. It added that section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act had been amended, limiting the right to family re-unification to children under 15 years instead of under 18 years. It was preferable for foreign minors living in Denmark to arrive as early as possible and spend as many of their formative years as possible in Denmark. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant's parents sent her voluntarily to Kenya to live with family for an indefinite period. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on 19 January 2008. 30 October 2008 the High Court upheld the City Court’s decision. By letter of 27 January 2010 the Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien's Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. She has not applied for asylum so far and the case is currently pending.
