The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) by a Somali national, Mrs Sahro Osman (‘the applicant’), on 19 July 2009. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8 of the convention. The Danish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Thomas Winkler, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and their Co-Agent, Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen, from Ministry of Justice. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court. Immigration Service ruled that the applicant's father's residence permit had not lapsed. The applicant had taken care of her grandmother, who had fallen seriously ill, until some of the grandmother’s children had arrived from Somalia to take over the care of their mother. The Immigration Service found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permit under section 9 c, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act. They also considered that she was not entitled to a new residence permit since the applicant was 17 years old and the said provision only extended a right to family reunification to children below the age of 15. It also found that she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months because she had not contacted the Immigration Service. The applicant appealed against the decision to withdraw her residence permit in April 2007. The Migration Service upheld the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. In June 2007 the applicant re-entered Denmark clandestinely to live with her mother. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg, Denmark. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs (Ministeriet for flygtninge, indvandrere og integration) stated that there is no information available that would lead to [the applicant’s] residence permit being deemed not to have lapsed. The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret) The applicant’s representative in his written submissions stated that the applicant remained in Kenya. In April 2008 it found against the applicant. It added that section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act had been amended, limiting the right to family re-unification to children under 15 years instead of under 18 years. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention as invoked by the applicant in her appeal to the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret) On 11 December 2007 the Immigration Service brought the case concerning section 17 and section 9,. subsections 1, 2, and 3, of the Immigration Act before the city court of Copenhagen. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on 19 January 2008. 30 October 2008 the High Court upheld the City Court’s decision. Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien's Act and the possibility of submitting an application for asylum under section 7 of the Aliens Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. The Court of Appeal ruled that the applicant failed to fulfil the conditions of a residence permit.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3084/07) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant company alleged that a court judgment under the Media Act ordering it to pay damages had infringed its right to freedom of expression under Article 10. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 January 2009. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The Court ruled in favour of the applicant company and ordered the Austrian Government to pay a fine. Elaine B. (name changed, ed.) had been ill-treated by police officers in Cameroon. She was placed with 18 other women in ‘stinking, damp cells’ for having demonstrated on behalf of her son, abducted by the authorities. Her case was so well documented that Austria, in the form of the normally very strict Federal Refugee Office, granted her asylum quickly and without red tape. But then this country revealed its other side. Elaine B., 35, a well-groomed businesswoman and mother of three, holds on tight to her handbag during the interview and breaks down in tears repeatedly, says her life is a mess. She can no longer trust the authorities here because they treat her like a liar and a prostitute. Security officers at the centre later state in court that female asylum seekers could be paid for quick sex. They also tell of pimps rolling up to the centre in their cars. ‘Please help us!’ pleaded the women. The Interior Ministry stated at the time that the police were confronted with a ‘wall of silence’ Elaine B. from Cameroon demanded an interview with the head of the Traiskirchen [branch of the] Gendarmerie. She described ‘through her tears’ how a drunken security officer had pursued her for days, pointing to his uniform and threatening to have her thrown out of the centre and to slit her throat. Elaine B. describes with precision how the man locked the door and removed the key. She tells of the pains in her lower abdomen afterwards and how she washed herself with warm water for weeks. She immediately identifies the security officer in a photo. For the first interview in the interview room no trained interpreter can be found. In their minutes the police officers at times refer to Elaine B. not by her name but as ‘the nigger woman’ She is repeatedly linked to prostitution. Police: ‘Could the woman have left the room if she’d wanted to?’ ‘No, only I had a key’ Elaine B. denies this version of events. She says that she had other things on her mind at the time. She felt repelled by this fat man with a moustache who smelled of alcohol, she was afraid of him. If she had really been hoping to be granted asylum, why would she then have defamed the security officer? Next to take the witness stand are the employees of the bakery. Saleswoman R.Z.: ‘She gave him a kiss. She was fairly young, I’d say between 20 and 25. I couldn’t describe the woman’ When confronted with Elaine B. says: ‘I’m not quite sure whether it’s her’ According to the court, the bakery employees could not have identified Elaine. No evidence is taken either from other asylum seekers or from the female staff in the women’s quarters. Judge I.K. acquits the security officer. ‘He is a very simple man’ and it therefore spoke in his favour ‘that he himself admitted that intercourse with the witness was not easy to achieve’ The ‘black African’ on the other hand, appeared ‘very confident’, with the result that ‘it is hard to imagine that she could have felt so intimidated by the accused, who appears somewhat unsure of himself’ Elaine B. must appear before the investigating judge ‘or be brought by force’ She could face up to five years in prison. ‘That’s just routine, nothing unusual’ says a Justice Ministry spokesman. Judge I.K. brought an action for defamation against the applicant company under section 6 of the Media Act and Article 111 of the Criminal Code. The judge ignored relevant evidence and delivered a scandalous judgment (“The judgment fails to give rise to a scandal”) Justice Minister K.M. has promised to do more to protect the victims of crime. She should study this case. The applicant company argued that the impugned statements were true. It sought to prove the truth of those statements by asking the court to call several witnesses and admit as evidence the files of the proceedings concerning K.’s asylum request and the criminal proceedings against H.P. In October 2005 the applicant company sought the disqualification of Judge N.F. for bias. The president of the Vienna Regional Court dismissed the motion on 17 October 2005 and held that the issue raised by the applicant was not sufficient to give rise to doubt that the judge would not decide the case objectively. In December 2005 the Regional Court held another hearing in the defamation proceedings in which it examined two of the witnesses proposed. The third witness proposed did not appear. The Regional Court found that the contents of the article had given a biased account of the taking of evidence at the trial of H.P. The judge had acted arbitrarily and out of racist motives and had disregarded evidence produced, whereas the rape asserted by K. had been described as proven and the assessment of evidence by the Regional Court as absurd. I.K. was therefore entitled to compensation, which it set at 7,000 euros (EUR) It also ordered the applicant company to publish a summary of the judgment. An earlier version of this article stated that the accused was acquitted on the basis of the principle of in dubio pro reo. We are happy to clarify that this was not the case. The Regional Court found that the applicant company had not succeeded in proving the truth of the impugned statements. The accusation that a judge, who was under the duty to act objectively and impartially, had deliberately disregarded evidence in order to acquit an accused from the same country had to be qualified as defamation. The term scandal of justice was a value judgement, which, however, was based on assertions of fact which had been disproven in the proceedings. An error in the translation of that statement could not be excluded, but that did not allow the conclusion that there had been no basis in the file for the above finding of Judge I.K. The Regional Court referred to the case of Prager and Oberschlick v. Austria (26 April 1995, Series A no. 313), and observed that the press had the right and the duty to impart information on matters of public interest. It was therefore necessary to protect public confidence in the judiciary against destructive attacks that were essentially unfounded. Taking these principles into account, the sharp critique of Judge I.K. in the impugned article, which had lacked any sufficient factual basis, had been excessive. The Regional Court found that the amount of EUR 7,000 in compensation was appropriate. The applicant company appealed on 8 March 2006 against the Regional Court’s judgment. On 19 June 2006 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment.

The hearing was adjourned on 19 December 1995 and legal aid was granted to enable their solicitor to travel to Italy where, it was believed, Rudi Steiner was in custody awaiting trial. The applicants' solicitor was able to obtain a number of documents relating to the Italian proceedings, including transcripts of interviews with Mr Steiner. The applicants added a further ground of appeal, alleging that the prosecution had failed to make full disclosure of the evidence in its possession concerning Mr Steiners. The case was adjourned until after the conclusion of the trial in Italy in the Autumn of 1996. In the event, however, MrSteiner was released on bail and his whereabouts were unknown at the time of the applicants’ appeal hearing in February 1997. He was called by the defence to give evidence. He said he would be willing to appear as a witness in the Court of Appeal. Court of Appeal ruled that justice did not require disclosure by the Crown of the public interest immunity evidence. The applicants and their lawyers were not permitted to be present when the court delivered its judgment on disclosure. It observed: “Little, if any, of the material [put before the Court of Appeal by the applicants’ counsel] would have been admissible at the trial. That is not only because it is largely hearsay and unspecific as to events and dates, but simply because much of it is wholly irrelevant to the central issue in this case’. The court dismissed the application for leave to appeal on 20 February 1997. Prosecuting counsel suggested that the only way Steiner could have been sure of achieving such an end would have been to persuade the officers to ‘plant’ the drug on, or falsely attribute it to, Thierry or Terrasson. Such a conspiracy between Steiner and the officers would have was hard for them to organise to an assured outcome. There are also a number of other questions indicating the impossibility of the Atlans’ defence. Why, if they thought they were to collect diamonds from Steiner, not drugs, did they immediately check their luggage onto the return flight without apparently enquiring by telephone why he had not turned up or whether he had been delayed? Why did Smolny and the two of them make no contact in Copenhagen and ignore each other on the plane to Heathrow? ‘Whatever Steiner’s possible role as an informer, the Atlans’ guilty participation in cocaine smuggling is clear.’ ‘All that activity pointed only to their involvement in the high value and high risk activity of drug smuggling, not some black market dealing in gems under Brazilian law' ‘The evidence against them, which had been thoroughly and robustly tested at the trial, was overwhelming. ...’‘Their lies on arrest and in interview. name: Ahmet Sürgit
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Ahmet Sürgit asked for compensation in an amount equal to half the value of the flat he and his former wife had bought in 1998. The applicant was unemployed and unable to provide even a basic level of financial support for his wife. It was concluded that, given his financial situation, the applicant could not have contributed enough to the purchase of the Flat in question to be entitled to claim a share in it. The court further noted that, at the time of purchase, the legal matrimonial regime was the system of separation of property. The Court of Cassation rejected the applicant's appeal and rectification requests. The flat was registered in the wife's name. The appeal was dismissed on 29 December 2005 and 14 April 2006 respectively. The application was brought by the wife of a former mayor of the city. The case was settled out of court in 2005. The wife was awarded damages of £10,000. She appealed the decision, but it was rejected in April 2006. The couple's appeal was rejected again in December 2005. Their appeal was also dismissed in March 2006. It was decided that the flat should be registered in the wife’s name.

It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in İzmir. He and his wife bought a flat in 1998. In 1999 the applicant’s wife initiated divorce proceedings against the applicant and in 2000 the divorce was pronounced. The court held that the applicant could not have contributed enough to the purchase of the flat in question to be entitled to claim a share. On 29 December 2005 and 14 April 2006 respectively, the Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s appeal and rectification requests. the flat was registered in the wife's name. the appeal was rejected and the wife was allowed to move in with her husband. The couple married in 2003 and have a daughter, a son, and a daughter-in-law. They have a son and daughter who were born in 2007 and 2008. The wife was granted a restraining order in 2010 and the couple have a new son, a boy, born in March 2011. The application was rejected on April 14, 2012 and the family was awarded a settlement on April 23, 2012.

The Appeal was rejected on December 29, 2005 and again on April 14, 2006 respectively. The appeals were dismissed on both occasions.

name: Martha Nölkenbockhoff
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 28 January 1986. It originated in an application (no. 10300/83) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6. The Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Lutz and Englert cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality. The Government had until 1 July 1986 to file memorials and that the Delegate of the Commission should be entitled to reply in writing within two months. The applicant’s memorial - drafted in German - was lodged with the registry on 1 July. The Government's memorial was lodged on 19 November. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government, by. Mr. Weitzel for the Commission and by Mr. Bergemann for the applicant, as well as. their replies to its questions. The Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court (Rule 50). Martha Nölkenbockhoff is the widow of Mr. Theodor Nölbockhoff, who died in 1981. Her husband was a senior manager in a holding company, Stumm AG, whose trading activities centred on iron, steel and fuel, including motor fuel. On 13 November 1974 he was arrested under a warrant issued by the Essen District Court on 11 November; he was suspected among other things of bankruptcy offences. The trial hearings began on 29 October 1976 before the 6th Criminal Chamber (6. Grosse Strafkammer) and lasted until 11 July 1980, two or three hearings being held each week. The applicant’s husband was defended by two counsel, one of whom was assigned by the court. Mr. Nölkenbockhoff entered an appeal on points of law on the same day that judgment was given. In determining the sentences, the Regional Court took into account as extenuating circumstances the length of the proceedings and, in respect of the applicant’s husband, his detention on remand for some three years. The Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof) had not given a decision by the time he died on 13 November, so that the proceedings came to an end without any decision being taken on his appeal. Three of the co-defendants, who had likewise challenged the regional Court’S judgment, later withdrew their appeals. The fourth person convicted, Mr. M, was dismissed by the Federal Court on 7 July 1982 as being manifestly ill-founded. Essen Regional Court found against Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff. Decision read as follows: “... The applications are admissible ... but ill-founded.” Where proceedings are terminated by reason of a defendant’s death, his necessary costs and expenses are normally borne by the Treasury. This does not apply where, were it not for this technical bar, the defendant would almost certainly have been convicted or his conviction almost certainly has been upheld. The defendant had already been found guilty, in a judgment that had not become final, after lengthy court proceedings in a trial (Hauptverhandlung) lasting more than three and a half years. The court declines to award compensation for the time spent in detention on remand, pursuant to section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. The court does not consider it necessary to defer judgment until a decision has been given on the co-defendant M’s appeal on points of law. “The applicant appealed to the Hamm Court of Appeal against that decision on 11 March 1982. In written pleadings dated 18 March, she challenged, inter alia, the Regional Court's finding that, had her husband not died, he “would almost certainly have been convicted or his conviction almost certainly would have been upheld“. The Regional Court disregarded the presumption of innocence in stating that the grounds of appeal afforded no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The applicant had requested an adjournment to await the judgment of the Federal Court of Justice in the appeal proceedings brought by one of the co-defendants. Since criminal law was based on the principle of individual guilt, it was quite simply unacceptable - and, once again, contrary to Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) - to judge the deceased. The Hamm Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 14 July 1982. It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss) of criminal proceedings, a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy, under Article 467 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act (see paragraphs 24-26 below) The application was dismissed on 7 July 1982 by the Federal Court of Justice. Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court. A bench of three judges of the Constitutional Court refused to entertain the constitutional complaint. The reasons for its decision were as follows: “The presumption of innocence, which is founded on the principle of the rule of law, precludes treating as guilty a person who has not been finally (rechtskräftig) convicted. That does not mean, however, that in every case costs must be reimbursed where the proceedings are terminated without guilt having been established (Schuldnachweis) ...“ The decision on the claim for compensation is based on section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. Both provisions confer on the courts a degree of discretion. The courts’ reference to the lack of success of the appeal proceedings instituted by the co-defendant M. and to the withdrawal of the appeals on points of law entered by the other defendants is clearly to be regarded as an additional argument, and the impugned decisions are not based on it. Nor do the grounds advanced in support of the constitutional complaint show the unreasonableness of the Regional Court’s opinion that, had the proceedings been continued, a conviction would have been more likely than an acquittal. The only relevant issue for the order as to costs. the proceedings had they been continued was whether the deceased defendant had been convicted of the offences of which he was convicted.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 28 January 1986. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 2. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Lutz and Englert cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Government and the Commission were asked to file memorials. The Court heard the oral proceedings on 23 February 1987. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government, Mr. Weitzel for the Commission and by Mr. Bergemann for the applicant. The Commission filed a number of documents and written comments either at the Court’s request or of their own motion. The case is still pending and will be heard by the Court of Appeal at the end of the year. The decision will be published in full at the bottom of this article. Martha Nölkenbockhoff is the widow and heir of Mr. Theodor N Ölken bockhoff. Her husband was a senior manager in a holding company, Stumm AG, whose trading activities centred on iron, steel and fuel. He was found guilty inter alia on several charges of breach of trust (Untreue), criminal bankruptcy (Bankrott) and fraud (Betrug) and given an aggregate sentence of eight years’ imprisonment. His four co-defendants were also sentenced to prison terms - two of them, for more or less identical offences and a few additional ones, to nine years, nine months. Mr. Nölkenbockhoff was convicted in 1980 on charges of aggravated DWI and money laundering. He had been detained on remand for three years. He filed a full appeal on points of law on the same day that judgment was given. The Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof) had not given a decision by the time he died on 13 November, so that the proceedings came to an end without any decision being taken on his appeal. Three of the co-defendants, who had likewise challenged the Regional Court’s judgment, later withdrew their appeals. The fourth person convicted, Mr. M, was dismissed by the Federal Court on 7 July 1982 as being manifestly ill-founded. In 1982, the Essen Regional Court found against Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff. The defendant had already been found guilty, in a judgment that had not become final, after lengthy court proceedings in a trial (Hauptverhandlung) lasting more than three and a half years. The judgment convicting the three co-defendants ..., who were likewise sentenced to several years’ imprisonment, has become final. Three of the defendants ... have withdrawn their appeals on points of law, thereby confirming the judgment against them, argues decisively in favour of the correctness (materielle Richtigkeit) of the judgment. The submissions made by the defence afford no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted had the proceedings continued. The court declines to award compensation for the time spent in detention on remand, pursuant to section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. In view of the reasons given for the judgment, it was much more likely, having regard to the adverse financial position of the Stumm holding company, that if the proceedings had continued, the defendant would have been convicted on the counts in question. The court does not consider it necessary to defer judgment until a decision has been given on the co-defendant M’s appeal on points of law. ....“The applicant appealed to the Hamm Court of Appeal against that decision on 11 March 1982. She claimed that that statement was erroneous and infringed the Basic Law (Grundgesetz) The Regional Court disregarded the presumption of innocence in stating that the grounds of appeal afforded no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The applicant pointed out in addition that from the outset her husband had denied having committed any offences and had indeed been acquitted on several counts. Since criminal law was based on the principle of individual guilt, it was quite simply unacceptable - and, once again, contrary to Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) - to judge the deceasedby the conduct of three of the co-defendants. On 28 December 1981, the Bochum public prosecutor submitted that, having regard to the state of the proceedings, there was every likelihood (hohe Wahrscheinlichkeit) that the conviction would have been upheld. The Hamm Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 14 July 1982. It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss) of criminal proceedings, a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy, under Article 467 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) claiming a breach of the Basic Law. On 30 September 1982, a bench of three judges of the Constitutional Court refused to entertain the constitutional complaint. The reasons for its decision were as follows: “The presumption of innocence, which is founded on the principle of the rule of law, precludes treating as guilty a person who has not been finally (rechtskräftig) convicted.” The decision on the claim for compensation is based on section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. Both provisions confer on the courts a degree of discretion. The courts' reference to the lack of success of the appeal proceedings instituted by the co-defendant M and to the withdrawal of the appeals on points of law entered by the other defendants is clearly to be regarded merely as an additional argument, and the impugned decisions are not based on it. (bb) Nor do the grounds advanced in support of the constitutional complaint show the unreasonableness of the Regional Court’s opinion that, had the proceedings been continued, a conviction would have been more likely than an acquittal ... [in connection with the charge in respect of which the proceedings had been provisionally stayed] ... ....“

The Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof) had not given a decision by the time he died on 13 November, so that the proceedings came to an end without any decision being taken. The appeal lodged by the fourth person convicted, Mr. M, was dismissed by the Federal Court as being manifestly ill-founded. The trial was held in Essen, Germany, in 1982. Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff had already been found guilty, in a judgment that had not become final, after lengthy court proceedings in a trial (Hauptverhandlung) lasting more than three and a half years. Three of the defendants have withdrawn their appeals on points of law, thereby confirming the judgment against them. The judgment convicting the three co-defendants ..., who were likewise sentenced to several years’ imprisonment, has become final. Co-defendant M is maintaining his appeal on points  of law. The submissions made by the defence in its full pleadings afford no reason to suppose the defendant would have been acquitted had the proceedings continued. The court declines to award compensation for the time spent in detention on remand, pursuant to section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. The court does not consider it necessary to defer judgment until a decision has been given on the co-defendant M’s appeal on points of law. The applicant appealed to the Hamm Court of Appeal against that decision on 11 March 1982. In written pleadings dated 18 March, she challenged, inter alia, the Regional Court's finding that, had her husband not died, he “would almost certainly have been convicted or his conviction almost certainly would have been upheld’. The Regional Court disregarded the presumption of innocence in stating that the grounds of appeal afforded no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The applicant had requested an adjournment to await the judgment of the Federal Court of Justice in the appeal proceedings brought by one of the co-defendants. Since criminal law was based on the principle of individual guilt, it was quite simply unacceptable - and, once again, contrary to Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) of the Convention. The Hamm Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 14 July 1982. It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss), a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy, under Article 467§ 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act (see paragraphs 24-26 below) The application was. dismissed. on 6 July 1982, after the applicant had pointed to the indictment, the judgment convicting the defendants, and the appeals. Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff applied to the Federal Constitutional Court claiming a breach of the Basic Law. A bench of three judges of the Constitutional Court refused to entertain the constitutional complaint. The reasons for its decision were as follows: “The presumption of innocence, which is founded on the principle of the rule of law, precludes treating as guilty a person who has not been finally (rechtskräftig) convicted” The case was settled in 1982. The decision on the claim for compensation is based on section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. The court's refusal of the applications for an order that the Treasury should bear the deceased defendant’s necessary costs and expenses was upheld. The courts’ reference to the lack of success of the appeal proceedings instituted by the co-defendant M and to the withdrawal of the appeals on points of law entered by the other defendants is clearly to be regarded as an additional argument, and the impugned decisions are not based on it. Nor do the grounds advanced in support of the constitutional complaint show the unreasonableness of the Regional Court’s opinion that, had the proceedings been continued, a conviction would have been more likely than an acquittal ... ....’”. “Eine derartige Einschätzung enthält indessen nicht die Feststellung einer Schuld, sondern lediglich die Fest stellung  einer fortbestehenden Verdachtslage’.

name: John Blackgrove
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2895/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant and his wife had two children, born in 1982 and 1987. He applied for benefits equivalent to those which a widow, whose husband had died in similar circumstances to those of his wife, would have been entitled, namely a Widow’s Payment (Wpt) and a Widowed Mother's Allowance (WMA) On 17 October 2000 his application was rejected as these benefits were only available to women. On 5 October 2000 the applicant applied to the Benefits Agency for the payment of social security benefits. This decision was reconsidered without alteration on 25 October 2000.

name: Mark Anthony Grieves
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 57067/00) lodged on 26 April 2000 with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that he did not receive a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law in violation of Article 6. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section. On 6 May 2003 a Chamber of that Section relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber. The Grand Chamber notified the parties that it might decide to examine the merits of the complaint before it at the same time as its admissibility. The parties decided to put an additional question to the parties. The applicant was convicted of unlawfully and maliciously wounding with intent to do grievous bodily harm. He was sentenced to three years' imprisonment and to be dismissed from the service and reduced in rank. The Government and the applicant each filed written observations on the admissibility and merits together with separate submissions on the applicable domestic law and practice. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 1 October 2003 (Rule 59 § 3 of the Rules of Court). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr J. Grainger, Agent, Mr P. Havers, Q.C., Counsel, Ms T. Jones, Mr H. Morrison, Mr E. Latham, Air Vice-Marshal R. Charles, Commodore J. Blackett, Commander S. Taylor, Brigadier T. Paphiti, Advisers. The applicant chose to be represented by a naval barrister. The Judge Advocate directed the members of the court-martial as follows: “As Judge Advocate it's my role to ensure that the trial is conducted in accordance with the law and I am here to advise and guide you” On 29 September 1998 the Navy Board decided not to vary the trial's verdict and sentence. On 30 June 1999 a single judge of the Courts-Martial Appeal Court rejected his appeal, as did the full court on 20 January 2000. In his advice to the Navy board, the Judge Advocate of the Fleet commented that. the trial had been “well conducted by all concerned”, that the main directions of law in the. Judge Advocate's summing up were “impeccable” and that any errors were, in any event, favourable to the applicant.

name: Oliver Riepan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35115/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him, relating to charges of threatening behaviour, he did not have a public hearing. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 15 June 2000 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 29 August 2000 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr W. Okresek, Head of the Constitutional Law Section at the Federal Chancellery, Agent, Mrs E. Schindler. Steyr Regional Court decided to hold the hearing at Garsten Prison, which is situated about 5 km from Steyr. It set down 29 January 1996 as the date for the trial. The summons indicating the date and place of the hearing was served on the applicant as well as on his official defence counsel a month before the hearing. On account of these incidents, criminal proceedings on charges of threatening behaviour (gefährliche Drohung) were instituted against the applicant. The hearing list was distributed by the public prosecutor's office to the media, namely to the most important national and regional newspapers. The Government were unable to provide the list for the week of 29 January1996, as these lists are not kept. The applicant filed an appeal on points of law and fact, as well as against sentence (Berufung wegen Nichtigkeit, Schuld und Strafe) He complained, in particular, that the hearing on 29 January 1996 had not been public since it took place in the closed area of Garsten Prison. He also claimed that the room in which the hearing was held was too small to accommodate any spectators and alleged that not even the witnesses had been able to stay in the room simultaneously. Finally, he complained that the sentence was too severe. On 5 July 1996 the Linz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) held a public hearing in the court building in the presence of the applicant and his counsel. Hearing was public in the sense that any interested person would have been allowed to attend. No such persons wishing to attend the trial had been present at the beginning of the hearing. The Court of Appeal stated that it had no doubts regarding the Regional Court's evaluation of the evidence and its establishment of the facts. The appellate court also confirmed the legal view that the applicant had, by threatening prison personnel with arson or assault, committed the offence of threatening behaviour. Finally, it found that the sentence was commensurate with the applicant's guilt. The trial was held in a closed area of the prison, as the prison governor was not concerned that interested persons should not be granted access.

There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr W. Okresek, Head of the Constitutional Law Section at the Federal Chancellery, Agent, Mrs E. Schindler, Federal Ministry of Justice, Adviser, and for the applicant Mr H. Blum. The Steyr Regional Court (Landesgericht) decided to hold the hearing at Garsten Prison, which is situated about 5 km from Steyr. It set down 29 January 1996 as the date for the trial. The summons indicating the date and place of the hearing was served on the applicant as well as on his official defence counsel a month before the hearing. The public prosecutor's office at the Regional Court issued a hearing list (Verhandlungsspiegel) in the middle of each week for the following week. This information would also include the number of the court hearing room and would, if appropriate, indicate that the hearing would be held at the scene of the crime or the name of the prison at which it was to take place. The applicant, assisted by counsel, pleaded not guilty. The court heard the four prison officers to whom the applicant had allegedly addressed threats as witnesses. Following the hearing, the Regional Court convicted the applicant of threatening behaviour, finding that he had on three occasions threatened prison personnel with arson or assault. The applicant filed an appeal on points of law and fact, as well as against sentence (Berufung wegen Nichtigkeit, Schuld und Strafe). He complained, in particular, as a ground of nullity, that the hearing on 29 January 1996 had not been public since it took place in the closed area of Garsten Prison. The Court of Appeal dismissed the case. The Court of Appeal had no doubts regarding the Regional Court's evaluation of the evidence and its establishment of the facts. It also confirmed the legal view that the applicant had, by threatening prison personnel with arson or assault, committed the offence of threatening behaviour. Finally, it found that the sentence was commensurate with the applicant's guilt. The judge was not informed of any potential spectators at the beginning of the hearing. The trial was public in the sense that any interested person would have been allowed to attend. Had the prison governor been concerned that interested persons should not be granted access to the closed area, he would have had to prohibit the conduct of the trial in that area.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him, relating to charges of threatening behaviour, he did not have a public hearing as the trial was held in the prison where he was detained. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 29 August 2000 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr W. Okresek, Head of the Constitutional Law Section at the Federal Chancellery, Agent, Mrs E. Schindler, Federal Ministry of Justice, Adviser, and for the applicant Mr H. Blum. The Steyr Regional Court (Landesgericht) decided to hold the hearing at Garsten Prison, which is situated about 5 km from Steyr. The summons indicating the date and place of the hearing was served on the applicant as well as on his official defence counsel a month before the hearing. The hearing list was distributed by the public prosecutor's office to the media, namely to the most important national and regional newspapers. The Government were unable to provide the list for the week of 29 January 1996, as these lists are not kept, but asserted that it would, in accordance with the usual practice, have indicated Garsten prisons. The applicant had allegedly threatened prison personnel with arson or assault. The applicant filed an appeal on points of law and fact, as well as against sentence (Berufung wegen Nichtigkeit, Schuld und Strafe) On 5 July 1996 the Linz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) held a public hearing in the court building in the presence of the applicant and his counsel. The hearing lasted three-quarters of an hour. It heard the applicant as regards the alleged lack of publicity of the hearing on 29 January 1996. It also heard him on the various counts of threatening behaviour, questioning him as regards statements made by the witnesses at the trial. The Court of Appeal ruled that the sentence was commensurate with the applicant's guilt. The court also confirmed the Regional Court's legal view that the applicant had, by threatening prison personnel with arson or assault, committed the offence of threatening behaviour. The hearing was public in the sense that any interested person would have been allowed to attend. The judge had not been informed of any potential spectators at the beginning of the hearing. The applicant was sentenced to five years in prison for threatening prison staff with arson and assault. He was also sentenced to three years in jail for threatening the prison governor with arson. The trial was held in a closed area of the Steyr Regional Court. name: Jonathan Moore
train_texts: The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applications were introduced on 10 June and 7 August 1997 and were registered on 16 June and 18 August 1997 under file nos. 36529/97 and 37393/97, respectively. The applicants complained, under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, that they were denied a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. The first applicant also submitted that he was denied a voice in the choice of venue for his court-martial. The Government, represented by Mr Martin Eaton, Agent, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, responded by letter dated 21 August 1998, stating that the Government did not have any observations to make. On 2 March 1999 the Chamber decided to join the cases and not to hold a hearing on the merits. The Chamber also declared the applications admissible. Mr Moore was found guilty of common assault contrary to the Criminal Justice Act 1988 and he was fined £400, although the 1988 Act provides for a maximum sentence of six months’ imprisonment (see paragraph 16 below). His subsequent petitions and appeals, as far as the single judge of the Courts-Martial Appeal Court, were unsuccessful. Mr Gordon was found. guilty of two charges of disgraceful conduct of an indecent kind (in the. nature of indecent exposure, contrary to section 66 of the 1955 Act) and was sentenced to a reduction in rank.

name: Jerzy Biśta
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22807/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Polish national, Mr Jerzy Biśta (“the applicant’), on 29 May 2007. The applicant was arrested by officers of the Internal Security Agency (Agencja Bezpieczeństwa Wewnętrznego) on suspicion of revealing State secrets and bribery. The court found that there was a reasonable suspicion that the applicant, while at liberty, would have had unlimited opportunities to contact other persons who were directly linked to his criminal activities. The applicant was charged with revealing state secrets and bribery. His detention was prolonged on several occasions, inter alia on 7 November and 29 December 2005 by the Szczecin District Court. In all their decisions regarding detention the authorities repeatedly relied on the original grounds given for the applicant’s detention. The judge ruled that the risk that the accused might influence the outcome of the evidentiary proceedings had ceased to exist. No other preventive measure was used to keep the applicant in custody. The applicant was released on 11 October 2007 after his application for release was unsuccessful. The court held that even if grounds for the initial detention of the applicant still remained valid, they no longer sufficed to justify extending it further beyond the permissible period of two years. The applicant received a letter from the Szczecin Regional Court with a stamp “censored’ (“ocenzurowano”) on 22 October 2007. The Kraków Appeal Prosecutor appealed. On 6 November 2007 the applicant could be released if he put up bail of 50,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) In addition, an order was given to seize his passport and he was placed under police supervision. The applicant appealed and requested that the amount of bail be reduced. It appears that the applicant was eventually released on payment of the bail, at the latest on 15 December 2007. It seems that the criminal proceedings are currently pending.

name: Mohammad Kuranbay Babajanov
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49867/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr A. Yılmaz, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The Government were further requested to submit copies of administrative courts’ decisions in cases concerning removal of asylum seekers rendered subsequent to the entry into force of the Foreigners and International Protection Act (Law no. 6458) The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Turkey. He fled from Uzbekistan to Tajikistan because of pressure from the police. He feared, in particular, that if he stayed in Uzbekistan, he would face persecution from the State authorities. In 2005 he arrived in Iran, where he settled in Zahedan. In 2007 he decided to flee from Iran following deportation threats. He claimed that the threats had been a response to certain disagreements with the Iranian authorities over their living conditions. In November 2007 he entered Turkey illegally through Van and went to Ankara to apply for refugee status at the UNHCR. He was given a temporary residence permit until 24 September 2008 and was ordered to report to the police three times a week for signature. The applicant and Iran were granted similar certificates and permits after following the same procedural steps. The applicant was allegedly ill‑treated and threatened by the police during deportation. Iran together with the applicant were captured and held hostage by people smugglers, who demanded 5,000 U.S. dollars to spare their lives and to release them. The asylum seekers contacted some other Uzbeks who had managed to escape deportation from Turkey and obtained the ransom fee. The smugglers made them walk for three days to Yüksekova, a town close to the Iranian border of Turkey, where they were released. They requested legal advice from the Van Bar Association, which, along with two Turkish non-governmental organisations, published a report on 28 September 2008 regarding the Uzbek asylum seekers’ collective expulsion. It was argued in the report, inter alia, that the expulsion of the Uzbek by the Turkish State authorities had had no legal basis. The applicant and a number of other Uzbek nationals were deported to Iran in 2008. The applicant has been living in Turkey in hiding since then. On 4 December 2013 and 28 March 2014 he was interviewed by officers from the UNHCR’s Ankara office regarding his application for refugee status. He has not received any information from the Turkish authorities as to his request for asylum. The UNHCR also sent a letter to the Turkish government requesting the latter to grant the applicant and the other deportees residence permits with a view to legalizing their status in Turkey pending the completion of the procedures with regard to their cases. The application for asylum is still under consideration by the UNHCR. The applicant applied for asylum in Turkey in December 2007. He informed the authorities that he had been granted refugee status in Iran by the UNHCR. His application was registered and he was asked not to leave the city of Van. On 14 February 2008 the applicant left Van and returned there on 26 August 2008. He subsequently repeated his asylum request. He cannot appoint a lawyer to undertake the necessary legal and procedural actions on his behalf before the domestic authorities. The case originated in an application (no. 33379/96) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the length of the civil proceedings were in breach of the “reasonable time” requirement laid down in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 14 January 1998 the Commission decided to communicate the applicant’s complaint. The Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court. The Court found that the applicant had reduced the sums due following the annual statements of account, challenging the Court's decision to dismiss the application. The Federal Constitutional Court declared the relevant parts of the Act on the Use of EC Coal in the Electricity Supply (Gesetz über die weitere Sicherung des Einsatzes von Gemeinschaftskohle in der Elektrizitätswirtschaft) unconstitutional. The Second Division (Senat) of the Federal Constitutional court rendered a decision (of about 30 pages) upon the applicant's constitutional complaint. The Court found that, pursuant to the above legislation which continued to be in force until 31 December 1995, the applicant had to pay the above sum representing the coal-mining contribution.

train_texts: The case originated in an applications (nos. 265/07) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the decision to expel the first applicant to Nigeria with a prohibition of re-entry into Norway for a period of five years constituted a violation of Article 8 of the convention. By a decision of 22 November 2007, the Court declared the application admissible. The application was brought by Mr Louis Osaze Darren Omoregie, a Nigerian national; Mrs Elisabeth Skundberg Darren, a Norwegian national; and their daughter Selma. The first applicant applied for a work permit on the ground of family reunification. The Directorate of Immigration rejected the application on 26 April 2003 and ordered him to leave Norway. On 14 May 2003 the first applicant again appealed and requested stay of execution. Local police notified him thereof on 19 October 2003 with an order to leave the country by 30 October 2003. No judicial appeal was lodged against the above decisions, which became final on 2 February 2003. The first and second applicants got married. The case was decided by the Immigration Appeals Board on 7 October 2002, and the decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 7 September 2002. The decision was appealed, but the appeal was rejected on 1 October 2002. The Directorate of Immigration on 4 July 2003 warned him that it was contemplating to expel him pursuant to section 29(1)(a) of the Immigration Act. The Directorate considered that he had seriously contravened the provisions of the Act and had evaded implementation of the order to leave the country. The Immigration Appeals Board upheld the Directorate's rejection of his request for family reunification and its decision that the basic conditions for expelling the first applicant were fulfilled. It found that the applicant's alleged ignorance of the unlawfulness of his gainful occupation was no excuse. The Oslo City Court quashed the Immigration Appeals board's decision of 21 July 2004 as being invalid. The High Court found it established that the applicant had stayed lawfully in Norway from 25 August 2001 to 30 September 2002. He had reason to believe (as from February 2003) that he had a right to stay and to apply for a work permit and a residence permit. This was, relatively speaking, not a very serious offence, which fact counterbalanced his relatively weak links to Norway. To impose a prohibition on re-entry for five years would constitute a disproportionate measure towards the applicant and his family in the sense of section 29 of the Immigration Act. It could easily lead to the dissolution of the family. The second applicant would presumably have great difficulties of adaptation in the first applicant's home country. Even if he could apply for re- entry after two years, he would probably only be granted permission to come for shorter visits. The High Court observed that the central issue was the one of proportionality. He had arrived in Norway aged 22 years, without any links to the country. At the time of the impugned decision he had lived there for less than three years, parts of the time unlawfully. His stay in Norway had been very short and could not have given him any legitimate expectation of being able to live there. This was not significantly altered by his marriage to the second applicant, which had been entered into shortly before the disputed decision and in breach of the provisions on marriage. In this case there was no indication that expulsion would entail extra burdens of any kind beyond what followed from the separation. The High Court considered that the balance of interest was not in his favour. Were it to be otherwise, expulsion would be possible only in very rare cases. The High Court, taking into account the Strasbourg Court's case law, did not find that the disputed decision would be incompatible with Article 8 of the Convention. The applicants, represented by a lawyer, submitted an application under the Convention, which was received at the Registry on 3 January 2007. They complained that the first applicant's expulsion would entail a splitting of the family in breach of Article 8. It would not be possible for the second and third applicants to accompany him to Nigeria. Neither Article 8 nor the United Nations Children Convention could imply a different solution. On 5 January 2007 the President of the Section decided, in the circumstances, not to indicate to the Government of Norway, under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, the interim measure requested. The applicants' lawyer informed the Court that they wished to maintain their application notwithstanding the refusal to apply Rule 39. In the meantime, on 7 March 2007 the Implementation Group of the Oslo Police District expelled the first applicant back to Nigeria. The request had been made on the basis of a provision in the Immigration Regulation. which was applicable to cases of unmarried parents and therefore did not cover the applicants' case.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40016/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Supreme Court's decision not to recognise his right to succeed to a tenancy after the death of his companion amounted to discrimination on the ground of his sexual orientation. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 11 September 2001 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. On 7 December 2001 the President of the Chamber granted ILGA-Europe (The European Region of the International Lesbian and Gay Association), Liberty and Stonewall leave to intervene as third parties. The landlord of the flat brought proceedings against the applicant for termination of the tenancy. In 1994 Mr W. died after designating the applicant as his heir. In 1996 the Vienna Regional Civil Court dismissed the landlord's appeal. In 2000 the applicant died and his mother waived her right to succeed to the estate. In 2002 the public notary handling the applicant's estate had traced other heirs. The Court struck the application out of its list before the notary had traced the other heirs to the applicant. The application has since been appealed and the case continues to be heard by the Supreme Court of Austria. The case has been described as one of the most important cases in the history of the Rent Act.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42007/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, a breach of his right under Article 6 § 1 to a fair hearing within a reasonable time. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it partly inadmissible on 26 September 2000. The Third Section declared the application admissible insofar as the applicant complained about the length of the ‘Blackspur’ proceedings. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The hearing was to have lasted until July 1992, but was adjourned until July 1993. The hearing was called off because of lack of time, and two of the defendants were found guilty. The other two, however, were found not guilty and the case was dismissed. The case was eventually dismissed in May 1995, and the appeal was heard again in May 1996. The decision to dismiss the case again was made in August 1996, and was upheld by the Court of Appeal. The appeal was dismissed again in July 1997, with the final decision to continue the trial in March 1998. The judge found that the case should be dismissed because the evidence had not been presented in full. In the event, however, the Blackspur proceedings against the applicant were discontinued on 12 January 1998, after a “Carecraft” agreement (see paragraph 23 below) was reached between the applicant and the Secretary of State in other proceedings under the CDDA. As part of the settlement, the applicant agreed to pay the secretary of state's costs of GBP 94,000. The court observed that the delay had not affected the timing of the hearing or prejudiced the applicant, and that, once the proceedings had commenced, “the respondents' main concern was to delay the proceedings until after the conclusion of the criminal trial, not to hurry them on”

The Court declared the application partly admissible as regarded the applicant’s complaint of lack ofaccess to court, inadmissible as regards her children. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). An interim maintenance assessment (IMA) was issued with effect from 5 October 1995. Mr K’s liability changed many times after that date, inter alia as his employment changed and it proved difficult to obtain information. By March 1996 arrears of GBP 4,244 had accumulated. On 21 June 1996 a liability order was applied for because he had breached the agreement. Payments were not made and bailiffs were instructed to levy distress, but were unsuccessful. Following this Mr K again stopped paying. EOs on the company of which he was a director proved unsuccessful. Consideration was given to a committal order but the policy was to use this only as a last resort. The judge ruled that the Act was HRA compliant and she was not entitled to a declaration of incompatibility. The state has an interest, most directly in cases where public funds are disbursed, but also more generally that children should be adequately supported. The 1991 Act cannot in my opinion be interpreted as conferring any right on a parent in the position of Mrs [K]. She concluded that this was just the sort of policy choice in a socio-economic field which the courts were usually prepared to leave to the judgment of Parliament. All money owed to the applicant was paid by 27 April 2005 and her case was closed. She would therefore have allowed the appeal and restored Mr Justice Wall’s order. Payments were not made and bailiffs were instructed to levy distress, but were unsuccessful. In an interview with the CSA Mr K alleged that he had stopped paying as two of the qualifying children had been living with him for five years and a third had moved in recently. A payment of GBP 1,500 was made on 30 December 2002. The exclusion of the claimant from the enforcement process imposed a procedural bar on the prosecution/enforcement of the claim. The court held that under the scheme the applicant had no legal right in domestic law to a child maintenance payment of any particular amount or at all and that she was unable to assert an arguable civil right under Article 6 which entitled her to a determination by a court. The state has an interest, most directly in cases where public funds are disbursed, but also more generally that children should be adequately supported. The 1991 Act cannot in my opinion be interpreted as conferring any right on a parent in the position of Mrs [K]. But the right which she had enjoyed under the former legislation was removed, and the right to recover the maintenance has been vested in the CSA. The merits of that scheme are not for the House in its judicial capacity to evaluate. But plainly the scheme did not lack a coherent rationale. Baroness Hale noted that there was undoubtedly a legitimate aim. to the extent of the obligation but also as a limit to its enforcement. She concluded that this was just the sort of policy choice in a socio-economic field which the courts were usually prepared to leave to the judgment of Parliament. She considered that the public authority charged by Parliament with securing those rights was under a duty to act compliantly with Article 6. name: Gerard O’Halloran
train_texts: Case originated in two applications (nos. 15809/02 and 25624/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two British nationals, Mr Gerard O’Halloran and Mr Idris Richard Francis (“the applicants”), on 3 April 2002 and 15 November 2001 respectively. The applications were allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) On 11 April 2006 the Chamber relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, none of the parties having objected to relinquishment. Luzius Wildhaber and Matti Pellonpää continued to sit following the expiry of their terms of office. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 27 September 2006 (Rule 59 § 3) The Court heard addresses by Mr Emmerson and Mr Perry and their answers to questions put by judges. The applicants were born in 1933 and 1939 and live in London and Petersfield respectively. Mr O'Halloran (application no. 15809/02) was the registered keeper of T61 TBX. He was asked to furnish the full name and address of the driver of the vehicle on the relevant occasion or to supply other information that was in his power to give and which would lead to the driver’s identification. The applicant was convicted and fined 100 pounds sterling (GBP) and ordered to pay GBP 150 costs and his licence was endorsed with six penalty points. The application was refused in the light of the decision of the Privy Council in Brown v. Stott [2001] 2 WLR 817. Thereafter the prosecution relied upon the photograph of the speeding vehicle and the admission obtained as a result of the section 172 demand. The applicant sought to exclude the confession made in response to the Notice of Intended Prosecution, relying on sections 76 and 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 read in conjunction with Article 6 of the Convention. The applicant was summoned to the Magistrates’ Court for failing to comply with section 172(3) of the Road Traffic Act 1988. He was convicted and fined GBP 750 with GBP 250 costs and three penalty points. The applicant states that the fine was substantially heavier than that which would have been imposed if he had pleaded guilty to the speeding offence. He writes: ‘The penalty on conviction for failure to supply the information is similar to that for the offence itself, i.e. a fine and penalty points’ The applicant says he was the owner/keeper/driver or user for the above vehicle at the time of the alleged offence, and you are required to provide the full name and address.

The applicant sought to exclude the confession made in response to the Notice of Intended Prosecution, relying on sections 76 and 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 read in conjunction with Article 6 of the Convention.
