name: Louise O’Keeffe
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Irish national, Ms Louise O’Keeffe (‘the applicant’), on 16 June 2009. The applicant mainly complained that the system of primary education had failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court. The Chamber, unanimously, struck out the complaints regarding the length of the domestic proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy in that regard, given the friendly settlement reached between the parties on those issues. It also declared admissible the remaining complaints. The applicant attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned, through trustees, by the Catholic Bishop of the Diocese of Cork and Ross. The manager (S.), acting on behalf of the bishop, was the local parish priest. The Court heard addresses by Mr Holland and Mr McDonagh. The applicant also attended. the school. The term “manager” used below refers both to Ó. and to the management function he performed. The School had two teachers, one of whom (. the latter being elderly and infirm, a local priest (Ó.) was the de facto manager who acted on. behalf of, and in the interests of, S. The applicant was subjected to approximately twenty sexual assaults by L.H. during music lessons in his classroom. The applicant suppressed the sexual abuse. While she had significant psychological difficulties, she did not associate those with the abuse. In 1996 she was contacted by the police who were investigating a complaint made in 1995 by a former pupil of Dunderrow National School against L. h. L. H. was charged with 386 criminal offences of sexual abuse involving some twenty-one former pupils of the school during a three-year period in the 1970s and 1980s. He was found not guilty of any of the charges against him and retired in 1995. In 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was sentenced to imprisonment. His licence to teach was withdrawn by the Minister for Education (“the Minister”) under Rule 108 of the National School Rules 1965. An initial award (44,814.14 euros (EUR)) was made by a single judge. The applicant appealed to a CICT panel. She claimed that the CICT gave her the option of continuing her appeal (at the risk of finding that her CICT application would be rejected as out of time) or of accepting the initial offer. The State is never a party to CICT proceedings, it became aware of this award later before the High Court (see directly below). The High Court awarded damages payable by L.H. in the sum of EUR 305,104. The first payment was received in November 2007 so that she has been paid in the region of EUR 31,000 to date. The State Defendants applied for a direction to strike out the case. When the applicant’s case concluded, the State Defendants application for adirection to strike. out the Case. If the child-protection protocols existing in 2003 had been in place in 1973, it was very likely that the applicant's abuse would have been acted upon in a manner which would have ensured the promotion of her welfare. The applicant took enforcement proceedings and she obtained an instalment order of EUR 400 per month. The High Court accepted the State Defendants’ application on 9 March 2004. It found that the action was not statute barred. It concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the sexual assaults perpetrated by L.H. given the relationship between the State and the denominational management of national schools. In May 2006 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. Her Notice of Appeal challenged the finding on vicarious liability. By a majority judgment of 19 December 2008 (Hardiman J and Fennelly J, with whom Chief Justice Murray and Mr Justice. Mr Justice Fennley J, found that no action lay for a breach of a constitutional right where existing laws protected that right. Dissenting churches and the Catholic Church wished to ensure that children of their denominations be educated in schools controlled by the denomination and not by the State. Those churches were “remarkably successful” in achieving this aim. State funding was accorded on a proportionate basis to all denominational schools, the population was at the time overwhelmingly Catholic so that the majority of national schools had Catholic patrons and managers. The Catholic Church had responded that there could be no interference whatever with the “inherited tradition of managerial rights of schooling”. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. Hardiman J went on to describe as ‘remarkable’ the fact that, whilst in nineteenth-century Europe firmer distinctions were being drawn between Church and State. Hardiman J referred to the “urgent desire” of the denominations to maintain their role in primary education. As a result there were approximately 3,000 national schools in Ireland: most were under the control of Catholic patrons and managers. Hardiman J noted that, in recent times and after more than a century and a half, the provision of education was belatedly and at least partially placed on a statutory basis by the Education Act 1998. Prior to that Act the system had been administered by the 1965 Rules as well as by other ministerial letters, circulars and notes. The end result of the process was a voluntary resignation followed by the employment of [L.H.] in the Education Department. Hardiman J concluded that, having regard to the relevant test for vicarious liability and to the above-described arrangements for the control and management of national schools, the State Defendants were not liable to the applicant for the wrongs committed against her. The relationship of L.H. and the State – a “triangular one with the Church’ – was entirely sui generis and a product of Ireland’s unique historical experience. The manager was “the nominee of the patron, that is of a power other than the Minister and he did not inform the Minister of any difficulties with, or complaints about, [L.H.]” He was the agent not of the Minister, but of the Catholic Church. Hardiman J said the Minister was simply providing assistance and subvention to private and corporate endeavour, leaving the running of the school to the private or corporate entities. Kenny J pointed out in Crowley v Ireland [1980] I.R. 102 that the claim could more appropriately be made against the manager who had the power to put in place appropriate measures and procedures. Fennelly J said it was surprising that the court was confronted for the first time with questions relating to the liability of institutions including the State. for sexual abuse of schoolchildren in a national school by a teacher. Nothing in the judgment could be interpreted as suggesting liability on the part of the Church and, in any event, it was quite impossible to do so. Fennelly J accepted the expert’s evidence that it was not a State system but rather a “State-supported system’ He noted the clear division of power between the State (funding and fixing the curriculum) and the manager (day-to-day running of the school including hiring and firing teachers) He concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the acts of L.H. or for the failure of the manager to report the 1971 complaint to the State. Geoghegan J dissented. He accepted that neither the Department nor its inspectors had any knowledge of the assaults. He considered that, for all practical purposes, most primary education in Ireland took the form of a joint enterprise between Church and State. The applicant was legally represented throughout the civil proceedings, although she did not have legal aid. Geoghegan J relied, notably, on the role of school inspectors. If an allegation of sexual assault by a teacher on a national-school pupil was considered well-founded by an inquiry set up by the Department, it could lead to the withdrawal of recognition or to a police investigation. By a judgment of 9 May 2009 the Supreme Court vacated the High Court order for costs against the applicant since it was not disputed that hers was an important and complex test case. It determined that each party had to bear its own costs related to the action against the State Defendants.

The case originated in an application (no. 35810/09) against Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Irish national, Ms Louise O’Keeffe. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court. The Chamber, unanimously, struck out the complaints regarding the length of the domestic proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy in that regard, given the friendly settlement reached between the parties on those issues. It also declared admissible the remaining complaints. On 20 September 2012 that Chamber (Angelika Nußberger, substitute judge, replaced Ganna Yudkivska) relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber. The applicant attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned, through trustees, by the Catholic Bishop of the Diocese of Cork and Ross. The manager (S.), acting on behalf of the bishop, was the local parish priest. The term “manager” used below refers both to Ó. and to the management function he performed. The applicant also attended the same school. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 6 March 2013 (Rule 59 § 3). The Court heard addresses by Mr Holland and Mr McDonagh. The parties objected to relinquishment (Article 30 of the Convention and Rule 72). In 1971 a parent of a child complained to the manager that L.H. had sexually abused her child. That complaint was not reported to the police, to the Department or to any other State authority and was not acted upon by the manager. In September 1973 other parents brought to the applicant’s parents’ attention similar allegations concerning L.h. Following a meeting of parents about this, L. h. went on sick leave and in September 1973 he resigned from his post. The applicant suppressed the sexual abuse. While she had significant psychological difficulties, she did not associate those with the abuse. In 1996 she was contacted by the police who were investigating a complaint made in 1995 by a former pupil of Dunderrow National School against L. H. He was charged with 386 criminal offences of sexual abuse involving some twenty-one former pupils of the school. In 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was sentenced to imprisonment. His licence to teach was withdrawn by the Minister for Education (“the Minister”) under Rule 108 of the National School Rules 1965. An initial award (44,814.14 euros (EUR) was made by a single judge. The applicant appealed to a CICT panel. She claimed that the CICT gave her the option of continuing her appeal (at the risk of finding that her CICT application would be rejected as out of time) or of accepting the initial offer. The award was made on an ex gratia basis. Since the State is never a party to CICT proceedings, it became aware of this award later before the High Court. Since L.H. did not file a defence, on 8 November 1999 the applicant obtained judgment in default against him. On 24 October 2006 the High Court assessed and awarded damages in the sum of EUR 305,104. The first payment was received in November 2007 so that she has been paid in the region of EUR 31,000 to date. She registered a judgment mortgage against that part of the family home owned by L.T. The applicant took enforcement proceedings and she obtained an instalment order of EUR 400 per month. When the applicant’s case concluded, the State Defendants applied for a direction to strike out the case. High Court accepted the State Defendants’ application on 9 March 2004. On 20 January 2006 the High Court delivered judgment. It found that the action was not statute barred. It also concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the sexual assaults perpetrated by L.H. given the relationship between the State and the denominational management of national schools. In May 2006 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. Her Notice of Appeal challenged the finding on vicarious liability. By a majority judgment of 19 December 2008 (Hardiman J and Fennelly J, with whom Chief Justice Murray and Mr Justice. Mr JusticeFennelly) the appeal was dismissed. The costs of the proceedings were awarded against the applicant. Dissenting churches and Catholic Church wished to ensure that children of their denominations be educated in schools controlled by the denomination and not by the State. State funding was accorded on a proportionate basis to all denominational schools, but the population was at the time overwhelmingly Catholic so that the majority of national schools had Catholic patrons and managers. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. Hardiman J described in detail the legal status of national Schools in Ireland in the early nineteenth century. The Irish Free State was formed in 1922 and the system of national education began in 1831. The Catholic Church had responded that there could be no interference whatever with the “inherited tradition of managerial rights of schooling”. The Constitution reflected a largely State-funded, but entirely clerically administered, system of education. As a result there were approximately 3,000 national schools in Ireland. Most were under the control of Catholic patrons and managers. Hardiman J referred to the “urgent desire” of the denominations to maintain their role in primary education. He said: “No complaint, on the evidence, was directed to the Minister or to any State body. The matter was handled, so to speak, ‘in house’ at the election of the complainants. The end result of the process was a voluntary resignation followed by the employment of [L.H.] in the Education Act 1998” Hardiman J concluded that, having regard to the relevant test for vicarious liability and to the above-described arrangements for the control and management of national schools, the State Defendants were not liable to the applicant for the wrongs committed against her. The relationship of L.H. and the State – a “triangular one with the Church’ – was entirely sui generis and a product of Ireland’s unique historical experience. The manager was “the nominee of the patron, that is of a power other than the Minister and he did not inform the Minister of any difficulties with, or complaints about, [L.H.]” Hardiman J: "The Minister can hardly be responsible for a failure to ‘cease’ a course of action of whose existence he was quite unaware” Kenny J: “... this is a claim which could more appropriately be made against the manager. It was he who had the power to put in place appropriate measures and procedures governing the running of the school.” Fennelly J: The “calamity of the exploitation of authority over children so as to abuse them sexually” had shaken society to its foundations’ Hardiman J concluded by pointing out that nothing in the judgment could be interpreted as suggesting liability on the part of the Church and, in any event, it was quite impossible to do so. The judge said that L.H. was not employed by the State but, in law, by the manager. He said the inspection regime did not alter the division of responsibilities between the State and the manager, the inspectors having no power to direct teachers in the carrying out of their duties. Fennelly J concluded that there can be no liability for the failure of the manager to report the 1971 complaint. Geoghegan J dissented. He accepted that neither the Department nor its inspectors had any knowledge of the assaults. For all practical purposes, most primary education in Ireland took the form of a joint enterprise between Church and State and he considered that that relationship was such that there was a sufficient connection between the state and the creation of the risk. Supreme Court vacated the High Court order for costs against the applicant since it was not disputed that hers was an important and complex test case. It determined that each party had to bear its own costs related to the action against the State Defendants. The applicant was legally represented throughout the civil proceedings, although she did not have legal aid. Geoghegan J relied, notably, on the role of school inspectors. He noted that if an allegation of sexual assault by a teacher on a national-school pupil was considered well-founded by an inquiry set up by the Department, it could lead to the withdrawal of recognition or to a police investigation.

It also declared admissible the remaining complaints. The school was owned, through trustees, by the Catholic Bishop of the Diocese of Cork and Ross who was recognised by the Department of Education and Science as the school’s patron. The manager (S.), acting on behalf of the bishop, was the local parish priest. The latter being elderly and infirm, a local priest (Ó.) was the de facto manager. The term ‘manager’ used below refers both to Ó. and to the management function he performed. The Court heard addresses by Mr Holland and Mr McDonagh. That complaint was not reported to the police, to the Department or to any other State authority and was not acted upon by the manager. In September 1973 other parents brought to the applicant’s parents’ attention similar allegations. Those allegations were not reported at that time. In 1996 she was contacted by the police who were investigating a complaint made in 1995 by a former pupil of Dunderrow National School. The applicant made a statement to the. police in January 1997 and was referred for counselling. During the investigation a number of other pupils made statements. L.h. was charged with 386 criminal offences of sexual abuse. In 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was sentenced to imprisonment. His licence to teach was withdrawn by the Minister for Education (“the Minister”) under Rule 108 of the National School Rules 1965 (‘the 1965 Rules’) In October 1998 the applicant applied to the CICT for compensation. An initial award (44,814.14 euros (EUR)) was made by a single judge. The applicant appealed to a CICT panel. The award was made on an ex gratia basis. Since the State is never a party to CICT proceedings, it became aware of this award later before the High Court (see directly below) The High Court assessed and awarded damages payable by L.H. in the sum of EUR 305,104. The first payment was received in November 2007 so that she has been paid in the region of EUR 31,000 to date. She registered a judgment mortgage against that part of the family home owned by L.'s father. The applicant took enforcement proceedings. L. claimed he had insufficient means and she obtained an instalment order of EUR 400 per month. The State Defendants applied for a direction to strike out the case. The High Court hearing against the State Defendants began on 2 March 2004. The judge asked Counsel for the applicant as follows: “What evidence do I have, or what should I have deduce[d] from the evidence that has been given?” High Court accepted the State Defendants’ application on 9 March 2004. On 20 January 2006 the High Court delivered judgment. It found that the action was not statute barred. It also concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the sexual assaults perpetrated by L.H. given the relationship between the State and denominational management of national schools. In May 2006 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. Her Notice of Appeal challenged the finding on vicarious liability. By a majority judgment of 19 December 2008 (Hardiman J and Fennelly J, with whom Chief Justice Murray and Mr Justice. Mr JusticeFennelly ruled), the appeal was dismissed. The costs of the proceedings were awarded against the applicant. Dissenting churches and the Catholic Church wished to ensure that children of their denominations be educated in schools controlled by the denomination and not by the State. Those churches were “remarkably successful” in achieving this aim. State funding was accorded on a proportionate basis to all denominational schools, the population was at the time overwhelmingly Catholic so that the majority of national schools had Catholic patrons and managers.Hardiman J went on to describe as ‘remarkable’ the fact that, whilst in nineteenth-century Europe firmer distinctions were being drawn between Church and State and Church influence in the provision of public services (including education) was ebbing. Hardiman J referred to the “urgent desire’ of the denominations to maintain their role in primary education. The Constitution reflected a largely State-funded, but entirely clerically administered, system of education. As a result there were approximately 3,000 national schools in Ireland. Most were under the control of Catholic patrons and managers, while a few were under control of other denominations. Hardiman J noted that, in recent times and after more than a century and a half, the provision of education was belatedly and at least partially placed on a statutory basis by the Education Act 1998. Before that Act the system had been administered by the 1965 Rules as well as by other ministerial letters, circulars and notes. Hardiman J concluded that, having regard to the relevant test for vicarious liability, the State Defendants were not liable to the applicant for the wrongs committed against her. The relationship of L.H. and the State – a “triangular one with the Church’ – was entirely sui generis and a product of Ireland’s unique historical experience. He concluded that it was quite impossible to do so because those authorities had not been heard by the Supreme Court since the applicant had not sued them. Fennelly J, who delivered the other majority judgment, began by noting that the “calamity of the exploitation of authority over children so as to abuse them sexually” had shaken society to its foundations. Cases of sexual abuse had preoccupied the criminal courts and Supreme Court for many years and it was surprising that that court was confronted for the first time with questions relating to the liability of institutions including the State for sexual abuse. Fennelly J accepted the expert’s evidence that it was not a State system but rather a ‘State-supported system’ He noted the clear division of power between the State (funding and fixing the curriculum) and the manager (day-to-day running of the school including hiring and firing teachers) He concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the acts of L.H. or for the failure of the manager to report the 1971 complaint to the State.Geoghegan J dissented. He accepted that neither the Department nor its inspectors had any knowledge of the assaults. He considered that, for all practical purposes, most primary education in Ireland took the form of a joint enterprise between Church and State. Geoghegan J relied, notably, on the role of school inspectors. If an allegation of sexual assault by a teacher on a national-school pupil was considered well-founded by an inquiry set up by the Department, it could lead to the withdrawal of recognition or to a police investigation. If the police found the complaint justified, the teacher’s licence to teach would be withdrawn. The Supreme Court vacated the High Court order for costs against the applicant since it was not disputed that hers was an important and complex test case. It determined that each party had to bear its own costs related to the action against the State Defendants.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48247/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the length of his pre-trial detention and of criminal proceedings against him had exceeded a “reasonable time” The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 of the Convention and decided to examine the merits of the application. The first hearing was held on 21 January 2005. Subsequently, hearings were held at regular intervals. On 18 May and 17 August 2006 the Gdańsk Court of Appeal granted the applications and extended his detention. The Court also considered that the District Court could not be held responsible for not having completed the trial as there had been objective procedural difficulties in hearing all the witnesses. The applicant’s applications for release from detention and his appeals against the decisions extending the preventive measure were dismissed. The proceedings are still pending before the trial court. On 20 November 2006 he was released from remand and returned to his home town.

name: Thomas Richard Sylvester
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that the non-enforcement of the final return order under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction had violated their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the admissibility and merits. The Court decided to join the applications and to communicate them to the respondent Government. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court. The first applicant married an Austrian citizen in April 1994. The marriage was concluded in the United States of America, where the couple set up their common residence. On 11 September 1994 their daughter, the second applicant, was born. Under Michigan law the first applicant and his wife had joint custody of their daughter. The first applicant's wife, without obtaining his consent, left the U.S. and took her to Austria. The Graz District Civil Court ordered that the child be returned to the first claimant at her former place of residence in Michigan. The court found that the first applicants' wife had wrongfully removed the child within the meaning of Article 3 of the Hague Convention. The case started in December 1995 in Graz, Austria. The first applicant filed an application for enforcement of the return order of 20 December 1995. In April 1996, the first applicant started divorce proceedings before the Oakland Circuit Court (Michigan). By a decision of 16 April 1996 the court pronounced a default judgment of divorce. Further, it awarded the first. applicant sole custody of the second applicant and ordered that the second. applicant should reside with the first Applicant in the event of her. return. On 7 May 1996 the file arrived again at the Graz District Civil Court. On 8 May 1996, an attempt to enforce the return. order was made in accordance with the terms set out in. Article 13 of the Hague Convention. The case was brought by the mother of the second applicant, who was seeking sole custody of her daughter. The mother was accused of international parental kidnapping in the U.S. The Graz Regional Civil Court quashed the Graz District Civil Court's enforcement order of 8 May 1996 and referred the case back to it. The first applicant appealed against the transfer of jurisdiction and the case was heard in Graz again in August 1996. The case was finally settled in August 1999. The second applicant was awarded full custody of the daughter of the first applicant. The court ruled in favour of the mother and awarded her full custody. The judge ruled that the child's well-being had to be taken into account in so far as a change in the situation had occurred. Austrian Supreme Court dismissed an appeal by the first applicant and set aside the enforcement order of 8 May 1996. Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention made clear that the child's well-being took priority over the Convention's general aim of preventing child abduction. Reasons of general deterrence or, in other words, the aim of showing that child abduction was not worthwhile could not justify exposing a child to a grave risk of physical or psychological harm. The court acknowledged that particularly difficult problems arose in cases in which the abductor had created the situation in which a return represented a serious danger to the child’s well- Being. In the main proceedings, the courts had denied that there was any risk of psychological harm (as a result of the alleged sexual behaviour of the first applicant) exclusively on account of the child's tender age. In these circumstances, it could not be excluded that the child, who was now more than two years old and had been living solely with her mother for more than a year, would suffer grave psychological harm in the event of a return to her father. Thus, the question whether the return order could be enforced by coercive measures needed further examination, including an opinion by an expert in child psychology. It might also prove necessary to assess whether or not the mother's allegations were at all true. The application for enforcement of the return order had to be dismissed. The court noted the first applicant's statement of 28 April 1997 and his offer within the meaning of the ‘safe harbour’ case-law. It considered that this offer did not guarantee that the second applicant's relationship with her main person of reference would be preserved in the long run. Following appeal proceedings the judgment became final on 31 March 1998. The first applicant was granted a couple of hours of supervised access to the secondApplicance. The second applicant was awarded sole custody of the second applicants by the Graz District Civil Court on 29 December 1997. The case was settled by the Supreme Court of Germany.

The case originated in two applications against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that the non-enforcement of the final return order under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction had violated their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. In a decision of 24 October 2000 the Court decided to join the applications and to communicate them to the respondent Government. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case. The first applicant married an Austrian citizen in April 1994. On 11 September 1994 their daughter, the second applicant, was born. Under Michigan law the first applicant and his wife had joint custody of their daughter. The first applicant's wife, without obtaining his consent, left the U.S. with the daughter and took her to Austria. On 31 October 1995 the first. applicant, relying on the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (“the. Hague Convention”), requested the Austrian courts to order the second. applicant's return. 26 September 2002 the Court declared the applications admissible. The second applicant's mother was ordered to return to the United States in December 1995. She appealed against the decision, but the case was dismissed in January 1996. In April 1996 the first applicant filed an application for enforcement of the return order. In May 1996 the Graz District Civil Court ordered the enforcement of a return order under section 19 (1) of the Non-Contentious Proceedings Act (Ausserstreitgesetz) The first applicant had started divorce proceedings before the Oakland Circuit Court (Michigan) By a decision of 16 April 1996, the court pronounced a default judgment of divorce. Further, it awarded the firstApplicant sole custody of the second applicant and ordered that the second Applicant should reside with the first Applicant in the event of her return. The case was brought by the mother of the second applicant. The second applicant's mother appealed against the decision of 8 May 1996. On 29 May 1996 the U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Michigan, issued an arrest warrant against the mother on suspicion of international parental kidnapping. The Graz Regional Civil Court granted an appeal by the first applicant against the transfer of jurisdiction and quashed the Graz District Civil Court's enforcement order. name: Fazia Ali
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40378/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a parent of two young children, is a homeless person in priority need of accommodation within the meaning of Part VII of the Housing Act 1996 (“the 1996 Act”). The applicant applied to Birmingham City Council for assistance in October 2006. The Council determined that the applicant was homeless, eligible for assistance and not intentionally homeless. The authority therefore accepted that it owed the applicant the “main housing duty” to provide accommodation to her and her family. The applicant viewed the property on 19 March 2007 but declined the offer as she was not happy with the condition of the communal area. The applicant appealed to Birmingham County Court under section 204 of the 1996 Act, which allowed for an appeal on a point of law only. In her grounds of appeal the applicant claimed that the Council had discharged its main housing duty to her under section 193 of the Housing Act. The County Court upheld the decision that the applicant’s refusal of the offer of accommodation had discharged the Council’S main housing duties to her. The case was heard at Birmingham Crown Court in April and May 2007. The appeal was heard on 29 August 2007, on which date the judge noted that the only ground of appeal argued before him was that the letter of offer had failed to arrive. The applicant submitted that the County Court should hear evidence on the matter so that it could determine it for itself. Although the judge accepted that the Homelessness Review Officer was not an independent or impartial tribunal, he found that the decision whether or not the letter had been received was properly and fairly to be made by her and he declined to hear evidence.The applicant subsequently appealed to the Court of Appeal and then to the Supreme Court. At each level, the grounds of appeal were that the. decision taken by the Council’s Homelessness. Review Officer had constituted a determination of the applicant’'s civil rights for the purposes of Article 6. 1 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The House of Lords stressed that although the Officer had been called upon to resolve some disputed factual issues, these findings of fact were “only staging posts on the way to the much broader judgments” concerning local conditions and the availability of alternative accommodation. Although the Officer could not be regarded as independent, since she was employed by the Council which had made the offer of accommodation which the claimant had rejected, statutory regulations provided substantial safeguards to ensure that the review would be independently and fairly conducted, free from improper external influences. Any significant departure from the procedural rules would have afforded a ground of appeal. Thomas LJ said the decision of the House of Lords in Runa Begum applied to all County Court appeals under section 204 of the 1996 Act. He further held that the decision in Tsfayo, which concerned the housing benefit scheme, did not affect appeals brought in homelessness cases. “I consider that it does whether the decision turns on a simple issue of primary fact or a conclusion of fact based on primary facts (such as a conclusion on suitability),” he said. ‘The present scope of the appeal provides a real measure of protection for homeless appellants. It demonstrates, as Lord Bingham observed, that the scheme properly operated should ensure fair treatment.’ The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, finding that the determination by the Council, that its duty to secure accommodation for the applicant had ceased, was not a determination of her civil rights within the meaning of Article 6.1. Lord Hope of Craighead said: “... I would be prepared now to hold that cases where the award of services or benefits in kind is not an individual right of which the applicant can consider himself the holder, do not engage article 6(1). In my opinion they do not give rise to ‘civil rights’ within the autonomous meaning that is given to that expression for the purposes of that article” Lord Hope commented that separating simple, formal questions of “gateway” facts, such as the letter issue, from the expert assessment of suitability would needlessly complicate a scheme designed to be simple to administer. The court went on to observe that the fact that a County Court did not have a full fact-finding jurisdiction when hearing an appeal under section 204 of the 1996 Act did not mean that the applicant was deprived of what was required to satisfy the guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention. Unlike the County Court, the Supreme Court appeared to consider whether or not the Council had discharged its duty to the applicant under section 193(5); however, it appeared to accept that a formal letter of offer was required.

name: Geoffrey Dennis Peck
train_texts: The case was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant complained about the disclosure to the media of closed-circuit television footage, which resulted in images of himself being published and broadcast widely. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing was required. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. The Council installed a CCTV surveillance system in Brentwood in April 1994. In August 1995 the applicant was suffering from depression as a result of personal and family circumstances. On 20 August 1995 at 11.30 p.m. he walked alone down the high street towards a central junction in the centre of Brentwood with a kitchen knife in his hand and he attempted to commit suicide by cutting his wrists. He was unaware that a CCTV camera, mounted on the traffic island in front of the junction, filmed his movements. The Council's first press feature, the CCTV News, was released on 9 October 1995 and included two photographs taken from the CCTV footage of the applicant. The applicant was intercepted with a knife and a potentially dangerous situation being defused as a result of the CCTV system. The applicant's face was masked at the Council's oral request. However, that masking was later considered inadequate by the Independent Television Commission (see below) The applicant became aware that he had been filmed on CCTV and that footage had been released because a neighbour told his partner that the former had seen him on television. He did not take any action then as he was still suffering from severe depression. A number of people recognised the applicant. A letter of 25 April 1996 from the Yellow Advertiser opined that the applicant was not identifiable. The Council agreed to mask the man's face in a broadcast of ‘Crime Beat’ in 1996. The man’s identity was not revealed until after the programme was broadcast in 1998. The BBC says it cannot find a signed copy of the agreement. The original agreement was signed by the producers of 'Crime Beat' and the BBC. The full agreement can be found at: http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/features/features-features/crime-beat-features-the-man-who-will-never-be-seen-again-after-he-was-masked-by-the BBC-in-1998. The applicant complained to the ITC in respect of the broadcast by Anglia Television. The ITC found that the applicant's identity was not adequately obscured and that he was readily identifiable. The Broadcasting Standards Commission upheld both of his complaints. The BBC was directed to broadcast a summary of the adjudication of the BSC with the episode of “Crime Beat” on 12 June 1997. The applicant later chose to speak publicly about this incident, but this did not alter the infringement established. He also had his photograph published in the Yellow Advertiser on 25 October 1996 and on 5 August 1997 on BBC 1's “You Decide”. The applicant complained to the Press Complaints Commission (PCC) in respect of the articles published in the Yellow Advertiser. The PCC rejected the applicant's complaint without a hearing and the decision was communicated to the applicant by letter dated 2 August 1996. The applicant applied to the High Court for leave to apply for judicial review of the Council's disclosure of the CCTV material arguing, inter alia, that that disclosure had no basis in law. The High Court found that the purpose of section 163 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 was to empower a local authority to provide CCTV equipment in order to promote the prevention of crime or the welfare of victims of crime. The High Court judge had some sympathy with the applicant who has suffered an invasion of his privacy. He argued that by failing to consult the police to see if he had been charged with a criminal offence and to impose sufficient restrictions as regards disclosure of his identity, the Council had facilitated an unwarranted invasion of privacy. But the judge did not consider it correct in law. Unless and until there is a general right of privacy recognised by English law (and the indications are that there may soon be so by incorporation of the European Convention on Human Rights into our law), reliance must be placed on effective guidance being issued by Codes of practice or otherwise. Anglia TV failed to mask the applicant's identity adequately. The BBC failed to disguise the applicant at all in the trailers. Brentwood Borough Council contacted the BBC and received assurances that his image had been masked. In the event, unknown to the Council, it had not been adequately masked in the programme. An application to the High Court for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal was rejected. A subsequent leave application to a single judge of the CourtOfAppeal was rejected on 21 January 1998. The Council was neither acting outside its statutory authority nor irrationally in making the film and photographs available to the media. The injury, of which complaint is made, arises from a failure on the part of the media to sufficiently disguise the person involved.

The case originated in an application (no. 44647/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained about the disclosure to the media of closed-circuit television footage, which resulted in images of himself being published and broadcast widely. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing was required. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. In the section headed “Closed-Circuit television (CCTV) and the relevant footage’, we look at the case of Geoffrey Dennis Peck. In August 1995 the applicant was suffering from depression as a result of personal and family circumstances. On 20 August 1995 at 11.30 p.m. he walked alone down the high street towards a central junction in the centre of Brentwood. He stopped at the junction and leaned over a railing facing the traffic with the knife in his hand. The police were notified by the CCTV operator and arrived. They took the knife from the applicant, gave him medical assistance and brought him to the police station. He was detained under the Mental Health Act 1983. His custody record refers to the self-inflicted injuries to his wrists on arrival and notes that he was examined and treated by a doctor. In late October or November 1995 the applicant became aware that he had been filmed on CCTV and that footage had been released. He did not take any action then as he was still suffering from severe depression. Anglia Television sought, and the Council provided, footage of the incident involving the applicant. On 17 October 1995 extracts from that footage were included in its news programme about the CCTV system. The applicant's face had been masked at the Council's oral request. However, that masking was later considered inadequate by the Independent Television Commission (see below), the applicant's distinctive hairstyle and moustache making him easily recognisable to anyone who knew him. The BBC agreed to show the image of the man in a new series of “Crime Beat’s” “Right to Reply” in 1996. The BBC agreed that the man's face would be masked in the programme. The man's name was revealed in a newspaper article in 1997. In 1998, the BBC agreed not to show his face in any further programmes. The decision was later overturned on appeal by the BBC. The film was shown in a second series of the series, which was called ‘Right to the Point’. The programme was screened on BBC1 on Monday, May 27, 1997, at 9pm and 10pm. The Broadcasting Standards Commission upheld both of the applicant's complaints. The BBC was directed to broadcast a summary of the adjudication of the BSC with the episode of ‘Crime Beat’ on 12 June 1997. The applicant complained to the ITC in respect of the broadcast by Anglia Television on 1 May 1996. The latter had already apologised to the applicant and conceded that it had breached the privacy requirements. The ITC noted that the implication was that a man carrying a knife was likely to be intent on a criminal act. It found that section 2(2) and (5) of the Code had been breached and the decision was published in its Programme Complaints and Interventions Report of June 1996. The applicant complained to the Press Complaints Commission (PCC) in respect of the articles published in the Yellow Advertiser. The PCC rejected the applicant's complaint without a hearing and the decision was communicated to the applicant by letter dated 2 August 1996. The applicant applied to the High Court for leave to apply for judicial review of the Council's disclosure of the CCTV material arguing, inter alia, that that disclosure had no basis in law. The High Court found that the purpose of section 163 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 (“the 1994 Act”) was to empower a local authority to provide CCTV equipment. High Court judge had some sympathy with the applicant but did not consider it correct in law. He said the Council had facilitated an unwarranted invasion of his privacy. He argued that by failing to consult the police to see if he had been charged with a criminal offence and to impose sufficient restrictions as regards disclosure of his identity, the Council facilitated an invasion of privacy. The judge said that unless and until there is a general right of privacy recognised by English law, reliance must be placed on effective guidance being issued by Codes of practice or otherwise, in order to try and avoid such undesirable invasions of a person's privacy. But he said that the decision of the Council to distribute the film footage could not be said to be irrational or unreasonable. Anglia TV failed to mask the applicant's identity adequately. BBC failed to disguise the applicant at all in the trailers. Brentwood Borough Council were notified about that by the applicant. The Council contacted the BBC and received assurances that his image had been masked in the programme. In the event, unknown to the Council, it had not been adequately masked. An application to the High Court for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal was rejected. The subsequent leave application to a single judge of the court of appeal was rejected on 21 January 1998. Following an oral hearing before the full Court of appeal, the applicant’s leave application was dismissed on 19 February 1998.

The case was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant complained about the disclosure to the media of closed-circuit television footage, which resulted in images of himself being published and broadcast widely. By a decision of 15 May 2001 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merit of the case was required. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. The application was transferred to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. In the section headed “Closed-Circuit television (CCTV) and the relevant footage”, we discuss the case of Geoffrey Dennis Peck. In August 1995 the applicant was suffering from depression as a result of personal and family circumstances. He attempted to commit suicide by cutting his wrists. He was unaware that a CCTV camera, mounted on the traffic island in front of the junction, filmed his movements. The operator was solely alerted to an individual in possession of a knife at the junction. The police were notified by the CCTV operator and arrived. They took the knife from the applicant, gave him medical assistance and brought him to the police station. His custody record refers to the self-inflicted injuries to his wrists on arrival and notes that he was examined and treated by a doctor, after which he was released without charge. The applicant's face was masked at the Council's oral request. However, that masking was later considered inadequate by the Independent Television Commission. The applicant became aware that he had been filmed on CCTV and that footage had been released because a neighbour told his partner that the former had seen him on television. He did not take any action then as he was still suffering from severe depression. It appears that a number of people recognised the applicant. A letter of 25 April 1996 from the Yellow Advertiser opined that the applicant was not identifiable. The application was rejected and no further action was taken by the Council or Anglia Television. The BBC agreed to show the footage as long as the faces were masked. It was later revealed that the man in the footage was the presenter of ‘Crime Beat’ The man made a number of media appearances in response to the incident. The BBC has refused to comment on whether the man was the star of the programme or if he had been identified as such through the masking. The man's identity has never been officially released. The case is now before the European Court of Human Rights, which has the power to order the mask to be removed. For more information on the case, go to: http://www.justgiving.com/the-case-of-the-couple-who-were-caught-in-a-sexually-exploiting-their-child’s-paedophile-cnn-story-tweeting. The Broadcasting Standards Commission upheld both of his complaints. The BBC was directed to broadcast a summary of the adjudication of the BSC with the episode of ‘Crime Beat’ on 12 June 1997. The ITC found that the applicant's identity was not adequately obscured and that he was readily identifiable and easily recognisable by those who knew him. Given the admission and apology by Anglia Television, no further action was taken by the ITC. The applicant later chose to speak publicly about this incident did not alter the infringement established. The BSC also considered the masking during the programme inadequate as the applicant had been recognised by viewers who had not seen the trailer. The Press Complaints Commission (PCC) rejected the applicant's complaint without a hearing. The applicant applied to the High Court for leave to apply for judicial review of the Council's disclosure of the CCTV material. On 26 June 1996 a single judge refused leave. High Court granted leave on a renewed request and leave to amend the application to include a complaint that the disclosure was irrational, even if lawful. The High Court rejected the application for judicialreview in November 1997. It found that the purpose of section 163 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 was to empower a local authority to provide CCTV equipment in order to promote the prevention of crime or the welfare of victims of crime. The High Court judge had some sympathy with the applicant but did not consider it correct in law. He said reliance must be placed on effective guidance being issued by Codes of practice or otherwise to try and avoid such undesirable invasions of a person's privacy. The evidence is that the CCTV cameras in public places play an important role in both crime prevention and crime detection. In this case, the film footage showed a man walking in the High Street carrying a large knife in his hand. It did not show him attempting to commit suicide. It was plainly a potentially dangerous situation which the Council's monitoring employee quite properly put to the police, as a result of which the man was arrested. ... It was not unreasonable for the Council to conclude that the footage was a useful example of how a possibly dangerous situation can be avoided. The Council contacted the BBC and received assurances that his image had been masked. In the event, unknown to the Council, it had not been adequately masked in the programme. Brentwood Borough Council was neither acting outside its statutory authority nor irrationally in making the film and photographs available to the media. The application to the High Court for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal was rejected. The subsequent leave application to a single judge of the court of appeal was rejected on 21 January 1998. The applicant's leave application was dismissed on 19 February 1998.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 61444/00) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had not had his case heard within a ‘reasonable time’ The applicant’s wife informed the Court’S Registry that the applicant had died on 30 December 2004. She stated that she wished to continue the proceedings before the Court in her late husband's stead. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant and his wife sued E.W. and W.W., the owners of a company, in the Zielona Góra Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) in Poland. They were seeking compensation for the serious damage to the applicant's house allegedly caused by the defendants. The court ordered the experts to revise their report on 2 December 1996. On 17 July 1997 the plaintiffs modified their claim. On 19 November 1998 the court gave judgment and dismissed the claim. The plaintiffs appealed. On 20 February 2000 the expert report was submitted to the court. On 9 May 2000 the court heard evidence from the expert. The Government said the plaintiffs had altered the amount of the damages they had sought. The plaintiffs applied for an exemption from payment of the court fee. for the increased claim. On 12 October 2000 the court refused their application. That decision was later upheld by the Poznań Court of Appeal. Eventually, on 16 March 2001, the particulars of that claim were returned to them on account of their failure to pay the fee. The Government maintained that at the hearing held on 8 May 2001 the plaintiffs had increased their claim and had stated that they would not seek an exemption. The applicant maintained that, in a pleading of 11 May 2001, he had indeed extended the amount of the damages sought to 300,000 Polish zlotys (PLN), mostly because he had been forced to do so by the court.

Case originated in an application (no. 61444/00) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had not had his case heard within a “reasonable time”, as required under Article 6 § 1 of the convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26: 1. On 2 February 2005 the applicant’s wife, Mrs Józefa Krasuska, informed the Court’S Registry that the applicant had died on 30 December 2004. The case was brought by the applicant and his wife against E.W. and W.W., the owners of a company W. ona Góra, Poland. In September 1980 his licence was revoked and thereafter he was continuously ‘unlawfully at large’ He was arrested in April 1989, having returned from South Africa in possession of a false passport. The application was successful and the applicant was released from prison on 1 July 1997, but for the revocation of his life licence, the applicant would have been released on the expiry of his sentence for fraud, pursuant to provisions whereby prisoners serving determinate sentences of more than two years are eligible for release. He asserted that he could lawfully detain a post-tariff mandatory life prisoner solely because there was a risk that he might commit further non-violent imprisonable offences. The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that his detention after recall on life licence had ceased to be justified by the original sentence. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 29 May 2001 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section, composed of the following judges: Mr J.-P. Costa, President, Mr W. Fuhrmann, Mr P. Kūris, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mr K. Jungwiert, Sir Nicolas Bratza and Mr. Traja. The case was heard in the Court of Appeal on 20 February 2002 (Rule 59 § 2) The applicant was convicted of murder in 1967 and released on licence in 1979. His licence required him to cooperate with his probation officer and to remain in the United Kingdom. He left the UK in breach of his licence and went to live in South Africa. In September 1980 his licence was revoked and thereafter he was continuously ‘unlawfully at large’ He was arrested in April 1989 for possession of a false passport. In July 1994 he was convicted on two counts of conspiracy to forge travellers' cheques and passports and sentenced to six years' imprisonment. In 1996 the Parole Board conducted a formal review of the applicant's case and recommended his release on life licence. In 1997 the Secretary of State rejected the Board's recommendation in the following terms: “... [The Secretary of state] notes with concern the circumstances surrounding your two recalls to prison ... Both these occasions represent a serious and grave breach of the trust placed in you as a life licensee and demonstrate a lack of regard for the requirements of supervision.” On 10 June 1997 the applicant was granted leave to seek judicial review of his decision. On 1 July 1997, but for the revocation of his life licence, the applicant would have been released from prison on the expiry of his sentence. The Secretary of State acknowledged in the proceedings that there was not a significant risk that the applicant would commit further violent offences. But he asserted that he could lawfully detain a post-tariff mandatory life prisoner solely because there was a risk that he might commit further non-violent imprisonable offences. The applicant is now serving the equivalent of a determinate sentence of about five years, albeit in open conditions. This term has not been imposed on him by way of punishment, because he has already served the punitive terms which his previous, very serious, offences have been thought to merit. It is not submitted that the term imposed bears any relation to the gravity of any future imprisonable offence which the applicant might commit. House of Lords dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Court of Appeal's decision. In his speech, Lord Steyn held that section 35(2) of the 1991 Act conferred a wide administrative discretion on the Secretary of State to decide upon the release on licence of mandatory life prisoners. He expressly repeated Lord Bingham's concern that the imposition of a substantial term of imprisonment by exercise of administrative discretion was hard to reconcile with ordinary concepts of the rule of law. On 22 December 1998 the applicant was released on licence by the secretary of state. He was never convicted of any offence. He is currently serving a sentence of life with a minimum term of 15 years.

name: Volkan Şahin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34400/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 6 August 2002. On 6 May 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the length of the proceedings. On 8 September 2006 it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time, pursuant to Article 29 § 3 of the Constitutional Convention. The application was brought by a Turkish national, Volkan Şahin (‘the applicant’), who was accused of forging a bond. The case was referred to the trial court for a new trial. The trial court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to one year and eight months’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed. On 13 February 2002, after having held a hearing, the Court of Cassation upheld the new trial court’s decision. On 22 October 2001 the Principal Public Prosecutor submitted his written observations to the Court. These observations were not communicated to the applicant. He was convicted on 11 April 2000, during its first hearing in thenew trial, and sentenced to a year and a half in prison. The application was dismissed on 13 April 2002, and he was released on bail.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41355/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had prevented him from having access to his home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 1 February 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. The Court also received third-party comments from the Government of Cyprus, which had exercised its right to intervene in the case. The decision was published in full on 4 December 2000. In support of his claim of ownership the applicant produced the relevant certificates of registration and affirmations of ownership issued by the Republic of Cyprus. The applicant alleged that from 14 August 1974 onwards he had not been able to return to his house and had been continuously prevented from exercising his property rights and enjoying his properties. The appeal was denied by the Supreme Court of Cyprus and the appeal was upheld by the Court of Appeal. The case was heard in Nicosia, Cyprus, on November 6 and 13, 2014. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant and handed down a verdict of not guilty. The decision was quashed on November 14, 2014, and a new hearing will take place on November 16, 2015.

name: Fırat Karatay
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained about the length and the lawfulness of their detention on remand. They complained that during their detention they were never brought before a judge, which deprived them of the possibility of effectively arguing for their release pending trial. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was made by three Turkish nationals, Mr Fırat Karatay, Fesih Karatays and Mr Şeyhmus KaratAY. The first and second applicants were arrested and detained on remand on 7 July 2001 and 1 May 2001, respectively. The third applicant was not brought before the court at the hearings of 11 June 2001 and 9 July 2001. The applicants' lawyer, who was present before the Bornova Criminal Court for the first time, requested the applicants' release pending trial. The court dismissed the lawyer's request in view of the state of the evidence and the nature of the offence. It also reiterated its order to transfer all three applicants to Buca Prison. The first applicant confessed to his guilt in a letter to the court dated 9 July2001. In the meantime, the court sent a letter rogatory to the Kızıltepe Criminal Court of First Instance. The first and the third applicants were accused of embezzling money from a textile company. The first applicant confessed to his guilt, while the others refuted the allegations. The court ordered their release pending trial as requested by the Bornova Criminal Court, in its decision dated 21 November 2001. The applicants alleged that they were not aware of the fact that a second case had been brought against them, at the time they gave these statements. At the hearing of 9 October 2002 the Karşıyaka Criminal Court of First Instance acquitted the third applicant due to lack of evidence and found the first applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to five years and four months' imprisonment. On 26 January 2004 the Court of Cassation quashed the first instance court's decision. The Karşıyaka Criminal Court refused the lawyer's request to release the applicant in view of the state of the evidence and the nature of the offence. On 17 January 2005 the Criminal Court decided to acquit the second and third applicants and convicted the first applicant. It sentenced him to five years and four months' imprisonment. The case is pending before the Court of Cassation. The first applicant's appeal is pending. The second applicant is currently serving a three-year sentence for possession of a firearm and ammunition with intent to commit murder. The third applicant is serving a two-and-a-half year sentence for possessing a firearm.
